Swami Vidyāraṇya— the fourteenth-century statesman,
savant, and saint— was known as Mādhavācārya prior to his taking *saṃnyāsa*. He played a very important role in the founding of...
the Vijayanagara Empire; and served as the spiritual and temporal advisor to the first three kings of Vijayanagara, namely Harihara I (crowned A.D. 1336), Bukka I, and Harihara II.
A prolific writer possessed of encyclopedic knowledge,
Vidyāraṇya has to his credit many important works on diverse subjects ranging from astronomy to Vedānta. At a ripe age...
He composed the *Pañcadaśī* and the *Jīvanmuktiviveka*, two excellent works intended for advanced students of Vedānta and seekers of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*).
Jīvanmukti, the subject matter of the present treatise, is a problem of Indian philosophy. It pertains to the authentic Vedānta,
which is based entirely upon the teachings of the Upaniṣads.
The Brahmasūtras and the Bhagavad-Gītā— which is otherwise known as the Advaita Vedānta philosophy— advocate *jīvanmukti*, or liberation while living.
The *Jīvanmukti-viveka* treats its subject matter both systematically and according to tradition. It consists of five *prakaraṇas*, or chapters.
In the first chapter, after describing the two kinds of...
The two forms of renunciation— namely *vividiṣā-saṃnyāsa* and *vidvat-saṃnyāsa*—
the nature and scope of *jīvanmukti*, its scriptural evidence, and the characteristics of a *jīvanmukta* are presented here.
The second and third chapters deal with the means to *jīvanmukti* and *videhamukti*, namely *tattvajñāna*—
the knowledge of Reality— and *vāsanākṣaya*— the effacement of latent impressions.
desires; and *manonāśa*—the dissolution of the mind.
The fourth chapter deals with the purposes of *jīvanmukti*, namely, *jñānarakṣā*—the preservation of knowledge; *tapas*—;

Penance (namely, the *sapta yoga-bhūmayaḥ*—the seven successive stages of yoga); absence of controversy (*viṣamvādābhāva*), whether in the form of dispute or censure; cessation of suffering (*duḥkha-nāśa*).

[The other chapters deal with] pain and the *Sukhāvirbhāva*— the manifestation of bliss. The fifth chapter treats at length the *vidvat-saṃnyāsa*, the renunciation of the knower, which is conducive to *jīvanmukti*.
Although both formal types of renunciation— Vividiṣā-saṃnyāsa and Vidvat-saṃnyāsa— have been emphasized and encouraged, the knowledge of Reality, Brahma-jñāna, can be acquired by anyone.

In any stage of life— namely, Brahmacharya, Garhasthya, or Vanaprastha— one may renounce mentally while still performing the specific duties of that stage. However, for all knowers of reality (Vidvats), [this applies as follows]:
Sannyāsa is prescribed for the unimpeded bliss of jīvanmukti.
Vidyāraṇya defends his positions with cogent arguments and further supports them by citing passages from the Upaniṣads.
The Bhagavad-Gītā, Yoga-Vāsiṣṭha, Bhāgavata, Mahābhārata, Purāṇas, Smṛtis, and Dharma-Śāstras.

An Inquiry into the Nature of Emancipation while Living (*Jīvanmuktiviveka*).
The First Section: On the Evidence for Liberation while Living (Jīvanmukti)
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose very breath is the Vedas and who fashioned the entire universe from the Vedas. 1.
I pray to Vidyātīrtha, the Supreme Lord, who created the entire universe from the Vedas, which are his own vital breath.

I shall explain, according to their distinction, the renunciation of the seeker (vividiṣā-nyāsa) and the renunciation of the knower (vidvat-nyāsa), which are respectively the causes of liberation while living (jīvanmukti) and liberation after death (videhamukti). ||2||
I shall expound the renunciation of the seeker and the renunciation of the knower, distinguishing between the two,
which are the causes for liberation after death.
"Death" refers to deliverance through liberation from the body,
and "liberation in life" refers to emancipation while still alive.

Detachment is the cause for renunciation; "on whatever day one becomes dispassionate, on that very day one should go forth"—such is the Vedic injunction, while its specific classifications are found in the Purāṇas.
The cause of renunciation is a sense of revulsion toward worldly things, as prescribed in the Veda:
"On the day one feels aversion for the world, on that day he should renounce."
"Indeed, [this is] the state of one who has renounced" (Jābāla Upaniṣad 4). The various types of this renunciation are found in the Purāṇas:
"Renunciation is said to be of two kinds: intense and intensely intense."
But only when [the desire] is truly intense should the yogi renounce [worldly life] as a *kuṭīcaka*.
But one who is capable [should practice] in Bahūdaka; when [the craving] is more intense, in that known as Haṃsa;
and one desiring liberation [should practice] in the supreme Haṃsa, which is the direct means for attaining higher knowledge. ||5||
Indifference toward worldly objects is said to be of two kinds:
strong and stronger. In the case of strong aversion, the renunciant remains in the stage of a *kūṭīcaka*, that is, a yogi who...
He dwells permanently apart from inhabited areas in a hut or similar place;
and when capable, he enters the *bahudaka* state— that is,
he becomes one who moves from place to place without any fixed residence.
With intensified detachment and desiring liberation,
he attains the state of a haṃsa, which, upon maturation, leads him to the state of a paramahaṃsa— the direct means to the ultimate goal.
Upon the loss of children, wife, wealth, and so forth, the immediate thought "Fie upon this worldly existence!"— such is indeed the feebleness of dispassion. (6)
A thought such as "this worldly life is not worth it" may arise temporarily upon the loss of a son, a wife, or wealth; this is considered weak detachment.
The firm resolve that "In this life, may I have no sons, wives, and so forth" is the intensity of dispassion. (7)
The resolve not to have children, a wife, and so forth in this life is called strong detachment (*tīvra-vairāgya*). [It is expressed as:
"May there be no world for me whatsoever that involves returning again."
Thus, there would be an intensity [of suffering] that is even more acute; for indeed, there is no placement [of the self] whatsoever in one who is dull-witted.
The thought, "May the world with its cycle of rebirth and so forth not be for me," is considered the stronger form of detachment.
There can be no renunciation in the case of weak detachment.
According to one's capacity or lack of capacity for travel, there are two types of renunciation in the intense [degree]:
the *kuṭīcaka* and the *bahūdaka*; both of these are holders of the triple staff (*tridaṇḍin*).
In strong detachment, two types of renunciation— namely,
the *kuṭīcaka* and the *bahūdaka* varieties— are possible,
corresponding respectively to the absence or presence of the capacity for movement.
From place to place, and so forth; both of them are *tridaṇḍins* (carriers of three thin staffs tied together).
These two [distinctions] arise from the difference between the world of Brahmā and liberation, according to their more intense asceticism.
He is the destroyer of the ignorance of reality in this world; he is the supreme *parahaṃsa* in this world. ||10||

The other two varieties of *saṃnyāsa*, namely the *haṃsa* and the *paramahaṃsa*, are possible when there is a stronger aversion toward worldly life and its objects. The distinction between them is as follows:
The former leads to the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*), and the latter to liberation (*mokṣa*), that is,
to complete emancipation. The *haṃsa* renunciant realizes the absolute truth in the world of Brahmā, whereas the *paramahaṃsa*...
The renunciant attains this very state even here and now.
The conduct of these [orders] has been declared in the Pārāśara-smṛti;
however, in this commentary, it is the Parahaṃsa who is being analyzed by us here. (11)

While commenting upon the *Pārāśara-smṛti*, the forms and practices of all these various types of renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*) have been treated; here, however, we shall deal only with the *paramahaṃsa* type.
For the purpose of discussion:
the Parahaṃsa is considered to be of two kinds—the seeker of knowledge (jijñāsu) and the possessor of knowledge (jñānavat).
The Vājasaneyins declare that renunciation (nyāsa) is for the sake of attaining knowledge for the seeker. (12)

There are two kinds of *paramahaṃsas*: the seeker (*jijñāsu*) and the knower (*vidvān*). According to the Vājasaneyi school of the Vedas, the renunciation of the seeker is for the sake of attaining knowledge.
"For those wandering mendicants indeed go forth desiring this world";
the meaning of this shall now be explained in prose for the sake of those of dull intellect. (13)

"Sannyāsins desiring this world (the world of the Self) renounce their worldly life" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22, adapted). The meaning of this passage is now being elaborated in prose for the benefit of those [who seek clarity].
They are slow to understand.
For the world is twofold: the world of self and the world of non-self.
There are two kinds of worlds: one is the world of self—
The world of the self and the world of the non-self (anātmaloka) are [distinguished].
Among these, the threefold nature of the world of the non-self is heard in the third chapter of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "Now, there are indeed three..."

"The worlds are the world of men, the world of the ancestors, and the world of the gods. This world of men is to be won only by a son, and not by any other rite; by ritual action the world of the ancestors is won, and by knowledge the world of the gods" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.16).
In the third chapter of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, three...

The various types of the selfless world (*anātmaloka*) have been described: "Indeed, there are then three worlds—*lokas*: the world of men, the world of the ancestors, and the world of the gods. The world...

"The world of men is attainable only through a son and by no other religious rites; the world of the ancestors through religious acts; and the world of the gods through knowledge" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.16).

And the Self as the world is heard of in that very same place: "Verily, he who departs from this world without having seen his own world—him, being unknown, it does not support" (4.15); and also, "One should meditate upon the Self alone as the world; for him who meditates upon the Self alone as the world, his work is never exhausted" (4.15).
The world of the Self is also described there: "Whoever,
without knowing his own world— that is, the *ātmanloka*— departs from this world (of men), being unknown, is not protected."

"By means of the *ātmaloka*" (Br. Up. 1.4.15). And likewise: "One should be intent upon the pursuit of this *ātmaloka*; for one who devotes himself to this *ātmaloka*, his efforts do not fail him" (ibid).
The actual text reads: "Desiring this very world, mendicants renounce the world. Regarding the *Jīvanmuktiviveka*:

he who dies without knowing his own world—which is characterized by the aggregate of the body, flesh, and so forth, and is called the Supreme Self—through the realization "I am Brahman," that world of his, the Supreme Self, remains unknown and is veiled by ignorance (*avidyā*).
It does not consume—that is, it does not protect by removing the defects such as grief and delusion—the deceased who has passed away, even one who was ignorant.

Indeed, the ritual act (*karman*) of a devotee (*upāsaka*) certainly does not perish; it is not exhausted by the yielding of a single fruit, but rather bestows all desired fruits as well as liberation (*mokṣa*). This is the meaning.
He who, not knowing from the mass of flesh and so forth that his own world called the *paramātman* or Supreme Self is one with himself—
that is, failing to realize "I am Brahman"— dies, him...

That his own world, the Supreme Self, being separated by ignorance and thus unknown as one’s own self, does not relieve one from the torments of grief, delusion, and so forth; and also [the state] of the seeker—
Acts of devotion are not exhausted by yielding only one or two fruits; rather, they lead him to liberation (mokṣa) through self-realization,
which is the fulfillment of all desires.
Also in the sixth chapter [of the Aitareya Āraṇyaka]: "For what purpose shall we study? For what purpose shall we sacrifice? (AiĀ 3.2.6);

and "What shall we do with offspring, we for whom this Self is this world? (4.4.22). "Those wise ones who desired offspring entered the cremation grounds; those wise ones who did not desire offspring attained immortality. (AiĀ 2.5.1)

For [the gods] indeed partook [of it]. And thus, in the passage, "Seeking this very world, mendicants go forth into homelessness" (4.4.22), it is understood that the "world of the Self" (*ātmaloka*) is intended, because the word "this" (*etad*) refers back to the Self introduced in the phrase, "Now, this great unborn Self" (4.4.22). A "world" (*loka*) is so called because it is perceived or experienced.

Thus, the intended meaning of the Śruti, "Therefore, desiring the experience of the Self, they go forth [into renunciation]," is established. And there is a Smṛti: "For the sake of attaining the knowledge of Brahman, one who is called a Parahaṃsa should be endowed with all the means, such as tranquility (śama), self-control (dama), and so forth."
—(Nārada Parivrajaka Upaniṣad 6.26). Thus [it is said].
Also in the sixth chapter: "For what purpose should we study?
For what purpose should we worship the gods? (Aitareya Āraṇyaka 3.2.6). "What shall we do with children, since to us..."

“This world of the Self is supreme” (Br. Up. 4.4.22). “Those who desire offspring go to the cremation ground; those who do not, they attain immortality. Thus it is stated in the text cited in the verse.
13: "Desiring only this world, the *saṃnyāsins* renounce. "This world" means the *ātmaloka*. This is from the text beginning with: "He... [as quoted by Ācārya Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda in his *Bhāṣya*].
In the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* (5.1.1) and elsewhere, as well as in the passage quoted by the Great Sage (*Maharṣi*)—
"This indeed is that great, unborn Ātman" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.4.22)—
the Ātman is referred to by the word "this" (*ayam*). That which is seen...
That which is experienced and realized is *loka*. Therefore, the intended meaning of the text is:
"Renounce while desiring self-realization.
There is also a *smṛti* [text] concerning one who is named a *paramahaṃsa*:
"One should acquire qualities such as control of the mind, body,
and senses, which are considered the means for the realization of the knowledge of Brahman" (Nārada Parivrājaka Upaniṣad).

Because this [renunciation] is accomplished through the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā*) produced by the proper performance of Vedic recitation and other duties in this life or in another birth, it is designated as "renunciation born of the desire for knowledge" (*vividiṣā-saṃnyāsa*). Furthermore, this renunciation which is a cause for [attaining] knowledge is of two kinds: that which consists merely in the abandonment of desire-driven actions (*kāmya-karma*) that bring about rebirth, and that which is preceded by the utterance of the [teacher's] command (*preṣa*).
And [the renunciant] takes the form of the stages of life (āśrama) beginning with the carrying of the staff.

It is said: "By the mere utterance of the command, the mother and the wife obtain human birth; and by the power of this [renunciation], he becomes established in Brahman, virtuous in conduct, and a man of knowledge. Furthermore, renunciation (tyāga) is heard of in the Taittirīya and other texts: "Not by ritual action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone—some..."
"They have attained immortality" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.10.21). And in this renunciation, even women are entitled [to participate].
By the term "female mendicant" (*bhikṣukī*), [it is indicated that] women also [are entitled] either before marriage or after widowhood.

It has thus been shown that they have the qualification for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*); therefore, according to the *Mokṣadharma*, they must perform the practice of begging for alms, listening to the scriptures on liberation,
and meditating on the Self in solitude, and they must carry the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*) and other such emblems.

In the *Caturdharī-ṭīkā*, within the dialogue between Sulabhā and Janaka, the passage beginning with "Vācaknavī" is heard in the *Śārīrakabhāṣya* (Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya), in the fourth pāda of the third adhyāya, under the section concerning the qualification of the widower (*vidhura*) by means of the logic of the *Devatādhikaraṇa*. For this very reason, the statement of Maitreyī is recorded in scripture: "What should I do with that by which I would not become immortal? What indeed does the Blessed One know?"

"Tell me that very thing" (4.5.4). When the adoption of the stage of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa-āśrama*) is obstructed for *brahmacārins*, *gṛhasthas*, or *vānaprasthas* due to some cause, the mental abandonment of action for the sake of knowledge is not contradicted even while performing the duties of one's own stage of life; for such knowers of reality are recognized in the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, *Itihāsa*, and *Purāṇa*, as well as in the world.

This is because such [renunciants] are observed in great numbers. As for the Paramahaṃsa stage of life, which has the bearing of the staff and so forth as its cause for experiencing [liberation], that has been explained in many ways by previous teachers; therefore, we shall desist from further elaboration. Thus ends the section on the Renunciation of the Seeker (vividiṣā-saṃnyāsa). ||1||
Āpastamba says:
"Now they cite two ancient verses: 'There were eighty-eight thousand sages who were eager for progeny...'"
By the southern path of Aryaman, they have gone to their cremation grounds. ||3||
The eighty-eight thousand seers who led their progeny along the northern path of Aryaman indeed attain immortality. ||4||
—Āpastamba-Dharma-Sūtras (2.9.23:3,4). ... *Vividiṣā-sannyāsa*. By means of the study [of the Vedas] in this life or in previous lives...
From the Vedas and other religious acts prescribed by the Vedas,
the desire for self-realization arises; the renunciation brought about by this desire is called "renunciation of [action]."
The seeker. This renunciation, which is the means to knowledge, is of two kinds: the renunciation of only those actions performed with selfish motives that lead to rebirth and so forth; and...
The other consists of taking up the orders by muttering the *praiṣa* formula and accepting the *daṇḍa* (staff) and so forth. By means of the *praiṣoccāraṇam*—
the muttering of the *praiṣa*— the renunciant becomes...
"O knower of the Self, you are gentle and absorbed in the contemplation of Brahman; and his mother and wife are reborn as males. (Source untraced)
The Taittirīya branch of the Vedas and other Upaniṣads speak of renunciation: "Some have attained immortality not by work, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation."

"Renunciation alone" (T.A. 10.10.21; Kena Upaniṣad 1.3). Women also possess the right to this renunciation. By the use of the term *bhikṣukī*—meaning a female mendicant—it is demonstrated that [they are entitled].
That women have the right to *sannyāsa* either before marriage or after the death of their husbands. [This is stated] in the *Caturdharī-ṭīkā* on the *Mokṣadharmaparvan* (*Mahābhārata*, 12.168ff).
12.353) concludes its treatment of the dialogue between Sulabhā and Janaka by stating that, like their male counterparts,
women are entitled to subsist on alms and study the scriptures.

Dealing with the scriptures concerning liberation, such as the Upaniṣads and so forth; meditating upon the Self in solitude; and carrying the triple staff (tridaṇḍa)—three slender sticks bound together—which is the symbol of saṃnyāsa.

The portion of the text beginning with "bhikṣukī-iti-anena" and ending with "sulabhā-janaka-saṃvāde" appears to be an interpolation, as Nīlakaṇṭha Sūri’s Caturdharī-ṭīkā was not composed until the last quarter of the seventeenth century.
AD, see Mahābhārata (ed. V. S. Sukthankar), Ādiparvan, Prolegomena, p. LXV. Translator.
Following the debate regarding the right of a widower to renounce the world (*sannyāsa*),...
In the *Devatādhikaraṇa* of the fourth chapter of the third book of the *Sārīrakabhāṣya*, the name "Vācaknavī" and others have been cited; thus, the words of Maitreyī [are authoritative].
It is said: "What should I do with that [wealth] which does not lead me to final liberation? Tell me that which your holiness knows" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.4).
For students, householders, and forest-dwellers who, for some reason,

were unable to enter the stage of renunciation (*sannyāsa*), even the performance of their specific duties pertaining to their respective stages of life (*āśrama*) was not incompatible [with the goal].
They were white with the mental renunciation aimed at attaining knowledge.
There is no lack of references to such enlightened beings in the Vedas, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and Itihāsas, as well as in...
In contemporary society, the state of the *paramahaṃsa*,

This triad, beginning with the "knot," because it is produced by ignorance, is ceased through the vision of the Self.
This same point is also found in the *Smṛti*:
"The state of Hiraṇyagarbha and so forth..."
That which is attained by an individual through sacrifice and other such means is the highest (*para*) in this world;
yet even that is inferior (*avara*) compared to that which is called the supreme-and-inferior (*parāvara*), namely Brahman.
The superimposition of the identity of the witness with the intellect through beginningless ignorance is like a knot that tightly entangles these two; therefore, it is called a "knot."
Is the Self merely a witness, or is it also an agent? Granting that it is a witness, is it Brahman, the Supreme Self, or not? Even if it is Brahman, is it intelligible or not?
If it is intelligible, does the mere knowledge of It lead to liberation? These are the doubts (*saṃśayāḥ*). Karma—the latent impressions of actions—is the cause of the future.
Birth. These three things—namely, the knots, the doubts, and the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*)—are composed of ignorance (*avidyā*);
therefore, through the knowledge of the Self, they become non-existent. In...
The Smṛti text also conveys the same meaning: "He whose state of being is not characterized by egoism, whose intellect is not tainted—
even having slain these worlds, he does not slay, nor is he bound."
(Bhagavadgītā 18.17) Thus:
"He who does not consider himself the agent of actions, whose conscience is clear— even if he were to slay the entire world— [is free from sin]."
"He never kills, nor is he bound" (Bhagavad Gītā 18.17).

For that knower of Brahman, whose state (*bhāva*), existence (*sattā*), essential nature (*svabhāva*), or self (*ātman*) is not "made of ego" (*ahaṃkṛta*)—that is, not internally veiled by the superimposition of identity with the ego—the "stain of the intellect" (*buddhilepa*), which is doubt, does not exist. In the absence of that [doubt], even by the slaughter of the three worlds...

It is not bound; the meaning is that it is even less so by any other karma. Now, this being the case, since future births have already been warded off by the very knowledge of reality—which is the fruit of the renunciation of the seeker (vividiṣā-saṃnyāsa)—how could the remainder of the present birth [be destroyed] without experience?

If it be argued that since [the body] cannot be destroyed, what is the use of this effort toward the renunciation of the knower (*vidvatsaṃnyāsa*)? It is not so, because the renunciation of the knower is the cause of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). Therefore, just as the renunciation of those desiring knowledge (*vividiṣāsaṃnyāsa*) is to be undertaken for the sake of realization, so too must the renunciation of the knower be accomplished for the sake of liberation while living. Thus ends the section on the renunciation of the knower. 2.
"Whose"—*yasya*—means the knower of Brahman. "Being"—*bhāvaḥ*—means the true state, truth, or reality;
the true essence, nature, or own state of being, that is, the Self. Not...
"By one who has not made the mind"—
that is, by one whose mind has not been [subjected to] the superimposition of identity with the self, such that one conceives oneself as the agent of actions.
Obscured by the ego;
attachment of the intellect (*buddhilepa*) is doubt. In the absence of these...
(Regarding these two things— the ego and doubt— one is never subjected to bondage by any action, even by destroying the three worlds.)— *Jīvanmuktiviveka*
Objection: Well then, if this is the case,
there is no purpose in undergoing such great effort for the renunciation of the knower (*vidvatsaṃnyāsa*), since [the result] is already attained by the seeker (*jijñāsu*).
The renunciation of the seeker (*vividishā-saṃnyāsa*) itself leads to the realization of the ultimate reality, which in turn prevents future birth as well as the remainder of the present life.
It must be lived through because there is no other way to rid oneself of it (the *vidvatsaṃnyāsa* being of no use).
Response: No. That cannot be, because of the cessation of the *vidvatsaṃnyāsa*.
*Nyāsa* is liberation in this very life; for the attainment of knowledge, *vividiṣā-saṃnyāsa* is necessary. Similarly, for the attainment of liberation in life, *vidvat-saṃnyāsa* is necessary.
Thus far concerning the renunciation of the knower (*vidvat-sannyāsa*).
Now, one might ask: what is this liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), what is the authority for it, how is its attainment achieved, and if it is attained, what is its purpose?

Objection: Now the question arises: what is this liberation-in-life (jīvanmukti)? What evidence is there for it, if any exists? And even if it were to exist, how could it be accomplished? Furthermore, even if it were accomplished—
What purpose will that serve?

It is said: for a living person, the mental state characterized by agency, enjoyership, pleasure, pain, and so forth, constitutes bondage because it consists of afflictions (*kleśa*); the removal of that is liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*).
Reply: The answer is: In his life, a person experiences pleasure and pain through the functions of his mind, which conceives itself as the performer of all actions and the enjoyer of their fruits.
These worldly anxieties regarding their fruits constitute bondage (for one worn by anxieties is unable to taste the bliss that is his own nature);
the cessation of these is liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). *Jīvanmuktiviveka*.

Now, is this bondage to be removed from the witness (*sākṣin*), or from the mind (*citta*)? Not the first, because it has already been removed by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) alone. Nor the second, because it is impossible. For only if fluidity could be removed from water or heat from fire would the removal of agency and so forth from the mind be possible; however, the fact of being inherent (*svābhāvikatva*) is the same in all cases.

Objection: The question is whether this bondage belongs to the witness (*sākṣin*) or to the mind (*manas*). For if it belongs to the witness, it is removed by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*); and if [it belongs to the mind]...

Regarding the mind, this is impossible, because it is inherent in the very nature of things. The agency of the mind in all actions could be removed only if the fluidity of water or the heat [of fire were removed].
It might be removed from fire; however, this is impossible because these qualities are equally natural to such things.
Not so; for even though absolute removal is impossible, suppression is possible. Just as the fluidity residing in water [is suppressed by heat].
The heat of fire is overcome by the application of clay, or by means of gems, mantras, and the like; likewise, all fluctuations of the mind can be overcome through the practice of yoga.
Response: It is not so. Although it is not possible to remove it [entirely],...
It is not entirely impossible to overcome;
for just as the fluidity of water is counteracted by adding earth, and the heat of fire is neutralized by means of a gemstone.
Similarly, every single state of mind can be neutralized through the practice of *yoga-samādhi*.

Now, it may be argued that *prārabdha* karma acts as an obstacle to the realization of truth (*tattva-jñāna*), which is engaged in destroying the entirety of ignorance (*avidyā*) along with its effects.

Having performed its function, it maintains the body, senses, and so forth for the purpose of yielding results; yet, the experience of pleasure, pain, and the like cannot be accomplished without the activity of the mind. Therefore, how can there be subjugation?
[Objection: But the *prārabdha* karma (the karma that has begun to bear fruit) ...

The karma that has begun the present life and will remain active until its end will maintain the body and its sense organs in order to bring about its own fruition, because it must experience pleasure and pain.
and so forth, are impossible without the mind being in its proper state of functioning. Therefore, *prārabdha* karma prevents knowledge from destroying ignorance along with [its effects].
Therefore, no neutralization of its effects is possible.

[The author replies: It is not so; for even liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), which is accomplished by overcoming [the force of past actions], is essentially a form of supreme bliss and is thus included within the very fruits of *prārabdha* (commenced) karma. [Objection: In that case, karma alone will bring about liberation while living; let there be no human effort.
If it is argued that [this fault applies], then the same objection applies equally to agriculture, trade, and so forth.
Response: It cannot be said so. The liberation-in-life (*jīvanmukti*), which results from the neutralization [of karma], is of the nature of the supreme [liberation].
Since happiness is thus within the scope of *prārabdha* karma,
it cannot be said that liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) is accomplished by *prārabdha* karma alone; therefore, there is...
Human effort is required because similar objections could be raised in the case of agriculture, commerce, and so forth;
for karma, being itself of an unseen nature, is incapable of producing a fruit without the accompaniment of seen means, and thus depends [upon them].
If it is argued that human effort is required for agriculture and the like, [we reply:
action (karma) is by nature invisible and requires certain visible auxiliaries to produce its fruit; that is, karma remains ineffective until—
Thus, certain means are employed; consequently, agriculture and the like depend upon human effort and other factors.

Even in the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), there is an equal requirement for composure. For even when human exertion is present, the culmination of the fruit of agriculture and such activities [depends on other conditions].

Where [the result] is not seen, there an obstruction by another powerful karma must be postulated. And that powerful karma obstructs only after having brought about a visible set of conditions (dṛṣṭasāmagrī) unfavorable to itself, such as the absence of rain.
Response: This applies equally to the case of liberation.
In this world, that is, through the assistance of yogic practice, the result is brought about.
Even despite human effort and so forth, where the expected result—

When the results of agriculture and so forth are not obtained, it is imagined that a more powerful karma is obstructing its course. That very powerful karma, by creating both favorable and visible means—

Such factors as drought and the like constitute an obstruction. And that obstruction is removed by a counteracting, more powerful supporting action in the form of rituals such as the *kārīrī-ṣṭi*. That ritual, having brought about its own favorable perceived causal complex characterized by rain, [accomplishes its effect].

It removes the obstacle. Why say more? For you, who are intensely devoted even to *prārabdha* karma, it is impossible even to conceive in your mind the futility of human effort in the form of the practice of yoga. Alternatively, just as *prārabdha* karma is more powerful than the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), let the practice of yoga be even more powerful than that karma.
And thus, the voluntary abandonment of the body by yogins such as Uddālaka, Vītahavya, and others, is logically established.
That obstacle is countered by rival obstructive karmas of much greater force, such as the Karīrī sacrifice; that karma...

The generation of favorable visible conditions, such as rain and so forth, removes the obstacle. Without further elaboration, we state that [the efficacy of] human effort— such as the practice of yoga and the like— is rendered futile by you.
Those who are obsessed with *prārabdha*-karma cannot even conceive of this.
Or, let it be so that since operative (*prārabdha*) karma is stronger than knowledge, likewise let there be the practice of yoga.
It is more powerful than *prārabdha* karma. In this manner,
the relinquishing of the body by yogis such as Uddālaka, Vītahavya, and others, is justified.
Even if such a yoga is not possible for us who have short lifespans, nevertheless,
what effort is required for a yoga that consists merely in the cessation of mental fluctuations such as desire and the like, provided there is scriptural exertion?
If its preeminence is not accepted, then it would follow that everything from medical science up to the scriptures on liberation would be rendered useless.
It may be that for short-lived people like us, such yoga...
It would not be accomplished; however, there can hardly be any difficulty in controlling such mental states as desire and the like.
If the efficacy of human effort as prescribed by the competent [authorities]...
If the authority of the *śāstra*— that is, the sacred scriptures and so forth— is not accepted,
then all authoritative disciplines, beginning with medicine and extending to the treatises on liberation, would become useless.

Indeed, one can never bring about weakness [of a system] merely because of a single instance where the fruit of an action does not correspond to its cause; otherwise, seeing a single occasional defeat, all kings would abandon their armies of elephants, horses, and so forth. For this very reason, the teacher Ānandabodha said:
"One does not abandon food for fear of indigestion, nor does one refrain from placing the cooking pot on the fire out of fear of beggars."
"Or the abandonment of clothing out of fear of lice.
Thus, sometimes the result does not correspond to the effort. By that alone, the futility of effort cannot be proven; otherwise, [the same would apply to all actions].
The actual text reads:
"Or, due to fear, there is the release of the lower garment for one afflicted by cold. (See *Pramāṇamālā*, p.
21). All kings, at some point or another, have experienced defeat.
One would not have paid any attention to their armed forces, consisting of elephants, cavalry, and so forth. Regarding this, Ānandabodhācārya said: "No one abandons food out of fear of indigestion."
"No one stops cooking for fear of beggars; no one throws away wrappers for fear of lice" (*Pramāṇamālā*, p. 21).
The preeminence of scriptural effort is clearly understood from the dialogue between Vasiṣṭha and Rāma: "For everything here is always [the Self]."
This is stated in the passage beginning with these words and ending with "thereafter, having even that relinquished, remain well.
The efficacy of the practices prescribed in the scriptures is clearly known from the dialogue between Vasiṣṭha and Rāma.
In the *Yogavāsiṣṭha*, beginning with "All this here always" (*Y.V.* 2.4.8) and so forth, up to "Thereafter, having abandoned even that" (*Y.V.* 2.9.43) and so forth.
Vasiṣṭha: "O descendant of Raghu, in this world of saṃsāra, everything is always obtained by everyone through human effort when it is properly applied. (Yogavāsiṣṭha, Mumukṣuvyavahāraprakaraṇa, 4.8)

All fruits— such as sons, wealth, the heavenly world (*svargaloka*), and the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*)— are [attained through] human effort (*pauruṣa*). Human effort is characterized by the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice and the meditative worship of Brahman (*brahmopāsanā*),
as well as by rites for the desire of sons (*putrakāmeṣṭi*), agriculture, and trade.
Vasiṣṭha: "O scion of the Raghus, everything in this world can always be certainly attained by everyone through the proper application of effort" (Yogavāsiṣṭha 2.4.8).

"Everything" (*sarvam*) refers to the results, such as sons, wealth, the celestial realm, and the world of Brahmā. "Human effort" (*pauruṣam*) means the performance of sacrifices for the sake of obtaining offspring.
Agriculture, commerce, the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the worship of Brahman, and so forth—such are human efforts.
"Human effort is traditionally held to be of two kinds: that which is contrary to the scriptures and that which is in accordance with the scriptures."
"In that regard, that which is contrary to the scriptures leads to misfortune, while that which is in accordance with the scriptures leads to the supreme goal" (ibid., 5.5).

"Contrary to the scriptures (*ucchāstra*) refers to acts such as stealing the property of others and adultery with the wives of others. *Śāstrita* refers to the performance of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites and so forth.
*Anartha* is hell; among *arthas*—such as heaven and the like—the supreme is liberation (*mokṣa*), which is the ultimate goal (*paramārtha*).
Vasiṣṭha says: 'Exertions are divided into two categories—one..."

That which is enjoined by the scriptures and the like is [to be followed], while that which is prohibited is [to be avoided]. By acting in the prohibited manner, an evil fruit is produced; by the prescribed effort, a good fruit [is attained].
"against the scriptures" (*uc-chāstram*) means efforts contrary to the sacred texts. (Ibid., 2.5.5)
The injunctions regarding sacred adultery, theft, and so forth;
and effort according to those injunctions— this is what is meant by *śāstrita*.
The performance of daily and occasional rites and so forth; evil (*anartha*) is hell, and good (*artha*) is heaven and so forth;
among these (*artheṣu*), the supreme (*parama*) is liberation.
The supreme Good (*paramārtha*):

"By means of qualities such as the study of scriptures and association with the virtuous, practiced sufficiently from childhood, that beneficial goal is accomplished through human effort" (ibid., 5.28).

*Alam* means "complete" or "perfect. The word *yuktena* ("endowed with") is to be supplied [as the object of the adjective]. *Hitaḥ* means "beneficial," having the nature of the highest good (*śreyaḥ*).
Vasiṣṭha says: "Qualities such as the study of the scriptures, keeping the company of holy men, and so forth, are acquired through proper..."
"Practice [this] right from early life; these, when accompanied by effort, achieve the excellent result" (ibid. 2.5.28).
The word *alam* means "fully and correctly"; after—
“By means of qualities” (*guṇaiḥ*) is to be understood as “endowed with,” that is,
possessing the qualities or together with the qualities; “beneficial” (*hitaḥ*) means the bliss of final liberation (*nirvāṇa*).
Śrī Rāma said: "O Sage, I remain exactly as my past web of latent impressions (vāsanā) impels me;
being a wretched man, what can I do?
Vāsanās are the latent impressions residing in the individual soul (*jīva*), consisting of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).
Śrī Rāma said: "O Sage Vasiṣṭha! It is these impressions of my past actions that lead me wherever [I go]."

1. The original text reads: "Since one's own purpose is accomplished through the qualities (*guṇas*), human effort, and action in whatever manner, I, being entirely powerless, must comply" (ibid., 2.9.23).

Vāsanā refers to the good and evil desires within an individual. Vasiṣṭha says: "Therefore indeed, O Rāma, you shall attain eternal welfare only through human effort brought about by your own exertion, and not otherwise."
—(In that very same place, 9.24) ||

Since you are dependent upon latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it is precisely for the sake of removing that dependence that human effort (*puruṣavyāpāra*)—generated by mind, speech, and body and accomplished through your own exertion—is required.
Vasiṣṭha said: "O Rāma, for this reason..."
"Regarding past actions, you must exert yourself; accompanied by such effort, you shall accomplish eternal bliss;
there is no other way" (ibid. 2.9.24).

Since you are subject to the impressions of your past actions, in order to eliminate this subjection, you must take the initiative with full enthusiasm for a total effort— physically, mentally, and spiritually.
"O Rāma, the accumulation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is of two kinds— wholesome and unwholesome— and it exists from the past as either one or both. (Tatraiva 9.25)

Is it that both dharma and adharma impel you, or is it one or the other? This is the first alternative. Even within the latter case, the further alternative—whether it be auspicious or inauspicious—is established by implication.
Vasiṣṭha says: "Desires are of two kinds, the auspicious and the inauspicious; your..."
"O Rāma! Do these desires arising from past actions belong to both types, or to either one of the two? (Ibid.
"Both the auspicious and the inauspicious lead you, or either one of them."
This is the alternative; the other alternative implied is: if it is neither both, then which one? Is it good or evil?
1. The original reading is *ata eva hi rāma tvam* | *Jīvanmukti-viveka*.
"If you are led away from there by a pure flood of latent impressions (*vāsana*), then by that very means you will swiftly attain the eternal state in due course. (Ibid., 9.26)

In that regard, among those alternatives: *tat tarhi* (then, in that case); *tenaiva krameṇa* (by that very sequence); *śubhavāsanāprāpitenaiva ācaraṇena* (by conduct attained through pure latent impressions alone);
*prayatnāntaranirapekṣeṇa* (independent of any further effort); *śāśvataṃ padaṃ mokṣam* (the eternal state, which is liberation).
Vasiṣṭha: "Of the three alternatives, if you are led by..."
"Then, through those very good desires, you shall attain that eternal state" (ibid. 2.9.26). Among these, *tatra* means "among the alternatives"; *tat* [refers to that state].

The word "then" (atha) means at that time; "by that very sequence" (tenaiva kramena) means by means of no other effort, namely, through the very activities brought about by virtuous desires; "the eternal state" (śāśvatam padam).
This means liberation:
"But if this impure state should involve you in distress,
then that former [state] must be conquered by you yourself through effort."
— (in that very same place, 9.27) ||

*Bhāva* is latent impression (*vāsanā*). Therefore, that [effort] is the practice of scriptural dharma which is opposed to the unwholesome. By that, it must be conquered by oneself; it cannot be conquered through another person, as if seeking death in the mouth of battle.
Vasiṣṭha: "But if evil desires are leading you toward..."
"Then, you yourself must exert effort in order to overcome that former impression" (ibid. 2.9.27).
*Bhāvaḥ* means desire; *tat* means "then"; *yatnaḥ* means effort.
The practice of anti-evil rites prescribed by the sacred scriptures.
By means of that and through one's own effort—not by employing others such as soldiers—a battle is won. 28.
"The river of latent impressions, flowing along both auspicious and inauspicious paths, should be directed onto the auspicious path by means of human effort. (Ibid., 9.30)

In both cases, however, even if the auspicious portion occurs independently of effort, one should ward off the inauspicious portion through scriptural effort and practice only the auspicious in its place.
Vasiṣṭha says: "Desires flow like rivers through the auspicious and..."
"Evil courses; by manly effort it should be directed toward a good channel" (ibid. 2.9.30).
When both types are present, the good lot is...
There is no need for any guidance for those who are already established; however, for the wicked,
their course must be altered and directed toward goodness through means sanctioned by the scriptures.
"O best among the strong, by means of human effort and power, draw your own mind away from impure things and establish it in pure things alone. (In that same work, 9.31).
Regarding the impure, such as the wives and wealth of others; regarding the pure, such as the study of the scriptures, the meaning of the teachings, and meditation on the deity;
by means of human effort—that is, by human exertion—and by force—that is, by a powerful force—Vasiṣṭha says: "O greatest of the powerful! If your mind..."
"Then, being attached to the unwholesome, one should, through powerful efforts, bring it down to a wholesome course" (ibid. 2.9.31).
"Unwholesome" (*aśubha*) here refers to the desire for theft, adultery, and so forth.
Good—*śubha* means contemplating the essence of the *śāstras* and the deities; *puruṣārthena* means by human effort; *balena* means by great power.
"The mind of a living being, like that of a child, moves from the impure to the pure, and from that [the pure] again to the other. Therefore, one should forcibly steady it.
(Ibid., 9.32) — *Jīvanmuktiviveka*
Just as a child is restrained from eating clay and directed toward eating fruit, and is restrained from pulling at jewels and pearls and directed toward pulling at balls and the like.
In the same way, the mind can also be restrained from harmful attachments by means of objects that are their opposite.
Vasiṣṭha: "The mind of an individual resorts to the good when it is removed from the evil; likewise, it may do the reverse.
The mind is like a child; therefore, it must be disciplined rigorously."
"By association with the virtuous, through the consolation of equanimity, quickly— that is, not suddenly, but gradually. (Ibid., 9.32)
"One should cherish the child of the mind with manly effort. — (Ibid., 9.33)
Just as a child is prevented from eating earth and induced to eat fruit, or prevented from catching pearls, jewels, and the like,
and instead allowed to play with balls and such, so too the mind— by means of...
Through the help of good company, one can be prevented from falling into the company of the wicked and from objects of attraction that are not wholesome.
There are two means for leading a restless beast into its place of bondage: the display of green grass, and...
[These are] scratching [the body] and so forth, harshness of speech, and threatening with sticks and the like. By the first of these, one is made to enter [the womb] suddenly;

by the second, one is made to enter slowly while running here and there. Likewise, the realization of equality toward enemies, friends, and others, and human effort such as breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*)—these two are means for the pacification of the mind. Among them, by the first, which is gentle yoga (*mṛdu-yoga*), [the mind is pacified].
One should train it quickly. By means of the second method, *haṭhayoga*, one should not train it abruptly, but rather very gradually.
Vasiṣṭha: The mind, which is like a child, should be disciplined into tranquility through persuasion and consolation.
By caressing it in this soothing manner, it is disciplined all at once;
however, by attempting to hasten the process and resorting to harsher measures, one only achieves the desired result gradually (ibid).
1. There are two ways to subdue a refractory animal: one is by caressing and enticing it with fresh grass, and the other is by scolding and striking it with a staff. By the former method, the...

The animal is led to its stall immediately; however, by the second way, the animal—running hither and thither, that is, resisting until the very end—is made to enter gradually by force. Similarly, in the process of persuasion...
He brings the mind to equanimity, by convincing it that there is no distinction between friend and foe, and through such manly efforts as the control of the breath and the restraint of the mind.

function—these are the two ways. By the first way, namely the easy and comfortable method of training, the mind becomes calm quickly; however, by the forceful method of physical yoga, the result [is achieved differently].

"When you see the same everywhere, whether in the name or the nameless, then you shall attain the state of Brahman" (ibid. 2.9.87). "When you see the same everywhere, whether in the concept or the
In Haṭhayoga, when wholesome aspirations arise, they should be appreciated as the result of practice; one should not doubt their impossibility on account of their having occurred so quickly.
"Even when there is doubt, cultivate only that which is exceedingly auspicious;
for, my dear, when auspicious latent impressions increase, there is no fault whatsoever."
— (In that very same place, 9.38) ||
When there is doubt as to whether the cultivation of virtuous impressions (*śubhavāsanā*) has been completed or not, one should continue to cultivate the virtuous ones.
For example, when the tenth hundredth repetition in a session of recitation (*japa*) is doubtful, one should repeat it a hundred times again;
if it was incomplete, its completion will bear fruit, and if it was already complete, the repetition does not invalidate the hundred-fold recitation because of that increase—it is just like that.
Vasiṣṭha: "Even if you have doubts, continue with the practice to acquire virtuous impressions; my dear, there is no harm whatsoever in the increase of noble desires" (ibid).
While practicing wholesome aspirations, doubt may arise regarding the completion of the practice; in such a case, one should continue with the practice,
just as in the instance where one has already begun.
If, while reciting a mantra a thousand times and counting as one goes along, one has doubt regarding the tenth hundred, then one should recite it once more for another hundred. If...
If it is incomplete, it shall now be completed; and even if it were complete, an increase in the number does not in any way harm the requirement of one thousand recitations.
"As long as your mind is unrefined and you have not realized that state of reality..."
"Practice that which has been determined by the authority of the Guru and the scriptures" (ibid.,
Vasiṣṭha: "As long as your mind is not capable of reflecting the unity of Brahman and Ātman, and that supreme state has not yet been realized, continue to practice."
"In accordance with the teacher, scripture, and other valid means of knowledge" (ibid. 2.9.41).
"Then, by one whose impurities have been ripened and who has truly realized the reality..."
"Even this stream of pure latent impressions must be abandoned by you who seek cessation.

"And when the obstacle consisting of the desires of love and hatred has ripened— that is, when it will no longer cause hindrance— and you possess the direct and immediate awareness of ultimate reality,"

Then you, striving for the complete tranquility of the mind, should abandon the entire collection of desires, even those that are most auspicious and practiced by the noble ones (ibid., "That which is exceedingly fortunate and practiced by the noble ones...").
Having followed what is auspicious, through the purity of a pleasing disposition.
"Attain that state which is forever free from sorrow; thereafter, having even abandoned that, abide in excellence. (Ibid., 9.43).

Because the possibility of being overcome by desire and other afflictions exists even for one liberated while living, the meaning [of such liberation] is not clearly evident. Therefore, one must strive through the practice of yoga.
Thus ends the nature of liberation while living (jīvanmukti). ||3||
“With the aid of wholesome desires, you should follow the path trodden by the great ṛṣis that leads to the supreme good and realize the state of non-duality (advaita); thereafter, abandon them.”
"May all things—that is, those means by which the knowledge of non-duality (*advaita-jñāna*) is accomplished—be well-established in your true nature" (ibid).
The meaning of the preceding verses is clear. Thus, by...
Since the practice of yoga can neutralize passion and other afflictions,
"liberation while living" (jīvanmukti) should no longer be contested. Thus,
the nature of jīvanmukti has been explained.

The statements of the Śruti and Smṛti are the authorities for the existence of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). These are recited in the Kaṭhavallī and other texts; therein, the Kaṭhavallī states: "He who is already liberated is liberated" (5.1). This means that one who is already liberated from the visible bonds such as desire while still alive, is especially liberated from future bondage upon the fall of the body. This is due to [the realization of] knowledge.

Even previously, by the accomplishment of tranquility, self-control, and so forth, one was indeed liberated from desire and the like; nevertheless, there, the cessation of arisen desires and the like occurs through effort. Here, however, due to the absence of mental modifications (*dhīvṛtti*), there is simply non-arising. Therefore, it is said [to be] "specifically.
Likewise, when dissolution (*pralaya*) or the fall of the body occurs, one is liberated from the future bondage of a body for some time; here, however, it is absolute.
The word "especially" (*viśeṣeṇa*) is used with the intention of [distinguishing] liberation (*mokṣa*).
The existence and attainability of *jīvanmukti* are indicated by Vedic and Smṛti texts; they are found therein.
*Kaṭhavallī* and other texts. In that *Kaṭhavallī*, it is read:
"The 'especially liberated' one is liberated outright" (*Kaṭha Upaniṣad* 5.1).
Being especially free from the visible while still alive...

The bondage of passion and the like becomes entirely free from future bondage upon the fall of this body; even before such realization, it is so through the practice of restraint over the internal and external organs.
One becomes free from desire and so forth through the mind and other faculties; however,
in this case, the restraint of desire and so forth that has already arisen occurs through effort, whereas for the *jīvanmukta*, desire and so forth do not arise at all.
Since there is no transformation of the mind, it is said that he is "especially liberated. And likewise, during the dissolution of the universe and after the falling away of the body...
An individual is liberated from the bondage of a future body for a period of time; however, in the case of the *jīvanmukta*, liberation is absolute. Bearing this in mind, it is said:
Specifically, it is recited in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad:
"When all the desires that dwell in his heart are liberated, then the mortal becomes immortal; he attains Brahman even here."
The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad reads: "When all the desires dwelling in his heart have departed, then he, having been mortal,
becomes immortal and attains Brahman in this very body."

In another Śruti as well: "Though possessing eyes, he is as if sightless; though possessing ears, he is as if deaf; though possessing a mind, he is as if mindless; though possessing breath, he is as if breathless. This may be cited elsewhere as well. In the Smṛtis, [the state of] the one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*)...

He is designated here and there by such names as "one of steady wisdom" (sthitaprajña), "devotee of the Lord" (bhagavadbhakta), "one who has transcended the qualities" (guṇātīta), "the Brāhmaṇa beyond the castes and stages of life" (ativarṇāśramī), and so forth. In the dialogue between Vasiṣṭha and Rāma, the one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) is described in the passage beginning with "Of men who are solely established in knowledge" and ending with "nothing whatsoever remains."
In another Śruti also it is said: "Though possessing eyes, he is, as it were, without eyes; though possessing ears, he is, as it were, without ears;
though possessing a mind, he is, as it were, without a mind; though possessing life..."
It is, as it were, devoid of life. Similar examples are found in other texts as well.
In various *smṛtis*, the *jīvanmukta* is indicated by different [terms].
Names such as: *sthitaprajña*—one who has attained the supreme, unshakable wisdom; *bhagavadbhakta*—one who is completely absorbed in the Lord; *guṇātīta*—one who has transcended the qualities...

He has transcended this phenomenal existence composed of the three *guṇas* or qualities; he is a *brāhmaṇa* who has attained the Self; he is an *ativarṇāśramī*, one who is beyond the reach of the social orders and stages of life.
Regarding the four castes and the four stages of social life (*āśrama*),
a *jīvanmukta* (one liberated while living) is described in the section of the text concerning the dialogue between Vasiṣṭha and Rāma.
"Among men who are absorbed in knowledge... (YV 3.9.2) up to "existence alone remains" (ibid.; as quoted by Ācārya Śaṅkara in his commentary on Brahmasūtra 1.1.4).
Vasiṣṭha:
"For men who are solely devoted to knowledge and who investigate the knowledge of the Self, that state of liberation while living arises, which is like liberation after death. (88)

(Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 5.88): Exclusive devotion to knowledge and the renunciation of worldly and Vedic rituals constitute the two types of liberation; the distinction between these two lies solely in the existence or non-existence of the body and the senses, and not in experience, because dualistic perception is absent in both cases.

Vasiṣṭha: Among those men who are solely engaged in the pursuit of knowledge through the contemplation of self-knowledge, there arises that state of "liberation while living" (jīvanmukti) which is identical to final liberation.
"after the dissolution of the body" (Laghu Yogavāsistha Rāmāyaṇa 5.88). The state of being in the "pursuit of knowledge alone"—

"Exclusive devotion to knowledge" (jñānaikaniṣṭhā) means the renunciation of all other activities, both Vedic and worldly. The distinction between the two types of liberation mentioned is based solely on the presence or absence of [the body].
The body and the sense organs; the experience is the same, because in both cases there is an absence of the perception of multiplicity.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Brahman, [tell me] the characteristics of one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) and one liberated after death (videhamukta)."
Speak so that I may likewise strive with a vision won through the mastery of the scriptures.

Śrī Rāma said: "O Brahman, please describe the specific characteristics of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) and one liberated after death (*videhamukta*), so that I may strive toward that goal in accordance with the instructions of the scriptures. (Ibid.)

Vasiṣṭha: He for whom this world remains as it is, even while engaged in worldly affairs, and who perceives that which stands as having gone to its setting—like the sky—he is called one liberated while living (jīvanmukta). (90)
—(In that very same place, 5.90) ||

This perceived world, consisting of mountains, rivers, oceans, and so forth, along with the body, senses, and activities of the perceiver, is withdrawn by the Supreme Lord during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) and comes to an end through the destruction of its own nature. But here it is not so;
for [it is said]: "by the vision of the scripture" (*śāstradṛśā*); the readings *śāstragayā dṛśā* and *śāstradṛśādhiyā* are also found. — *Jīvanmuktiviveka*

However, the conventional functioning of the body, senses, and so forth does indeed exist. Furthermore, mountains, rivers, and the like—since they have not been withdrawn by the Supreme Lord—persist as before and are clearly perceived by all other living beings. For one who is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), because of the absence of mental modifications that would cognize those objects, everything has set, as if in deep sleep; yet it remains self-luminous.

Only a small portion remains. Although there is a similarity in the absence of mental modifications (*dhīvṛtti*) for a bound soul during deep sleep, he does not possess the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmuktatva*) because the seeds of future mental modifications still exist.
Vasiṣṭha says: "He is the one liberated while living to whom this world..."
"Although he lives and moves within it, the existence of the senses has ceased; only the all-pervasive *vyoman*—that is, Knowledge—remains" (ibid. 5.90).
This apparent world of mountains, rivers, oceans,
and so forth, together with the individual perceivers and their bodies, senses, and so on, having been dissolved by the Great Lord.

At the end of a cycle, [the world] becomes non-existent, being devoid of forms due to their destruction; but in this case, it is not so, because the body, the senses, and their functions continue to operate. The mouth—
Mountains, rivers, and so forth, not being withdrawn by the Great Lord,
exist as before and are clearly perceived by other beings;
however, in the case of the *jīvanmukta*, because there is no mental...
Upon transformation, everything becomes non-existent, as in deep sleep; only the self-luminous, all-pervading Consciousness remains. During deep sleep, the absence of the mind...
For the time being, the transformation is equal to that of a *jīvanmukta*, yet it cannot be equated with the state of a *jīvanmukta* because the seeds [of bondage] still remain [in deep sleep].

Regarding future mental transformations, Vasiṣṭha says: "He whose facial radiance neither rises nor sets in pleasure or pain, but remains steady as things occur, is called one liberated while living. (91)
—(In that very place, 5.91) ||
The radiance of the face is joy (*harṣa*). Even when pleasures such as ointments, sandalwood paste, and hospitality are obtained, joy does not arise as it does for those in *saṃsāra*.
The fading of the radiance of the face is dejection (*dainya*). Even when suffering such as the loss of wealth or public reproach is encountered, one does not become dejected.
[This refers to] alms-food and the like, which arrive through the continuous flow produced by previously commenced karma, without requiring any special effort on one's part at present.

"Yathāprāptam" means remaining as one has attained; it is the preservation of the body through the firmness of *samādhi*. Because of the absence of the perception of external objects such as sandalwood paste and the like due to the stability of *samādhi*, and because even during the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*) there is an absence of the notion of what is to be rejected or accepted by virtue of the gift of discrimination (*viveka*), the state of being free from joy and other such emotions is logically established.
Vasiṣṭha: He whose face neither beams with joy nor becomes drawn with pain, and whose body is sustained solely by whatever food comes by chance—he is called a *jīvanmukta*. (Ibid.)
Sometimes,
even when something has been perceived,
a facial glow indicates happiness, even after it has been received.

Flowers, sandalwood paste, honors, and other such things that cause pleasure do not cause his face to flush, unlike that of ordinary mortals. The absence of flushing indicates the presence of affliction. The loss of...
Wealth, infamy, and so forth, which cause grief to others,
do not affect one who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta). Whatever comes of its own accord (yathāprāptam)— that is, whatever occurs spontaneously.

This means that, without any effort at the present time, one remains— i.e., maintains oneself— by the ordinary course of events through the alms and other provisions brought about by *prārabdhakarman*.
of the body. When in intense concentration, he is unaware of flower garlands and so forth; yet, upon emerging from such meditation, he perceives such objects as if they were present.
By the sheer power of his discernment, he has no thought of either accepting or rejecting anything; therefore, the "absence of pleasure" and so forth is justified.
Vasiṣṭha: "He who is awake while remaining in deep sleep, for whom no waking state exists, whose consciousness is free from latent impressions—he is called liberated while living. (Ibid., 5.92)
Because the sense organs, such as the eye, remain in their respective sockets and have not ceased their activity, [the self] is awake;
yet, because it is devoid of mental fluctuations (*manovṛtti*), it is as if situated in deep sleep. For this very reason, regarding the statement "the perception of objects through the senses,"...

It exists. Even though awakening has occurred, because the defining characteristic of waking is absent, there is no state of being awake; rather, there is the defect of the intellect consisting of the conceit of being a knower of Brahman and so forth, as well as desires produced for the sake of enjoyment, which constitute latent impressions (*vāsanā*), due to the absence of mental modifications (*vṛtti*).
Due to the absence of those defects, there is the state of being free from latent impressions (*nirvāsanatva*).
Vasiṣṭha says: "He is called *jīvanmukta* who, though in deep sleep, remains awake, for whom there is no state of waking."

"Whose knowledge is devoid of desires" (ibid. 5.92). "Awake"—*jāgarti*—because all his sense organs, such as the eyes and so forth, function in their respective locations. "In deep sleep"—*suṣuptisthaḥ*—because of the absence of mental states.
‘No waking state’— *jagranna vidyate*— because the waking state is known through the perception of objects via the senses,
and that is not present here. ‘Knowledge devoid of latent impressions’— *nirvāsanah*.

Enlightenment (*bodha*), because even in that knowledge, such pride as "I am the knower of Brahman" arises; furthermore, through the objects of enjoyment, desires and so forth are generated— these and...
Pride defiles the mind, and that defilement is *vāsanā*; since his mind is free from such modifications, such stains are absent.
Vasiṣṭha: "Even while acting in accordance with passion, hatred, fear, and the like, he who is as utterly transparent within as the sky is called one liberated while living. (Ibid., 5.93)
Activity such as eating in accordance with passion; turning away from Buddhists, Kāpālikas, and others in accordance with aversion;

retreating from snakes, tigers, and so forth in accordance with fear; and by the word "and so forth," the performance of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to a greater degree than other yogis in accordance with envy—even when such conduct occurs during the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*), it is due to prior practice.

For one whose mind has attained rest, there is extreme clarity due to the absence of turbidity; just as the sky, though filled with smoke, dust, clouds, and the like, possesses an excellence of transparency because its nature is untainted, so it is here.
Vasiṣṭha: He is the *jīvanmukta* who, although responsive...
"Even when spurred by love, hatred, fear, and the like, he is as utterly pure of heart as space" (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 5.93).
Responses to love and so forth are of the same nature as acts such as eating.

To hatred, such as turning away from the Bauddhas, Kāpālikas, and others; and to fear, such as moving away from snakes, tigers, and the like. Other stimulations, such as envy, are likewise responded to.
Due to the intensified practice of concentration by other yogins, even during the intervals when such habitual behavior is observed, the mind remains pure because it has...

He attains tranquility, just as the sky remains clear—its very nature—even in the presence of dust, smoke, clouds, and so forth. Vasiṣṭha says in the *Jīvanmukti-viveka*: "He whose state of being is not characterized by egoism, and whose intellect is not defiled..."
Whether acting or not acting, he is called one liberated while living. (Ibid., 5.94)

The first half [of the verse] has been explained in the context of the renunciation of the wise (*vidvatsaṃnyāsa*). In this world, for a bound person performing scriptural action, the conscious self (*cidātman*) becomes identified with the ego through the thought "I am the doer," and the intellect (*buddhi*) is stained by joy through the thought "I shall attain heaven in the future. However, for one who does not perform [action], there is the ego-identification of "I have renounced," as well as the dejection of not attaining heaven.

[This is] an ointment. In this manner, [the analysis] should be applied as appropriate to prohibited actions and to worldly actions. However, for one who is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), because of the absence of superimposition of identity (*tādātmyādhyāsa*) and the absence of joy and so forth, the two defects do not exist.
Vasiṣṭha says: "He is the *jīvanmukta* whose inner self is not..."
"Affected by egoism, yet whose mind is free from all mental fluctuations, whether engaged in scriptural activities or not" (La. Yo. 5.94).
The first part of this verse has been explained in the section on *vidvat-saṃnyāsa*. When an individual, while still bound, performs a ritual act according to the scriptures, his self—
He is affected by the thought, "I am the doer. His mind undergoes transformation with the pleasant thought, "I shall go to heaven. And while not performing [the action], he is affected by...
‘I have abandoned it,’ and the dejection of the mind is due to the loss of heaven. In this manner,
this should be understood with reference to other worldly actions and karmas.
Both are prohibited in the scriptures. The *jīvanmukta* is free from both, because he possesses neither the superimposed identification nor [the experience of] pleasure and so forth.
Vasiṣṭha: "He from whom the world does not tremble, and who does not tremble from the world; he who is free from joy, resentment, and fear—he is called one liberated while living. (Ibid., 5.95)

He is not agitated. Because he does not engage in reviling, beating, and so forth, people do not likewise engage in reviling him; even if some wicked person should so engage, it does not affect his mind.
And because such conceptual constructions do not arise, he too does not tremble.
Thus, Vasiṣṭha says in the *Jīvanmukti-viveka*: "The *jīvanmukta* is he who does not fear."
"He is neither attached to the world nor afraid of the world; he is free from joy, anger, and fear" (Laghu Yogavāsiṣṭha 5.95).
Because he never goes to insult or beat others, therefore...
The world is not afraid of him; for this very reason, no one does anything of the sort to him. Even if some wicked person should ever engage in such activity against him, he remains unperturbed.
Since such things cannot bring about any transformation in his mind.
Vasiṣṭha says: "One whose mental constructions regarding worldly existence have been stilled is partless, even though possessed of parts."
"He who, though possessing a mind, is mindless— he is called liberated while living" (ibid., 5.96).
[This refers to] conceptual constructions such as enemy and friend, honor and dishonor, and so forth.
The sixty-four sciences are the arts (*kalās*); he is one for whom the manifestations of *saṃsāra* have been stilled even while those arts exist.
Because of the absence of both conceit regarding them and worldly activity, he possesses the state of being partless (*niṣkalatva*).

Even though the mind exists in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), it is "without mind" (*niścitta*) because mental modifications (*vṛtti*) do not arise. Alternatively, according to the reading "though possessing thought, he is without thought," even when the modification of meditation on the Self (*ātmadhyāna-vṛtti*) exists due to the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it is "without thought" (*niścinta*) because of the absence of worldly modifications.
Vasiṣṭha says: "He is the one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) who is free from all..."
"Engaged in worldly conduct; though skilled in the arts, devoid of them;
as it were, without a mind, though possessing one" (Ibid. 5.96).
Friend, enemy, honor, dishonor, and so forth—all these dualities are merely the ways of the world, which no longer exist within him.
The sixty-four types of arts are called *kalās*; although he [is possessed of them],...
Having accomplished these, he neither employs them nor is he conceited on account of them;
thus, he is as if without them. The very nature of the mind is indeed present within him, yet because of the absence of any...
Even when there is modification, he is, as it were, without it. If the reading is *sacintopiniścintaḥ*, the meaning will be: by the force of former impressions, his mind assumes the form of...
"Vasiṣṭha said: 'One should contemplate the Self, yet remain free from other worldly transformations, as if devoid of them.'"
"He who, though engaged in all kinds of worldly affairs, remains cool as if toward the interests of others, being full in his self— he is called liberated while living. (Ibid., 5.97)

Just as one who has gone personally to another's house on occasions such as a wedding festival might engage in their affairs for the sake of their pleasure, yet does not experience the mental distress consisting of joy or dejection regarding gain or loss— even so this liberated one remains cool even toward his own affairs. His state of coolness arises not only from the absence of distress, but also from the constant contemplation of his own perfect nature.
Thus ends the definition of one liberated while living. || 4 ||
Vasiṣṭha: The *jīvanmukta* is he who, though engaged in all manner of affairs, remains cool as if the matter concerned another person, being one whose self is whole. (Ibid.)

Just as one who has gone to another’s house on an occasion such as a wedding or the like, partakes in the activities there personally for the sake of pleasing the host, yet remains unattached and unaffected; so too is the yogin.

Just as one remains unmoved by the joy or sorrow caused by gain or loss, so too does the liberated one remain cool even regarding matters concerning himself. He is cool not only because of the absence of anxiety, but...
as well as for the awareness of his self as a complete whole. Thus far are the characteristics of the *jīvanmukta*.
Now, the characteristics of the *videhamukta*—
Having abandoned the state of liberation while living when his own body has been surrendered to time, he enters the state of disembodied liberation, just as the wind enters a state of motionlessness.
(In that very same place, 5.98) ||
Just as the wind sometimes abandons its movement and remains in a state of stillness,
so too the liberated self, having abandoned the cycle of transmigratory existence produced by limiting adjuncts, remains in its own essential nature.
Now, concerning the one liberated while in the body (jīvanmukta):
Vasiṣṭha: When life expires, the body dissolves and one abandons the state of *jīvanmukta*. One then enters the state of *videhamukti*—liberation after disembodiment—just like the wind.
"becomes motionless" (Ibid. 5.98).
Just as the wind sometimes ceases blowing and reaches a state of calm and motionlessness, so too does the liberated soul.
Having departed from this world composed of limiting adjuncts (upādhi), one remains in one's own true nature.

The one liberated while in the body (jīvanmukta) neither rises nor sets, nor does he cease to exist; [likewise] the one liberated after death (videhamukta) neither rises nor sets, nor does he cease to exist.
"I am neither existent nor non-existent, neither far away, nor am I not this, nor something other.
(5.99, in that same work)

Rising and setting are joy and sorrow. He does not become tranquil, nor is he one who abandons them, because the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*) is dissolved right here. That which is designated as "existent" is the cause of the world, having ignorance (*avidyā*) and *māyā* as its limiting adjuncts; it is not the Lord (*Īśvara*) in the state of deep sleep (*prājña*). That which is designated as "non-existent" is neither the elements nor their derivatives. By the statement "not standing at a distance," it is not beyond *māyā*. And by the statement "nor [is it]... [it is not the case that...].
Even one situated near the gross enjoyer is excluded. "I am not" excludes the universal aggregate (*samaṣṭi*); "nor another" excludes the individual manifestation (*vyaṣṭi*).
The meaning is that there is no conceptual construction whatsoever capable of worldly transaction.
Vasiṣṭha says: "He who is liberated after death does not rise..."
He neither sets nor does he rest; he is neither existent nor non-existent;
he is neither distant nor near, and he is neither "I" nor "another. (Ibid. 5.99)
"Rising and setting" (*udayāstamayau*) means joy and sorrow; "does not rest" (*na śāmyati*) means he does not abandon them, because his subtle body (consisting of the mind...)
...and so forth— has dissolved right here. "Existent" (*sat*) refers to *prājña* conditioned by *avidyā* and *īśvara* conditioned by *māyā*,
which are the causes of the world— the disembodied liberated one (*videhamukta*).
He is neither *sat* (existent), that is, the cause; nor is he *asat* (non-existent), that is, the effect, which is matter or a material object.
*Na dūrasthaḥ* means he is not beyond *māyā*. Nor... these.
The two words signify that He is not near; that is, although He is present nearby, He does not experience gross sensory objects. "Neither 'I'" (*na ca aham*) means not *samasti*, i.e., not *Virāt*.
Neither Hiraṇyagarbha, nor Īśvara.
Nor "the other"—*netara* meaning not *vyasti*, that is, not Viśva, nor Taijasa, nor Prājña. In Him there is no diversity.
alternatives related to ordinary practice:
"Thereafter, neither brilliance nor pervasive darkness remains; something existent, indescribable and unmanifest, persists. (100)
—(In that very same place, 5.100) ||

In this way, it should be understood that the degree of excellence and superiority of liberation while in the body (videhamukti) corresponds precisely to the degree of transcendence of conceptual construction (vikalpa).
Vasiṣṭha: "Then that which remains is something existent, calm and profound, neither light nor shrouded in pervasive darkness, nameless and unmanifest" (Ibid. 5.100).
By the statement of similarity, even in the case of *jīvanmukti*, to the extent that—
[the resemblance of *jīvanmukti* with *videhamukti* has been described in the preceding verses; the greater the excellence...]
Insofar as there is non-differentiation in *jīvanmukti*, it is superior [to other states].
In the second chapter of the *Bhagavadgītā*, the one of steady wisdom (*sthitaprajña*) is described:
Arjuna said:
"O Keśava, what is the description of one whose wisdom is steady, who is established in samādhi? What does the one of steady intellect speak, how does he sit, and how does he move? (54)

Wisdom (*prajñā*) is the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). It is of two kinds: stable and unstable. Just as the intellect of a woman who is infatuated with a lover dwells only upon that lover in all her activities—even while performing household chores that have been correctly measured by valid means of cognition—she immediately forgets them; so it is for one endowed with supreme dispassion (*paravairāgya*).
