When the knowledge of reality has arisen in one whose mind has been completely mastered through proficiency in the practice of yoga, the intellect meditates upon that reality uninterruptedly, as if it were an aged relative; this is "steadfast wisdom" (*sthita-prajñā*). However, even if the knowledge of reality should occasionally arise in one devoid of the aforementioned qualities due to some particular merit, that reality is forgotten right there, like household chores; this is "unsteadfast wisdom" (*asthita-prajñā*).
In the second chapter of the Bhagavadgītā, the one of steady wisdom (sthitaprajña) is described as follows:

Arjuna said: "What is the definition of that person who is steady... [The Blessed One replied: "...who, having abandoned all desires, remains satisfied with the self alone, free from longing for any object, whose mind remains unperturbed amidst pleasures, and who is unshaken by adversity, whose senses are fully withdrawn, and who is called 'one of steady wisdom'—he is indeed a sage. (BhG 2.55–58) This concludes the excerpt from *Jīvanmuktiviveka*.
"In the supreme knowledge and in profound meditation—O Keśava! how does he whose intellect is steady speak, sit, and walk? (Bhagavadgītā 2.54)
Supreme Knowledge—*prajñā*—means the knowledge of Reality. It is of two kinds: one is stable and the other is not. This is like the case of a woman who is engaged [in worldly affairs].

In an illicit love affair, she constantly thinks of her paramour in all her activities; while attending to the household chores that she normally perceives through her senses, she easily forgets them.
Similarly, for one who has attained the highest degree of detachment, whose mind has been fully mastered through proficiency gained by the practice of yoga, and upon whom—
The highest knowledge dawned; he who constantly contemplates the Truth like a lover—this is "abiding knowledge.
One who lacks such qualities as mentioned, however, by...
Through the power of some merit, one may at times realize the Truth;
yet one soon forgets it, just as a lover forgets household chores, and thus this is unstable knowledge.
Intending this very point, Vasiṣṭha said:
"A woman devoted to another man, even while busy with household chores, relishes within herself that very elixir of union with another. (58)
"Thus, the steadfast one who has attained rest in the supreme, pure reality,
savors that very [reality] within, even while engaging in external activity.
(Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 27.58, 59)

In this regard, the one of steady wisdom (*sthitaprajña*) is of two kinds according to the difference in time: the composed (*samāhita*) and the emerged (*vyutthita*). He asks for the characteristics of both of them through the first and second halves [of the verse]: "What is the description (*bhāṣā*) of the one of steady wisdom who is established in *samādhi*?
By what words expressing his characteristics is he described in all respects? And what is the [description] of the one of steady wisdom who has emerged?"
Does he engage in verbal discourse? Regarding his sitting and walking, how are they distinct from those of the dull-witted?
With this point in mind, Vasiṣṭha said:
"A woman who has an affair with a paramour, even while engaged..."

Just as a woman engaged in household duties inwardly relishes the experience of lovemaking she previously felt, so too does the wise person who has found rest in the stainless, ultimate Reality rejoice within.
"that experience, though engaged in worldly activities externally" (Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 27.58, 59).
There are two states of the one whose wisdom is steady (sthitaprajña) according to time:

One is established in abstract meditation (*samādhi*) and the other arises from it. Their characteristics are inquired about by Arjuna through the first and second halves of the verse, respectively. What...

What is the definition of one whose wisdom is steady while in deep meditation? By what kind of descriptive words is such a person spoken of by all? How does one whose wisdom has arisen speak? And how does he sit?
In what way are those who walk [the path] different from ordinary people? The Blessed One said:
"When one renounces all desires residing in the mind, O Pārtha..."
But when one is satisfied in the self alone by means of the self, then one is said to be "steadfast in wisdom" (śrīmadbhagavadgītā 2.55).

Desires are of three kinds: external, internal, and those consisting of mere latent impressions (*vāsanā*). External desires are things like sweets that have been acquired; internal desires are things like sweets imagined through longing; and those in the form of latent impressions are those perceived at first sight, like grass fallen on the road. One who is concentrated (*samāhita*) abandons all of them due to the total cessation of all mental fluctuations (*dhīvṛtti*). And he possesses this:

Contentment is to be understood through the sign of the clarity of the face; and that contentment does not reside in sense-objects, but rather in the Self alone, because sense-objects have been renounced and because the intellect is directed toward the reality of the Self in the form of supreme bliss. Furthermore, in this state, the bliss of the Self is not delineated by a mental modification (*manovṛtti*) as it is in the case of *samprajñāta-samādhi*; rather, it is [experienced] by the Self in its nature as self-luminous consciousness (*svaprakāśa-cid-rūpa*). Moreover, contentment is not itself a mental modification; what then...
But it consists of the impressions (*saṃskāra*) thereof; thus, by means of words expressive of such characteristics, he who is composed is described.
The Lord said: "O Pārtha! when a person abandons all desires that exist in his mind and becomes..."
When one is satisfied in the Self by the Self alone, then he is called *sthitaprajña*, firmly established in the highest knowledge (*Bhagavadgītā* 2.55).
Desires are of three kinds: material, mental, and potential.
Sweet things already obtained are material or external; the hope for obtaining sweet things is mental or internal; and those desires which...
They are merely perceived incidentally, like one who happens upon blades of grass while walking along a path, and remain as latent tendencies within the mind.
For one who is in intense contemplation, because of the totality...
The absence of mental fluctuations causes him to relinquish all three types of desire. His contentment is evident from his joyful countenance;
this contentment does not arise from the fulfillment of desires, but—
Of the Self. His mind, being liberated from all desires,
has become blissful, as it has come closest to the Self (for that is the supreme bliss).
In *samprajñāta* samādhi— a variety of concentration wherein the object of meditation remains distinct from the subject— the mental transformation takes the form of:
The bliss of the Self is not like that in this case. Here, in *samādhi*, the Self—which is self-luminous, self-manifesting, and absolute knowledge and bliss—remains manifest. This is contentment.

Furthermore, it does not exist in the form of a mental state, but only as the impression of that form. The person who is in abstract meditation is described by these words expressing its specific characteristics.
One whose mind is unperturbed by sorrows, who is free from longing for pleasures,
and from whom passion, fear, and anger have departed— he is called a sage of steady wisdom.

—(ibid., 2.56) *Duḥkha* is a contrary mental state consisting of torment, characterized by a transformation of the *rajas* quality, and produced by causes such as passion (*rāga*). When such suffering has arisen, one thinks: "I am a sinner; fie upon me!"
"Agitation" (*udvega*) is a mental state consisting of remorse, which takes the form of a delusion due to being a transformation of the quality of *tamas*.

Although this appears to be discernment (*viveka*), it must be understood as a delusion because, while it might have served a purpose in a previous birth by acting as an obstacle to the commission of sin, it is now useless. [The next term is] "pleasure" (*sukham*).

The sattvic mental modification (*cittavṛtti*) is one that is favorable and takes the form of affection, arising from such causes as the birth of a son or the acquisition of a kingdom. When that pleasure exists, the tamasic mental modification is *spṛhā* (longing), which is the vain expectation of such future pleasure without performing the merit (*puṇya*) that is its cause. Furthermore, since both pleasure and pain are brought about by *prārabdha-karma*, for one whose mind has emerged [from samādhi], [these states persist].

And because of the possibility of [right] conduct, both of those are appropriate. However, agitation and longing do not occur for one who possesses discrimination. Likewise, passion, fear, and anger do not exist in him, as they are not brought about by action characterized by tamas.
One who is thus defined by these characteristics—
The meaning is that, by manifesting his own experience, he speaks words that indicate freedom from agitation, lack of desire, and so forth, for the purpose of instructing his disciples.
"He who is not troubled by sorrow and does not hanker after happiness, from whom passion, fear, and anger have departed— he is called a sage of steady wisdom" (Bhagavadgītā).
Sorrow (*duḥkha*) is an unfavorable mental state arising from attachment and so forth; it is a transformation of... (Bhagavadgītā 2.56).

The quality of rajas causes anguish. Being thus afflicted, there arises a remorse such as "I am a sinner; shame on me, the wicked one," and so forth, which is a transformation of the quality of tamas.
Such a mental transformation is anxiety (*udvegaḥ*); although it resembles discrimination (*vivekaḥ*) between the good and the bad, it is not [true] discrimination.
It is indeed so. Had it existed in previous lives, it would have prevented unwholesome action and thus would have been beneficial;
now, however, it serves no purpose, and for this reason it is regarded as [useless].
Delusion.
This happiness (*sukham*) is that which is pleasing and favorable.
The mental state formed by the *sattva-guṇa* and caused by the acquisition of a kingdom, a son, and so forth;
following the experience of such happiness, the longing for...
To expect that the same thing will happen again without performing the requisite meritorious actions and hoping in vain—
such happiness is a mental state formed from the quality of *tamas*.
That which is eager desire— *spṛhā*.
When the sage has arisen from meditative absorption, there may be mental transformations, and he experiences pleasure and pain.

They are justified insofar as they are brought about by *prārabdha* karma; however, anxiety and craving are impossible for a discriminating soul. Likewise, passion, fear, and anger [are likewise impossible].
Being products of *tamas* and not brought about by action, these do not exist in him. By these characteristics, this man of steady wisdom is known.
Using wooden marks, he spoke to his disciples of his own experiences to instruct them, implying an absence of anxiety and craving:
"He who is without attachment everywhere, whatever good or evil he encounters..."
"He who neither rejoices nor feels aversion—his wisdom is firmly established. (Ibid., 2.57)
That in which, when there is decrease or increase in another, these are superimposed upon oneself.

Affection (*sneha*) is a specific modification of the *tāmasa* mind directed toward such other objects. A "wholesome object" (*śubho viṣayaḥ*) is one that causes happiness, such as one's own wife and so forth.

"Appreciation" (*abhinanda*) is a mental modification that impels one to speak of the virtues of such an object. In this context, since the speaking of virtues lacks the purpose of inspiring others, it is futile; therefore, the appreciation that is its cause is *tāmasa*. It is *tāmasa* because it becomes a cause of suffering by generating envy.
The knowledge and other qualities belonging to another are an inauspicious object for this [person]. The mental modification that incites censure toward them is hatred (*dveṣa*).
That too is *tāmasa*, because it is futile since it lacks the purpose of preventing such censure. How could these *tāmasa* qualities possibly exist in one who possesses discrimination?
"He who is without attachment on any side, neither rejoices nor feels aversion upon obtaining the good or the evil, his wisdom is firmly established" (Bhagavadgītā 2.57).
Affection (*sneha*) is that specific transformation of the mind regarding others, caused by the quality of darkness (*tamas*), which,
when it occurs, brings about the superimposition of the loss of those others.
And he gains for himself.
"Good" (śubha) means pleasing things, such as one's wife and so forth. "Rejoicing" (abhinanda) is that mental state.
which leads one to praise such things as a wife; here, the purpose of praising a wife and so forth is not to inspire others. Therefore, it is futile, and the mental state (joy) that causes this is—
The form of *tamas*.
Evil (*aśubha*) refers to disagreeable things, such as the acquisitions of others and so forth, which give rise to envy. Disgust—48.

Hatred (*dveṣa*) is that mental state which impels one to disparage another on account of their acquisitions. This, too, belongs to the quality of darkness (*tamas*), because such disparagement is futile; for this reason...
They are not intended to restrain anyone from anything. Since these are composed of the quality of *tamas*, how could they possibly affect one who possesses discernment?
"And when he withdraws these senses from their objects in every way, as a tortoise draws in its limbs, his wisdom is firmly established. (2.58) (In that same work, 2.58).

The absence of all tamasic modifications in one who has emerged [from meditation] was stated in the two preceding verses; however, the intention here is that for one who is absorbed in samādhi, the modifications themselves do not exist—how, then, could there be any suspicion of tamasic nature? "Furthermore, when he withdraws the senses from their objects..."
"When one withdraws the senses from all sides, as a tortoise draws in its limbs [into its shell], then his knowledge is firmly established" (Bhagavadgītā).
By the preceding two verses, it was stated that in a...
Even when one whose wisdom is established is not in deep meditative absorption,
there is an absence of all tamasic transformations; and when in deep meditative absorption, there are no transformations at all.
Since this is not the case at all, the verse implies: how, then, could there be any doubt regarding the transformations of *tamas*?
"The objects of the senses recede from the embodied one who abstains from food, with the exception of the taste [for them]; even that taste ceases for him upon seeing the Supreme. (Ibid., 2.59)

Prārabdha karma itself brings about certain objects that serve as causes for pleasure and pain—such as the rising of the moon or darkness—while it brings about others, such as houses and fields, through human effort. Among these, the rising of the moon and so forth cease only through samādhi characterized by the complete withdrawal of the senses and other faculties, and not otherwise; whereas houses and the like [cease through other means].

Even in the absence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), [worldly attachments] cease. "Bringing forth" (*āharaṇa*) means effort (*udyoga*). For one who is effortless, objects such as home and so forth cease, but the "taste" (*rasa*) does not cease. "Taste" is mental thirst (*mānasī tṛṣṇā*).
That too ceases from causes of minor pleasure when there is the vision of the Supreme Brahman, whose nature is supreme bliss—as it is said: "What shall we do with offspring, for us..."
This is because of the Vedic scripture: "Neither this self nor this world [exists for him]" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22).
"The objects of the senses turn away from the one who abstains, yet the longing for them remains; but even that longing ceases."
"who sees the Supreme" (Ibid. 2.59).
Certain objects that cause pleasure and pain are brought about by *prārabdha* karma alone, such as the rising of [the sun].

The moon, darkness, and so forth; others, such as houses, lands, and the like, through the assistance of human effort. The rising of the moon and other such phenomena cease to exist during abstract meditation, when all the sense faculties [are withdrawn].
[They] are completely withdrawn and not by any other means. However, houses and the like cease even without *samādhi*.
*Āharaṇa* means accomplishing; *āhāraḥ* means bringing about.
Udyoga means strenuous and continuous endeavor.
The household and such things turn away from one who lacks enterprise.
Rasa means mental thirst—that is, the intense longing for the household.
...and so forth, remains. This longing for the objects of the senses, which yield little joy, ceases upon finding the Self that is absolute bliss.
The Upaniṣad says: "What shall we achieve through..."
"O children, we who have attained this Self, this world" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22).
"For even for a wise man, O son of Kuntī, though he strives..."
The turbulent senses violently carry away the mind.
"Restraining all these, one should sit disciplined, intent on Me;
for he whose senses are under control, his wisdom is firmly established.

Even for one who exerts effort toward exertion, renunciation, and the vision of Brahman, the practice of *samādhi* is necessary to avoid occasional lapses of heedlessness. This is the answer to the question, "What was that? [It is said:
"O son of Kuntī, the turbulent senses indeed carry away..."
"The mind forcibly carries away the intellect of even a discerning man who is constantly striving for perfection" (Bhagavadgītā 2.60).
Having brought all those senses under control, he should...
"Fix your mind on Me with single-minded concentration; for he whose senses are subdued has his wisdom firmly established" (Ibid. 2.61).
Despite his attempts to abandon personal effort and...

Even while realizing the Self, there may be occasional lapses in attention; to avoid this, he should practice abstract meditation (samādhi). Thus, this is the answer to the question, "How does he sit?"
"For a person dwelling on sense-objects, attachment to them arises.
From attachment, desire is born; from desire, anger is produced.
From anger comes delusion; from delusion, the confusion of memory. (62)
"From the loss of mindfulness comes the destruction of the intellect; from the destruction of the intellect, one perishes. (Ibid., 2.62, 63)

In the absence of the practice of concentration (*samādhi*), the following forms of negligence have been set forth: attachment (*saṅga*) is the proximity to the object of meditation; delusion (*saṃmoha*) is the turning away from discrimination (*viveka*); confusion of memory (*smṛtivibhrama*) is the lack of inquiry into reality;
and the incapacity of knowledge—which is obstructed by the defect of the accumulation of contrary mental impressions—to bestow liberation.

“From the contemplation of the objects of the senses comes the destruction of the intellect. From that destruction of the intellect arises attachment to them; from attachment springs longing, and from longing—”
Longing gives rise to anger;
from anger comes delusion, from delusion comes loss of mindfulness, and from loss of mindfulness proceeds ruin.
"From discrimination arises delusion, and from the ruin of discrimination he perishes" (Bhagavadgītā 2.62, 63).
In the absence of the practice of *samādhi*, how can negligence...

The occurrence [of these states] is described as follows: attachment (*saṅga*) means the mental preoccupation with an object of thought; bewilderment (*sammoha*) means the turning away from discernment; and loss of memory—

*Smṛtivibhramaḥ* means the failure to seek the Truth. *Buddhināśaḥ*— the destruction of discernment— means the incapacity of the intellect to effect liberation due to obstacles arising from [ignorance].
"By moving among sense objects with the senses that are free from attachment and aversion,
and which are under his own control, the self-governed man attains serenity. (64)
— (In that very same place, 2.64) ||
"Submissiveness of self" (*vidheyātmatva*) means having the mind brought under control. "Clarity" (*prasāda*) is purity, which is freedom from bondage.

One who is engaged in the practice of *samādhi* attains perfect clarity even while functioning through the senses during the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*), by the power of that latent impression (*vāsanā*). This is the answer to the question, "What would he go toward? Furthermore, by the extensive subsequent text, the one of steady wisdom (*sthitaprajña*) is described.
It has been explained:
"But a man, with a disciplined mind, moving among sense objects with his senses under control and free from..."
"one who has subdued the pairs of opposites, such as love and hatred, attains tranquility" (Bhagavadgītā 2.64).
*Vidheya-ātmā* means the self (the mind) that is subject to discipline—that is, the controlled mind. *Prasādam puri*—
*Ty-* means free from obstruction. One who practices *samādhi*,
even while engaging with sense objects during the waking state, attains perfect purity through the power of [that practice].
The impressions of *samādhi*. This answers the question, "How does he move? The one whose wisdom is established (*sthita-prajña*) has been described in the following several verses.
Now, prior even to the stability and arising of wisdom, freedom from passion, hatred, and so forth is required as its means.
It might be asked: since it is a means for the realization of the supreme truth, it is necessary to be free from love and hate.
...and so forth, as well as for the purpose of making that realization firm after its attainment.
"Certainly; nevertheless, there is a distinction, and that has been shown by the authors of the *Śreyomārga*:
'Those which previously served as means for the establishment of knowledge are to be accomplished through effort.'"
"Furthermore, those [characteristics] remain by their very nature established in one whose wisdom is steady;

they call this state 'liberation while living' (jīvanmukti), which consists in the realization of the Self that is firmly established, wherein the appearance of duality has been sublated by the power of the uncontradicted realization of the Self. Thus [it is said].
Indeed, it is so. However, there is a certain distinction, which has been pointed out by the author of the *Śreyomārga*:
all those factors leading to realization must be brought about.
Through effort, these are the means. When his knowledge becomes steady, they remain within him as inherent characteristics.
"This state of abiding self-knowledge is called *jīvanmukti*, liberation while living, wherein all sense of separateness is countered as a consequence of unimpeded [Self-awareness]."
Regarding "If-knowledge" (jñāna-yoga): the devotee of the Blessed One has been described by the Blessed One in the twelfth chapter as follows:
"One who is not hateful toward any being, but is friendly and compassionate..."
Free from the sense of "mine," free from egoism, equal in suffering and happiness, and patient. ||13||
"The yogi who is always content, self-controlled, and firm in resolve;
whose mind and intellect are dedicated to Me—he, my devotee, is dear to Me.
(Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā 12.13–14)

Because one who is composed has no concern for anything else due to having a mind surrendered to the Lord, and because even when withdrawn from that state, there is an absence of joy or dejection due to maintaining an attitude of indifference, there is an equality of pleasure and pain. This is likewise to be understood in the cases to be described hereafter.
It is to be seen among the pairs of opposites.
The true devotee of the Blessed Lord has been described in the twelfth chapter [of the Bhagavadgītā].
The Lord (Kṛṣṇa):
“He who harbors no hatred toward anyone, who is friendly and compassionate toward all, and who is free from the sense of ego and possessiveness...”
mine, equanimous in pain and pleasure, patient, ever-contented, steadfast in meditation, self-controlled, resolute, and with his mind and intellect fixed upon me— he who...
Thus devoted to Me, he is dear to Me (*Bhagavadgītā*).
In the state of *samādhi*, the mind is fixed upon God; therefore, no other thought can arise. However, when not in *samādhi*—
Although the mind perceives objects, it experiences neither the feeling of happiness nor sorrow due to its equanimity;
thus, there is an equal state of mind toward pleasure and pain. In this manner, in the following—
In these verses as well, the pairs of opposites are to be understood.
"He by whom the world is not troubled, and who..."
"He who is not troubled by the world, and who is himself free from joy, envy, fear, and anxiety— he is dear to Me" (ibid., 12.15):
"He from whom the world does not tremble, and who does not tremble from the world..."
He who is free from joy, impatience, fear, and agitation—he too is dear to me. (15)
“He who is without expectation, pure, skillful in action, indifferent, and undisturbed, who has renounced all undertakings— he, my devotee, is dear to me” (Ibid. 12.16).
He who is free from expectations, pure, skillful, impartial, and free from distress;
who has renounced all undertakings—that devotee of mine is dear to me. 16.
"He who neither rejoices nor hates, neither grieves nor desires, and who has renounced both good and evil— "
"He who neither rejoices nor hates, neither grieves nor desires, who has renounced both good and evil, and who is possessed of devotion— he is dear to Me" (12.17).
He is the same toward enemy and friend, as well as toward honor and dishonor;
he is the same in cold and heat, in pleasure and pain, and is free from attachment. 18.
"He who is the same toward praise and blame, silent, content with whatever comes, homeless, steady-minded, and full of devotion—that man is dear to Me. (19) Thus [it is said].
"He who is equal toward friend and foe, as well as toward the good..."

One who has a bad reputation, who is the same in cold and heat, pleasure and pain, and is free from attachment; to whom blame and praise are equal, who is silent, and content with whatever comes— him they call a sage.
"He who comes [to Me], homeless, steadfast in mind, and full of devotion— that man is dear to Me" (Gītā 12.18–19).
Here too, as before, the distinction has been shown by the author of the Vārttika.
"For one in whom self-awakening has arisen, qualities such as non-enmity and the like occur effortlessly, and not in the form of [deliberate] means" (Naiṣkarmyasiddhi 4.69).
Here too, as before, a certain distinction is shown by the Vārttikakāra (*Sureśvarācārya* in the *Naiṣkarmyasiddhi*):
"In one who has realized the Self, virtues such as freedom from hatred [arise]."
"They are present without any effort, not as a means to an end (as is the case for an aspirant)" (ibid. 4.69).
One who has transcended the qualities (*guṇātīta*) is described in the fourteenth chapter:
The state "beyond the qualities" (*guṇātīta*) is described in the fourteenth chapter of the *Bhagavadgītā*:
Arjuna said:
"By what marks, O Lord, does one become transcendent of these three qualities?
What is his conduct, and how does he pass beyond these three qualities?
(Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā 14.21)

The three qualities (guṇas) are sattva, rajas, and tamas; from their specific transformations, the entire cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra) proceeds. Therefore, the state of transcending the qualities is the state of being beyond worldly existence; that is to say, it is liberation while living (jīvanmukti).
The marks (liṅgāni) are those that indicate his transcendence of [ordinary] qualities. Conduct (ācāra) is behavior; it is the manner in which his mind moves.
"How? is a question regarding the method of practice.
Arjuna said: "By what marks, O Lord, is one known who has transcended these three *guṇas*? What is his way of life, and how does he go beyond these three *guṇas*?"
(Bhagavadgītā 14.21).
The three modes— the *guṇas* (constituents)— are *sattva* (lightness/goodness), *rajas* (movement/passion), and *tamas*.
—heaviness/dullness; all mental and material phenomena are the outcome of the evolution of these [three]. Therefore, the state of "beyond the three modes" is not [of those three].

The *liṅgāni* (marks) of *jīvanmukti* (liberation while living) indicate to others the state of one who has transcended the *guṇas* (the modes of nature). *Ācāraḥ* (conduct)— that is, the mode of life— is the manner [of such conduct].
In which [state] his mind will react— [under given conditions].
How (*katham*) means inquiring about the methods that lead to the state beyond the *guṇas*.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O Pāṇḍava, he who does not hate illumination, activity, and even delusion when they arise, nor longs for them when they cease. (22)
He who sits like one indifferent, not shaken by the qualities (guṇas), and remains established in the thought "it is only the qualities that are acting," and does not waver—[he is a sage]. 23.
Equanimous in pain and pleasure, established in his own self, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal;
the wise one is the same toward the pleasant and the unpleasant, and equal in blame and self-praise. ||24||
He who is the same in honor and dishonor, the same toward the parties of friend and foe,
and has renounced all undertakings— he is said to have transcended the qualities.
The Blessed Lord said: "O Pāṇḍava, he who does not loathe illumination, activity, and delusion when they arise, nor longs for them when they cease;
"He who sits as if unconcerned, untroubled by the modes, standing apart and unmoved, knowing that it is only the modes that act;"
Alike in pleasure and pain, established in his own Self,
he looks upon a clod of earth, a stone, and a piece of gold as the same.
He who is of equal worth, impartial toward the pleasant and the unpleasant, steadfast, regarding both censure and praise as one;
he who remains the same in honor and dishonor, and...
He who is equal toward friend and foe and has renounced all undertakings is said to have transcended the modes (*bhagavadgītā*: "And he who serves Me with unswerving yoga of devotion...").
Having transcended these qualities, he becomes fit for the state of Brahman.
“He who serves Me with unchanging devotion of love transcends the three modes; he too is fit for becoming Brahman” (Ibid. 14.26).

The qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are respectively characterized by illumination (*prakāśa*), activity (*pravṛtti*), and delusion (*moha*). These operate during the states of waking and dreaming;

they cease to function during the states of deep sleep, meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and the state of the empty mind (*śūnyacittavṛtti*). Furthermore, activity is of two kinds: favorable (*anukūla*) and unfavorable (*pratikūla*).

And so it is said. In that regard, the deluded person hates contrary activity during waking and desires agreeable activity; however, for one who has transcended the *guṇas*, because of the absence of the superimposition of the agreeable and the contrary, hatred and desire do not exist. Just as some bystander, observing two people engaged in a quarrel, himself—

He remains indifferent, not being moved hither and thither by victory or defeat; likewise, the discerning one who has transcended the qualities (*guṇātīta*) remains indifferent of his own accord. Through the discernment that "the qualities act upon the qualities, but I do not," there is indifference. The superimposition (*adhyāsa*) that "I myself am the agent" is agitation, and he does not possess that. This is what is meant by the question, "What is his conduct? regarding this person.

The answer to the question: equanimity toward pleasure, pain, and so forth, as well as service to the Supreme Self through the practice of knowledge and meditation accompanied by unwavering devotion—this is the answer to the question concerning the means for transcending the qualities (*guṇātīta*).
Illumination, activity, and delusion are the three modes—sattva, rajas, and tamas. They are active during the waking state and the dream state; they cease to function in the state of deep sleep.
Sleep, concentration, and vacant-mindedness.
Activity is of two kinds: agreeable and disagreeable.
Therein, in the waking state, the unwise hates the disagreeable.

One performs actions and seeks those that are agreeable. However, for one who has transcended the *guṇas* (*guṇātīta*), there is no superimposed impression of actions as either agreeable or disagreeable; therefore, such a person possesses neither aversion nor desire.
The discerning one who has transcended the *guṇas* remains entirely indifferent,
just as a bystander standing apart and watching two parties fighting each other remains unconcerned with the outcome.

Remaining unmoved in either case by success or failure, this indifference arises from the realization that the *guṇas* (modes) act upon themselves and not upon me. Such misconceptions as "I am the doer" [are thus dispelled]. *Jīvan-mukti-viveka*.
It is the cause of restlessness, and he does not possess this. Thus, this is the answer to the question: "How does he act?
Equanimity toward pleasure, pain, and so forth, are his characteristics.
By which one is known as *guṇātīta*. Service rendered to the Supreme Self through the practice of knowledge and meditation,
together with unfailing loving devotion (*bhakti*), constitutes the means to be employed.
"Adopted by him"— this answers the question, "How is one to transcend the modes?
A Brāhmaṇa is described by Vyāsa and others.

"The gods know him as a Brāhmaṇa who wears no upper garment, who sleeps on the bare ground without a mat, who uses his arm as a pillow, and who is peaceful. (Mahābhārata, Śāntiparvan, Mokṣadharma 269.29)

The word *brāhmaṇa* denotes one who knows Brahman, as described in the scripture: "Now, the *brāhmaṇa*" (*atha brāhmaṇaḥ*). And since the knower of Brahman has the qualification for the renunciation of the wise (*vidvatsaṃnyāsa*), [this is so] because of scriptural passages such as "wearing his natural form" (*yathājātarūpadharaḥ*, Jābāla Upaniṣad 6) and "the Paramahaṃsa moves about without clothing" (*nācchādanaṃ carati paramahaṃsaḥ*, Paramahaṃsa Upaniṣad 1.2), which indicate the absence of possessions.
Because he is designated as the primary [knower] and because there is no one superior to him, it is logical that he possesses such qualities as being "unexcelled" (anuttarīya) and so forth.
Regarding the term *brāhmaṇa*— the knower of Brahman— it is described by Vyāsa and other sages as follows:
"He who possesses no garment whatsoever to cover either the upper or the lower parts of his body, sleeps upon the bare ground with nothing spread over it, using his own arm as a pillow."
"He who uses the earth as his bed and is ever tranquil is known as a *brāhmaṇa* by the gods" (Mahābhārata, Śāntiparvan, Mokṣadharmaparvan 261.29).
The word *brāhmaṇaḥ* here denotes the knower of the supreme Self, as described by the Śruti text: "Then [there is] the knower of Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.5.1). For it is he alone...

is entitled to the "renunciation of the knower" (*vidvatsannyāsa*). Such scriptural texts as— "The *paramahaṃsa*, as soon as he is born, wanders about unclothed"— (Jābālopaniṣad 6.3) and so forth [establish this].

The *Paramahaṃsopaniṣad* (1–2, adapted), and other such texts, demonstrate the importance of being without possessions; therefore, the statements "he has no garments whatsoever," and so forth, are entirely appropriate.
"Clad in whatever [garment], fed by whatever [food],
and sleeping wherever [he may be]— the gods know him as a Brāhmaṇa.
(Mahābhārata 5.97.14)
Even when there is a dependence on food, clothing, bedding, and shelter for the maintenance of the body, one does not investigate the merits or defects regarding the acquisition of food and so forth;

for since the maintenance consisting of filling the stomach and nourishment is the same [regardless of the source], the investigation of merits and defects is purposeless and constitutes a defect of the mind.
‘The gods know him to be a brāhmaṇa who is covered by any garment, fed by any food, and sleeps at any place’ (Mahābhārata 5.97.14).

Food, clothing, and a place to sleep are, of course, required to maintain the body or life; however, he does not seek out their qualities— whether good or bad— for the sake of mere satiation and sustenance.
Such cases are equal whether qualities are taken into account or not; and the consideration of quality serves no purpose,
being rather a defect of the mind.
For this very reason, it is recited in the *Bhāgavata*:
"What is the use of much description? The characteristic of virtue and vice is as follows: the perception of virtue and vice is itself a vice; virtue, however, is that which is free from both."
(Śrīmadbhāgavatam 11.19.45)
With this in view, it is said in the *Bhāgavata*:
"There is no purpose in dwelling upon the nature of merit and demerit, since the consideration of merit and demerit..."

"Non-merit in itself and the absence thereof is merit": "Clad in a rag from a funeral pyre and a loincloth, bearing a staff, and intent on meditation, he who always delights in solitude—the gods know him as a Brāhmaṇa. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa)
(Viśveśvara’s *Yatidharmasaṃgraha*, page 37)
“The gods recognize him as a brāhmaṇa who, wearing a loincloth and a patched garment, carrying the staff, absorbed in meditation, always remains alone” (Yatidharmasaṃgraha of Viśveśvara).

When there is a desire to favor living beings through the instruction of Brahman and so forth, one should bear the marks such as the staff and the loincloth (kaupīna) in order to generate faith by making known one’s excellence; [as it is said]: "The loincloth, the staff, and the covering are for the sake of the use of one's own body."

For it is stated in the scripture (*Parama Upaniṣad* 1): "And one should accept [the disciple] for the sake of benefiting the world. Even out of a desire to favor him, one should not personally attend to his domestic affairs and such matters; rather, one should remain intent on meditation. For it is stated in the scripture (*Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* 2.2.5): "Know Him alone as the One Self; abandon other words."
"Having realized that very [Self], the wise Brahmin should practice wisdom;
he should not ponder over many words, for that is a weariness of speech.
(Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.21)
And because of this scriptural statement:
"He should put on the loincloth and carry the staff and other such marks to inspire faith among the people."
His eminence in favoring them with instructions concerning the supreme Self; for it is said in the Śruti: "He should possess a loincloth, a staff, and a wrap in order to benefit..."
"for the sake of the people and for his own personal use as well" (Paramahaṃsa Upaniṣad 1).
Although the Brāhmaṇa is intent upon showing kindness to...
A householder should not engage in worldly talk but remain absorbed in meditation, for the Upaniṣad says: "Know that one Self alone; abandon other discourses."
(Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.5), and the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad also says:
"The resolute brāhmaṇa should know that Self alone [through the scriptures and instructions of the teacher]."

Having received instruction from the teacher, one should then strive for superior wisdom through the practice of *samādhi* as described in the *Jīvanmuktiviveka*; one should not indulge in contemplating many words, for they weary the organ of speech.
The instruction regarding Brahman is not a different kind of speech; thus, it does not contradict meditation (*dhyāna*). Furthermore, that meditation becomes free from obstacles when one is alone.
For this very reason, it is stated in another *Smṛti*:
"A single monk is as described; two are considered a pair;
three are declared to be a village, but beyond that, it becomes like a city."

“They should not establish a city, nor a village, nor likewise a settlement of couples; their discourse with one another should concern the king and such matters, as well as the practice of mendicancy. (Dakṣasmṛti 7.35–37)
Teachings concerning Brahman do not constitute other discourses;
therefore, they are not opposed to meditation. That meditation becomes unimpeded when one is alone. This is enjoined in other Smṛtis.
Thus: “A religious mendicant is truly such [as prescribed] when he is alone. When two of them come together, they are called a pair; three of them constitute a village, and more than that a town.”
"Three or more make a city. Therefore, a mendicant should avoid forming a city,
a village, or a pair, for they will speak among themselves of state affairs and the like, as well as of the availability of alms."

"The gods know him as a Brāhmaṇa who is free from desire for rewards, free from worldly undertakings, free from ritual salutations, and free from recitation of hymns; who is undecaying and whose karma has been exhausted. (Dakṣa Smṛti 7:35–37)
(The Mahābhārata, Mokṣadharmaparvan 237.24):
"The gods regard him as a brāhmaṇa who neither bestows blessings nor possesses any impulse for action; who neither salutes nor..."
"Praise anyone who is never dejected and whose desire for action has been extinguished" (Mbh. 12.237.24).
A blessing is bestowed by distinguished beings upon those persons who bow down to them, according to whatever each individual requires.

A benediction (*āśis*) is the prayer for the increase of such and such [qualities] in each respective person. And thus, because men have diverse tastes, the worldly impression (*lokavāsanā*) increases in one whose mind is preoccupied with seeking after what is desired by them; and that [worldly impression] is an obstacle to knowledge.
Accordingly, another *smṛti* states: "By the worldly impression and by the impression of the scriptures, the living being..."
"Through the latent impression of the body, knowledge does not arise exactly as it is.
(Muktikopaniṣad 2.2; Sūtasamhitā, Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa, Pūrvārdha 14.15; Vivekacūḍāmaṇi 202).

Distinguished householders bestow blessings upon men who pay them homage. The wish for success in the attainment of one’s desires is what is called a blessing. Since men desire various things, [the blessing is accordingly varied].
Life creates mental unrest in one who seeks to know these things and leads to attachment for worldly people;
this is contrary to knowledge. Another *smṛti* states thus: "One..."
"One cannot realize the Truth in its proper form, being distracted by the desire for people, scriptures, and one's own body" (Muktikopaniṣad 2.2).

This should also be understood to apply to the undertaking of activities such as prostrations and the like. "Undertaking" refers to the exertion toward acquiring houses, fields, and so forth, whether for one's own sake or for the benefit of others. Both these—blessings and undertakings—must be abandoned by the liberated one.
Furthermore, one should not fear that men who prostrate will suffer distress due to the absence of blessings; for both worldly habituation and distress must be avoided.

Because the word *Nārāyaṇa* is employed as a representative of all blessings for the sake of avoidance; however, every undertaking is indeed flawed. And so says the Smṛti: "For all undertakings are enveloped by defect, just as fire is by smoke."
(Śrīmadbhagavadgītā 18.48). Thus,
it should be understood that the same applies to the cases of salutation, the commencement of an undertaking, and so forth.

The exertion to acquire houses, land, and so forth, whether for one's own use or for the benefit of others, is called the initiative of action (*karmārambha*). These two things— blessing (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and initiative— are to be...
It is abandoned by one who is liberated.
It cannot be argued that if he were not blessed, the person offering salutation would feel unhappy; for [the Blessed One acts] in order to exclude unhappiness in others.
And to prevent attachment in a liberated person toward worldly beings, the term "Nārāyaṇa" is employed, which signifies all auspicious blessings.
— is prescribed. All kinds of undertakings are evil.
Thus it is said in the *smṛti*: "All undertakings are obscured by defects, as fire is by smoke" (*Bhagavadgītā* 18.48).
Even salutation has been prescribed for the seeker-renunciant (vividiṣā-saṃnyāsī): "If there be one who was previously a renunciant and is indeed equal in terms of dharma,
to him a prostration must be performed, but never to anyone else."
(Yājñavalkya Upaniṣad 1).

In that regard, the mind becomes distracted by deliberating upon the priority [of one rite] or its equality with another duty. For this very reason, many are observed quarreling over mere acts of salutation.
Salutation is prescribed for the *vidvatsaṃnyāsin* as follows:
"An elder monk belonging to the same monastic order (*nikāya*) is to be saluted, but no one else is ever to be saluted."
The mind is agitated by the effort to determine the seniority of a mendicant and his order; hence, many [such disputes] are found.
Regarding the dispute over salutation,
the cause for this has been shown by the authors of the Vārttikas:
"Those who are negligent, whose minds are directed outward, who are backbiters, and who are eager for quarreling..."
"Even renunciants are seen whose inner dispositions have been corrupted by fate."—
(Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-vārttika 1.4.1584). Thus,
the Vārttikakāra (Sureśvarācārya) has demonstrated the cause.

Regarding this, it is said: "There are even *saṃnyāsins* whose minds are corrupted by misfortune, who are found to be negligent, interested in worldly affairs, backbiters, and quarrelsome" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*).
(Vārttika 1.4.1584).
The absence of salutation for one who is liberated has been shown by the venerable Bhagavatpāda:
"When one is established in the non-dual, supreme sovereignty, which is the Infinite beyond name and the rest..."
"Then, one who knows the Self—whom would he bow to? At that time, no action remains to be performed.
(Upadeśasāhasrī 17.64).

His Holiness Śaṅkarācārya has demonstrated that the liberated one has no concern for salutation, as follows: "To whom should the knower of the Self offer salutation, if he is established in his own glory?"

What is that which is infinite, non-dual, and beyond name and so forth? For such a person, ritual actions then have no utility (Upadeśa Sāhasrī 17.64). [From] Jīvanmuktiviveka, even regarding prohibition:
Salutation, which is a cause of clarity, is accepted as a remedy for salutation that is a cause of mental turbidity; and thus says the Smṛti:
"The Lord, the Blessed One, has entered [the world] by means of a portion of the individual soul."
"One should prostrate like a staff on the ground before a horse, a caṇḍāla, a cow, or a donkey" (Śrīmadbhāgavata 3.29.34–2,
11.29.16–2). Thus, although salutation that causes a commotion is prohibited, [the following applies]:
Salutation that brings about perfect tranquility through the realization of the equality of all things is permitted. In this regard, the Smṛti states: "One should salute by prostrating oneself."
Even a dog, a *caṇḍāla*, a cow, and a donkey acknowledge Him as God Himself, because that Almighty One has entered into and is present within everything in His form.

"...the individual soul" (Bhāgavata 3.29.34 & 11.29.16). It is praise directed toward a human being that is prohibited, but not praise directed toward the Lord. And so says the Bṛhaspati-smṛti: "Just as one praises a wealthy man with respect out of a desire for wealth..."
"If this were so, who would not be released from bondage by [worshipping] the Creator of the Universe?
(Varāhopaniṣad 3.13; Garuḍapurāṇa 225.50).
Through the perception of universal equality, there is neither exhaustion nor dejection. For this very reason, the Smṛti states:
"The praise of men is forbidden, but not that of the Lord. The Smṛti...
It is thus stated by Bṛhaspati: "Who would not be liberated from bondage if they were to praise the Creator of the Universe, just as one desiring wealth respectfully praises a wealthy man?"

"Should one not be despondent if food is not obtained at a certain time, nor should the steadfast man rejoice upon obtaining it? For both [outcomes] are dependent on destiny. (Varāhopaniṣad 3.13; Garuḍapurāṇa 225.50). Thus [it is said].
"Never dejected"—*akṣīṇam* means never miserable.
Regarding this, there is a *smṛti*: "He who is steadfast should not be sad if, at some place or at some time, he does not obtain a meal."
Nor should he be joyful when he obtains it; for both [obtaining and not obtaining] are governed by destiny. (Source untraced; cf.
Śrīmad Bhāgavatam 11.18.33). Jīvanmuktiviveka.

The state of having exhausted all karma is independence from injunctions and prohibitions, as is recorded in the *Śukāṣṭaka*: "For one who walks upon the path beyond the three qualities (*nistraiguṇya*), what injunction is there? What prohibition is there? With this very point in mind, the Blessed One also said:
"The Vedas have the three qualities as their domain; be free from the three qualities, O Arjuna."
Free from the pairs of opposites, eternally established in purity, devoid of the desire for acquisition and preservation, and possessed of the Self.
(Śrīmadbhagavadgītā 2.45). Thus,
the state of having one's duties exhausted (*kṣīṇakarmatva*) means being free from the injunctions of the scriptures.
prohibitions; for, as the Smṛti says: "What injunction or prohibition can there be for those who walk the path beyond the three guṇas? (the refrain of the Śukāṣṭaka). Bearing this in mind...
The Blessed Lord said: "The Vedas deal with the activity of the threefold modes;
therefore, O Arjuna, be free from these three states of nature."
"Be free from the pairs of opposites, be ever-balanced, free from the desire for acquisition and preservation, and be established in the Self" (Bhagavadgītā 2.45).
Nārada said:
"Viṣṇu should be remembered constantly and never forgotten at any time;
all injunctions and prohibitions are but servants to these two."
(Nāradapañcarātra 4.2.23).
Thus spoke Nārada: "Always remember the Lord Viṣṇu (the all-pervading Self); never forget Him. [All] scriptural injunctions..."
Prescriptions and prohibitions are subordinate to these two rules (that is, these two rules are the objects of all injunctions and prohibitions) (Nārada-pāñcarātra 4.2.23).
The gods know him as a Brahmin who fears a crowd like a snake, honor like death, and women like a corpse.
(The Mahābhārata, Śāntiparvan, Mokṣadharma 237.13):
"The gods know him to be a brāhmaṇa who fears the crowd as he would a serpent, and honor as he would death."
Regarding the phrase "like a woman who is a corpse" (*Mahābhārata*, Śāntiparvan):
since it is stated that "for them, there may be talk of kings and such," fear of the group [of followers] is justified, as it is like a snake.
Because honor is a cause of attachment and thus opposed to the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*), it is to be shunned like death. This is expressed by the phrase "as if from hell."

Or there is this reading: "Fear of the crowd as of a serpent" (*sarpavad gaṇād bhītiḥ*). This is justified by the fact previously stated: "They will indulge... [and so forth]. Thus says the *Smṛti*: "Fear of the crowd as of a serpent."

In politics and the like, attachment arises from honor, which is contrary to the purpose and goal of life; therefore, it should be avoided as if it were death. It is like [escaping] from hell—*narakādiva*—as the other [extreme].
Therefore, the *smṛti* states as follows:
"From lack of honor, ascetic power increases; but from honor, ascetic power perishes.
A Brahmin who is honored and worshipped languishes like a cow that has been milked dry."
(Padma Purāṇa, Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, 19.340)
Intending this very point, dishonor is remembered as something to be embraced:
"Dishonor increases the power of austerity (in the form of meditation), but honor diminishes it; the *vipra* who..."
"One who has been worshipped and venerated becomes exhausted like a cow after milking" (Padmapurāṇa, Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa 1.19.340).
In accordance with this idea, the acceptability of insult is...
It is described thus in the Smṛti:
"The yogin should indeed conduct himself in such a way, recollecting the dharma of the virtuous,
so that people may disregard him and not seek his company."
—(Nāradaparivrājakopaniṣad 5.30). Thus.
"The yogi, remembering the ways of the wise, should conduct himself in such a manner that people treat him with contempt and never seek his company" (Nārada Parivrājaka Upaniṣad).
(Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.30).

There are two kinds of faults regarding women: their being prohibited and their being loathsome. Of these, the mere fact of their being prohibited may sometimes be transgressed due to passion or the force of past karma (*prārabdha*). (Jīvanmuktiviveka)

In the case of women, there are two kinds of faults: one is their being forbidden to renunciants (saṃnyāsins), and the other is their being loathsome by nature. This prohibition is sometimes transgressed.
This occurs for one who is deeply attached and impelled by powerful *prārabdha* karma.
With this in mind, the *Smṛti* says:
"One should not share a bed or a seat with one's mother, sister, or daughter;
for the powerful collection of the senses drags away even a learned man. (Manu 2.215)
With this in view, the *smṛti* states:
"One should never share a bed or a seat even with one's mother, sister, or daughter; for the groups of sense-faculties are powerful."
"Both the objects of the senses and one's own actions drag down even a wise man" (Manusmṛti 2.215).
And thus, loathing [for these] has been described in the Smṛtis.

"Even though there is no difference between the unmentionable parts of women and a moist wound from a vein, people are generally deceived by a difference in their minds. (Nāṭyaśāstra, Paribhāṣāprakaraṇa, 3.29)
"A piece of hide, split in two and fumigated by the upward breath of excrement—that which men take pleasure in; what greater folly than this?
(Viśveśvara’s *Yatidharmasaṃgraha*, p. 93).
In the *smṛtis*, loathing is described as follows:
"There is little difference between the unspeakable region of a woman and a discharging fistula; however, regarding it..."
"By another light, one is often deceived" (Nārada Parivrājaka Upaniṣad 3.29).
"Can there be anything more audacious than those men who are fond of that piece of skin with a hole?"
"In the middle [of the body], it is putrid with the foul wind emitted from the posterior opening" (Viśveśvara’s *Yatidharmasaṃgraha*, p.
93). *Jīvanmuktiviveka*.

Or there is another reading: "Those who take delight therein, how are they not like worms? Thus, with the intention of expressing both prohibition and disgust, the simile of a corpse (*kuṇapa*) is stated here.
"They are fond of [such things]," and so forth. Here, the example of a corpse is given to express both prohibition and loathsomeness.
"By whom alone the sky always becomes as if filled..."
‘The gods know him to be a brāhmaṇa for whom that which is crowded with people is empty.
(Mahābhārata, Śāntiparvan, Mokṣadharma 237.11) ‘The gods know him to be a brāhmaṇa, to whom when...’
"Alone, space appears to be ever-full, and a crowded place appears to be empty" (Mahābhārata, Śāntiparvan).
[This refers to] the dwelling of worldly beings in solitude.

Because it is a cause of fear, indolence, and other such obstacles, [the company of people] is to be avoided; whereas a multitude of people, being of a different nature, is to be accepted. For the yogi, however, the opposite is true. When one is alone, if meditation proceeds without hindrance, the entire sky appears as if filled with the perfect self of supreme bliss.
Therefore, fear, laziness, sorrow, delusion, and the like do not arise;
for one who knows, "In whom all beings have become the Self alone," what delusion can there be, and what sorrow for him who perceives this oneness?
Thus says the scripture (Īśā Upaniṣad 7).

Solitude causes fear, lethargy, and other such states; therefore, householders should avoid living alone and instead lead a communal life that is free from fear and similar afflictions. In the case of [the ascetic], however, this is exactly the opposite.

of a yogi. Being alone and absorbed in unimpeded meditation, the yogi experiences the Self, which is supreme bliss pervading the entire expanse of space. Therefore, for him, fear, lethargy, and sorrow—
and delusion and so forth do not occur.
For, as the Īśa Upaniṣad says: "When, for one who knows, all beings have indeed become one with his own self..."

"Then, for one who has seen the oneness, what delusion and what sorrow can there be? (Īśa Upaniṣad 7). A place crowded with people, because it is opposed to meditation due to talk of kings and the like, is devoid of the realization of the blissful Self; it is as if empty.
It means that the mind becomes afflicted because of the falsity of the world and the fullness of the Self.
A crowded place acts as an obstacle to meditation through various kinds of talk, such as politics, and because of the absence [of solitude].
The awareness of the Self within that state— which is supreme bliss— afflicts the mind like a void, owing to the unreality of the world and the fullness of the Self.
The *ativarṇāśramī* (one who has transcended the castes and stages of life) is described by the Supreme Lord to Viṣṇu in the fifth chapter of the *Muktikhaṇḍa* of the *Sūtasamhitā*.
And the stages of (social) life have been described by Parameśvara to Viṣṇu in the fifth chapter of the section on liberation in the Sūta Saṃhitā as follows:
"The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the mendicant—even these who have transcended the stages of life (varṇāśrama)—are progressively superior when they are wise. (9)

"The student (*brahmacārin*), the householder (*gṛhastha*), the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), the religious mendicant (*bhikṣuka*), and the one who has transcended all [castes and stages of life] (*ativarṇāśramin*)."
If they are well-versed in their respective vocations,
then they are superior according to the order mentioned [in Sūta Saṃhitā 9] (that is, each subsequent one is superior to the preceding).
"The Guru is declared to be beyond the castes and stages of life (ativarṇāśramī) and is the authority for all;
he shall not be the disciple of anyone, just as I am, O Puruṣottama. (14)
"The *ativarṇāśramin* is said to be the preceptor of all men who are entitled to the aforementioned occupations, O Puruṣottama; like me, he never becomes [subject to worldly conditions]."
A disciple of anyone at all (*Sūta Saṃhitā* 14). *Jīvanmukti Viveka*: "The one who has transcended the stages of life and caste (*ativarṇāśramī*) is said to be the direct teacher of teachers;
there is no doubt that in this world there is none equal to him, nor indeed any superior. (15)
It is said that the *ativarṇāśramin* is indeed the teacher of all teachers; there is no doubt that in this world there is no one equal to him, nor anyone superior (Ibid. 15).
"He who [knows] the one distinct from the body, senses, and so forth; the witness of all; ultimate consciousness; whose nature is bliss; and who is self-luminous. (16)

He who knows the Supreme Reality, the Witness of all, distinct from the body and the senses, self-luminous, and absolute bliss, becomes one who has transcended the castes and stages of life (ativarṇāśramī).
And through the hearing of the great Mahāvākyas of Vedānta alone, O Keśava, one becomes the *ativarṇāśramin* who possesses supreme intelligence and supreme truth (Ibid. 16–17). [17]
"He who,
by hearing the great words of Vedānta, O Keśava, knows the Self who is the Lord, becomes an *ativarṇāśramī*."

Śrī Śaṅkarācārya (Ibid 5.17, second line & 18, first line): "He who is free from the [distinctions of] caste and stage of life, the witness of the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep]... [18]
He who knows Mahādeva becomes one who has transcended the castes and stages of life.
“He who knows the Great Lord, who is beyond the castes and stages of life and is the witness of the three states, becomes an *ativarṇāśramī*. (Ibid. 18–2nd line & 19–1st line)
The castes, stages of life, and so forth, are imagined within the body through Māyā. ||19||
"Those [attributes] never belong to me, who am of the nature of consciousness";
he who knows this through the Vedāntas becomes one who has transcended the castes and stages of life (ativarṇāśramī). || 20 ||
— Caste, stage of life, and so forth, are conceptual constructs superimposed upon the body through the delusion of *māyā*;
they have no connection with Me, nor do they ever exist in Me, who am...
The Self, which is absolute intelligence— he who knows this from the Vedānta becomes an *ativarṇāśramin* (Ibid., 19, second line & 20).70
Just as the world moves by its own accord in the presence of the sun,
so too does the entire universe move through my presence.
Thus, he who knows through the Vedāntas becomes one who transcends the castes and stages of life (ativarṇāśramī).
“He who knows from the Upaniṣads that the universe is active because of my presence, just as men are active...”
When [the self] manifests itself in the presence of the Sun, it becomes the *ativarṇāśramī* (ibid. 21 & 22, first line).
"In gold, there are necklaces, armlets, bracelets, svastikas, and so forth. (22)
Just as that [world] is imagined through illusion, so too the universe always exists within me alone;
he who knows this through the Vedāntas becomes one who transcends the castes and stages of life (ativarṇāśramī). || 23 ||
"He who, through the Vedānta, knows that the various ornaments— such as the *hāra*, *keyūra*, *kaṭaka*, and *svastika*—
are composed of gold (and are nothing other than pure gold)..."
Just as the universe is perpetually projected within me through māyā-delusion, so too do I become the ativarnāśramin (ibid., 22,
second line & 23).
Just as silver is imagined in mother-of-pearl through illusion,
so too the world, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat), consisting of illusion, is imagined in me alone.

Thus, he who knows through the Vedāntas that the entire universe, beginning with Mahat— the Great Principle— is [of this nature], becomes one who has transcended the castes and stages of life (ativarṇāśramī).
Projected by me through māyā— delusion— just as a pearl is falsely perceived in mother-of-pearl, he becomes the *ativarṇāśramin* (Ibid.
24 & 25, first line).
Whether in the body of a Caṇḍāla, in the bodies of animals and so forth, or in the form of Brahman—[it is the same]. ||25||
O Supreme Person, while others exist according to degrees of gradation,
You are eternally all-pervading like space and entirely free from all attachments.
"Mahādeva exists as a single form; I am He, the supreme nectar.
He who knows this through the Vedāntas becomes one who transcends the castes and stages of life (ativarṇāśramī). ||27||
"O Puruṣottama, he who knows from the Vedānta that the Great Lord is one, free from all relations, and like the all-pervading ether, becomes an *ativarṇāśramī*."
"It pervades all beings, whether small or great—the body of a candāla, a bird, a beast, a brāhmaṇa, or any other being, high or low—[realizing]: 'I am indeed He, the Supreme Immortal One. (Ibid.)

Just as the directions appear as before even to one whose confusion regarding the directions has vanished, so too does the world appear to me, though it has been destroyed by right knowledge; yet in reality, it does not exist. 28.
Thus, he who knows through the Vedāntas— that the quarters are alike even after the correction of error— becomes one who has transcended the castes and stages of life (ativarṇāśramī).

Just as the world appears to me through the aid of the stars and so forth, even after it has been negated by supreme knowledge, it truly does not exist; thus, I become one who transcends the castes and stages of life (*ativarṇāśramī*). (Ibid.)
"Just as this manifold world of dreams is a manifestation of my own māyā. (28 & 29, first line) ||29||
Likewise, he who knows through the Vedāntas that even this waking world is a manifestation of Māyā within me—he becomes one who transcends the stages of life and caste (ativarṇāśramī). || 30 ||
"He becomes an *ativarṇāśramin* who, from the Vedānta, knows that the world of my waking state is a fabrication of *māyā*— illusion— just like the world of my dream."
The creation of delusion (Ibid 5.29–30):
"For one whose conduct regarding caste and stage of life has dissolved through the vision of the Self, he stands established in his own Self, having transcended all castes and stages of life. (31)
Through the realization of his Self, he has cast aside all the conventions of caste and stage of life; transcending all such things, he is established in his own Self (ibid., 5.31).

"The man who, having abandoned his own stages of life (āśramas) and castes (varṇas), abides in the Self alone, is declared by those who know the meaning of all the Vedas to be one who has transcended the castes and stages of life (ativarṇāśramī). ||32||
“The man who, having renounced his *varṇa* and *āśrama*, abides in the Self, is called an *ativarṇāśramin* by those who know the meaning of the Vedas” (Ibid. 32).

"It is neither the body, nor the senses, nor the vital breath, nor the mind, nor the intellect, nor the ego; it is neither the consciousness, nor indeed Māyā, nor the world consisting of space and the rest. (33)
Neither an agent, nor an enjoyer, nor likewise one who causes enjoyment;
in reality, the Self is solely Brahman, which is consciousness, existence, and bliss. 34.
‘The Self is neither the body, nor the senses, nor life, nor the mind, nor the intellect, nor the ego, nor the thinking faculty, nor Māyā, nor the creation beginning with...’
It is space; it is neither the agent nor the enjoyer, nor does it cause these; in reality, the Self is Brahman, which is absolute knowledge, existence, and bliss (Ibid. 33, 34).

Just as the sun appears flickering solely due to the movement of the water, so too does the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra) belong to the Self solely through its association with the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra). //35//
"Just as the sun appears to move through the movement of the water [in which it is reflected], even so the Self identified with the ego appears to possess *saṃsāra*-mutations" (Ibid. 35).
Therefore, O Keśava, the castes and stages of life belonging to others are merely superimposed upon the Self through delusion; those who perceive them as such do not know the Self. (36)
“Thus, O Keśava, the castes (varṇas) and stages of life (āśramas), though existing within the ego, are superimposed upon the Self solely through delusion;
the knower of the Self has no concern with them.”
(As stated in the same work, verse 36):

"For those who possess the knowledge of the Self, there is neither injunction nor prohibition, nor the conceptualization of what is to be avoided and what is not to be avoided; likewise, O Janārdana, there is nothing else. (37)
"O Janārdana, for those who have realized the Self,
there is neither injunction nor prohibition, nor the notion of what is to be avoided or not avoided; indeed,"
"Nothing else exists for them" (Ibid.
37). "O lotus-eyed one, mortals perpetually deluded by *māyā* do not at all understand this state of those who possess self-knowledge" (Ibid. 38).
“O lotus-eyed one, ordinary mortals, under the spell of *māyā*— delusion— would never know of such a state of those who have realized the Self” (Ibid. 38).
"O Keśava, this culmination of the realization of Brahman cannot be seen by the fleshly eye; it is self-established for the wise. (39)
‘This state of the knowers of Brahman is not visible to the fleshly eye, but to the knowers, O Keśava, it is self-evident’ (Ibid. 39).
"Where people are always asleep, there the self-controlled one is awake;
where they are awake, O Keśava, there the wise man is in deep sleep. (40)
“Where all beings always sleep, there the self-controlled one is awake; where they are awake, O Keśava, there the knower is asleep” (Ibid. 40).
"Thus, one should know the Self as free from duality, formless, stainless, eternally pure, without appearance, consisting of pure existence and consciousness, and the supreme nectar. (41)

"He who knows [this] through the Vedāntas and has become certain by means of his own direct experience—he is declared to be one who transcends the castes and stages of life; he alone is the supreme guru. Thus [it is said].
"He who knows from the Vedānta and [then is] firmly..."
Convinced of It through his own direct and immediate self-awareness—
that which is beyond dualities, formless, stainless,
eternally pure, and free from delusion— and which is...
Pure consciousness, supreme existence and bliss, is called the *ativarṇāśramin*, and he alone is the best preceptor—
the *guru* (Ibid. 41, 42).

Thus, it is established that such scriptural passages as "The liberated one is being liberated," along with the Smṛti statements defining the jīvanmukta, the sthitaprajña, the devotee of the Lord (bhagavadbhakta), the guṇātīta brāhmaṇa, and the ativarṇāśramin,
constitute the authorities for the existence of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). Thus ends the section on the authorities for *jīvanmukti*.

Thus, in this manner, by means of Śruti texts such as "Once liberated, one is liberated again" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.1) and Smṛti texts demonstrating the *jīvanmukta* who is *sthitaprajña*, [the state of liberation is established].
It is conclusively established that *jīvanmukti* is a reality by means of the terms *bhagavadbhakta*, *guṇātīta*, *brāhmaṇa*, and *ativarṇāśramin*.
This concludes the evidence for *jīvanmukti*.
Thus ends the first chapter, on the Proof of Liberation while Living, in the *Jīvanmuktiviveka* composed by the venerable Vidyāraṇya.
Thus ends the first chapter, concerning the proof of *jīvanmukti*, in the *Jīvanmuktiviveka* composed by Śrī Vidyāraṇya. The Second Chapter: On the Effacement of Latent Impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*).
Now we shall describe the means for liberation while living (jīvanmukti).

The knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), the dissolution of the mind (manonāśa), and the exhaustion of latent impressions (vāsanākṣaya) are its means. For this very reason, at the conclusion of the section on tranquility (upaśama-prakaraṇa) in the Vāsiṣṭha Rāmāyaṇa:
In this context from the *Laghu-yogavāsiṣṭha* (28.1), which begins with the words "of the bodies of those liberated while living" (*jīvanmuktaśarīrāṇām*), Vasiṣṭha says:
Now we shall discuss the means to liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). The...
Knowledge of the Truth, the cessation of the mind,
and the effacement of the impressions of latent desires are the means to *jīvanmukti*; for this, at the conclusion of the [first] part—
In the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa*, the chapter on perfect tranquility of the *Vāsiṣṭha-Rāmāyaṇa*, Vasiṣṭha,
while discussing the bodies of the *jīvanmuktas*, says:

"O Mahāmati, the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*), the realization of consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the dissolution of the mind (*manonāśa*), when practiced for a long time, become fruit-bearing simultaneously. (116)

The simultaneous practice, over a long period of time, of the effacement of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*), [the means to] knowledge, and the annihilation of the mind, O wise one (Rāma), brings about...
Regarding the result (*Laghu-yoga-vāsiṣṭha* 28.116): having stated the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), he states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—
in the aforementioned verse, [he describes] the relationship between the means and their...
The conclusion has been shown; now it is being demonstrated that in the absence of the means, the result will also be absent:
"These three, as long as they have not been thoroughly practiced repeatedly, [will not yield their fruit]."
"Until then, the attainment of the state does not occur, even in hundreds of aeons. Thus [it is said].
“Until these three means are repeatedly and well practiced together, the realization of that state does not occur even in hundreds of years” (Ibid. 28.115).
He states the obstacle that arises when there is no simultaneous practice:
"If these [mantras] are practiced one by one with long effort, they do not bestow success, like words that are merely strung together. (117)
He describes how it obstructs the result if not practiced together as follows:
"If they are practiced one by one, even for a long time..."
"Even with strenuous effort, they do not yield results, just as mantras— the scriptural formulas— fail to produce results if recited in fragments and with intervals" (Ibid., 117).

Just as in the ritual of the twilight ablution (*saṃdhyāvandana*), when the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.9.1) are enjoined to be used together for the act of sprinkling, the scriptural performance is not accomplished by reciting only one verse each day;
or just as there is no accomplishment [of the rite] with only one of the six ancillary mantras (*ṣaḍaṅga-mantra*); or as in common worldly practice.
Just as a meal is not accomplished by any single item such as vegetables, soup, or rice, so it is here. He states the purpose of long-term practice:
the three *ṛc* mantras beginning with *āpo hi stha* (RVŚ 10.9.1), "O Waters, you are... and so forth, are prescribed.
Regarding the recitation performed during the purification with water as part of the twilight rites (*saṃdhyā*): if,
instead of reciting all three mantras every day, only one *ṛc* is recited, [the following applies].
The scriptural observance does not succeed; or a six-limbed mantra will not yield results if employed in parts with intervals; or in worldly matters such as the evening meal.
If only a single course— namely, either the vegetables, or the soup, or the rice—
is served instead of all of them together, the intended purpose is not fulfilled.

The necessity of long-term practice is described as follows in the *Jīvanmuktiviveka*: "By these three, when practiced for a long time, the firm knots of the heart are severed without a doubt, just as fibers are cut by the slicing of a lotus stalk. (118)
He states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of that very point:
"By the long-term practice of these three means, the firm fetters of the heart are undoubtedly broken, just as..."
"O Rāma, this persistence of worldly existence, practiced through hundreds of previous births, is never destroyed without the yoga of long-term practice. (Laghu-Yoga-Vāsiṣṭha 1.119)
This is demonstrated by the following contrary statement:
"O Rāma, the appearance of the world arises from its being experienced through hundreds of births, and without..."
"Through the prolonged practice of yoga, it cannot be dissolved anywhere" (Ibid.
Not only is there an absence of fruit from the practice of each [element] individually, but even its very nature is not accomplished; thus [it continues].

"Knowledge of reality, the dissolution of the mind, and the destruction of latent impressions—having become mutual causes for one another, these indeed remain difficult to accomplish. (113) Thus it is said.
When attempted individually, these means not only fail to produce [the result]...
Since these results are even impossible to accomplish, he says this:
"The knowledge of the truth, the dissolution of the mind."
and the eradication of latent tendencies— these three means, being mutually related as cause and effect, make [the goal] all the more difficult to attain (Ibid. 28.113).

Among these three, by combining each pair, there are three dyads. Regarding the mutual causality of the dyad consisting of the dissolution of the mind (*manonāśa*) and the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*), he states it by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) therein: 78. [The verse follows: "If the mind is dissolved, the latent impressions are destroyed; if the latent impressions are destroyed, the mind is dissolved. By this, he shows that the dissolution of the mind and the destruction of latent impressions are mutually causal. If the mind is not dissolved, the latent impressions are not destroyed; if the latent impressions are not destroyed, the mind is not dissolved. Thus, through the method of exclusion, he demonstrates their reciprocal causality.
"As long as the mind has not dissolved, so long there is no destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā);
as long as the latent impressions have not been destroyed, so long the mind does not become tranquil.
From these, three pairs are derived through mutual association.

The means: among these, the pair consisting of the dissolution of the mind (*citta-vilaya*) and the effacement of latent impressions (*saṃskāra-saṃkṣaya*) possesses a reciprocal causal relationship, which is here described by way of negation.
Thus:
"As long as the mind has not been dissolved, there can be no eradication of the latent impressions (vāsanās); and until the latent impressions [are eradicated, liberation cannot be attained]."
"as long as they are not effaced, the mind does not dissolve" (Ibid. 28.110).

The substance of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which transforms in the form of a continuous stream of activity—like the succession of flames of a lamp—is called "mind" (*manas*) because its nature is that of thinking (*manana*). Its destruction consists in its abandoning transformation into the form of activity and becoming suppressed (*niruddha*).
Transformation (*pariṇāma*). And so Patañjali formulated in the *Yogaśāstra*:
"The suppression and manifestation of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of emergence and suppression [respectively] is the transformation of suppression" (3.9).
The sequence of moments of consciousness at the time of cessation;
the internal sense-faculties, which take the form of a series of mental transformations, like the series of flames of a lamp.
The lamp is called "mind" because of its mental functions. Its dissolution means its relinquishing of transformations in the form of modifications and remaining in its own essential nature.
The control of transformations prevents them from undergoing further modification.
Patañjali has formulated this in the *Yoga Sūtras* as follows:
"When the mental modification subsides and the restraining impression arises (that is, when the mind is withdrawn from further transformation), this moment of cessation..."

When [the mind] connects with the mind, it is called "transformation into cessation" (Yoga Sūtras 3.9). The latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of emergence are overcome; the latent impressions of cessation appear; [the mind] is joined with cessation.
The moment is followed by the mind; this should be understood as the dissolution of the mind (*manonāśa*).
When the impressions of transformation are neutralized, the impressions of restraint appear—this is the moment of *jīvanmukti*.
Control is connected with the mind— this state is to be understood as the dissolution of the mind.
The cause of a specific mental modification such as anger, which arises suddenly without prior reflection on what precedes or follows it, resides within the mind.
*Saṃskāra* is latent impression (*vāsanā*), because the mind is perfumed by successive prior practices;
it refers to a mental transformation such as anger that arises suddenly without reflecting on the past.
Or [the perception of] the future is due to the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) in the mind— those desires left behind by previous experiences in the mind (just as a piece of cloth...).
