Just as a cloth in contact with flowers retains their fragrance,

the destruction of that latent impression (*vāsanā*) means that even when external causes are present, anger and the like do not arise, provided that firm, pure impressions such as tranquility and self-restraint born of discrimination (*viveka*) are established.
The eradication of this *vāsanā* means that anger and the like do not arise even in the presence of an external cause;
this occurs when there is the presence of pure impressions, such as those of the Self.
The impressions (*saṃskāra*) and so forth produced by discrimination are engraved [upon the mind].

In that regard, in the absence of the dissolution of the mind (*manonāśa*), while mental modifications (*vṛtti*) are arising, there is no [cessation of bondage] because anger and other states may occasionally arise due to external causes.

The dissolution of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*). However, as long as the latent impressions have not been dissolved, mental modifications will continue to arise in that same manner, and thus there is no dissolution of the mind.
If the mind remains undissolved, transformations will persist, and at some point or another...

Since anger and the like would arise caused by external stimuli, there would be no eradication of *vāsanā*. Likewise, if the *vāsanā* were not eradicated, transformation would continue to occur; thus, there would be no dissolution.

Regarding the mutual causality between the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) and the dissolution of the mind (*manonāśa*), he states it by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): "As long as there is no realization of reality, how can there be the pacification of the mind?"
"As long as there is no tranquility of the mind, so long is there no realization of reality. (111)

The knowledge of reality and the dissolution of the mind stand in a relationship of mutual causality, which is now being described through negation: *Jīvan-mukti-viveka* (Discrimination of Liberation-in-life)
‘Until there is knowledge of Reality, how can the mind be calm? The knowledge of Reality cannot arise so long as the mind is not calm’ (Laghu-Yoga-Vāsiṣṭha 8.111).

The knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is the certainty that "all this is indeed the Self alone; however, the world consisting of perceived forms, tastes, and so forth, is composed of illusion (*māyā*) and does not exist in reality. In the absence of such [knowledge], while objects such as form and taste continue to exist, the mental modifications (*cittavṛtti*) directed toward them cannot be restrained, just as it is impossible to stop [the fire] when fuel and other materials are being thrown into it.

Just as a flame of fire cannot be extinguished [by mere words], so too, when there is no tranquility of the mind and forms and other objects are being grasped by the mental modifications (*vṛtti*), one might—due to the suspicion of contradiction with direct perception—[object] against the scriptural statement "Brahman is non-dual" (*brahmādvitīyam*), just as one might object to the Vedic text "The sacrificial grass-bundle is the sacrificer" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*) on the grounds that it contradicts what is perceived. This is in accordance with the Śruti: "There is not even the slightest diversity here" (*neha nānāsti kiṃcana*, Kaṭha Upaniṣad 4.11).
Thus, such a certainty regarding reality would not arise.
Brāhmaṇa: "All this is indeed the Ātman, the apparent world beginning..."
The firm conviction that "form, taste, and so forth are illusory and do not truly exist" is the knowledge of reality. In the absence of such knowledge and in the presence of...
Sense objects such as forms, tastes, and so forth, along with the mental transformations that take their shapes, cannot be stopped;
just as when fuel is added to a fire, its flames cannot be extinguished.
In the absence of mental tranquility, forms, tastes, and so forth will be experienced through the transformations of the mind;
consequently, doubt will arise regarding the truth of such Śruti.
“There is no duality whatsoever in this” (*Katha Upaniṣad* 4.11),
just as in the case of the passage: “The sacrificial seat (*barhis*) made of *kuśa* grass is...”
[The notions of] "sacrificer" and so forth [are untenable], for both contradict objective experience. Therefore, the firm conviction that "Brahman is one without a second" will never arise.
He states the mutual causality between the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
It is described conversely in the *Jīvan-mukti-viveka* as follows:
"As long as there is no destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), how can there be the attainment of reality (*tattva*)?
As long as there is no attainment of reality, there is no destruction of latent impressions. (112)

‘How can knowledge arise as long as the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) have not been wiped away? And until the attainment of knowledge, there can be no wiping away of the latent impressions. (Laghu-Yoga-Vāsiṣṭha)

(Śiṣṭha 28.112) As long as the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of anger and the like have not been destroyed, true knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) does not arise due to the absence of the means such as tranquility (*śama*) and self-restraint (*dama*). Furthermore, as long as the non-dual reality of Brahman remains unknown, the delusion regarding the reality of the causes of anger and so forth does not depart, and thus the latent impressions are not exhausted.
We shall illustrate, by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), how these three aforementioned pairs serve as mutual causes for one another:
if the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of anger and so forth remain uneffaced, the knowledge of reality cannot arise.

This is due to the absence of the means, such as self-restraint and the like. Without the realization of Brahman as the "non-dual ultimate reality," the illusory nature of the causes [remains unperceived].
Since the [notion] of anger and so forth is not sublated, the eradication of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is impossible. We shall now describe,
by means of examples, the mutual causal relationship of the three aforementioned factors.
Pairs [of opposites] are reconciled in a positive manner.

When the mind (*manas*) has perished, and the external cause that awakens latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) is no longer perceived, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) is exhausted. When the latent impression is exhausted, the mind perishes because, in the absence of its cause, mental fluctuations such as anger do not arise. This is as follows:
The pair consisting of the dissolution of the mind and the destruction of latent impressions [is achieved];
for once the mind has dissolved, external causes that arouse those impressions are no longer perceived.
The *vāsanās* are wiped away. And when the *vāsanās*— the latent impressions— are destroyed, mental transformations such as anger and so forth do not arise, owing to the absence of their cause.
Therefore, there is the dissolution of the mind. Thus, this is the pair consisting of the dissolution of the mind and the effacement of latent impressions.

From the Śruti text, "But it is seen by a refined intellect" (Kaṭhopaniṣad 1.3.12), it is understood that the destruction of all other mental modifications is the cause of the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), because the modification directed toward the unity of the Self is the means of perception. And when the knowledge of reality exists, the world, being illusory, [is regarded] like a man’s horn and so forth.
Due to the non-arising of mental modifications and because the Self has already been perceived, there is no further utility for such modifications; thus, like a fire without fuel, the mind perishes.
This constitutes the union of the dissolution of the mind and the knowledge of reality.
As the *Kaṭha Upaniṣad* (1.3.12) states: "The Self is seen..."

"by means of sharp intelligence. From this *śruti*, it is understood that the mental transformation directed toward the oneness of the Self leads to realization; therefore, [all other modifications] cease.
Of all other transformations, this alone is the means for the realization of Truth. When the Supreme Reality is known,
the world becomes unreal, and no mental modification [remains].
This unreal world occurs just as a transformation into the form of "human horns" never occurs; furthermore,
no further mental transformation is necessary, because the Ātman is [already that].
Since it has already been seen, the mind dissolves, just as a fire is extinguished in the absence of fuel. This concerns the dyad consisting of the dissolution of the mind and knowledge.
Regarding the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), the author of the *Vārttika* states that it is the cause for the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) such as anger:
"For one who perceives the same identity in enemy, friend, and one's own body..."
"How can there be anger in one who possesses discernment, any more than toward the limbs of one's own body?
(Naiṣkarmyasiddhi 2.18).
It is well known that tranquility (*śama*) and other qualities, which consist in the exhaustion of latent impressions such as anger, serve as causes for knowledge. Vasiṣṭha also says:
"The qualities such as tranquility arise from knowledge, and likewise, knowledge arises from tranquility and the other qualities; these two increase one another like two lotus ponds.
(Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 4.107).
This, then, is the dyad of the exhaustion of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the knowledge of the ultimate reality (*tattvajñāna*).
Knowledge of the ultimate reality leads to the effacement of latent impressions such as anger and so forth.
Such is what was described by the Vārttikakāra Sureśvarācārya in the *Jīvanmuktiviveka*:
"From where could anger arise for a man of discrimination..."
"He who sees that same single Self in the bodies of his friends,
enemies, and himself, just as one perceives that same single body in all its own limbs" (Naiṣkarmyasiddhi 2.18).
Self-restraint and the like are synonyms for the eradication of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and it is well known that these—
self-restraint and so forth— are the means to knowledge.
Vasiṣṭha also says:
"Virtues such as self-restraint flourish through knowledge,
and knowledge thrives through virtues, just like a lake."
And the lotuses flourish together (Laghu-Yoga-Vāsiṣṭha 4.107). This is the pair consisting of the knowledge of truth and the effacement of *vāsanā*.
He states the means for accomplishing the triad beginning with the knowledge of reality:
"Therefore, O Rāghava, having abandoned the desire for enjoyment far away, one who is discerning should, with human effort, take refuge in this triad."
(Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 4.114).
Thus, the methods for attaining the three means— the knowledge of truth and so forth— are described as follows:

"Therefore, O Rāghava, a discerning person, through resolute effort, should abandon the desire for enjoyment and take refuge in these three: namely, the knowledge of truth, [the practice of yoga, and the company of the wise]."
The dissolution of the mind and the effacement of *vāsanās* (Ibid.):
"Human effort" (*pauruṣo yatnaḥ*) is persistence in the form of such enthusiasm as, "By whatever means possible, I shall certainly accomplish this.

"Discrimination" (*viveka*) is the determination reached through analysis—that the means for the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) consists of hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, while [the means] for the destruction of the mind...

Yoga consists in the production of counter-vāsanās to the destruction of vāsanās. It is said to be "far off" because, if even a slight desire for enjoyment were admitted, its excessive proliferation would be unavoidable according to the maxim: "Like a fire fed with ghee, it only increases all the more" (Manu Smṛti 2.94).
*Pauruṣaḥ yatnaḥ* (determined effort) means "I must certainly accomplish this by some means or other"— such persistence in the form of enthusiasm. *Vivekaḥ* (discrimination).
It means arriving at a conclusion after distinguishing and sorting out matters: namely, that the hearing (study) of the scriptures and so forth are the means to the knowledge of reality.
Yoga is the means for the dissolution of the mind; the cultivation of contrary impressions is the means for the eradication of latent tendencies. Desire for...
If enjoyment is permitted even in the slightest degree,
it will know no bounds, just as the sage Manu has said: "Just as a fire continues to grow larger..."
"As long as it is nourished with clarified butter" (Manu-smṛti 2.94)— [this practice] should therefore be abandoned from afar;
that is why it is said, "from afar."

Now, it may be objected that in the previous section a distinction was described wherein the fruit of the renunciation of the seeker (*vividiṣā-saṃnyāsa*) is the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*), while the fruit of the renunciation of the knower (*vidvat-saṃnyāsa*) is liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*); and this being so, it would appear that one must first accomplish the knowledge of reality and only afterwards, having performed the renunciation of the knower,
effect the destruction of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and mental fluctuations (*mano-vṛtti*) which constitute bondage for oneself while living.
If it is argued that there is a contradiction between what precedes and what follows because, in this context, the simultaneous practice of the knowledge of reality and so forth is enjoined—
whereas previously, such an arrangement was described as being based on the fact that the knowledge of reality is the result [of yoga]— then [the response follows].

the renunciation of the seeker (*pārivrājya*), and *jīvanmukti*— the result of the renunciation of the knower (*vidvat-saṃnyāsa*). If that is the case, then one should first attain knowledge and subsequently take up *vidvat-saṃnyāsa*.
It appears that one should strive, while still alive, to liberate oneself from the bonds of *vāsanā* and mental states by effecting their destruction; however, [now] knowledge and the rest—
Since the means are being prescribed for simultaneous practice,
there is a contradiction between the former and the latter injunctions. Jīvan-mukti-viveka.
This is not a fault, because this systematic arrangement is logically tenable.

In the case of the seeker-renunciant (*vividiṣā-saṃnyāsī*), true knowledge (*tattvajñāna*) is primary while the dissolution of the mind (*manonāśa*) and the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*) are secondary;
for the knower-renunciant (*vidvat-saṃnyāsī*), however, it is the reverse. Therefore, the simultaneous practice of both is not contradictory in either case. Nor is there...
It should not be suspected that for one who has achieved their purpose through the mere arising of the knowledge of reality, what further use is there for the exertion of subsequent practice;
for this will be refuted by the demonstration of the purpose of liberation while living (jīvanmukti).
Reply: There is no harm in this, as their compatibility can be demonstrated.
from the standpoint of their mutual relationship as primary and secondary. For the seeker, the knowledge of Truth is essential, as is the dissolution of the mind and...
The obliteration of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*) is secondary;
for the Knower (*jñānin*), it is exactly the reverse. Thus, there is no contradiction in the simultaneous practice of these three.
This applies to both cases.
It cannot be doubted that some purpose will be served by the subsequent effort to practice the means once [the result] has already been attained.
One has accomplished everything through the attainment of supreme knowledge alone; for we shall demonstrate its utility for the sake of *jīvanmukti*, and thereby—
Settle this doubt:

Is it not the case that for a renunciant who has realized the Truth (*vidvatsaṃnyāsin*), since the performance of means such as hearing (*śravaṇa*) for the sake of knowledge is futile, and since knowledge— which by its very nature cannot be performed, not performed, or performed otherwise— is not something to be practiced, there can be no subsequent practice even if it were merely subordinate?
If it is asked, "Of what nature is this?", [the response is:
Objection: For the *vidvatsaṃnyāsin*, the practice of study and so forth—the means to knowledge—is futile, and the knowledge...
Virtue itself is beyond the scope of action, for no one can create it, destroy it, or alter it; thus, even if its subordinate status were conceded, of what nature would it be?

What is the subsequent practice? We say it is the repeated recollection of reality by whatever means possible. And such a practice is demonstrated in the *Līlopākhyāna* (the sixth book of the *Laghu-yogavāsiṣṭha*):
Answer: We reply that the Truth should be recollected by whatever means, again and again. This practice has been described in the episode of Līlā as follows:
The wise know that the practice of knowledge consists of reflecting upon that, speaking of that, mutually awakening one another to that, and being solely intent upon that. 108.
“Reflecting upon that, conversing about that, mutually instructing one another in that, and being entirely devoted to that—
this, the wise know, is the practice of knowledge.”

"From the very beginning of creation, the visible world was never produced; it does not exist at all, always. To understand that 'this is the world' and 'this is I' [are unreal] is what the supreme ones call the practice of awakening. (Laghu-Yoga-Vāsistha 6.108).
“This manifest world was not created at the beginning of creation, nor was I created; neither this world nor ‘I’ has ever existed— this the wise know to be the supreme practice.”
...of knowledge" (Ibid. 6.111).

The practice of the dissolution of the mind (*manonāśa*) and the effacement of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*) are also shown in that very same place: [the practice of] the dissolution of the mind and the effacement of latent impressions.

The removal of *vāsanā* is also described in that same episode as follows: "Those who strive by means of reasoning and scriptures for the attainment of the absolute non-existence of both the knower and the object known, they are established therein as practitioners" (110).
Those who, through the practice of yoga and study of the scriptures, seek to realize that both the knower and the known are absolutely non-existent, are practicing [the path].
"The dissolution of the mind" (Ibid. 6.110):
the realization of the falsity of both the knower and the known is the attainment of non-existence; the non-perception even of its own nature is the attainment of absolute non-existence.
This "yukti" is yoga; this is the practice of the dissolution of the mind.
The comprehension of the unreality of the knower and the known is called the attainment of non-existence (*abhāvasampattiḥ*). When these two— the knower and the known— ...
Not even perceived in their own forms— it is called the attainment of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāvasampatti*). — *Jīvanmuktiviveka*
Yoga is *yuktiḥ*, the practice of concentration or union with the Supreme Spirit; this is the practice of the dissolution of the mind.
"Through the realization that the perceptible world is impossible [in ultimate reality], when passion, aversion, and the like have become attenuated,
that fresh delight which arises is called the practice of Brahman.
This is the practice of the dissolution of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣayābhyāsa*).
“When the non-existence of phenomena is realized, attachment, aversion, and the like become attenuated, and then a new kind of repose is experienced, which is called”
"the practice of Brahman" (Ibid. 28.112). This is the practice of the effacement of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
When these three practices are perceived in their general form, it is not possible to distinguish between their primary and secondary status.
If this is argued:
[Objection] These three practices appear identical in their importance, and one is unable to distinguish between them.

[It may be argued that] it is unclear which [of the two] occupies the primary position and which the subordinate state. This is not so, because they can be distinguished according to their respective purposes for a person seeking liberation (mumukṣu).

The two purposes are liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) and liberation after death (*videhamukti*). For this very reason, it is stated in the Śruti: "Being already liberated, he is liberated again" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.2.1). In that regard, for a person who is alive, liberation results from divine endowment (*daivī saṃpat*), while bondage results from demonic endowment (*āsurī saṃpat*). And this was declared by the Blessed One in the sixteenth chapter: "The divine endowment leads to liberation; the demonic leads to bondage."
"...is considered [to be the true devotee]. (Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā 16.5).
Response: Not so. They may be distinguished according to necessity. A person seeking liberation requires...
Both *jīvanmukti* (liberation while living) and *videhamukti* (liberation after death). Regarding this, the *Śruti* states:
"First liberated from ignorance while still living, he is liberated again upon disembodiment"—*vimuktaśca vimucyate*.
(Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.2.1) A man, while still alive, attains liberation through the Divine.
One remains bound by divine endowments and demonic treasures; this was explained by the Blessed Lord in the sixteenth chapter of the *Gītā* as follows: "The divine treasures..."
"are considered to lead to liberation, while the demonic leads to bondage" (Bhagavad Gītā 16.5).
These two types of wealth are also described in that very same place:
Fearlessness, purity of being, steadfastness in the yoga of knowledge, charity, self-restraint, sacrifice, study of the scriptures, austerity, and uprightness; 1.
In that same chapter, those two kinds of qualities are described as follows:
"Fearlessness, purity of mind, steadfastness in knowledge..."
Self-control, concentration, charity, restraint, sacrifice,
study of the scriptures, austerity, and uprightness;
non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, renunciation, tranquility, absence of malice;
Compassion toward living beings, freedom from greed, gentleness, modesty, and lack of fickleness. ||2||
Non-violence, truth, freedom from anger, renunciation, tranquility, aversion to fault-finding, compassion for living beings,
freedom from covetousness, gentleness, modesty, and absence [of greed].
“O Bhārata, vigor, forgiveness, fortitude, purity, non-malice, and lack of excessive pride— these belong to one born with the divine fortune. (3)
"Energy, forgiveness, fortitude, purity, freedom from malice and excessive pride— these, O Bhārata, are the qualities of one born with a divine nature."
(Bhagavad Gītā 16.1, 2, 3); from the *Jīvan-mukti-viveka*:
"Hypocrisy, arrogance, self-conceit, anger, harshness, and ignorance—these, O Pārtha, belong to one born with an asuric nature. (4) Thus it is said.
“Hypocrisy, arrogance, self-conceit, wrath, as well as harshness and ignorance— these, O Pārtha, are the qualities of one who is born with a demonic nature.”
(Bhagavad Gītā 16.4).

Furthermore, until the end of the chapter, the demonic nature (*āsura-saṃpat*) is elaborated upon. Therein, the demonic nature—which is contrary to the scriptures, innate, and characterized by evil tendencies—is contrasted with the divine nature (*daiva-saṃpat*), which is in accordance with the scriptures, achieved through human effort, and characterized by virtuous tendencies.

When [the impressions] have perished, liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) occurs. Just as the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*), the dissolution of the mind (*manonāśa*) is also heard in scripture to be a cause of liberation while living.
The demonic qualities are further described until the end of the chapter. Therein, it is indicated that *jīvanmukti*...

The time when the evil impressions of the unscriptural, innate demonic qualities are neutralized by the good impressions of the scriptural divine qualities obtainable through [association with] persons...
There is no effort required. Just as the eradication of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is a cause for liberation while living, so too is the dissolution of the mind; thus says the Śruti:
"The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings; attached to sense objects, it leads to bondage; free from sense objects, it is known to lead to liberation. (2)

“It is said that the mind alone is the cause of a person’s bondage and liberation; [the mind] attached to the objects of the senses leads to bondage, while [when it is] free from such [attachment], it leads to liberation.”
Attachment leads to liberation (*Amṛtabindu* or *Brahmabindu Upaniṣad* 1.2–5):
"Since the liberation of this mind, when it is free from objects, is desired..."
Therefore, one who seeks liberation should constantly make the mind free from objects. 3.
Therefore, the seeker of liberation should strive to keep the mind perpetually free from the objects of the senses; for,
as prescribed, the mind thus liberated attains [the goal].
When the mind, with its attachment to objects cast aside, is completely restrained within the heart and attains the state of *unmanī*, that is the supreme state. (Ibid., 3.90) (4)
When the mind, free from attachment to sensory objects,
comes to rest within the heart (the seat of the mind) and enters the state of formlessness (cessation), [it attains liberation].

When the mind, which is the instrument of deliberation, is thus restrained, then that Supreme State is attained. "It should be restrained only so long until it reaches dissolution within the heart. (Ibid. 4)
"This is both knowledge and liberation; the rest is merely the elaboration of the book. (Amṛtabindūpaniṣad 2.5)
“The mind should be held in that state until it dissolves in the heart (that is, until it is completely freed from its transformations). This is knowledge, and this is also liberation.”
"Rest" (scriptural discourse) is merely dwelling upon that in detail (Ibid. 5).
Bondage is of two kinds: intense and mild. Among these, [the latter] is intense because the demonic endowment is a direct cause of affliction.

Bondage: The mere perception of duality, however, is a mild bondage because it is not inherently of the nature of affliction and because it gives rise to the demonic endowment (*āsura-sampat*). Among these, through the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā-kṣaya*), only intense bondage is removed; but through the dissolution of the mind (*manonāśa*), both are removed. If it is argued, "In that case, the dissolution of the mind alone is sufficient, and the destruction of latent impressions is useless," the answer is no; for there remains the powerful *prārabdha* karma which is the cause of experience.

When the mind has been withdrawn [from its objects], the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are for the purpose of removing intense bondage, since enjoyment can still occur even through mild bondage. The *tāmasa* fluctuations constitute intense bondage; the two types of fluctuations, *sāttvika* and *rājasa*, constitute mild bondage.
And this is illustrated in the passage from the *Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā* (2.56): "One whose mind is unperturbed amidst sorrows, and who is free from longing amidst pleasures..."
This has been made clear.
Bondage is of two kinds: intense and moderate. Among these, the demonic endowment is the direct cause of...
Sorrow is the strong bondage. Since the perception of duality alone is not miserable in itself, and furthermore because it is the generator of demonic qualities, it is treated [as such].
By the eradication of the latent impressions (*vāsanās*), only the intense bondage is removed;
however, [the reading] "it is turned back" (*nivartyate iti vā pāṭhaḥ*) indicates that even moderate bondage is removed.
By [the eradication of the latent impressions], only the intense bondage is removed, but by...
When the dissolution of the mind occurs, both of these are removed.
It might then be argued that since the dissolution of the mind is sufficient in itself, the elimination of the latent predispositions (anuśaya) is unnecessary.
[Such] sessions are pointless. But this is not so, because when the powerful *prārabdha*— which is the cause for the experience of pleasure or pain— brings the mind into operation, then...
The eradication of latent impressions is required to remove strong bondage; the experience [of pleasure or pain] may be brought about by moderate bondage.
Furthermore, all mental transformations caused by the quality of tamas are to be known as strong bondage; and...
Transformations caused by the *sattva* and *rajas* qualities are to be known as moderate bondage. This was explained while discussing the one "whose mind is not shaken."
"...who is unperturbed by adversity and does not hanker after happiness" (Bhagavadgītā 2.56).

This being the case, since a mild bondage is accepted [as possible], and since intense bondage ceases only through the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), [the effort for liberation] would be useless.
If it is argued that this refers to the destruction of the mind (*manonāśa*),
the objection is: if it is thus that moderate bondage is to be accepted and strong bondage can be removed [by it],...

If it is argued that there is no need for the dissolution of the mind once the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) alone have been obliterated, we say no; for [the dissolution] serves as a remedy against those inevitable experiences brought about by weak *prārabdha* karma. Such experience...
Intending to show that [suffering] can be averted by remedial measures, they say:
"If there were a remedy for those experiences that are inevitable,
then Nala, Rāma, and Yudhiṣṭhira would not have been stained by sufferings."
(From the *Pañcadaśī*, 7.156).
Response: It cannot be said thus, because of the unavoidable experience of pleasure and pain brought about by a weak [karma].
Prārabdha is countered by the dissolution of the mind.
Keeping in mind that such experience can be removed through counteraction, it is said as follows:
"If it had been possible to prevent the inevitable experience [of pleasure and pain], then Nala, Rāma, and Yudhiṣṭhira would never have been struck by affliction. (Pañca)

Thus, in this way, with respect to liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*) and the dissolution of the mind (*manonāśa*) are primary because they are the direct means (*sākṣātsādhana*); however, the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is secondary because it is mediated by the production of both [the former]. That the knowledge of reality is the cause for the destruction of latent impressions—
It is heard many times in the Śruti:
"Having known the God, there is the falling away of all fetters" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.11).
Thus, the effacement of the latent impressions and...
The dissolution of the mind is essential, as it is the direct means to *jīvanmukti*; since the knowledge of Truth is an indirect cause by producing these two, it is secondary.
It has been stated many times in the Śruti that knowledge is the cause of the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanās):
"When God is known, all fetters fall away" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad).
"Having realized the Divine through the attainment of yoga directed toward the self, the wise man abandons both joy and sorrow" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.12).
"The wise man leaves behind both joy and sorrow" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.12);
"The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.3).
"He who knows the Self crosses over sorrow" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.3);
"What delusion, what sorrow can there be for him who perceives oneness? (Īśa Upaniṣad 7).

"Then what delusion and what sorrow can there be for him who perceives oneness? (Iṣā Upaniṣad 7). "Having known God, one is released from all fetters. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.9) *Jīvan-mukti-viveka* (The Discrimination of Liberation while Living).
(Svetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.1.8): "By knowing God, one is released from all fetters. (Svetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.1.8).

Furthermore, that the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is the cause for the dissolution of the mind is established by the *Śruti*. With reference to the state of *vidyā* (enlightenment), this is heard in such passages as:
"But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? By what and whom should he smell? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15).
The knowledge of Reality is also the cause of the dissolution of the mind, as is evident from the Śrutis. Referring to the state of realization, the Śruti says: "But when..."
"Verily, when everything has become one's very Self, then by what and whom should one see? Then by what and whom should one smell? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15)

And the teacher Gauḍapāda said: "When, through the realization of the reality of the Self, one no longer forms volitional constructions, one then attains the state of mindlessness; in the absence of an object to be grasped, there is no grasping."
Thus it is stated in the Māṇḍūkya-kārikā (3.32).
The teacher Gauḍapāda also says this:
"When the mind, having realized the knowledge that the Self alone is real, is freed from conceptual constructions, therefore it..."
"When one does not cognize anything due to the absence of objects to be cognized, then it ceases to be the mind" (Māṇḍūkya Kārikā 3.32).

Just as the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*) and the dissolution of the mind (*manonāśa*) are the means for liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), knowledge (*jñāna*) is primary because it is the direct means for liberation after death (*videhamukti*).
"From knowledge alone, however, is isolation attained, by which one is liberated," according to the Smṛti;
for the effacement of latent impressions and the dissolution of the mind are the primary causes of *jīvanmukti*.
That knowledge, being the direct means for attaining *videhamukti*, is considered the primary cause. Thus says the *Smṛti*:

The venerable teacher Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda adopted the reading *ātmasatyānubodhena* [from knowledge of the reality of the Self]. (Source: *Jīvanmuktiviveka*, "Through knowledge alone is *kaivalya*—the absolute unity of the spirit—realized, and by means of that, one is liberated.")
(untraced).

Kaivalya is the state of the absolute Self (ātman), which is the condition of being devoid of the body and so forth. And that is attained through knowledge alone, because the state of possessing a body is imagined by ignorance (ajñāna) and is therefore removable by knowledge alone. As for the phrase "by which one is liberated," its meaning is: by that state of isolation (*kevalatva*) attained through knowledge, one is liberated from all bondage.

Bondage is of many kinds, as it is designated by various terms here and there in the scriptures, such as the knot of ignorance (*avidyā-granthi*), non-Brahmanhood, the knot of the heart (*hṛdaya-granthi*), doubt, actions, lack of fulfillment of all desires, death, and rebirth. The fruit of knowledge.
Now, by this same logic, the non-commencement of future bodies is also not the fruit of knowledge. For instance: is the mere non-commencement itself the fruit?
What, then, is that preservation? It cannot be the first [option], because, being of the nature of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), it is established as beginningless.
Nor can it be the second.

For the preservation of the prior non-existence of the commencement of a future body is established simply by the cessation of the causal complex consisting of uncommenced karma and form; nor is that cessation itself the fruit [of knowledge], because the cessation of ignorance alone is the fruit of knowledge.
Objection: One might argue in the same manner...
That the non-commencement of the future body is likewise not the effect of knowledge. For instance: whether this non-commencement is the effect or the maintenance of that [body].
Regarding "non-commencement": the first position cannot be maintained because this absence of the commencement of the future body is eternally present; that is, this antecedent non-existence—
Existence has no beginning. Nor is the second position tenable,
because through the dissolution of the cause in the form of latent karma alone, the prior non-existence of the beginning [of existence] [is established].
The future body can be maintained. Furthermore, the beginninglessness of the future body cannot be the result of knowledge,
because the cessation of ignorance alone is the result of knowledge.

This is not a fault, because the fact that the non-commencement of future births and so forth are the fruits of knowledge (*vidyā*) is established by authoritative means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*). The scriptural passages cited therein, such as "from which one is not born again" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.8), are the authority for this. Nor is it the case that...

There is a contradiction [in your position] according to the principle that "knowledge is the remover of ignorance alone," because the Pañcapādikācāryas intended by the term "ignorance" (ajñāna) such things as non-Brahmanhood, which are necessarily co-existent with ignorance. Otherwise, [there would be no] experience...

There is no contradiction. For the cessation of non-Brahmanhood and so forth is indeed experienced just like the cessation of ignorance. Therefore, liberation while in the body (*videhamukti*), characterized by the absence of a future body, is simultaneous with knowledge. And thus the word of Yājñavalkya is heard in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* (4.2.4): "O Janaka, you have indeed attained fearlessness," and "This much, my dear..."

And [it is said], "He indeed becomes immortal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15). In another Śruti as well: "Knowing Him thus, one becomes immortal here" (Nṛsiṃhapūrvatāpanī Upaniṣad 1.6; Puruṣasūkta, Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.90.12).
If, even when the knowledge of reality has arisen, liberation from the body—which is its fruit—were not to occur at that time, but only at a later time...

If that were the case, then some kind of *apūrva* (unseen potency) produced by knowledge would have to be postulated, as in the case of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice and others; and thus the science of knowledge (*jñāna-śāstra*) would be subsumed within the science of ritual action (*karma-śāstra*) alone. Now, if it is argued that—like fire obstructed by mantras and so forth—knowledge, being obstructed by *prārabdha* (commenced karma), will grant liberation from the body (*videhamukti*) at a later time, this is not so, because there is no contradiction. For [the state we] maintain is not...

The liberation while disembodied (videhamukti), characterized by the absolute non-existence of future bodies, is not contradicted by the prārabdha karma which sustains only the present body, such that it would be obstructed.
Reply: There is no harm in this, because the non-beginning...
The cessation of future birth and so forth is the fruit of knowledge; it has been described thus in the scriptures:
"From which he is not born again" (Katha Upaniṣad 1.3.8).
and other such cited *śruti* passages serve as testimony.
Furthermore, the theory of the *Pañcapādikā*— that "knowledge alone destroys ignorance"— is not contradicted, insofar as...
The concomitants of ignorance, such as the notion of non-self and so forth, are implied by the term "ignorance";
otherwise, it would contradict experience. The destruction—
The cessation of notions such as "non-self" and the like is experienced simultaneously with the destruction of ignorance.
Therefore, *videhamukti* consists in the non-existence of—
The future body is attained simultaneously with knowledge.
In this regard, the words of Yājñavalkya are found in the Śruti as follows: "Truly, O Janaka, you have reached [the state of]..."
"there is no fear from anything" (Br. Up. 4.2.4), and "Such indeed, O Maitreyī, is the immortal life" (Br. Up. 4.5.15). In other Śrutis as well it is said:
"Knowing him thus, one becomes immortal even here."
"the body" (Nṛsiṃha Pūrva-tāpanī Upaniṣad 1.6).
If, upon the arising of the knowledge [of Brahman], liberation from the body (videhamukti) does not subsequently occur as its result, and...
If it occurs subsequently, then an *apūrva*— merit produced by knowledge—
is to be postulated, as in the case of sacrifices such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and others; thus, the practice of knowledge [is required].
will become merely a part of the ritualistic discipline (*vidhi*).
If it is suggested that knowledge is temporarily neutralized by *prārabdha-karma*— the karma that has already begun to bear fruit—

One might argue that this disembodied liberation (videhamukti) is later on effective, just as a fire neutralized by a mantra becomes effective once the mantra's influence has passed. We say this cannot be,
because there is no such contradiction.
According to our view, videhamukti—
characterized by the absolute non-existence of a future body— is not obstructed by *prārabdha* karma, which maintains [the present body].
Since only the existing body remains, there is no question of neutralizing the effect of knowledge.
Furthermore, how could knowledge—being momentary and thus itself non-existent at a later time—bestow liberation? [This would require] another knowledge...
If it is argued that the characteristic of the final direct realization will arise, we say no;
for there is an absence of means.

Since the manifestation of the entire world—including the teacher, the scriptures, the body, the senses, and so forth—ceases simultaneously with the cessation of the obstructing *prārabdha* karma, what need is there for a further means?

If you ask, "What then is the meaning of this scriptural passage, 'And finally, at the end, there is the cessation of the entire illusion' (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.10)?"— the meaning is simply that, at the conclusion of the prārabdha [karma], due to the absence of its cause, there is the cessation of all effects such as the body, senses, and so forth. Therefore, the liberation from the body (videhamukti) characterized by the absence of the present body is indeed attained.
"Let it be later," meaning after the fall of the body; however, that which is desired by us occurs simultaneously with knowledge.
With this very intention, the venerable Śeṣa said:
"Whether in a sacred place or in the house of a dog-cooker, even if one has lost consciousness while abandoning the body..."
"Released simultaneously with [the arising of] knowledge, he whose sorrow is destroyed attains isolation (*kaivalya*). (Paramārthasāra 81). Furthermore, how could momentary knowledge...

If [the means] itself ceases to exist subsequently, how can it bring about liberation at a later time? If it is suggested that another cognition in the form of final realization will arise, we reply that this is impossible. *Jīvanmuktiviveka*
Since no other means remain, with the cessation of the obstructive *prārabdha*, the entire world of appearance—
including the teacher, the scriptures, the body, and the senses— [comes to an end].
If [the object] ceases to exist in such a manner, what could serve as the means for that final cognition?
Nor can it be argued that, in this context, then...
This should be the meaning of the Śruti text: "In the end, there is a complete cessation from the illusion of the world" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.10).
The meaning is this: when the *ārabdhakarma* (projected karma) is exhausted,
all its effects— consisting of the body, the sense organs, and so forth— cease to exist, for an effect can never persist without its cause.

Therefore, let the *videhamukti* consisting in the absence of the existing body be accepted by you as occurring after the cessation of that existing body; however, the one we accept occurs simultaneously.
With this very idea in mind,
the Lord Śeṣa says as follows: "He who has been liberated simultaneously with the arising..."
One who possesses knowledge and is free from sorrow attains the state of the absolute existence of the Self, whether he casts off his body in a sacred pilgrimage site or in the house of a *caṇḍāla*.

"with complete amnesia"—(Paramārthasāra 81). Therefore, it is logically established that the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), which is the direct means to disembodied liberation (*videhamukti*), holds primacy. Since the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*) and the dissolution of the mind (*manonāśa*) are mediated by being means to knowledge, they possess a secondary status. [This applies] to that which effects the destruction of demonic tendencies (*āsuravāsanā*).

The fact that the latent impressions of divine devotion (*daivavāsanā*) serve as a means to knowledge is found in both the *Śruti* and the *Smṛti*. The *Śruti* states: "Having become calm, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and concentrated, one should see the Self in the very Self" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.4.23).
Thus, regarding the attainment of liberation while in the body (*videhamukti*), the superiority [of this means] is established.
The knowledge of reality, which is the direct means [to videhamukti], is established. The effacement of latent impressions and the dissolution of the mind, which are...
The means to knowledge occupy a subordinate position.
Those divine impressions which destroy demonic impressions are the means to knowledge; this is found in the Śrutis.
Smṛti: “Therefore, he who knows it thus,
having become calm, self-controlled, withdrawn within himself, patient, and concentrated, should behold the Self in his own self.”
(Brhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.23; the original reading is ‘paśyati’, meaning ‘he sees’).
There is also a Smṛti [text]:
Humility, unpretentiousness, non-violence, forbearance, uprightness,
service to the teacher, purity, steadfastness, and self-restraint.
Detachment from the objects of the senses, as well as the absence of egoism,
and the contemplation of the defects of birth, death, old age, disease, and suffering.
(Bhagavadgītā 13.8, 9) ||
In the Smṛti also it is said thus: "Humility, lack of pretension, non-violence, forbearance, uprightness, service to the teacher, purity, steadfastness..."
steadfastness and self-control;
indifference toward the objects of the senses, as well as the absence of egoism; and reflection upon the evils of birth, death, and old age.
disease, and pain (BG 13.8, 9); ‘Non-attachment, absence of clinging to children, wife, home, and so forth,
and constant equanimity of mind amidst the occurrence of the desirable and the undesirable’ (10).
‘Non-attachment and non-identification of the self with son, wife, home, and so forth; and constant equanimity amidst desirable and undesirable occurrences.’
(As stated in the same work, 13.10):
"And unwavering devotion to Me through the yoga of exclusive concentration;
resorting to solitary places; and a lack of delight in the assembly of worldly people. (11)
“Unwavering devotion to Me through the yoga of non-separation, resorting to secluded places, and a lack of relish for the company of people.”— *Jīvan-mukti-viveka*
"Constancy in the knowledge of the Self and the perception of the goal of the knowledge of reality—this is declared to be knowledge;
that which is contrary to this is ignorance.
"Steadfastness in the knowledge of the Self and comprehension of the ultimate goal of the knowledge of Truth— this is declared to be knowledge, and its opposite is ignorance."
(Bhagavadgītā 13.11–12).

Attachment (*abhiṣvaṅga*) is the notion of "I" with respect to that which is other [than the Self]. By the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) "that by which something is known," it means the instrument of knowledge (*jñānasādhana*).
That even the dissolution of the mind (*manonāśa*) is an instrument of knowledge is well-established in the Śruti and Smṛti: "Then he beholds Him, the partless..."

The Śruti says: "Meditating" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.8), and also: "Having realized the Divine through the attainment of the yoga of the inner self, the wise man abandons both joy and sorrow" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.12). The meaning is that by attaining samādhi upon the inner Self, one knows the Divine.

The identification of one’s own ego with another is called self-identification. Regarding the term *jñāna*—knowledge—in the passage cited above (*etajjñānam iti proktam*), it is derived as follows: [text continues]
The sense of "known by this" (*jñāyate anena*) means that which leads to knowledge.
The dissolution of the mind is also accepted as such a means.
"Then indeed, through meditation, he beholds Him who is partless"—thus it is stated in the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*.
And likewise in the *Katha Upaniṣad*: "The wise man..."
"By attaining concentration on the Self, one realizes God and leaves behind both joy and sorrow" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.12). The latter phrase (*adhyātmayogādhigamena*) means:
"By knowing God through the attainment of concentration on one’s essential Self—
those who are sleepless, have conquered their breath, are contented, and have restrained their senses. (106) [Bhagavad Gītā 6.13]
"Salutation to that Self of Knowledge, whom those who practice yoga behold as light.
(Mahābhārata, Śāntiparvan, Rājadharma 47.35)
Thus says the Smṛti:
"The yogis who have restrained their breath and..."
"whose senses are satisfied and who are no longer asleep, and through meditation behold that splendor which is absolute intelligence— to that, salutations! (Mahābhārata)
Thus,

it is established that among these three— knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) and the others— their status as primary or subordinate is determined by whether they result in liberation while living (jīvanmukti) or disembodied liberation (videhamukti).
Thus, in this manner, the mutual primary and secondary importance of the knowledge of Truth and the other factors is determined according to the requirements of *videhamukti*.

Regarding *jīvanmukti*, that is, for one seeking liberation while living, the destruction of the mind (*manonāśa*) and the exhaustion of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*) are the primary means; whereas for *videhamukti*, knowledge is the primary means.

Now, regarding these [virtues] accomplished by one who has renounced with the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā-saṃnyāsin*): do they merely persist after the renunciation of the knower (*vidvat-saṃnyāsa*), or is a renewed effort at their accomplishment required? It cannot be the first, because if the other two were established without effort—just like the knowledge of reality—it would follow that they lack the primary importance and respect accorded to them. Nor can it be the second, because if knowledge also depended on effort, just like the other two, [the distinction between them would vanish].
Because there would otherwise follow the undesirable consequence of the absence of indifference, which is necessitated by the fact that [the self] is subordinate to [the means].
Here, a doubt might arise as to whether a *vividiṣā-saṃnyāsin*, having accomplished these three means, upon reaching the stage...
In the case of *vidvat-saṃnyāsa*, is it necessary for him to strive anew for their acquisition,
or do they continue to exist? If they continue to survive, then like knowledge (*jñāna*), the other two [perfections]— *vairāgya* and *aiśvarya*— [would likewise persist].

The ‘Critical Edition’ reading is *sattvasthā*; for *santuṣṭāḥ* and *yogātmane*, it reads *vidyātmane*. In the *Jīvanmukti-viveka*, the state of being effortlessly available is not considered the primary goal. The other alternative is also untenable. If...
If knowledge were subjected to fresh effort in the same way as the other two,
it would not be regarded as subordinate. In that regard, the object of meditation—
If it were to proceed after having performed [the action],

then this would not be a fault, because it is accepted that for the other two [results], there is merely the persistence of knowledge while the effort is required for their accomplishment; and thus...
Indeed—the one qualified for knowledge is of two kinds: one who has performed meditation (*kṛtopāsti*) and one who has not performed meditation (*akṛtopāsti*).
If [the latter] performs meditation until it culminates in direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), then [he becomes qualified for knowledge].

When the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*) and the dissolution of the mind (*manonāśa*) have become exceedingly firm, renunciation for the knower (*vidvatsaṃnyāsa*) and liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) are accomplished spontaneously after the dawn of knowledge. Such a person alone is the primary candidate for knowledge intended by the scriptures. Consequently, because they are presented together in the scriptures with respect to him, renunciation for the knower and renunciation out of desire for knowledge (*vividiṣāsaṃnyāsa*), though distinct in their essential nature, appear to be conflated.

[The two appear]. However, those of the present day generally engage in knowledge (vidyā) impulsively out of mere curiosity, without having performed any prior spiritual practice (upāsti). They seek to achieve the temporary dissolution of latent impressions (vāsanākṣaya) and the destruction of the mind (manonāśa), and they carry out hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (śravaṇa-manana-nididhyāsana). Through these, when firmly practiced, ignorance, doubt, and error are dispelled.

The knowledge of reality arises perfectly. Because there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) for that arisen knowledge, and because there is no cause for the re-emergence of ignorance once it has ceased, that knowledge possesses no weakness. However, the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*) and the dissolution of the mind (*manonāśa*) do not occur due to the absence of firm practice, as [the mind] is driven by that which bestows experience.
And because it is being afflicted from time to time by prārabdha karma.
They cease instantaneously, like a lamp in a place exposed to the wind. And so Vasiṣṭha says:
[Reply: There is no harm; we admit that knowledge will continue to exist, while the other two are to be striven for.
For example: the disciple qualified for knowledge is of two kinds—
one who has undergone the discipline of worship and another who has not yet done so.
If one performs worship until he has attained the vision of his ideal and then endeavors toward knowledge, his dissolution of the mind and effacement of the latent impressions will [be accomplished].
Be stronger— that is, possess superior strength—
by virtue of which his *vidvatsaṃnyāsa* and *jīvanmukti* will occur spontaneously immediately after the dawn of knowledge. The scriptures testify to this.

Recognize him as the most excellent student fit for knowledge. For such students, although *vidvatsaṃnyāsa* and *vividiṣāsaṃnyāsa* are distinctly different, they have been mentioned together in [the scriptures].
Thus, the scriptures appear to be confused.
Yet, most modern students, even without prior practice of meditation, suddenly attempt to attain [realization] out of mere curiosity.
They achieve the attenuation of latent tendencies and the temporary dissolution of the mind. Furthermore,
by means of that, they also accomplish study, reflection, and meditation.
Through the repeated and vigorous practice of Vedānta, ignorance, doubt, and contrary notions are destroyed, whereby the knowledge of Reality arises perfectly. In...
In the absence of any counteractive cause to that knowledge,
and in the absence of any cause for the previously destroyed ignorance to reappear, the knowledge remains firmly established.

However, in the absence of rigorous practice and due to being influenced from time to time by the ripening operative karma (*prārabdha-karma*), *manonāśa* (the dissolution of the mind) and *vāsanākṣaya* (the destruction of latent impressions) are [interrupted].
It is extinguished just like a lamp by a gust of wind.
Vasiṣṭha also said this:
"Indeed, this [path] is considered more difficult than all previous efforts."
"The abandonment of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is more difficult to accomplish than even uprooting Mount Sumeru" (Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 28.109).
Among the efforts previously mentioned, this one is considered...
It is far more difficult to be red. The renunciation of desires is a task even harder than uprooting Mount Sumeru— so says Arjuna.
"For the mind, O Kṛṣṇa, is restless, turbulent, powerful, and obstinate;
I consider its restraint to be as difficult as that of the wind" (Bhagavadgītā 6.34).
And Arjuna also spoke thus regarding the destruction of the mind: "The mind, O Kṛṣṇa, is indeed restless, turbulent, powerful, and obstinate; I consider its control to be exceedingly difficult."

"like that of the wind" (BG 6.34). Therefore, it is established that for contemporary *vidvat-sannyāsins*, there is merely the persistence of knowledge; however, the dissolution of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*) and the destruction of the mind (*manonāśa*) must be accomplished through effort.
Thus, it is maintained that for the *vidvatsannyāsins* of the present day,
only knowledge persists, whereas the dissolution of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*) and the destruction of the mind (*manonāśa*) must be accomplished through effort.
If it is asked, "What indeed is this latent impression (*vāsanā*) for the destruction of which one must strive?", Vasiṣṭha describes its nature as follows:
"It is that which, through intense contemplation, has abandoned all consideration of what precedes and what follows."
The grasping of an object is proclaimed to be that which is called "latent impression" (vāsanā). ||48||
O mighty-armed one, that very [state] which has been cultivated by oneself through intense spiritual urgency quickly becomes his, as all other memories fade away. (49)
For a person of such a nature, rendered helpless by latent impressions (vāsanā), becomes utterly deluded when he perceives this very thing and thinks, "This is a real entity. (50)
"Due to the helplessness caused by the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it abandons its true nature;
one with faulty vision sees everything as deluded, like one under the influence of intoxication.
(Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 28.48–51).
But what is this latent impression (*vāsanā*) for the eradication of which effort must be exerted? The nature of *vāsanā* is described by Vasiṣṭha as follows:
“The perception of objects through intense reflection, having abandoned even the consideration of their priority or posteriority (that is,
having abandoned all hesitation), is described as [perception].”
Regarding *vāsanā* (LY V28.48):
"By that very powerful imagination, whatever he conceives himself to be, he immediately becomes that [being], O mighty-armed one."
Even forgetting everything else (ibid.
28.49)— such a man, thus deluded and completely enslaved by *vāsanā*, regards as real whatever he perceives.
“He who is subdued by the influence of *vāsanā* cannot grasp the true nature of things; whatever he sees, [he perceives only through that lens].”
"sees falsely, just like a person under the influence of an intoxicant" (ibid. 28.51).
And herein, regarding the various local customs, family traditions, and linguistic differences, as well as the corrupt and correct words occurring therein, [there is] for living beings—

*Abhiniveśa* (clinging) is an example in general. However, having stated its specific divisions, we shall provide examples later. With reference to the aforementioned *vāsanā*, it is heard in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*: "As is one's desire (*kāma*), so is one's resolve (*kratu*); as is one's resolve, so is the action (*karman*) one performs; and whatever action one performs, that is what one attains" (BṛU 4.4.5).
Thus it is said.
In this regard, there is the adherence of people to the respective traditions, conventions, customs, and religious practices of their own countries.
Belief, modes of expression, and correct or incorrect words therein,
and so forth, may be cited as general examples of *vāsanā*; we shall treat this in detail later.
With regard to their diversity, the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad states as follows:
"Whatever he desires, he resolves upon; whatever he resolves upon, he acts."
"What he works out, that he attains" (Br. Up. 4.4.5).
The distinction between latent impressions (*vāsanā*) has been shown by Vālmīki:
"Latent impressions are said to be of two kinds: pure and likewise impure."
When impure, it is the cause of birth; when pure, it is the destroyer of birth.

"Characterized by a dense form of ignorance and possessed of thick egoism, the wise declare that impure latent impression (*vāsanā*) brings about rebirth. Having abandoned the sprout of rebirth like a parched seed, it remains [extinguished]. (Jīvanmuktiviveka)
"Having known what is to be known, she is maintained for the sake of the body and is called 'pure'.
(Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 1.10–12).
Thus, Vālmīki describes the variety of *vāsanā*.
‘Vāsanā is of two kinds: pure and impure; the impure one brings about birth, and the pure one brings it to an end. (Layv 1.10)
“The impure *vāsanā* consisting of solidified ignorance and stubborn ego is said by the learned to be the cause of rebirth” (ibid. 1.11).
“They say that the pure *vāsanā* is that which has known what was to be known (the Self) and, like a parched seed devoid of sprouting, remains only for the sake of the existing body.”

"having been liberated from future birth" (ibid. 1.12). Ignorance (*ajñāna*) is that which veils the distinction between the five sheaths, beginning with the body, and the conscious Self (*cidātman*) who is their witness. That which has a form thoroughly solidified by this [ignorance] is "she whose form is made dense by ignorance" (*ajñānasughanākārā*). Just as milk becomes solidified through the addition of buttermilk, or as...

Or, just as clarified butter that has melted is placed for a long time in an extremely cold place and becomes very solid, so too should latent impressions (*vāsanā*) be understood. And here, "solidification" refers to a succession of delusions. Regarding this, the Blessed One spoke in the *Asurasaṃpadvivaraṇa*:
"Ignorance conceals the distinction between the body..."
The Self, which is absolute consciousness, consists of the five sheaths and their witness.
The phrase "ajñānasughanākārā" refers to the latent impression (*vāsanā*) that has become dense with ignorance.

I have become quite dense through that ignorance. Just as milk coagulates upon contact with curds, or as melted clarified butter becomes solid if left for a long time in a cold place, so it is with me.
Thus, this density of *vāsanā* is to be understood as the result of successive delusions caused by ignorance. The Lord has referred to this impure *vāsanā* while describing [the nature of the world].
Thus are the demonic endowments:
"The people who are demonic know neither what should be undertaken nor what should be desisted from;
in them there is neither purity, nor right conduct, nor truth."
They say that this world is without truth, without a foundation, and without a Lord;
it is produced by mutual union, caused solely by desire—what else could there be?
Holding fast to this view, those of ruined souls and small intellects,
full of pride, arrogance, and insolence, and resorting to insatiable desire, arise as performers of cruel deeds for the destruction of the world and its enemies.
Having grasped false attachments out of delusion, they engage in impure observances.
Resorting to immeasurable anxiety that ends only with death,
they are devoted solely to the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, convinced that this is all there is.
"Bound by hundreds of snares of hope, devoted to desire and anger,
they strive for the sake of sensual enjoyment to amass wealth by unjust means. —
(Bhagavad Gītā 16.7–12).
"Those of a demonic nature do not know the way of action nor the way of renunciation. Neither purity, nor good conduct, nor truth is found in them. (BG 16.7)
They say that the universe is without truth, without a (moral) basis, without a God, brought about by mutual union and caused by desire and nothing else (ibid 16.8).
"Holding fast to this view, these ruined souls of small understanding and fierce deeds arise as the enemies of the world for its destruction" (ibid. 16.9).
‘Filled with insatiable desires, full of hypocrisy, pride, and arrogance, holding evil views through delusion, they act with impure intentions’ (ibid. 16.10).
“Overwhelmed by immense anxieties that end only with death, regarding the gratification of desire as the highest goal, and feeling certain that this is all” (ibid., 16.11). Jīvan-mukti-viveka.
"Bound by hundreds of ties of hope, surrendered to passion and anger, they strive to acquire through unjust means hoards of wealth for the enjoyment of the senses" (ibid. 16.12).

Those Asuras declared the world to be unreal; that is to say, they asserted that the world is such that there is no truth in it, such as the authority of the Vedas, Purāṇas, and so forth—the meaning is that they did not accept the validity of the Vedas. For this very reason, they declared the world to be such that there is no Lord who is its creator and ordainer. To the question, "In that case, from what do they say this world originates? he says:

Regarding the phrase *aparaspara*: "the other and the other" is *aparaspara*. From this mutual [union] of male and female, the world has arisen. What other cause is there for it? There is none whatsoever; rather, it is caused by desire (*kāmahaituka*).
The meaning is that they say the very desire of the male and female is its cause, existing in the form of a continuous stream. And there is a dense egoism (*ghanāhaṃkāra*).
It is illustrated in that very same place: "Those who are demonic say that the universe is without truth;
the authority of the Vedas, Purāṇas, and so forth is not true."
In which [universe]—such is, they say, the universe. This means that they do not accept the authority of the Vedas. Therefore, they say the universe is such wherein there is no God—the Creator.
and director. Then, from what do they say the creation of the world arises? It is said thus: from one and another—that is, mutually;
through the mutual union of the sexes, the universe is created. Is there...?

What other cause could there be for this? None other than lust. The meaning of their statement is that, in the form of a continuous succession, the mutual lust of the sexes is its cause. Excessive self-conceit also [arises from this].
It has been described there as follows:
"Today this has been gained by me; I shall attain this desire.
This is mine, and this wealth also shall be mine again."
"This enemy has been slain by me, and I shall slay others as well;
I am the lord, I am the enjoyer, I am successful, powerful, and happy."
"I am wealthy and of noble birth; who else is equal to me?
I shall sacrifice, I shall give gifts, and I shall rejoice"—thus deluded by ignorance, they are distracted by many thoughts and enveloped in the snare of delusion. (114)
"Those who are addicted to the enjoyment of sensual pleasures fall into an impure hell. — (Bhagavadgītā 16.13–16).
"This has been gained by me today; this desire I shall..."
"I have obtained this; this is mine, and this wealth also shall be mine in the future.
That enemy has been slain by me, and others as well I shall [slay]."
"Kill! I am the lord, I am the enjoyer, I am successful, powerful, and happy.
I am wealthy and well-born; who else is my equal?"
"I shall sacrifice, I shall give, I shall rejoice"— thus deluded by ignorance,
bewildered by manifold fancies, and shrouded by the snares [of craving].
"Deluded by ignorance and addicted to the gratification of lust, they fall headlong into a foul hell"—
by this, the cause of rebirth is illustrated, and that has been further elaborated upon.
Self-conceited, stubborn, and filled with the intoxication of wealth and pride, they perform sacrifices in name only, out of ostentation and contrary to scriptural injunctions. (17)
Resorting to egoism, power, arrogance, lust, and anger, these envious ones hate Me in their own bodies and in the bodies of others. 18.
Those hateful, cruel, and most base of men in the world of transmigration—I cast those inauspicious ones perpetually into demonic wombs alone. 19.
"Having entered the womb of an asura, deluded from birth to birth, they do not reach Me at all, O son of Kuntī; from there they go to the lowest state. (Bhagavad Gītā 16.17–20).
It has been demonstrated by the preceding discussion that this intense egoism is the cause of rebirth. This same point is further elaborated as follows:
*Jīvan-mukti-viveka* (The Discrimination of Liberation while Living)

Self-conceited, stubborn, and filled with pride and arrogance regarding their wealth, they perform sacrifices that are merely in name, characterized by ostentation and devoid of adherence to the prescribed rules.
“Endowed with egoism, power, and arrogance, as well as lust and anger, these wicked people hate Me who dwells within the bodies of themselves and others.”
"These malicious and cruel evildoers, the most debased of men— I cast them perpetually into the wombs of the Asuras alone within these worlds."
"Attaining the wombs of the *asurika* and being deluded birth after birth, failing to reach Me, they thus fall, O son of Kuntī, into an even lower state" (ibid., 16.19–20).

Pure latent impression (*śuddhavāsanā*), however, is that in which the object of knowledge has been known. The Blessed One described the true nature of the object of knowledge in the thirteenth chapter:
"I shall declare that which is to be known, by knowing which one attains immortality.
It is the beginningless Supreme Brahman; it is said to be neither being nor non-being. (13.12)
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces on all sides, and with ears everywhere in the world, It stands encompassing all.
It appears to possess the qualities of all the senses, yet it is devoid of all senses;
it is unattached and yet the sustainer of all; it is beyond the gunas, yet the experiencer of the gunas.
It exists both outside and inside all beings, both moving and unmoving;
because of its subtlety, it is incomprehensible; it is far away, yet it is near.
It is undivided, yet it exists as if divided among all beings;
it is to be known as the sustainer of beings, as well as their devourer and their progenitor.
That is the light even of lights; it is said to be beyond darkness.
It is knowledge, the object of knowledge, and that which is attainable through knowledge; it resides in the heart of every being. 17.
(Bhagavadgītā 13.12–17).
However, the pure *vāsanā* is that which has known what is to be known. The Lord, in the thirteenth chapter...

The Gītā has described the nature of the object to be known as follows: "I shall declare that which is to be known, by knowing which one attains immortality. It is without beginning... (Gītā 13.12) *Jīvan-mukti-viveka* states:
"I shall describe that which is to be known, by knowing which one attains immortality. It is the beginningless... (JMV 1.1)
The Supreme Brahman, who is said to be neither existent nor non-existent,
"with hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and..."
With faces everywhere and ears on all sides in the universe that exists pervading all;
shining by the functions of all the senses, yet without [them].
The senses; devoid of all attachment, yet sustaining all; free from the *guṇas*, yet the experiencer of them.
He is without and within all beings. He is unmoving and...
Also moving, yet incomprehensible due to its subtlety;
it is far away, yet it is near.
It is undivided, yet appears to be divided.
He is to be known as the supporter of beings, their destroyer, and their creator anew. He is the light of lights and is said to be beyond darkness.
"Knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the goal of knowledge— He dwells in the hearts of all.

Here, by means of both the indirect definition (*taṭasthalakṣaṇa*) and the essential definition (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*), [the nature of] His conditioned (*sopādhika*) and unconditioned (*nirupādhika*) forms is to be understood.

Two types of definitions have been presented: sometimes that which indicates [the object] through a relation with it is an incidental definition (*taṭasthalakṣaṇa*), as in "Devadatta’s house has a crow on it. Likewise, that which indicates [the object] through a relation existing in all three times is a definition of essential nature (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*), as in "the moon is that which possesses preeminent light."
The Supreme Self, in its finite and infinite aspects, is presented here for the purpose of promoting an understanding of It through *tatasthalakṣaṇa* and *svarūpalakṣaṇa*. That which indicates...
That which is defined by an accidental relation is called the *tāṭastha-lakṣaṇa* (indirect definition);
for example, the statement: "The house with a crow belongs to Devadatta. (*Jīvan-mukti-viveka*)
And that which indicates [an object] by its constant presence therein is called *svarūpalakṣaṇa* (essential definition); for example, the statement "the bright moon."

Objection: It has been stated that the definition of *vāsanā* is the state of having abandoned prior and subsequent reflection (*vicāra*); yet, the knowledge of the object of cognition (*jñeya-jñāna*) is produced by reflection. Therefore, that definition does not apply to pure [consciousness].

It consists in the relinquishing of all consideration regarding what precedes and what follows; however, the knowledge of the object to be known arises from an inquiry into it; therefore, that [is the case].
The definition does not encompass pure *vāsanā*.

It is not so, because it was stated in the definition that [the cause] is "firm cultivation" (*dṛḍhabhāvanā*). Just as, due to having been firmly cultivated over many lifetimes, impure *vāsanās* such as egoism (*ahaṃkāra*), possessiveness (*mamakāra*), desire, and anger arise in this life even without the instruction of another, so too—

Although the initial awakening arises from inquiry, when the reality has been cultivated through long-term, uninterrupted, and respectful practice, that reality subsequently flashes forth suddenly—without even the consideration of words or logical arguments—just like a jar standing before one.

The engagement of the senses accompanied by such a continuous flow of awakening constitutes pure latent impression (*śuddhavāsanā*). And that is employed solely for the maintenance of the body and life.
But it is not for the sake of producing the demonic qualities such as hypocrisy and pride, nor for the sake of producing merit and demerit which cause rebirth in another life;
just as parched seeds of rice and the like are used merely to fill a granary, and not for delicious food, nor for the production of a harvest, so it is in this case.

Reply: This is not the case, because the phrase "through strong impressions" (*vāsanā*) is added to the definition. For example, there are impure *vāsanās* consisting of egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) and the notions of "I" and "mine" (*mamakāra*).
Since desire, anger, and the like arise in this life without any instruction from others due to being deeply impressed by practice throughout many previous lives, the knower—
Knowledge of reality, although primarily arising from inquiry,
when practiced continuously for a long time with care, produces deep impressions and subsequently, without further assistance...
Through any kind of instruction, reflection, or suggestion,
reality becomes immediately visible, just like a jar or other objects situated directly before one. This occurs together with the functioning of the sense organs and...
The constant awareness of Reality is called pure *vāsanā*;
and this pure *vāsanā* is merely suitable for the maintenance of life and the body. Pure *vāsanā* is not capable of producing [further rebirth].
Neither the demonic endowments such as hypocrisy, insolence, and the like, nor the religious merit and demerit that lead to rebirth [are to be cultivated],
just as parched grains of rice and the like are suitable for filling the stomach.
Like a granary, it is incapable of producing fresh grain or a delicious dish.

Furthermore, impurity of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is threefold: the latent impression of the world (*lokavāsanā*), the latent impression of the scriptures (*śāstravāsanā*), and the latent impression of the body (*dehavāsanā*). All...

The worldly habit (*lokavāsanā*) is the attachment that thinks, "I shall always act in such a way that people do not censure me or that they praise me. Because it is impossible to fulfill this, it is impure. For instance:
"Who indeed in this world at present is virtuous, and who is heroic?"
(Rāmāyaṇa 1.1.2)
In these and other ways, Vālmīki questioned him in many respects.
Impure latent dispositions (*vāsanā*) are of three kinds: the desire for fame and reputation, the desire for learning, and the desire for the body.

The resolve to lead such a life that will win one acclaim from the people and avoid their censure is called the desire for worldly existence (*lokacchanda*). This desire is impure, because it is impossible—
Accomplish only renown and avoid blame. For example, Vālmīki questioned Nārada in various ways, asking:
"In these days, who is virtuous and who is brave?"
"Is there anyone in the world? (Rāmāyaṇa 1.1.2).
To this, Nārada gave the reply beginning with: "There is one born in the lineage of Ikṣvāku, known among people by the name Rāma" (Rāmāyaṇa 1.1.8).
Nārada replied as follows: "He is indeed Rāma, born in the ancestral lineage of Ikṣvāku, well-known to the people" (ibid).
Even regarding such a Rāma, it is impossible to hear [the account] of Sītā, the mother of the world and the crest-jewel of devoted wives.

Public scandal has broken out; what need is there to mention others? For indeed, a great deal of mutual derision is observed according to specific regions. Brahmins from the South are censured by Brahmins of the North as eaters of meat despite being knowers of the Vedas. And by those of the North, the Southerners are censured for marrying their maternal uncle’s daughters and carrying earthen pots on journeys.

They are censured. The followers of the Ṛgveda consider the Āśvalāyana recension to be more praiseworthy than the Kāṇva recension, whereas the Vājasaneyins hold the opposite view. Thus, the praising of one's own family, lineage, circle of kinsmen, and tutelary deity, along with the censuring of those belonging to others, is well known everywhere, from the learned down to the cowherds. It was with this very point in mind that it was said:
Even that very Rāma and his wife Sītā—the mother of the world and the paragon of feminine virtue—were scandalized; what need be said of others? For instance, people [acted] with complete freedom...
They speak ill of one another, referring to their respective local peculiarities.
The Brāhmaṇas of the South censure their counterparts in the North as flesh-eaters, even though they are well-versed in the Vedas.

The northerners reciprocated [this] because of their practice of marrying the daughter of their maternal uncle, and also because of their carrying earthenware (as cooking utensils) while traveling. The *Ṛg*—
The Vedic Brāhmaṇas consider the Āśvalāyana branch to be superior to the Kāṇva branch, whereas the Vājasaneyins of the Yajurveda think exactly the opposite. It is we—
