It is well known that people— from the learned down to women and even herdsmen— extol their own community, lineage, relatives,
deities, and so forth, while reviling others. With this in mind:
It is said thus:
"The *piśāca* is pure, restless, discerning, patient yet powerless, and strong yet wicked."
"A heartless thief, though handsome and full of desire, who is capable of pleasing the world? Thus it is said: "Indeed, there exists no means whatsoever..."
"He who brings satisfaction to the whole world—how can such a person be affected by talkative people? One should always practice what is beneficial for oneself. Thus it is said.
And: "No one can satisfy the people; they always speak ill of others—even a pure man is called a demon, and a wise man..."
One who is self-possessed is regarded as an arrogant man; a forgiving person is deemed weak; a strong man is thought to be wicked;
and one absorbed in contemplation is looked upon as a thief.
‘A handsome man is lustful’ (source untraced). And thus:
‘There is no way to please everyone; therefore, one should strive by all means to achieve one’s own welfare. What can [be done otherwise]?’
"What do talkative people [say]? (Source untraced).

Therefore, with the intention of showing that the worldly impression (*lokavāsanā*) is more defiled than the scriptural impression (*śāstravāsanā*), the Lord of Yogis [teaches] his state of being equal toward blame and praise.
It is described in the treatises on liberation as being threefold: first,
addiction to recitation;
There is the addiction to many scriptures and the addiction to ritual performance. The addiction to recitation is understood to reside in Bharadvāja.

For he, having studied many Vedas over three human lifespans, was tempted by Indra during his fourth lifespan to study even more remaining Vedas; yet, because that recitation was impossible to complete, it constitutes a defiled latent impression (*mala-vāsanā*).

Indra, having awakened him to that impossibility and turned him away from his recitation, taught him the knowledge of the Saguna Brahman for the sake of a human goal even greater than that. All of this is to be seen in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa. Likewise, the defilement resulting from an addiction to extensive scriptural study due to the absence of the ultimate human goal is observed in the Kāvaṣeya Gītā:
Considering the impurity of the desire for fame and reputation,
it is stated in the scriptures on liberation that a master yogi should remain equanimous toward both praise and blame.
The desire for learning is of three kinds: attachment to study, attachment to many disciplines, and attachment to ritual acts. Attachment to study is found in Bharadvāja, who—
Having studied the Vedas throughout three successive lifetimes,
he was enticed by Indra and again attempted to study the remaining portions of the Vedas in his fourth lifetime; this desire, too, is impure.
Since such study was impossible,
Indra, having restrained him from study by explaining its impossibility, instructed him in the discipline of...
The conditioned Brahman is intended for the attainment of a higher purpose in life. All of this is to be found in the *Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa*.
Similarly, attachment to the study of many scriptures [is likewise for a specific purpose].
This is an impure desire for learning, because the ultimate goal of life cannot be attained through it. This is found in the *Kāvaseya Gītā* as follows: [End of] *Jīvanmukti-viveka*.

"A certain sage, Durvāsas, having come with the weight of many kinds of scriptural books to pay homage to Mahādeva, was compared by the sage Nārada in that assembly to a donkey carrying a load; in anger, he cast his books into the salt ocean and was then initiated into the knowledge of the Self (ātma-vidyā) by Mahādeva. And this knowledge of the Self [is not for one] whose face is turned outward.
For one devoid of the compassion of a guru, [realization] does not arise through the mere study of the Vedas and Shastras.
Once, a certain sage named Durvasa, carrying a load of books on various subjects, came to pay homage to the Great Lord. In that assembly—
When the sage Nārada compared him to a donkey,
a beast of burden, he became enraged; he cast all his books into the Lavana Ocean and was instructed in the discipline of Śeṣa.
Self-knowledge arises through the Great Lord. Furthermore, self-knowledge does not arise through the Vedas alone for one who is not introverted and lacks the grace of the Guru.
And thus says the Śruti:
"This Self is not to be attained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing" (Kaṭhopaniṣad 1.2.23).
And the Śruti says thus:
"This Self cannot be attained by instruction, nor by intellectual power, nor even through much hearing" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad).
It is stated elsewhere as well: "What is the use of this futile rumination on the tattered rags of many scriptural discourses? (Up. 1.2.23; Mund. Up. 3.2.3).
"One who knows reality must diligently seek that inner light," and also:
"Having studied the four Vedas and the treatises on dharma many times,
one who does not know the reality of Brahman is like a spoon that does not know the flavor of the food it stirs."
(Muktikopaniṣad 2.63, 65)
In other places as well, it is said thus:
"There is no purpose served by the useless repetition of the collected texts of many scriptures, in the form of, as it were,"
A patched garment [is useless], just as a piece of such cloth being chewed by a cow or similar animal serves no purpose. Those who have learned of the Inner Light should strive to realize It.
(Muktikopaniṣad 2.63):
"Even after studying the four Vedas and all the Dharmaśāstras many times, one may not know the essence of Brahman."
"Just as a ladle has no knowledge of the taste of the food" (ibid. 2.65).
Nārada, although skilled in the sixty-four arts, being distressed by his lack of self-knowledge, approached Sanatkumāra.

Thus the Chandogas recite. A passion for ritual performance is observed in Nidāgha in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*, and in Dāśūra in the *Vāsiṣṭharāmāyaṇa*. For although Nidāgha was repeatedly awakened by Ṛbhu, he did not abandon his dull-witted devotion to ritual action for a long time. And Dāśūra, due to extreme dullness of faith, [sought] a pure place on the earth for the sake of performance.
I did not find it anywhere. Furthermore, this latent impression of karma (karmavāsanā) is impure because it is the cause of rebirth.
In the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, it is narrated that Nārada, though well-versed in the sixty-four branches of knowledge (*vidyā*), [was still dissatisfied].

Remorseful for his ignorance regarding the Self, Nidāgha approached Sanatkumāra (Chāndogya Upaniṣad, Chapter 7). Nidāgha’s attachment to ritualistic works is recorded in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (Chapters 2.15 and 16).
and of Dāśūra in the Vāsiṣṭha Rāmāyaṇa (chapters 4.48 through 4.55). Nidāgha did not relinquish his stubborn adherence to ritualistic observances for a long time, even after being persuaded—

Rbhu caused him to wander repeatedly. And Daśūra, due to his excessively stubborn adherence to ritualistic formalities, could not find even a single pure spot in the entire world suitable for the performance of sacrifice. This...
The desire for ritual acts is impure because it leads to rebirth.
Thus, the followers of the Atharvaveda recite: "Unstable indeed are these rafts in the form of sacrifice."
Those fools who rejoice in these eighteen inferior activities in which action is prescribed go back again and again to old age and death.
Existing in the midst of ignorance,
though wise themselves, they consider themselves learned;
these fools wander about, being tormented.
Just like blind men being led by one who is himself blind.
Existing in ignorance in many ways, fools imagine themselves to have achieved their goal;
for those engaged in ritual action do not perceive this due to passion.
Therefore, being afflicted and having exhausted their worldly existence, they fall away.
Thinking that sacrifices and charitable works are the highest good,
these deluded ones know no other excellence; having experienced the fruits of their good deeds on the heights of heaven—
They enter this world or one even lower than that.
(Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.7–10)
The Muṇḍakopaniṣad of the Atharvaveda reads as follows:
"Unsteady indeed are these boats of the eighteen forms of sacrifice, which are said to be inferior karma. The deluded..."
Those who delight in this as leading to the good fall again into old age and death (ibid. 1.2.7).
"Abiding in the midst of ignorance, wise in their own [estimation]..."
Esteeming themselves as learned, fools afflicted by distress wander about like the blind led by one who is himself blind (Ibid. 1.2.8).
“The immature, dwelling diversely in ignorance, think, ‘We have accomplished our goal. Since those who perform ritual acts do not understand [the truth] due to their attachment, therefore— ”
For they sink down, wretched, when their worlds (that is, the fruits of their merits) are exhausted (ibid. 1.2.9).
"Those deluded men, regarding sacrifices and works..."
"Regarding merit as most important and knowing no other good,
having enjoyed themselves in the lofty abode of heaven won by their virtuous deeds, they re-enter this world or one even lower than it" (ibid.).
The Blessed One has also said: "O Pārtha, those who are unwise, who delight in the ritualistic discourse of the Vedas and who assert that there is nothing else, utter this flowery speech. (Gītā 2.42)
Those whose nature is desire, who look toward heaven, [follow that path] which yields the fruits of birth and action,
abounds in various ritual acts, and leads toward the attainment of enjoyment and power.
For those who are deeply attached to enjoyments and power, whose minds have been carried away by that [attachment],
the intellect characterized by resolute determination is not established in meditative concentration.
The Vedas concern themselves with the three gunas; be free from these three gunas, O Arjuna.
Be free from the pairs of opposites, eternally established in purity (sattva), indifferent toward acquisition and preservation, and possessed of the Self.
"As much purpose as there is in a small reservoir when there is water overflowing everywhere,
so much [purpose] is there in all the Vedas for a Brahmin who possesses true knowledge. (Bhagavad Gītā 2.46)
In the Bhagavadgītā, the Lord has also said this:
"Those of little intelligence, who delight in the laudatory words of the Vedas and maintain that there is nothing else, O..."
O Pārtha, those who are full of desires and regard heaven as their supreme goal proclaim these flowery words,
which result in rebirth as the fruit of action, and prescribe various special rites.
...the intellect that discriminates between right and wrong belonging to those devoted to enjoyment and power (ibid).
"And whose minds are carried away by them, their intellect is not well-established" (ibid. 2.44).
"The Vedas deal with the activities of the three modes."
Be free, O Arjuna, from this threefold nature;
be free from the pairs of opposites; be firmly established in purity, indifferent to acquisition and preservation, and possessed of the Self.
"For the Brahmin who has realized the Self, all the Vedas are of as much use as a reservoir is when there is a flood."
"everywhere" (ibid. 2.46).

Furthermore, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the scriptures is impure because it is a cause of pride. The Chandogas [record] in the sixth chapter that Śvetaketu, having studied all the Vedas in a very short time, did not show humility even before his father due to pride.

Thus they recite: Bālāki, having understood certain meditations (*upāsanā*), became arrogant and, after traveling on a conquest of the quarters through many lands such as Uśīnara and insulting many Brahmins, displayed the audacity to instruct Ajātaśatru of Kāśī— the crest-jewel among knowers of Brahman— so state the Kauṣītakins and the Vājasaneyins.
Furthermore, the desire for learning is impure because it is the cause of arrogance. This is described in the sixth chapter of the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, where Śvetaketu, having—
Having mastered all the Vedas in a short time, he did not behave with humility even toward his own father due to pride.
Similarly, it is described in the fourth chapter of the...
In the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad and in the first Brāhmaṇa of the second chapter of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, it is told that Bālāki was very proud because of his knowledge of a few forms [of Brahman].
He worshipped; embarking on a victorious tour, he traveled to many countries, beginning with Uśīnara, and humiliated many Brahmins through the pre-eminence of his vast learning. Finally, in Kāśī...

He had the audacity to offer instructions to Ajātaśatru, the most eminent among the knowers of Brahman. The latent impression of the body (*dehavāsanā*) is threefold, due to the distinctions of [identifying the body as] the self (*ātmatva*), the attribution of qualities (*guṇādhāna*), and the removal of defects (*doṣāpanayana*). Regarding these, the author of the Commentary [states]: [the first is] the selfhood...

He stated: "Ordinary people and the Lokāyatikas maintain that the self is merely the body qualified by consciousness" (*Brahmasūtrabhāṣya* 1.1.1). By means of the passage beginning with "This person, indeed, consists of the essence of food" and ending with "Therefore, it is called food" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.1.2), [the author] refutes that very view held by ordinary people. *Jīvanmuktiviveka*
The Taittirīyas clarify this: "Even though Virocana was instructed by Prajāpati, due to a defect in his own mind,
he strengthened the notion that the body is the Self and taught it to all the Asuras"— thus the Chandogas record in the eighth chapter.
The desire for the body is also of three kinds:
the erroneous identification of the body with the self, the acquisition of good qualities, and the removal of faults. The commentary...
Śaṅkarācārya has described the erroneous identification of the Self as follows: "Ordinary people as well as the materialists of the Lokāyata school..."
The schools recognize the body alone to be the self endowed with sentience (Bhāṣya on Brahmasūtra 1.1.1). In the Taittirīya Upaniṣad (2.1.2), such a notion of the ordinary...
This false identification of the self with the body, which is "people," has been described thus,
beginning with "This, indeed, is the person consisting of the essence of food" and ending with "Therefore..."
It is called 'food'.
In the eighth chapter of the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, it is described that Virocana, although Prajāpati had instructed him...

In the context of self-knowledge, due to his impure mind, he became firmly convinced that this body possessed the nature of the Self, and proceeded to impart this erroneous conception to his fellow demons.

The cultivation of qualities (*guṇādhāna*) is twofold: worldly (*laukika*) and scriptural (*śāstrīya*). The production of correct sounds and so forth is worldly. For instance, people strive to drink oil and eat black pepper in order to sing or study with a soft voice; likewise, for the sake of a soft touch, people employ nourishing medicines and foods.

For the sake of beauty, they employ unguents, ointments, fine silken garments, and ornaments; for the sake of fragrance, they wear garlands and fragrant pastes; and to instill scriptural virtue, they perform ritual baths in the Ganges and visit sacred sites such as Śālagrāma.
The acquisition of accessory qualities (*guṇa*) is of two kinds:
the customary and the scriptural. Accomplishing a true voice or tone is an instance of the non-scriptural. People attempt at drinking...

People use oil and eat black pepper in order to acquire a sweet voice for singing or chanting. They employ medicinal substances and nutritious food to obtain smooth skin. For the sake of beauty, they use cosmetics.
Such as cream, powder, and so forth; they wear fine garments and ornaments.
To make the body fragrant, people put on garlands of flowers and apply sandalwood paste and other unguents.
To acquire the auxiliary qualities of the scriptures, people bathe in the sacred waters of the Gaṅgā, worship the Sālagrāma, and undertake pilgrimages.

The removal of defects is of two kinds: worldly, consisting of the application of medicines prescribed by physicians and the rinsing of the mouth and so forth; and Vedic, consisting of purification, ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and the like. The impurity of this latent impression (*vāsanā*) regarding the body will now be explained.
To begin with, the body’s status as the Self is impure because it lacks any authoritative basis and because it is the cause of all suffering. And on this point—

All the former teachers have exerted themselves [in this matter], yet we generally do not perceive the acquisition of [new] qualities. Indeed, many singers and reciters, despite their efforts, do not attain excellence of tone.
Softness of touch and physical robustness are not invariably present; even beauty and fragrance reside in things such as fine silk garments and flower garlands, and not [in the person].
It resides in the body. For this very reason, it is stated in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"The removal of defects is also of two kinds; of these, the conventional is by means of taking medicines prescribed by a physician."
The worldly [method] consists of using a tooth-stick, rinsing the mouth, and so forth; the scriptural method consists of purification through the sprinkling and sipping of water and the like.
It will be explained later that the desire for the body—
Impure.
To confuse the body with the Self is unfounded, and such identification is also the cause of endless suffering; therefore,
It is impure. All former teachers have exerted great effort in this regard (that is, they have employed cogent reasons to eliminate this false conception).
The acquisition of additional qualities is for the most part not found.
Even celebrated musicians and teachers, despite their efforts, fail to achieve a truly delightful voice. [This applies even to] tender skin and *jīvan-mukti-viveka*.
The nourishment of the body is not invariably achieved by food and the like;
rather, beauty and fragrance reside in the clothing, flower garlands, and so forth, not in the body itself. For this reason...
It is said in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (1.17.63) [and also in the Nārada Parivrājaka Upaniṣad 48] as follows: "In this collection of flesh, blood, pus, feces, urine, sinews, marrow, and bones..."
If that fool feels attachment to the body, he will find himself even in hell.
—(Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.17.63): "If a man is not repelled by the foul odor of his own body, what other cause for detachment could possibly be taught to him? * Thus it is said.
(Muktikopaniṣad 2.66)
"That deluded fool who is in love with this body— a mere conglomeration of flesh, blood, pus, excrement, muscle, sinews, marrow, and bone— will also love hell."
(V. Purāṇa 1.17.63; N.P. UP.
48) "For that man who is not repelled by the foul stench of his own body, what else could possibly cause him revulsion?"
"Prescribed" (Muktikopaniṣad 2.66; Padmapurāṇa, Bhūmikhaṇḍa 66.80–81).
Furthermore, a scriptural injunction for the cultivation of qualities is set aside by a more powerful contrary scriptural rule, as in: "One should not harm any living beings."

Regarding this [statement from the *Mahābhārata* 3.203.45], there is an exception by the rule "one should immolate an animal dedicated to Agni and Soma" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 6.1.11.6); likewise, this scripture is more powerful than other scriptures—
the scriptural acquisition of auxiliary qualities is invalid.
But that man who does not become disgusted by the foul odor of his own body is liberated by the more important and powerful injunctions of others. ||80||
What other cause for its impurity can be taught? The entire world is pure; only the body itself is supremely impure. (81)
—*Padampugaṇe* (in the *Gurumaṇḍalagranthamālā*), 2.66.80–81.
What other cause for revulsion could be taught for that man who is already repelled by the foul odor of his own body’s impurities? (80)

In that very work (*Ānandāśrama Granthāvalī*, no. 131), 2.66.80, from the *Jīvanmuktiviveka* scriptures, for example: "No living being whatsoever should be killed" (*Mahābhārata* 3.203.45; 12.269.5, 316.18). This is the precept.
It is recorded in one scripture that the victim of the Agniṣoma sacrifice should be killed, while this is contradicted by another [scripture] (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.1.11.6).
The scripture more powerful than any other is this:
"He who perceives the notion of self in a corpse composed of the three humors, the notion of his own in his wife and others, and the notion of sacrifice in the earth— "
"He who perceives a sacred ford only in water and never among wise men is indeed an ox or a donkey" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.84.13).
"The body is exceedingly impure, while the embodied self is exceedingly pure; having understood the difference between these two, for which one is purification prescribed? and so forth.
(Sūta-saṃhitā 2.14.19)
‘He who identifies the self with the body composed of the three humors— phlegm, wind, and bile— considers his wife and others to be his own, and regards [worldly] images as objects of worship.
"Who honors earth and stone, and regards water as an object of veneration but never those who are wise men— he is indeed a donkey carrying fodder" (Bhāgavata 10.84.13).
And thus:
"The body is extremely impure, while the Self, who possesses a body, is extremely pure; for one who has realized this distinction..."

"Should purification be prescribed? (That is to say, it should not be prescribed for anyone, because the Self has no need for it and the body cannot be purified. (Muktikopaniṣad 2.67 & Śaṅkarācārya’s Sadācāraḥ 4; Sūta-Saṃhitā)

Although by this teaching the removal of defects is prohibited rather than the instilling of virtues, nevertheless, since a virtue cannot be instilled when there exists a powerful defect that acts as an obstacle, the prohibition of the instillation of virtues follows by implication. This refers to extreme impurity.

And in this regard, it is heard in the Maitrāyaṇīya recension: "O Blessed One, what is the use of the enjoyment of desires in this body, which is defiled by bone, skin, sinew, marrow, flesh, semen, blood, tears, and rheum; a mere conglomeration of feces, urine, wind, bile, and phlegm; foul-smelling and devoid of essence? (1.1.2); and: "This body has arisen from sexual intercourse alone; it is bereft of consciousness, like a hell."

"It has emerged through the urinary passage, filled with bones, smeared with flesh, covered with skin, and packed full with feces, urine, bile, phlegm, marrow, fat, grease, and many other impurities—like a treasure chest filled with wealth.
Furthermore, the pacification of disease through medical treatment is not certain; even when a disease has been cured, it may sometimes arise again.

When impurities flow incessantly from the nine apertures and from the countless pores of the skin, who indeed could wash away the perspiring body with mere water? Thus it was said by the ancient teachers:
[Though the scriptural texts quoted above prohibit...]

Although there is an attempt to remove faults rather than acquire additional qualities, nevertheless, in the presence of powerful obstructive faults, no good quality can be acquired; thus, indirectly—
They strictly prohibit the acquisition of virtuous qualities. However, the extreme impurity of the body is described in the Maitrāyaṇīya branch of the Vedas as follows:
"Venerable Sir, in this foul-smelling, defiled,
and insubstantial body— a mere conglomeration of bones, skin, muscles,
marrow, flesh, semen, blood, mucus, tears, phlegm, and feces— "

"Since this body arises from sexual intercourse and is devoid of [purity], consisting only of urine, wind, bile, and phlegm, what is the use of the enjoyment of sensual pleasures? (Maitrāyaṇī Upaniṣad 1.2). "This body arises from sexual intercourse... [and so forth].
Consciousness, a veritable hell, then emerges through the urinary passage; it is constructed of bones,
smeared over with flesh, covered with skin, and filled with [impurities].
"With feces, urine, bile, phlegm, marrow, fat, grease,
and also with many other impurities, like a treasure-house full of wealth" (Maitrāyaṇī Upaniṣad 3.4).
Furthermore, the cure of disease through medical treatment is not certain; even when cured, a relapse cannot be ruled out. Who can purify the body, which is constantly discharging waste matter?
Through its nine apertures and moistened by the secretions from countless pores, [it remains foul] despite great effort. Thus it has been said by the former teachers:
"Bodies with nine apertures leak like water-jars;
they are not purified by external cleansings, nor does internal purity exist."
Therefore, the latent impression of the body is impure. Intending this very impurity, Vasiṣṭha said:
"Bodies with nine apertures constantly discharge [waste matter] like a porous earthen pot; they cannot be kept clean."
"By washing externally, there is no means of internal cleansing" (source untraced).
Therefore, desire for the body is impure. With this in mind:

The impure Vasiṣṭha spoke thus: "‘From head to foot, I am fashioned by my mother and father’— O Rāma, this is the singular conviction that arises from the perception of the unreal, leading to bondage."
(Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 20.42)
That path of the Kālasūtra hell, that snare of the Mahāvīci hell,
and that row of sword-leaf forests— all these are the state of "I" established within the body.
She should be abandoned with every effort, even when total ruin has arrived;
she must not be touched by a noble man, like a Pulkasī woman carrying dog-meat.
(Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 18.16–17):
"O Rāma, the conviction that 'I am built from head to foot by my father and mother' is due to false notion (mithyābhimāna)."
leads to bondage (LYV20.42). "The conviction that 'I am the body' is the path to the Kālasūtra hell, the snare for the Mahāvīci hell, and the staircase [to rebirth]."
To descend into the hell known as Asipatravana (ibid):
"This conviction must be abandoned by every possible effort, even if it results in disaster. A righteous person should never [hold onto it]."
"Come into contact with it as if with a *pulkasī* carrying dog-meat" (ibid. 18.17).
This triad of worldly, scriptural, and bodily impressions (*vāsanā*), although appearing as something to be accepted by those lacking discrimination, [is to be abandoned] by the seeker...
Because they are opposed to the arising of [true] feeling and because they oppose the establishment of knowledge in the wise,
these three desires— for fame, learning, and a faultless body— are to be abandoned by those possessed of discrimination; yet they may appear acceptable to the undiscriminating.

These [qualities] should be avoided by the wise, insofar as they obstruct the attainment of knowledge in seekers and prevent that knowledge from becoming firmly established in those who already possess it.
For this very reason, it is stated in the Smṛti:
"Due to the latent impression of worldly life, the latent impression of the scriptures,
and the latent impression of the body, knowledge does not arise in its true form for a living being."
(Sūta-saṃhitā 4.14.51).
Thus the Smṛti says: "Proper knowledge does not arise in one who hankers..."
After fame, pride in learning, and the longing for a flawless body (*Sūtasamhitā* 4.14.51).
As for that mental latent impression (*vāsanā*) which consists of the demonic wealth (*asurasampat*) such as hypocrisy and arrogance, because it is a cause for hell, [it must be abandoned].
This is very well known. Therefore, by whatever means possible, the destruction of the fourfold latent impressions (*vāsanā*) must be accomplished;
just as the destruction of the latent impressions must be accomplished, so too must that of the mind.
The mental desires in the form of the demonic...
Hypocrisy, insolence, and the like are regarded as impure, for it is well known that they lead to utter ruin. Therefore, by whatever means these four desires—

It must be destroyed. Just as there is the destruction of desires, so too must the destruction of the mind be accomplished. In the *Jīvan-mukti-viveka*, it is stated that the followers of the Vedas do not accept the mind—like the logicians—to be an eternal substance of atomic dimension, such that the destruction of the mind would be impossible.

[Otherwise] it would be difficult to establish [its permanence]. What then? According to the Tārkika school, the mind (manas) is a substance that possesses parts, is impermanent, and is always subject to various transformations, like lacquer, gold, and other such materials.
and of atomic dimension; therefore, its dissolution is hardly possible. Unlike the Tārkikas, the Vaidikas admit the mind to be composed of parts, a non-eternal substance that is always...
It is capable of assuming various forms, such as lac, gold, and so forth.

Regarding its characteristics and dimensions, the Vājasaneyins record in their tradition: "Desire, resolve, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, shame, intelligence, and fear—all this is nothing but the mind" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.3).
This is its definition.
The Vājasaneyins provide the definition and proof of the mind as follows:
"Desire, resolve, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, shame, intelligence, and fear—all these are but the mind. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.3). This is the definition.

The meaning is that the mind (*manas*) is the material cause of those functions such as desire and the like, which, arising in succession, appear with extreme clarity through the direct perception of the Witness (*sākṣipratyakṣa*), just as a jar or other objects are perceived by visual perception. This is supported by the scriptural passages: "My mind was elsewhere, I did not see; my mind was elsewhere, I did not hear" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.3), and "For with the mind one sees, with the mind one hears" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad).
This is the authoritative proof (for the statement):
"The mental impressions in the form of desire and so forth, which arise on occasion, become directly perceptible."

It is witnessed very clearly, just as the perception of jars and other objects occurs through the eyes and so forth. Thus, the meaning is that the mind is the material cause of them all. Therefore, [they say]: "My mind..."

‘When [the mind] was elsewhere, I did not see it; when [the mind] was elsewhere, I did not hear it’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.3); and likewise: ‘It is indeed by the mind that one sees; it is by the mind that one hears.’

(Brhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.3). Thus is the proof for the existence of the mind. A jar situated in the midst of bright light in proximity to the eye, and the Veda recited loudly in proximity to the ear—[these would not be perceived by the senses alone].

The meaning is that such an instrument, common to the perception of all objects, is established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka)— namely, that which is not perceived when there is a lack of attention, yet is perceived when there is attention. Therefore, for this reason as well...
"The mind perceives [the touch] from behind" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.3)— this is the illustrative example.
[It refers to] a jar situated in broad daylight and within the range of sight,
and a Vedic chant being loudly recited within the range of hearing.
That without whose attention such a thing is not perceived,
and with whose attention it is truly perceived, being a common factor in the perception of all objects, is known through positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
and by means of negative methods. Such is the meaning of the cited passage. And this is the illustration:
"Even if one is touched from behind, one knows it through..."
"...therefore [the mind exists]" (Br. Up. 1.5.3).
Since the mind is established by both its defining characteristic and its means of proof, it should be illustrated in this way:
even when touched from behind, Devadatta perceives specifically, "This is the touch of a hand; this is the touch of a finger. It is not [otherwise].

For in that case, the eye does not extend [to the object], while the sense of touch is exhausted merely by grasping softness or hardness. Therefore, the mind alone remains as the cause of specific cognition. And that is called "mind" (*manas*) because of its function of thinking (*manana*), and "consciousness" (*citta*) because of its nature as consciousness. Furthermore, that consciousness consists of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, and is characterized by illumination, activity, and delusion.
From the observation of effects such as existence (*sattva*) and so forth, it follows that illumination (*prakāśa*) and the other qualities are effects of the *guṇas*.
The characteristic of being beyond the *guṇas* is understood from the statement in the *Bhagavadgītā* (14.22): "O Pāṇḍava, [he who does not hate] illumination, activity, and even delusion.
In that regard:
And since the existence of the mind has been established by its own valid means of cognition,
Regarding the definition and the evidence, it should now be illustrated as follows: even if Devadatta is touched on his back by someone, he becomes specifically aware of that touch.

[It must be] either of the hand or of the finger. Since the eye cannot see that location and tactile perception is restricted to the sensation of hardness or softness, it follows by the principle of elimination [that it is neither].
The mind alone is the cause of such specific cognition.
Because of its function of deliberation, it is called *manas* (mind); and because it deals with external objects, it is known as the organ of thought.

The external world is called *citta*. And this *citta* is of the nature of the three *guṇas*— *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*— because their effects, namely illumination, activity, and delusion, [are observed therein].
The light and so forth are the effects of the *guṇas*;
they are found in the definition of one who has transcended the *guṇas* (*guṇātīta*) as follows (Bhagavadgītā 14.22):
"O Arjuna (Pāṇḍava), illumination (the effect of sattva), activity (the effect of rajas), and delusion (the effect of tamas)— thus have they been described."

In the Sāṃkhya treatise as well, it is stated: "Illumination, activity, and delusion are for the purpose of regulation. Here, "illumination" does not refer to the form of white light, but rather to knowledge.
As it is said: "From *sattva* arises knowledge, and from *rajas* indeed arises greed."
"Negligence and delusion arise from Tamas, as well as ignorance itself.
(Bhagavad Gītā 14.17)
Because it has been stated thus;
and it has also been said in the Sāṃkhya philosophy as follows:
"Light, activity, and delusion are employed for the purpose of..."
"Light is knowledge, for it illumines all objects of knowledge" (Sāṃkhya-kārikā 12,
adapted). Here, the word "light" does not mean whiteness and brilliance, but rather knowledge, since it has been stated thus [in the Bhagavadgītā]:
"From *sattva* arises wisdom, and from *rajas* greed;
misapprehension, delusion, and ignorance arise from *tamas*" (Bhagavad Gītā 14.17).
Happiness, like knowledge, is also an effect of *sattva*. As it has been said:
"O Bhārata, *sattva* attaches one to happiness; *rajas* to action;
but *tamas*, veiling knowledge, attaches one to negligence."
(Bhagavadgītā 14.9). Thus, like wisdom, happiness is also an effect of *sattva*; this has also been stated as follows:
"Sattva clings to happiness, and rajas to action, O descendant of Bharata; but tamas, indeed, veiling discernment, clings to ignorance."
As the *guṇas* transform incessantly like the waves of the ocean, at times one of them arises while the other two are suppressed.
As it has been said:
"O Bhārata, when *rajas* and *tamas* are overcome, *sattva* prevails."
"Rajas, sattva, and tamas, as well as tamas, sattva, and rajas [arise]—
just as waves in the ocean, they become the oppressor and the oppressed" (ibid., 14.10).
And as it is said in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* (5.1.20):
"Like the waves of the ocean, while undergoing constant change, sometimes one or another of the *guṇas* prevails."
The other two remain overwhelmed. Thus it has been said:
"Sattva arises, O descendant of Bharata, prevailing over rajas and tamas; and rajas [prevails] over sattva and..."
"Darkness [prevails] over goodness and passion" (BG 14.10). And likewise:
"They [the modes] are like the waves of the ocean..."
This is the state of mutual oppression (Viṣṇupurāṇa 5.1.20).
In that regard, when *tamas* arises, the demonic endowment (*āsurasampat*) emerges; when *rajas* arises, the three tendencies toward worldly existence and so forth (*lokādivāsanā*) come into being;
and when *sattva* arises, the divine endowment (*daivī saṃpat*) is produced. It is with this very intention that it has been said:
"When light arises through all the gates in this body,
and knowledge [arises], then one should know that *sattva* has increased" (Bhagavadgītā 14.11).
When *tamas* predominates, the demonic endowments arise. When *rajas* predominates, the three desires—such as for fame and so forth—take place. When *sattva* predominates, the...
Divine endowments arise. With this in view, it has been said:
"When, through every sense in this body, the light..."
"When knowledge flows forth, then it should be known that *sattva* is predominant" (BG 14.11).
Although the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) appears to consist of the three *guṇas*, nevertheless, *sattva* alone is its primary material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*).

Rajas and tamas, however, are the supporters (*upaṣṭambhaka*). The components that serve as the auxiliary causes for the material substrate (*upādāna*) are the supporters. For this very reason, when rajas and tamas have been removed through the practice of yoga by the knower, pure *sattva* alone remains as his essential nature (*svarūpa*).
With this very point in mind, it has been said: "The mind of the knower becomes non-mind; the mind of the knower is called *sattva*."
Although the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) appears to be composed of the three guṇas, sattva alone is its primary material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa).
Rajas and tamas are merely supports. Those parts which...
Those which become supports for the primary material cause are called *upastambhakas*— props. Therefore, through yogic practice,
when *rajas* and *tamas* are eliminated from the mind...
For the Knower, only *sattva* remains, which is his very nature. With this in view, it is said: "The mind of the Knower is not a mind at all, for it is called *sattva*" (LYV 6.3.13, adapted).

And that *sattva* is one-pointed because it is devoid of the quality of *rajas*, which is the cause of instability; it is subtle because it is devoid of the quality of *tamas*, which is the cause of the forms of gross objects whose nature as non-self is imagined through delusion. Therefore, it is fit for the vision of the Self. For this very reason, the Śruti says:
"But it is seen by those of subtle vision through a sharp and subtle intellect" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.12).
And that *sattva* is one-pointed because it is free from...
Rajas is the cause of motion; and it is also subtle, because it is free from tamas— the cause of the gross forms of non-self objects imagined through delusion.
Therefore, this *sattva* is fit to perceive the Self. Hence the Śruti says:
"It can be seen by those subtle-seers through their sharpened..."
and subtle intelligence" (Katha Upaniṣad 1.3.12).
Indeed, it is not possible to discern the characteristics of jewels, pearls, and the like by means of a lamp flickering in the wind;
nor is it possible to sew a fine cloth with a needle using a thick mattock. Such is this very *sattva* among those who are unattached (*ayogins*).
The mind becomes conscious through the quality of *rajas* permeated by the quality of *tamas*, conceptualizing through various dualistic constructions.
When that mind is dominated by the quality of *tamas*, it becomes swollen, accumulating the demonic (*āsuri*) disposition. Thus said Vasiṣṭha:
"In a light flickering with the wind, it is not possible..."
Nor can one ascertain the qualities of jewels, pearls, and the like [without the proper means]. Nor can fine cloth be sewn with a spade as it is with a needle.
Therefore, such *sattva* indeed becomes the *citta* for those who are not yogis.
Under the influence of *rajas* mixed with *tamas*, through the awareness of many dualistic thoughts,
this *citta* becomes fat by the accumulation of *tamas*.
Regarding the demonic endowments, Vasiṣṭha spoke as follows:
"By identifying the self with what is not the self, by the notion that the body is the self,
and likewise through children, wives, and family, the mind becomes swollen with attachment."
Through the transformation of egoism, by the play of the impurity of "mine-ness," and through the notion that "this is mine," the mind becomes swollen with attachment.
Through the play of mental and physical afflictions, through consolation in the cycle of existence,
and through the distinction between what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, the mind attains fullness.
Through affection, greed for wealth, the gain of jewels and women,
and that which is pleasant at first sight, the mind becomes swollen with attachment.
"By drinking the milk of false hopes, by the force of the wind of enjoyments,
and by the movement of grasping at existence, the serpent of the mind attains fullness.
(Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 24.17–21).
By regarding what is not-self as self, and by the thought "This is my body," and by [regarding] sons, wife, and relatives as "mine," the *citta* becomes swollen. (LYV 24.17) *Jīvan-mukti-viveka*
"Afflicted by the conceit of 'I,' delighting in the defiled sense of 'mine,' and with the notion 'this is mine,' the *citta* becomes swollen" (ibid. 24.18).
"By means of the faith and hope in this world— which is the playground of mental and physical illness and is imagined to consist of things acceptable and unacceptable— "
...the *citta* becomes inflated (ibid. 24.19).
"By means of affection (for worldly things), there arises lust for wealth and the acquisition of jewels and women, all of which appear..."
“Being very pleasing, the *citta* becomes inflated” (ibid. 24.20).
“The serpent of the mind, by feeding upon the milk of vain hopes, through the strength gained from the breath of...”
"By enjoying [them] and by wandering about to take up a place of dwelling, one becomes fat" (ibid. 24.21).
"Reliance" (*āsthā*) means the notion of reality regarding conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); its "taking up" (*ādāna*) is the acceptance [of it], and that itself is the "wandering" (*cāra*).
"By him" refers to the activity of going and coming. Thus, the nature of the two things to be destroyed—the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the mind (*manas*)—has been described.
*Āsthā* means the sense of reality regarding the phenomenal world; "taking" (*ādāna*) of that is its acceptance.
[It is] the non-existence (of the reality of the visible world); that alone is *carah*—wandering, going and coming by means of that—such is the meaning. Thus, in this manner, the nature of desire...
The mind that is to be dissolved is thus defined.

Now, the dissolution of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the destruction of the mind (*manonāśa*) are described in succession. Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha states the method for the dissolution of latent impressions:
"Bondage is indeed the bondage of latent impressions; liberation would be the dissolution of latent impressions."
Having abandoned latent impressions, abandon even the desire for liberation.
Having first abandoned mental impressions of sense objects,
take up the stainless impressions known as the meditations on friendliness and the other [divine abodes].
Having abandoned even those [internal impressions] within, and even while engaging with them,
remain with your inner affection most profoundly stilled, possessing only the latent impression of pure consciousness (cinmātra).
Having abandoned even that [consciousness] within, together with the mind and intellect...
"Remaining seated steadily in the remainder [of the practice], abandon that by which you abandon.
(Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 18.20–23). Now follows the effacement of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), such as desire.
The dissolution of the mind is being described respectively.
Regarding the destruction of desire, Vasiṣṭha spoke as follows:
“Bondage is indeed the bonds of desire, and liberation is their abandonment. Having renounced all desires, renounce even the desire for liberation” (ibid. 18.20).
"First renounce the desire for objects of enjoyment, then the desires of the mind, and possess within yourself pure desires such as thoughts of friendliness and so forth" (ibid. 18.21).

"Even while employing those thoughts of friendliness and so forth in practice, one should inwardly relinquish them and remain mentally unattached to them all, abiding solely in the desire for knowledge."
"Even that desire for knowledge, together with the mind and intellect, having abandoned internally, abiding in that..."
"Abandon that by which you renounce" (ibid. 18.23).
Here, by the term *mānasavāsanā* (mental impressions), the three previously mentioned impressions—of the world, of scripture, and of the body—are intended.

By the term *viṣayavāsanā* (sensory impressions), the demonic endowments such as hypocrisy, arrogance, and so forth, are intended. The distinction between mildness and intensity is the cause for this difference in their intended meaning.

Alternatively, sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are the objects (*viṣaya*). The latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by their state of being desired is *mānasavāsanā* (mental latent impression). The latent impression produced by their state of being experienced is *viṣayavāsanā* (object latent impression). In this view, the four previously mentioned [types of latent impressions] are included within these two alone, because no other latent impressions are possible apart from the internal and the external.

By the term *mānasavāsanā* (mental impression), the aforementioned three desires—namely, for fame, for learning, and for the body—are referred to. By the term *viṣayavāsanā* (desire for sense objects) [the other impressions are indicated]. *Jīvanmuktiviveka*.

*Viṣayavāsanā*—hypocrisy, insolence, and so forth—refers to the demonic endowments. These are mentioned individually because of their varying degrees of mildness and severity. Alternatively, it may be...
Let there be those sounds, touches, forms, tastes, and smells as objects;
the impressions formed while they are being desired are mental desire, and the impressions formed while they are...
The states that are being undergone are called desire for sense objects.
According to this interpretation, all four of the aforementioned desires are included within these two categories; since—
There is no desire other than internal and external desires.

Now, how can the abandonment of these latent impressions (*vāsanā*) be accomplished? For they possess no physical form by which we might lift them up with our hands and cast them outside, like dust and grass gathered by a broom.
Objection: How is this relinquishing of desires accomplished?
They possess no forms; otherwise, they could have been gathered together like dust and grass and taken up in the hands.

And [the objection that they] are cast out—let it not be so; for that is possible, as in the case of fasting and staying awake. Although the acts of eating and sleeping, which occur by natural necessity, are formless (*amūrta*), fasting and staying awake—which consist in the abandonment of those acts—are performed by everyone; let it be the same here as well.
Reply: It is not so. It is possible, just as in the case of fasting or forgoing sleep. Eating and sleeping are the natural activities of life;
though they are formless, people observe fasts and vigils in a formal manner.

If you argue that "renunciation" (tyāga) consists in remaining there with vigilance after having made a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) with a mantra such as, "Having remained today without food," and so forth— let it be the same way in this case as well.
Objection: In that case, remaining vigilant after undertaking the vow by reciting the formula, "I shall pass this day without food," and so forth, constitutes fasting— the renunciation of eating.
"Having remained today without food and having abandoned all enjoyments, tomorrow I shall eat, O Puṇḍarīkākṣa; O Acyuta, be my refuge."

In the *Padma Purāṇa*, *Uttara-khaṇḍa* (6.61.23), regarding this [practice] as well, it is not prohibited by that staff, because one is able to remain vigilant after having made a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) with the *preṣa-mantra*. This applies to those who lack the qualification for Vedic mantras.
If, then, there is the abandonment of the proximity of vegetables, soup, boiled rice, and so forth, even here;

and if, in that case, the mind were to be cherished with lutes and other instruments that cause one to forget hunger, sleep, laziness, and the like, then here too, one should cherish it with loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the other [immeasurables]. And as for loving-kindness and the others:

It was aphorized by Patañjali: "The clarification of the mind arises from the cultivation of friendliness, compassion, joy, and equanimity toward those who possess happiness, suffering, virtue, and vice" (Yoga Sūtra 1.33). Let it be understood through the commentary (*bhāṣya*) that this refers to volition (*saṃkalpa*). If therein...
Let there be the renunciation of proximity to garlands, sandalwood, and women;
let there be the listening to the Purāṇas, the worship of the gods, dancing, and singing.
Reply: In this case as well, that is not prohibited.
a staff. It is not impossible to remain alert after having taken the vow by uttering the *praīṣa* formula.
Those who are not entitled to pronounce the Vedic [mantras]...
Let them take the vow in their own language using the following formula: "If, in that case,
contact with rice, soup, vegetables, and so forth is avoided,
then in this case as well, let there be avoidance of contact with flower garlands."
One should avoid sandalwood paste and women. However, if in that state the mind is gladdened by the study of the Purāṇas,
the worship of deities, singing, dancing, and instrumental music, [it is permissible].
In order to keep it oblivious of hunger, sleep, and indolence,
so too in this case the mind should be caressed with thoughts of friendliness and the like. Friendliness and so forth—
It has been composed by Patañjali as follows: "Maitrī, karuṇā, muditā, and upekṣā, when cultivated with respect to objects that are happy, unhappy, virtuous, and non-virtuous respectively..."
"pacify the mind" (Patañjala Yogasūtra 1.33).
For the mind is indeed defiled by passion, hatred, merit, and demerit. And regarding passion and hatred, Patañjali set forth the aphorism:

"Attachment is that which lies latent in pleasure" (2.7); "Aversion is that which lies latent in pain" (2.8). A certain particular modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*) lies latent (*anuśete*) within the pleasure being experienced by oneself, [in the form]: "May everything of the nature of pleasure be mine. And because of the absence of the necessary collection of seen and unseen causes, that [desire] cannot be fulfilled. Therefore, that attachment turbidizes the mind.

When one cultivates loving-kindness (*maitrī*) toward those who are happy, thinking, "All these happy ones are mine," then, as one contemplates that their happiness has become one's own, attachment toward it ceases; just as, even in the absence of one's own kingdom, the kingdom of a son or other relative is considered one's own kingdom, so it is here. And when attachment has ceased, once the rains have passed—
The mind becomes serene like an autumnal river.
The mind is rendered impure by affection, aversion, virtue, and vice. Patañjali has also described affection and aversion in his aphorisms.
Thus it is said: "Attachment is that which dwells on pleasure" (2.7);
"Aversion is that which dwells on pain" (2.8).
When one experiences pleasure, there arises a certain mental transformation in the form "may all that is of the nature of pleasure be mine," which dwells upon that very pleasure.
Such desire for all kinds of pleasures remains unfulfilled due to the absence of means, whether visible or invisible.
Therefore, this attachment to pleasure [disturbs] the mind.
impure.
When one applies the thought of loving-kindness toward happy people in this way— "All these happy people are mine"— then by...
Thinking, "This happiness is, as it were, my own happiness," his attachment dissolves, just as one who possesses no kingdom of his own might think of his son’s kingdom as his own. When...
When the mind is freed from attachment, it becomes pure, just as an autumnal river becomes limpid after the rains have ceased.
Likewise, a certain condition dwells upon suffering, thinking: "May all such suffering never be mine at any time.

And that [suffering] cannot be prevented when diseases, enemies, tigers, and the like exist; nor can all causes of suffering be destroyed. Consequently, that hatred always burns the heart. When [one regards] all others as one's own self...
One should cultivate compassion toward suffering beings in this manner: "May there be no suffering that is contrary [to their wishes].
When enmity and other forms of hatred cease, the mind becomes serene. For this very reason it is recorded in the Smṛti:
"Just as one's own life is cherished, so too is the life of all beings."
The virtuous show compassion toward all living beings by treating them as they would themselves.

In the same way, there occurs a certain extraordinary transformation in the form of "may no such suffering ever befall me," which dwells upon the experience of suffering. This experience of suffering...
As long as diseases, enemies, tigers, and the like exist, they cannot be stopped; nor can all the causes of unhappiness be destroyed. Therefore, that hatred burns the heart at all times.

When one reflects, "Just as I do not wish for my own suffering, so too may the unfavorable suffering of all other beings not befall them," and thus feels compassion for all miserable creatures, then...
Hatred toward enemies and others dissolves, and the mind becomes pure. Therefore, the Smṛti says:
"As life is dear to me, so is it dear to other beings."
"The benevolent feel compassion for all beings, regarding them as equal to themselves" (Yatidharma-saṃgraha p. 31; Hitopadeśa, Mitralābha 19; Mahābhārata 13.116.21–22).
And great beings demonstrate that manner [of conduct] as follows:
"May all here be happy; may all be free from affliction;
may all behold auspicious things; and may no one experience suffering."
Great men demonstrate the manner in which this is done thus:
"May all here be happy and free from affliction; may they accomplish the welfare of their lives, and may none suffer pain."
In the Mahābhārata, the second line reads:
*śrīkṛṣṇa uvāca |* *bhagavaty āgate kāle kṣayaṃ yāsyanti mānavāḥ ||*

"Those of great soul and mature intellect should proceed by way of analogy with themselves. Thus it is said: "Living beings, by their very nature, do not practice virtue but rather practice sin. Regarding this, they say:
'Men desire the fruit of merit, yet they do not desire to perform the meritorious act.'"
"They do not desire the fruit of evil, yet they commit evil with great effort.
Thus it is said; for by their very nature, people do not practice virtue but indulge in vice.
"People desire the fruit of virtue but not virtue itself;
they commit evil with great care yet do not wish to experience its fruits. (Source untraced)
And those virtues and vices produce remorse; and that remorse is restated by the Śruti: "What good have I not done? What evil have I done? (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.9).
It describes thus: ‘Why have I not done what is right? Why have I done what is sinful? (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.9.1).
If one cultivates sympathetic joy (*muditā*) toward virtuous persons, then through that mental impression (*vāsanā*), one will spontaneously engage in meritorious deeds with vigilance.
Likewise, by cultivating equanimity (*upekṣā*) toward evildoers, one will personally refrain from evil. Thus, due to the absence of remorse, the mind becomes serene.
For one who cultivates loving-kindness (*maitrī*) toward those who are happy, not only is attachment (*rāga*) eliminated, but envy, jealousy, and other such states are also removed.
They cease. Envy (*asūyā*) is the manifestation of faults in others; jealousy (*īrṣyā*) is the inability to endure the virtues of others.
When, through the power of friendliness (*maitrī*), one regards that which belongs to another...

When that is accomplished, then, in accordance with what is appropriate, [compassion] is to be inferred toward the virtues of others. When hatred— which causes the killing of enemies and so forth— is eliminated for one who cultivates compassion toward those who suffer, then...

The pride conditioned by one's own happiness, which is the counter-positive of suffering, also ceases. And that pride was previously described in the section on egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) within the *asurasaṃpat*:
"Happiness is indeed one's own alone."
How could envy and the like possibly arise? In this same way, there is also the cessation of other defects.
If one practices sympathetic complacency (*muditā*) toward virtuous persons, then through that aspiration, one applies oneself with care.
righteous deeds. In the same manner, by practicing indifference toward the sinful, one becomes free from sin. Therefore, due to the absence of remorse, the *citta*...
becomes pure. *Jīvan-mukti-viveka*:
By exercising friendly thought toward the happy, not only is attachment discarded, but also malice and envy.
and so forth. *Asūyā* (malice)—meaning calumnious malignity—is finding fault with virtue; and *īrṣyā* (envy) is intolerance toward another’s [success].
virtue. When, through the influence of benevolent thoughts, the happiness of another truly becomes one’s own, then there remains...
There is no scope for finding fault with the virtues of others.
In the same manner, it should be understood that other defilements are likewise eliminated.
When hatred— the cause of killing enemies and so forth—
is removed from the mind through thoughts of compassion toward those who suffer, then pride is also eliminated.

This is caused by happiness, which is the opposite of misery. This pride was previously described in connection with the conceit of "I" (*asmimāna*) among the demonic endowments (*āsura-dharma*) as follows:
"I am the lord, I am the enjoyer, I am successful, powerful, and happy;
I am wealthy and well-born; who else is equal to me? (Bhagavad Gītā 16.14–15), and so forth.
"I am the lord, I enjoy, I am successful, powerful, and happy; I am wealthy and of noble birth. Who else is my equal?
Is it not said that for one who cultivates sympathetic joy toward those of meritorious nature, the engagement in merit becomes the fruit? And yet, that [joy] does not exist for the yogin.

[Objection: This is incorrect, because merit (*puṇya*) was previously included within "impure" (*malina*) mental impressions (*vāsanā*) derived from the scriptures, as has been illustrated before. [Reply: It is not so;

for in that context, rites performed out of desire (*kāmya*), such as *iṣṭāpūrta* and the like—which are causes for rebirth—were cited as examples of impurity. Here, however, what is intended is merit produced by the practice of yoga, which is neither white nor black (*aśuklākṛṣṇa*) and does not bring about rebirth.
Patañjali formulated [the aphorism] regarding the state of being neither white nor black:
"The practice of sympathetic complacency toward the virtuous results in [the accumulation of merit]. Objection: It has been stated that this leads to *jīvanmukti-viveka*.
And virtuous activity is not fitting for yogis, because it was previously described as being included within the impure desire for learning.

Reply: This need not be so. For, in that context, the *iṣṭāpūrta* karma—performed with desire and leading to rebirth—was described as impure; however, here it is that very same merit which is intended.
It does not lead to rebirth because, through the practice of yoga, it has become "neither black nor white. The state of being "neither white nor black" is described by Patañjali as follows:

"Karma is neither white nor black for the yogi; it is of three kinds for others" (4.7). Desirable karma is "white" because it is prescribed; prohibited karma is "black"; and mixed karma is "white-black. These three accrue to others, namely those who are not yogis.
And that [karma] bestows a threefold birth. Thus say the teachers of the Viśvarūpa school:
"For yogis, actions are neither white nor black;
for others, they are of three kinds— black, white, and mixed" (Yoga Sūtra 4.7).
Work performed with motivation is said to be white—pure; that which is prohibited is black; and that which is mixed is both white and black.
Thus, these three types of action pertain to other people who are not yogis.
And it brings about three kinds of birth. As has been stated by Viśvarūpācārya:
"By auspicious deeds one attains the state of a deity; by prohibited deeds, the destiny of hell."
"Helplessly, one obtains human birth through both merit and demerit.
— (Naiṣkarmyasiddhi 1.41).
"By good deeds, the state of a god is attained, and by [evil] deeds..."
"Those who are prohibited [from action] are consigned to perdition, and by both good and evil together they inevitably reach the human state" (Naiṣkarmyasiddhi 1.41).
If it is argued that although yoga is not black because it is not prohibited, it must nevertheless be white because it is enjoined—
How, then, is it said to be neither white nor black?
Not so; for the statement that it is not white is intended to mean that it is undesired. Therefore, the yogin’s engagement with merit that is neither white nor black is required.
Reply: This is not so, because yoga is described as "non-white" (aśukla) on the grounds that it is performed without motive.
Therefore, yogis practice such merit as is neither [black nor white].
Neither white nor black.

Now, one might object: "By this same logic, even yogins, having cultivated sympathetic joy (*muditā*) toward those whose nature is merit as appropriate, would proceed only toward meritorious actions."
Objection: By this method, even yogis who practice appropriate equanimity toward virtuous persons would be prompted to perform only virtuous deeds.
Let them indeed proceed; for those who clarify the mind through loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the other [immeasurables] are alone considered practitioners (*yogins*).

The tetrad beginning with loving-kindness is an illustration; by it, the divine endowment (*daivasampat*) such as "fearlessness, purity of being" (*Bhagavadgītā* 16.1), as well as the means to knowledge (*jñānasādhana*) such as "humility, lack of hypocrisy" (*ibid.* 13.7), are included.

It is so because it takes the form of auspicious latent impressions (*śubhavāsanā*), thereby bringing about the cessation of impure latent impressions (*malinavāsanā*), as described in such passages as those concerning the "one liberated while living" (*jīvanmukta*) and the "one of steady wisdom" (*sthitaprajña*);
furthermore, religious duties (*dharma*) are also indicated [by this].
Reply: Let them do so, for those who purify their minds through friendliness and other such qualities are indeed true yogis.

The quartet beginning with friendliness implies other analogous virtues— such as the divine endowments mentioned in the *Bhagavadgītā* (16.1), "Fearlessness, purity of heart," and so forth— as well as the means to them.
Knowledge such as "humility, unpretentiousness" (ibid.
13.7) and other such virtues mentioned in the descriptions of the *jīvanmukta* and the *sthitaprajña* are implied, since all of these...
If it is argued: "Noble desires eliminate impure desires.
But surely there are infinite noble tendencies (*śubhavāsanā*), and it is not possible for a single person to practice them all; moreover, such an effort in practice would be useless."
Objection: There are innumerable virtuous desires, and it is impossible to practice them all; therefore, the attempt to practice them is futile. *Jīvanmuktiviveka*
No, no; for it is impossible for all those impure latent impressions (*malinavāsanā*) that are to be removed by them—which are infinite—to exist within a single mind.
Indeed, it is not possible for one person to consume all the medicines prescribed in Ayurveda, nor can all the diseases to be cured by them be eliminated at once.

These arise within the body of a single individual. If this is so, then one should first examine one's own mind; whenever and however many defiled latent impressions (*vāsanā*) exist there, one should practice their opposites—namely, virtuous latent impressions—to that same extent.

Just as one who is tormented by children, friends, wife, and so forth, becomes detached from them and takes up the life of a wandering mendicant (*pārivrājya*) to bring about their cessation, so too [should one act].

One should practice discernment (*viveka*) against those impure latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) such as pride in learning, pride in wealth, pride in noble lineage, and pride in conduct; and that discernment was demonstrated by Janaka when,
being oppressed, he [perceived] its opposite.
"Those who today stand at the head of the great will, alas, fall low within days;
O mind, what kind of misplaced confidence is this of yours regarding greatness?
(Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 19.39).
Reply: This is not so, because all these endless impure desires, which are to be destroyed by those [remedies], do not arise in one's mind.
Furthermore, it is not possible for one person to take all the medicines.
Not all the diseases mentioned in the Āyurveda, nor all those curable by those medicines, actually occur in one’s body. Therefore,
one should first ascertain in one’s mind the number of [diseases].
At a given time, one should cultivate an equal number of wholesome aspirations that are the opposites of the impure desires; for example,
when one is distressed by a wife, children, and other relatives, and having become...
Becoming disgusted with all these, one takes to *saṃnyāsa* in order to eliminate them entirely. Likewise, one who is tormented by the pride of learning, wealth, and family lineage...
Those with such impure desires should practice the opposite discernment; and that discernment was described by Janaka as follows:
“Those who are at the pinnacle of greatness today will fall within a few days; alas, O mind, what kind of faith is this that you have in greatness? (LYV 19.39)
Where are the treasures of the lords of the earth, or where are the worlds of Brahmā?
Those of former times have passed away; what is this confidence of yours?
Millions of Brahmās have gone by, and successions of heavens have vanished.
"The kings have departed like dust; what stability can there be in my life?
"For whom the closing and opening of the eyes are the dissolution and arising of the world."
"Such men as those have perished; what account can there be of people like me? — (ibid., 19.49). "Where have the riches of kings gone? And where..."
"Have the earlier worlds of Brahmā also passed away? What kind of faith is this of yours [in eternity]? (ibid. 19.41).
"Tens of millions of Brahmās (the creators) have passed away..."
The successive heavens have also passed away; the kings have vanished like dust; what is this faith of mine in life?
“Those men, by whose closing and opening of the eyelids the dissolution and creation of the world were caused, have passed into oblivion; how could there be any counting of men such as we? (Ibid.)

Now, one might object: "Is this discrimination (*viveka*) not also prior to the arising of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), since the knowledge of Brahman is impossible without the means such as the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities? Here, however, the undertaking is to explain the means for the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*) and so forth for the sake of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) by one who has already attained the direct realization of Brahman; therefore, why this sudden, frantic dance? If you ask this:
Objection: This discrimination also precedes the arising of the knowledge of truth, since the knowledge of Brahman is not possible in the absence of its means.

In the form of the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal things and so forth; here, in this treatise, [it concerns] the means for one [to attain] *jīvanmukti*, such as the eradication of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the like.
Since one who has already realized Brahman is the subject under discussion,
why this sudden, frantic dancing (that is, the introduction of discrimination at this stage is entirely unnecessary)?

This is not a fault. That the knowledge of Brahman follows for one endowed with the fourfold means (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*) is the grand, royal road common to all persons. In the case of Janaka, however, through the ripening of a mass of prior merit, the knowledge of reality arose suddenly—like the falling of a fruit from the sky—as soon as he heard the *Gītā*. Therefore, this discrimination (*viveka*) is being undertaken for the sake of the mind’s rest.
"This *tāṇḍava* dance is appropriate only for the *kāṇḍa*.
Response: "There is no fault in this. One should first accomplish the fourfold means (*catuṣṭaya-sādhana*) and then [attain] knowledge."
This scheme, known as the "we-path" (*vayam-mārga*),
is well-known as the royal road for all people in general; however, as soon as Janaka heard the *Siddhagītā* (YV 5.8.9–18), he realized [the truth].
The truth came upon him suddenly; this windfall was, of course, the consequence of his accumulated past virtues. Thereafter, the practice of this discernment was undertaken.
In order to bring the mind to rest, it is highly relevant to introduce discrimination at this stage. But even so, what of this discrimination?

If it is argued that because [the mind] is cultivated immediately after knowledge, there is no lack of continuity and thus the practice of pure latent impressions (*śuddhavāsanā*) is not required, [then consider] the impure latent impression (*malinavāsanā*)—

Objection: Even if this were so, the application of pure desire (*śuddha-chanda*) is not required, since there is an absence of the continuity of impure desire (*aśuddha-chanda*) caused by conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).
It does not necessarily follow that [the knower] immediately follows [that knowledge];
for although there is no such following by the progenitor (janaka), we observe such following in the cases of Yājñavalkya, Bhagīratha, and others.
Indeed, Yājñavalkya, as well as his opponents Uṣasta, Kahola, and the rest, possessed a great pride of learning (*vidyāmada*), and all of them—
[Objection: Because this is occurring within a debate for victory (*vijigīṣukathā*).
[Reply: This is not so; for even though it is absent in Janaka, it is found in Yājñavalkya, Bhagīratha, and others.
Even Yājñavalkya and his opponents, Uṣasta, Kahola, and the others, all possessed vast pride in their learning, insofar as they all entered into debate desiring victory.
If it be objected: "They possessed only other branches of learning, but not the knowledge of Brahman," we reply: [as follows].
No,
for in that discussion,
both the questions and the answers are found to concern Brahman.
Brahman.

[Objection: Even though Brahman is the object of those [scriptural passages], there is only a superficial understanding (*āpātataḥ jñānam*), and not perfect knowledge (*samyagvedana*). If this is argued:
Since they possessed only indirect knowledge and not perfect knowledge,
if that were the case, it would follow that the Brahma-vidyā produced by their words in us would likewise be imperfect.
Reply: That cannot be said, because in that case, our knowledge of Brahman arising from those statements would also become imperfect— that is, indirect knowledge (parokṣa).
If it is argued that even though it is perfect, it is nevertheless only indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*), then [the response is as follows]:

No; for we observe that the specific questions asked were directed precisely toward the primary immediate [perception] of Brahman, as stated in *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.4.1: "That Brahman which is immediate and direct."
It is particularly concerned with the directness and immediacy of the knowledge of Brahman, as expressed in the passage: "That Brahman which is direct and immediate" (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.1).

Objection: But surely the Ācārya (Śaṅkara) does not accept that one who knows the Self may possess the pride of knowledge (*vidyāmada*); for it has been stated thus in the *Upadeśasāhasrī*: [text follows]
For the knower of the Self, there is no conceit regarding learning;
as it has been stated in the *Upadeśasāhasrī*: "One who possesses the knowledge of Brahman is truly a knower of the Self, and no other" (12.13).
"And he who also relinquishes the conceit of being a 'knower of Brahman' is a knower of the Self; others are not" (ibid. 12.13).
Also in the *Naiṣkarmyasiddhi*:
"Even the conceit of being a knower of the self does not exist for the wise one, because it is demonic in nature;
if even the wise one were demonic, the vision of Brahman would be fruitless" (1.75).
If this is argued,
it is also stated thus in the *Naiṣkarmyasiddhi* (of Sureśvarācārya):
"There can be no pride of learning in one who knows Brahman, for such qualities belong to the demonic; if even a knower of Brahman were to suffer from this demonic trait,"
"Then his knowledge of Brahman is futile" (ibid. 1.75).

This is not a fault, because what is intended there is the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) culminating in liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). Indeed, we too do not admit that those liberated while living possess the pride of learning (*vidyāmada*).
Reply: There is no harm; for the knowledge referred to in the cited passages is intended to culminate in *jīvanmukti*. Furthermore, we certainly do not approve of such pride.
Regarding the knowledge of those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*):
now, it might be argued that one who desires victory possesses no self-knowledge at all,
for "passion is the sign of a lack of awakening amidst the fields of mental exertion."
How can there be lushness for that tree in whose hollow there is fire?
If it is argued that this is because it has been accepted by the Teachers [in the *Naiṣkarmyasiddhi* 4.67],
[we reply: Furthermore, there is not even self-knowledge.
In one who desires to defeat others, since the Ācārya (Sureśvara) has agreed to this as follows: "Attachment to the grounds upon which the mind exercises [its functions]... [Jīvanmuktiviveka].
[The presence of] sound and so forth indicates the absence of knowledge. How can a tree remain verdant when there is fire within its hollow? (Naiṣkarmyasiddhi 4.67)
"No; let passion and the rest exist as much as they wish, for their presence does not constitute a fault.
(Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārttika 1.4.1539)
"Like a serpent whose fangs have been pulled out, what can ignorance do?
(In that same work, 1.4.1746).

This is not so, because the Ācārya [Sureśvara] accepts passion and the other afflictions in those very [states]. Nor is there any mutual contradiction here, since the two statements are appropriately applied to the one of steady wisdom and the mere knower respectively.
He himself approves of such matters in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka-vārttika* as follows:
"Let attachment and the rest remain at their ease; their..."
"Merely being present cannot cause offense. What harm can ignorance (*avidyā*) inflict, like a serpent whose fangs have been extracted? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Bhāṣya Vārttika 1.4.1539.2).
And there is no contradiction between these two positions, insofar as they can be so arranged as to apply respectively to one whose wisdom is established (*sthitaprajña*) and to a simple knower.
Now, if it is argued that if passion and the like are admitted for a person of knowledge, then there would necessarily follow rebirth by way of merit and demerit;
[this is the objection].
[If it is argued that] virtue and vice [are the causes], and these in turn lead to rebirth—
do not say so; for only desire and the like, preceded by ignorance, function as primary passion and so forth, and thus constitute the cause of renewed birth, just like an unburnt seed.

For the wise, however, passion and the like appear as mere semblances, like burnt seeds. With this very point in mind, it is said in the *Jīvanmuktiviveka*: "Passion and the like, as they arise, are burned at that very moment by the fire of discriminative knowledge; how then can they sprout?"
(Varāhopaniṣad 3.24–25).
Response: This is not so. Attachment and the other afflictions produced by ignorance are the actual [afflictions], just as uncooked seeds [are incapable of sprouting].
This is the cause of rebirth. As for those who have realized [the truth], however, their attachment and so forth— like parched seeds— are mere appearances and thus cannot cause rebirth.
The idea is expressed as follows:
"As soon as attachment and the other afflictions arise, they are incinerated right then and there by the fire of discernment. From where could they [re-emerge]?"
"Will they sprout again? (Vājasaneyi Upaniṣad 3.24–25). If it is argued: "Then let those [desires] belong to the one of steady wisdom as well," this is the objection.

No, because at that time, those things appearing as if they were primary are indeed sublaters; for even a rope-snake is perceived at that moment as being terrifying just like a real snake, and it is the same in this case.

Reply: Not so, because at that time even the apparent attachment and so forth act as obstacles to the state of one whose wisdom is steady (sthitaprajña), just like real ones. Even the [illusory] snake in a rope...

At the time of its perception, it causes fear just like a real snake. If it is argued that, in such a case, there is no sublation whatsoever because the continuous contemplation of its appearance-as-such persists, [we reply:]...
Objection: In that case, attachment and the rest would be unable to cause any obstruction if they were recollected merely as appearances.

May you live long! This indeed is our desired liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). Yājñavalkya, however, was not in such a state during his period of seeking victory (*vijigīṣā*), because he was about to undertake the renunciation of the knower (*vidvatsaṃnyāsa*) for the sake of the mind’s rest. In the *Jīvanmuktiviveka*, it is stated that he possessed not only a desire for victory, but even a great thirst for wealth, since [he encountered] many knowers of Brahman...
Having stolen away a thousand cows adorned with ornaments that had been placed before him, he himself said: "We pay homage to the one most devoted to Brahman;
we are merely desirous of cattle" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.1.2).
Response: (In that case,) we say, "May you live long. For this...
This is the *jīvanmukti* that we accept.
However, Yājñavalkya was certainly not in such a state while he was still desirous of victory in debate, since he was yet to...
