He took the *vidvatsaṃnyāsa* in order to bring his mind to rest.
Not only was he desirous of victory, but he also possessed a great thirst for wealth; for, while carrying away a thousand...
Having placed cows adorned with gold before an assembly of many knowers of Brahman, he himself spoke thus: "We bow to the most wise among the Brāhmaṇas, yet we merely desire to obtain— "
"the cows" (Br. Up. 3.1.2).
If it is argued that this is merely a certain rhetorical device intended to disparage other knowers of Brahman— Objection:
It may well be that he [uses this] to insult other knowers...

...of Brahman, spoke euphemistically. But then there is this further fault: other knowers of Brahman, thinking that their own wealth had been stolen by him, became enraged. Overcome by anger, he killed Śākalya with a curse. And for this slayer of a knower of Brahman—

One might suspect the absence of liberation; for the Kauṣītakins record: "His world is not destroyed by any deed—not by matricide, nor by patricide, nor by theft, nor by the slaying of an embryo" (3.1).
Reply: That is merely another enumeration of offenses. The other...
The knowers of Brahman became incensed, thinking that he had taken away their wealth; however, in a fit of anger, he cursed Śākalya to death. Indeed, one should not suppose—
This slayer of a Brāhmaṇa has no liberation, insofar as the Kauṣītakins read:
"By no action whatsoever of his is his world harmed."
"By stealing, not by killing an embryo, not by the killing of his mother, not by the killing of his father" (Kena Upaniṣad 3.1). Furthermore, Śeṣa said this in his own work, the *Āryāpañcāśīti*:
"Even if one performs hundreds of thousands of horse-sacrifices or commits hundreds of thousands of murders of Brahmins,
the knower of the ultimate reality remains stainless, untouched by merits or sins" (Paramārthasāra 77).
Śeṣa has also stated this in his *Āryāpañcāśīti* (Paramārthasāra 77):
"The knower of the supreme truth, being devoid of all..."
Impurities remain untouched by the merit earned through a hundred thousand horse-sacrifices and by the demerit of killing a lakh of Brahmins. (From the *Paramārthasāra* or *Āryāpañcāśikā*)
Śīti 77).
Therefore, what need is there for much? Even for those knowers of Brahman such as Yājñavalkya and others, there is indeed the persistence of impure latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Bhagīratha, however, although he had realized the Truth, while governing the kingdom, found that his mind lacked repose due to those impure latent impressions.
Vasiṣṭha relates that [the sage] rested only after renouncing everything; therefore, with this very intention, one's own present defect of impure latent impressions (vāsanā) is remembered as follows:
Having correctly observed the faults of others, one should practice their remedy;
just as one who is very skillful is devoted to the thorough observation of another's faults.
"If that were so, what skillful person would not be liberated from bondage?
(Varāhopaniṣad 3.25).
Thus, Yājñavalkya and other knowers of Brahman were not...
Since it is free from the persistence of impure desires, there is no need for further discussion.
Vasiṣṭha has related the story of Bhagīratha.
Though he knew the Reality, he could not find peace of mind due to impure desires while ruling his kingdom; subsequently, having renounced everything, he attained it.
Peace.
Therefore, one should investigate the fault of impure desire within oneself with as much care as one does in others, and strive to counteract it.

With this idea in view, it is said thus in the *Smṛti*: "People display extraordinary skill in finding the faults of others; if they were to display equal skill in finding their own faults," [the world would be transformed]. *Jīvanmuktiviveka*.
"Who will remain unfreed? (Varāha Upaniṣad 3.25).
Now, if it is asked: "In the first place, what is the remedy for the intoxication of knowledge?
[Objection: Then, in the first place, what is the cure for...
Regarding the pride of knowledge:
is it the intoxication directed toward others while rooted in oneself, or is it the intoxication directed toward oneself while rooted in others?
In the first case, one should constantly reflect that a downfall will inevitably occur somewhere; for example, Śvetaketu was intoxicated by his learning.

Having gone to the assembly hall of King Pravāhaṇa, when questioned by him regarding the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgni-vidyā*), he, being ignorant himself and unable to provide an answer, was severely rebuked by the king. Returning to his father, he expressed his despondency. But the father, free from pride, followed that very king and obtained that knowledge. And the arrogant Bālāki, having been rebuked by King Ajātaśatru, [lost his] pride.

Having abandoned the king, he approached [the sage]. Uṣasta, Kahola, and others, having engaged in conversation with pride, were defeated. One should reflect: "When pride, which is established upon another, prevails within my own domain, then let that other person, being intoxicated, revile me or despise me;
in every way, there is no loss for me. For it is thus:

Response: Is the pride [directed] toward oneself and others as the objects [of contempt], or is it directed toward another person while you are the object [of that feeling of inferiority]? If it is of the first kind, then always...
Remember that at some point or another, your pride will be pulverized. For instance, Śvetaketu, who was exceedingly proud of his learning, went to the court of King Pravāhaṇa and was unable—
When questioned regarding the Pañcāgni-vidyā, he remained silent out of ignorance and was greatly ridiculed by the king. He returned to his father and related his dejection. His father, as...

A certain humble man went to that same king and learned the Pañcāgni-vidyā from him. Then Bālāki, filled with arrogance, having been rebuked by King Ajātaśatru, cast off his pride and sat down before him.
He served at the feet of the king as a student. Then Uṣasta, Kahola, and others, out of pride, entered into debate and were defeated.
When pride resides in another and you are its...
Then one should think: "He is very proud; let him speak ill of me or insult me, it cannot harm me in any way.
As it is said, for example, in the *Jīvan-mukti-viveka*:
"If they reproach themselves, they indeed reproach their own selves;
if they reproach their bodies, in my opinion, they are my companions."
"For that yogi for whom censure and contempt are absolute ornaments, how can his mental distraction be caused here by talkative people? Thus:
"If they malign me—the Self—truly they are maligning..."
[They revile] their own self. If they revile me—the body—they are my trusted friends. (Source untraced).
“For the yogi, for whom slander and humiliation are complete...”
"Since he is adorned with such ornaments, how could his mind be distracted by talkative people? (Source untraced).
From the *Naiṣkarmyasiddhi*:

"When the body has been completely relinquished and determined to be a defect, if one were to speak of a fault in it, what would that matter to the speaker? (2.16). "In the same way, when both the gross and the subtle bodies have been abandoned through discernment..."
If he were to speak of a fault to those two, what would that avail the wise man there? (2.17)

"Sorrow, joy, fear, anger, greed, delusion, longing, and so forth— these, as well as birth and death, are seen to belong to the ego (ahaṃkāra), and not to the Self (ātman). (Bhāgavatapurāṇa 11.28.16).
The *Naiṣkarmyasiddhi* states as follows:
"If someone, perceiving feces as harmful and having voided them, should find fault with them, what does that matter to one who [has realized the truth]?"
...did he discharge them? (ibid. 2.16).
"In the same manner, when the gross and subtle bodies are abandoned through discrimination, and someone finds fault..."
"What is that to the knower (who has renounced them)? (ibid. 2.17).
"Sorrow, happiness, fear, anger, greed, delusion, desire..."
"and so forth, even birth and death are found to belong to the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*),
not to the Self" (Śrīmad Bhāgavatam 11.28.16). Furthermore, that censure is actually an ornament has been shown in the *Jñānāṅkuśa*:
If people find satisfaction in censuring me,
then this favor is indeed easily obtained by me without effort;
for men who seek their own welfare do so for the sake of pleasing others.
They relinquish even those riches that were acquired with great hardship.
In this world of living beings, which is devoid of happiness and where dejection is ever-present and easily found, if someone should derive pleasure from my censure,
let them revile me as they wish, whether in my presence or behind my back.
"For in this world of manifold suffering, the attainment of joy is rare.
Thus was the figure of speech *apavāda* (calumny) treated as an ornament, as described in the *Jñānārṇava*.
‘If people take delight in despising me, let them do so,
for this favor of mine is bestowed upon them without effort. For even men who desire their own welfare must spend their lives [in such service].’
hard-earned money for the benefit of others.
‘In this world, happiness is hardly found, whereas sorrow is always obtained very easily. In such a state, if anyone...’
"Let him who seeks to achieve happiness by maligning me malign me freely,
whether in my presence or behind my back; for in this world of suffering, felicity is difficult to obtain."
The fact that contempt is an ornament is recorded in the Smṛti:
"A yogi should indeed conduct himself in such a way as not to violate the dharma of the virtuous,
so that people may hold him in contempt and do not seek his company."
"...as it is stated [in the *Nāradaparivrājaka Upaniṣad* 5.30].
Thus, humiliation as an ornament is recorded as follows:
"The yogi, without transgressing the conventional conduct..."
"A renunciant should conduct himself in such a way that people treat him with disregard and avoid his company" (Nārada Parivrājaka Upaniṣad 5.30).

Just as the remedy for the two types of pride in learning— those centered on oneself and those centered on others— as seen in the cases of Yājñavalkya, Uṣasta, and others, is understood through discernment, so too should it be understood for the desire for wealth and anger.
"There is suffering in the acquisition of riches, and likewise in their preservation."
"Suffering in its loss, suffering in its expenditure—fie on wealth, which causes only affliction!
Thus is the discernment regarding wealth.
Just as discrimination is the remedy for the pride of learning in Yājñavalkya, Uṣasta, and others in the aforementioned manner,
so too should it be understood that it is the remedy for greed and anger.
This is discrimination. Discrimination regarding covetousness is as follows:
“The earning of wealth is troublesome, and its preservation is likewise.”
"If lost or spent, it causes pain; fie upon wealth, the source of affliction" (Mahābhārata 13. App. 15, 3971 pr. and Pañcadaśī, Tīrthadīpa 139).

Anger, too, is of two kinds: that which resides in oneself and has another as its object, and that which resides in another and has oneself as its object. Regarding the former—anger residing in oneself directed toward another—it has been said:
"If you feel anger toward one who harms you, why do you not feel anger toward your own anger?"
"Violently obstructing dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
— (Yājñavalkyopaniṣad 20)
"If he is useless, tormenting his own body for the sake of fruit, dharma, and fame, then he destroys both dharma and fame.
The *Mahābhārata* text reads as follows:
"There is suffering in the acquisition of wealth, and suffering in the protection of what has been acquired;
there is suffering in its loss and suffering in its expenditure. Fie on wealth, the vessel of suffering!
That which is not for the benefit of the virtuous either in this world or the next—" [162]
"How could anger take refuge in the minds [of such people]? Thus it is said.
Anger, moreover, is of two kinds: the first resides within oneself and has others as its object; the second...
It exists in others, and one is its object. Regarding the discrimination of one who is angry with others, it is said:
"If you are angry with him who harms you, then..."
Why not be angry with anger itself—which greatly obstructs the attainment of the four aims of life: *dharma*, *artha*, *kāma*, and *mokṣa*? (Yājñavalkya Upaniṣad 20)
"Even if it succeeds [in punishing the offender], it destroys the morality, reputation,
and wealth of the angry person; if it fails, it merely torments his own body."
And the mind. How could anger, which is beneficial neither in this world nor in the next, take refuge in the hearts of the wise?
(Source untraced)
Regarding one's own object as being established in another, it has been said thus:
"I have committed no offense; why do men harbor malice toward me without cause?"—one should not even think in this way.
"Since no atonement for the bonds of former existences was performed by me,
let this supreme transgression be reflected upon.
Homage be to the God of Wrath, who fiercely burns his own abode!"
"To me, who am full of faults, you have granted dispassion and awakened my understanding of defects.
(Yājñavalkya Upaniṣad 21)
Regarding the second variety—namely, anger directed toward others while one is the object—it is said as follows:
"Do not even think: 'I have committed no wrong, yet these people [are angry with me].'"
"Are you angry with me? Always remember the greatest offense you have committed by not liberating yourself beforehand from the bondage of this worldly life. (Source untraced) *Jīvan-mukti-viveka*
"I bow to the God of Anger, who consumes his own seat and bestows upon me— the object of his anger— detachment by imparting the knowledge of my own faults" (Yājñavalkya Upaniṣad).

Just as desire for wealth and anger are to be abandoned through discernment (*viveka*), so too must desire for women and sons be abandoned through discernment. In this regard, the discernment concerning women has been shown by Vasiṣṭha:
In this woman, who is a puppet made of flesh, whose cage-like body is set in motion by machinery, and who is adorned with sinews, bones, and joints— what indeed is beautiful?
—(Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 2.90)
Attachment to wife and children should be removed by applying discernment, just as one removes anger and desire for wealth;
Vasiṣṭha has described the discernment regarding women.
Thus:
"What is beautiful there in a woman— a doll of flesh, a mechanical device constructed of muscles and bones?"
"Having separated the skin, flesh, blood, and tears from the eyes, look closely at them; if they are beautiful, why do you delude yourself in vain? (LYV 2.91)
"Examine closely the pair of eyes of a woman after analyzing their contents—skin, muscle, blood, and tears; if there is anything therein so charming as to be worthy of affection? (Ibid. 2.91).
In which breast the splendor of a pearl necklace was seen to possess a brilliance comparable to the rush of the Gaṅgā’s waters as they surge against the slopes of Mount Meru’s peaks. (2.92)
In cremation grounds at the ends of the quarters, that very same breast of a woman is devoured by dogs in due time, like a small lump of food. (2.93)
“The breasts of a woman, upon which the movement of a pearl necklace appears so radiant and whose elegance is comparable only to the swift-flowing waters of the Gaṅgā.”
Over Mount Meru, in due course, they are greedily devoured like a small morsel of food by dogs in the cremation grounds on the outskirts (ibid. 2.92, 93).164
"Women, bearing hair like soot, difficult to touch yet pleasing to the eye, burn men like straw—being the flames of the fire of their own misdeeds. (2.94)

“Women are like the flames of the fire of evil deeds; like the soot of those flames, they have black hair upon their heads; they are as captivating to the eye as the flames themselves; and like fire, they consume.”
Their touch brings misery; and just as fire consumes straw, they carry men away (ibid. 2.94):
"Though blazing even from afar, and though full of moisture, they are yet devoid of essence."
For women are the lovely yet terrible fuel for the fires of hell. || 2.95 ||
"When a log burns at its far end, the sap oozes from the near end and appears succulent, even though the burning end is dry.
In the same way, women are like fuel for the distant fires of hell."
They appear very charming, but in reality they are the source of misery (ibid. 2.95):
"Scattered by the hunter named Desire among those of deluded minds..."
Women are the snares for binding the limbs of men, who are like birds. ||2.96||
"The hunter whose name is lust has set women as snares to capture the bewildered human birds" (ibid. 2.96).
"Of those who are like fish in the pond of birth, moving in the mud of the mind..."
For men, a woman is a baited hook upon the rope of evil latent impressions.
"Men are like fish in the pond of birth and death— that is, in this world; they take delight, as it were, in the turbidity of the mind, and impure desire is like the fishing line."
"With women as both the hook and the bait" (ibid. 2.97):
"May I always be thoroughly defiled by this woman, who is a small box for all the jewels of faults and a chain of suffering" (2.98).
"Women are, as it were, a casket containing the jewels of evil; they are like an endless chain of misery; I have no concern with them" (ibid. 2.98). *Jīvan-mukti-viveka*
"O Brahmin, in just a few days, a woman goes to ruin, [with the thought]: 'Here is flesh, here is blood, and here are bones. (2.99)
"O Brāhmaṇa (Vasiṣṭha)! This body of a woman will, in a few days, fall apart; her flesh, blood, and bones will be scattered here, there, and elsewhere" (ibid. 2.99).
"He who has a woman desires sexual enjoyment; for one without a woman, where is the ground for enjoyment?
Having abandoned the woman, the world is abandoned; having abandoned the world, one becomes happy. (2.100) "He who has a woman, wants to make love with her;"
And he who is devoid of woman is devoid of passion; by abandoning woman one abandons the world, and by abandoning this world one becomes happy (ibid. 2.100).
The separation from one's son is shown in the *Brahmānanda*:
"A son not obtained causes his parents long-lasting distress;
even when obtained, he afflicts them through miscarriage and the pains of childbirth."
(From the *Pañcadaśī*, 12.65)
Discrimination regarding a son has been described in the *Pañcadaśī*, in the section on *Brahmānanda*, as follows:
"If there is a delay in conceiving [a child], parents become unhappy..."
Childhood. Once conceived, they are in constant fear of miscarriage;
otherwise, there is still the pain of childbirth. As it is said:
"For one who has been born, there are the afflictions of seizing spirits and diseases; and for the youth, there is stupidity."
But when [a son] has been brought near, ignorance results; and for a learned man, there is no marriage.
"When born, parents are always anxious during childhood lest he should suffer from seizures or other diseases; then there arises the fear that the child might turn out to be..."
An idiot; when sent to the teacher, there is anxiety that he might be negligent in his studies, and if well-educated, he might not find a suitable match (ibid. 12.66).166

"Furthermore, there is poverty resulting from [the sin of] adultery with another's wife and so forth for the family members; there is no end to the suffering of one's parents; and if a wealthy man dies [under such circumstances], then [he too suffers]. (Pañcadaśī 12.65–67).

Furthermore, when the son has reached adulthood, the parents are anxious that he might commit adultery; if he is a householder, they fear he may suffer from poverty, or even if he earns sufficient wealth, [they worry about its loss].
"Even if one is wealthy, one eventually dies; thus, at no time are parents free from suffering" (ibid. 12.67).
Just as there is a remedy for impure latent tendencies (*vāsanā*)—such as those directed toward knowledge, wealth, anger, women, sons, and sense objects—through discernment (*viveka*):

One should also discern the defects of other latent impressions (*vāsanā*) as appropriate, through the scriptures and by one's own reasoning, and apply a remedy. Once the remedy has been applied, the supreme state characterized by liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) is attained. Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha said:
The way impure desires regarding learning, wealth, [and power...]
Anger, women, and children are cured by discrimination;
in the same way, other desires should be countered through discrimination that ascertains their faults by means of scripture.

One should perform the necessary rites and self-reflection as required. Once the counteractive measures have been applied, the supreme goal—described as *jīvanmukti* (liberation while living)—is attained.
As Vasiṣṭha has said:
"If you exert yourself sufficiently in the abandonment of latent impressions (*vāsanā*),
then all mental and physical afflictions will instantly become slackened.
(Yogavāsiṣṭha Rāmāyaṇa, Upaśama-prakaraṇa, 92.9)
"If you exert yourself sufficiently to renounce your desires, then all your afflictions— both mental and physical— will dissolve in an instant" (Yogavāsiṣṭha, Upaśama-prakaraṇa, 92.9).
"If you firmly establish your state by forcibly abandoning latent impressions through human effort, then you will surely attain the supreme state. (Ibid.,
‘If, through vigorous personal effort, you can eliminate desires and remain steadfast, then you will surely attain that state’ (ibid. 92.3, 4). Jīvan-mukti-viveka.

Now, in this context, human effort refers to the discernment of the defects of sense-objects mentioned previously. Even when that is practiced again and again, it is overcome by the powerful activity of the senses. As it was said by the Blessed One:
"For even for a wise man, O son of Kuntī, though he strives..."
The turbulent senses violently carry away the mind.
(Bhagavadgītā 2.60)
By "personal effort" here is meant the discernment of the faults— the evils— of the object of desire, as was stated previously. However, this is defeated even after repeated practice.
by the activities of the exceedingly powerful senses. And the Lord has said thus:
"The turbulent senses, O son of Kuntī (Arjuna), forcibly..."

"For even the wisdom of a wise man striving for perfection is carried away when the mind follows after the wandering senses; it snatches his discernment away, just as the wind carries off a ship upon the waters."
(tatraiva 2.67) Thus:
"For even one of the wandering senses, if the mind yields to it, carries away discernment, just as a gale carries away a ship."
"a ship upon the waters" (ibid. 2.67).
Thus, then, for the sake of protecting the discernment that has arisen, the senses must be restrained. That too has been shown in the two subsequent verses of that same work:
Restraining all these, let him sit disciplined, intent on Me;
for he whose senses are under control, his wisdom is firmly established.
— (In that very same place, 2.61) ||
Therefore, for the protection of the discernment that has arisen, the senses must be restrained. This too has been described there in the following two verses:
"The yogi restrains them all and remains intent on Me. Steady is his wisdom whose senses are under control" (Bhagavad Gītā 2.61).
"Therefore, O mighty-armed one, for him whose senses are completely restrained from the objects of the senses, his wisdom is firmly established. (Ibid., 2.68).
"Therefore, O mighty Arjuna, his wisdom is steady whose senses are completely restrained from their objects" (ibid. 2.68).
In another Smṛti as well: "A renunciant should not be fickle with his hands or feet, nor fickle with his eyes, nor indeed fickle with his speech; such is the characteristic of a disciplined man."
Another *smṛti* also states as follows: "The hands, feet, and eyes of an ascetic are not restless, nor are his words unrestrained; these are the marks [of such a one]."
"By which the wise man is known" (cf. Vasiṣṭha Smṛti 6.38;
Mahābhārata 14.45.18).
This very point has been clarified elsewhere through both summary and detailed exposition:
"One who is tongueless, a eunuch, a cripple, blind, deaf,
and deluded— a monk liberated by these six [conditions] has no doubt."
(Nāradaparivrājakopaniṣad 3.62) | This very same [truth] has been explained in other scriptures both briefly and in detail as follows:
“The mendicant who is tongueless, impotent, lame, blind,
deaf, and simple-minded is undoubtedly liberated through these six qualities” (Nārada Parivrājaka Upaniṣad 3.62).
(a) A Brahmin should not be fickle with his hands or feet, nor should he be fickle with his eyes; nor should he be restless—this is the sphere of conduct for the disciplined. (Mṛcchakaṭika 6.39)
(b) The sage who is not fickle with his hands or feet, nor fickle with his eyes, and who is not fickle in speech or limb—such a one is within the sphere of the disciplined. (Mahābhārata 14.45.18)
(c) He is not fickle with his hands or feet, nor fickle with his eyes, nor crooked;

he is not fickle with his speech, nor does he frequent the company of the uncultured. (Skanda Purāṇa, Māheśvara Khaṇḍa, Kumārikā Khaṇḍa, 41.139–40). "He who, even while eating, does not become attached, thinking 'this is desirable' or 'this is not,' and who speaks what is beneficial, true, and measured—that one they call 'tongueless' (ajihva). (3.63).
“He who, even while eating, does not concern himself with the pleasantness or unpleasantness of the food,
whose speech is wholesome, moderate, and truthful, is called— ”
"Regarding the 'tongueless' (ibid. 3.63):
'He who, upon seeing a woman whether she has just been born, is sixteen years old, or is a hundred years old, remains without any change of emotion—he is a eunuch. (3.64)
"He who remains as unperturbed at the sight of a sixteen-year-old girl as he would at the sight of a one-day-old infant or a hundred-year-old woman is called a eunuch" (ibid. 3.64).
He who wanders no further than a yojana for the sake of alms or for the evacuation of excrement and urine—he is in every respect truly a pañjura. (3.65)
"He who moves only for the sake of begging food and relieving himself, and even then no further than a *yojana* (no more than nine miles), is indeed a cripple" (ibid. 3.65).
"He whose vision does not reach far, whether standing or walking, having abandoned the earth with its four ages—that wanderer is called blind. (3.66)
“The sannyāsin is called blind whose range of vision is limited to sixteen cubits, whether standing still or moving about” (ibid. 3.66).
"He who, having heard speech that is beneficial, measured, pleasing, and dispelling of grief, does not hear it as if he were deaf—he is proclaimed to be a deaf man. (3.67)
"He who, though as if hearing, does not hear the moderate, wholesome, pleasing, and consoling words,"
"He is called the deaf" (ibid. 3.67).
"Though in the presence of sense-objects and capable with unimpaired senses, he who always behaves as if asleep is called a bewildered mendicant" (3.68). *Jīvan-mukti-viveka*.
The mendicant who is capable of enjoying and whose senses are in order, yet remains, as it were, perpetually asleep in the presence of objects of enjoyment, is called "simple."
"One should neither offer censure nor praise; one should not touch anyone's vital spot.
One should not be a speaker of excessive words; likewise, one should remain equanimous in all circumstances."
‘He should neither blame nor praise, not offend, nor speak harshly to anyone, and be the same toward all. (Source untraced)

"One should not converse with any woman previously seen, nor should one remember her; one should avoid talk about her and should not look even at her image in a painting. (Nāradaparivrājaka Upaniṣad 4.3)
"He should neither converse with women, nor should he recall one previously seen; he should avoid talk concerning women and should not look even at a painting of a woman."
(Nārada Parivrājaka Upaniṣad 4.3).

Just as someone who has taken a vow—having resolved upon vows such as eating only at night, fasting, or observing silence—protects them properly with vigilance and without failure, even so, one established in the vow of tonguelessness and the like should protect discernment with vigilance. Thus it is.

Through discernment (*viveka*) and the cessation of the senses (*indriyanirodha*), practiced for a long time, without interruption, and with devotion, when the meditations on friendliness (*maitrī*) and the other [immeasurables] are firmly established,

the impure latent impressions (*malinavāsanā*)— which constitute the demonic endowment (*āsurasaṃpad*)— are destroyed. Thereafter, in the world, by means of the latent impressions of friendliness and the rest, which proceed without human effort— like inhalation and exhalation, or like the closing and opening of the eyes— [the yogi remains].
Even while engaged in worldly affairs, one should abandon in the mind any consideration of their completeness or deficiency;

having diligently stilled all activities such as sleep, drowsiness, and mental fantasies, one should practice the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of pure consciousness alone. For this world, by its very nature, appears as consisting of both the conscious and the insentient, even though...

The sense organs were created solely for the manifestation of insentient objects such as sound and touch, according to the Vedic scripture: "The Self-existent pierced the openings outward" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.1.1). Nevertheless, because consciousness is the material cause [of all things], it is impossible to exclude it; thus, the insentient world shines only preceded by consciousness, as it is said: "Everything shines only after Him who shines."

"By its light all this shines" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.2.15); such being the case, having ascertained that the true nature of the insentient, which appears later, is indeed consciousness appearing first, one should disregard the insentient and dwell upon pure consciousness (cinmātra) in the mind. This is established through the questions and answers of Bali and Śukra.
It is clearly understood—
as when a certain devotee observes a vow such as eating only at night, fasting, maintaining silence, or the like—
Remaining thus properly vigilant and without transgression, likewise,
one who has taken the vow of silence and so forth should carefully maintain discernment. In this manner, through vigilance—

Through the full, continuous, and prolonged practice of discernment (*viveka*) together with the restraint of the senses, the thoughts of friendliness and the other [immeasurables] become firmly established; thereafter, the impure...
Desires in the form of demonic endowments dissolve. Thereafter, thoughts of friendliness and so forth continue to flow spontaneously, without any deliberate personal effort— just as...
or the closing and opening of the eyelids. Although he conducts his life in this world guided by thoughts of loving-kindness and so forth, he avoids the thought of whether he has practiced them.
Having fully or partially suppressed those [faults], and through effort bringing to rest such mental activities as sleep, discursive dreaming, drowsiness,
and so forth, he then practices the aspiration for absolute knowledge.

This entire universe manifests itself as consisting of both sentient and insentient entities. Although the sense organs were created for the purpose of manifesting insentient objects such as these, [the text continues].
As sound, touch, and so forth— as is known from the Śruti:
"The Self-made one pierced the openings."
"outward" (Katha Upaniṣad 2.1.1).
Nevertheless, since consciousness is the material cause of the universe, it cannot be excluded; and as for the insentient...
The universe consisting of consciousness manifests itself; and the Śruti declares this thus:
"When He shines, everything shines after Him; by His light all [shines]."
"This is illuminated" (ibid. 2.2.15). *Jīvanmukti-viveka*.
Therefore, having distinguished the true nature of the insentient as being solely consciousness, because it manifests after [the manifestation of]...
Upon the dissolution of consciousness, one should disregard the insentient and imprint the mind with the thoughts of pure intelligence. This is made very clear through the catechism.
Of Bali and Śukra.
"What is here? What is its measure? And what is it composed of?"
"Who are you? Who am I? And what are these worlds? Tell me quickly.
(Laghu-yogavāsiṣṭha 21.50)
"What is here in this world? What is its nature? Of what is it composed? Who are you and who am I?
And what are these worlds? Please tell me directly."

"Consciousness exists here; this is consciousness alone, and it is composed of consciousness. Consciousness-ness, consciousness, I, and these worlds—all are consciousness: such is the summary. (Laghu Yogavāsistha 21.50)
(tatraiva 21.52) Thus: "In this world, there is only pure Knowledge; this is Knowledge by its very nature, and it is composed of Knowledge."
"You are knowledge, I am knowledge, and all these worlds are knowledge; thus it is said in brief" (ibid. 21.52).
Just as one desiring gold, even when purchasing a bracelet, disregards the merits and defects of its circular shape and considers only its weight and color.

One desires to fix the mind; thus, the mind should be fixed upon pure consciousness alone. For as long as it takes for the mind’s activity toward pure consciousness to become natural—like breathing—by completely disregarding the insentient, one should strive in the cultivation of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of pure consciousness for that duration of time.
Just as a goldsmith, even when purchasing a bracelet,
focuses his attention solely on the color and weight of the gold, disregarding its circular shape and other such qualities;

Therefore, the mind should be concentrated solely upon pure knowledge. Until the mind becomes as naturally absorbed in the thought of pure consciousness as it is in the act of breathing, one must disregard all else.
Having completely abandoned all insentient things, one should proceed with the practice of imprinting the mind with the thought of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).

But surely, the impression of pure consciousness alone should be cultivated from the very beginning, since by that alone the impure impressions are removed; what is the use of this superfluous internal growth?
If it is argued that this is accomplished through the practice of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the other [immeasurables],
the objection is raised: Why not first practice the aspiration for ultimate knowledge (*jñāna*), since by that alone the impure desires are [eliminated]?
[Objection: Why remove [these] through the useless and superfluous practice of friendship and so forth?

[Response: No, because that would entail the consequence that the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of consciousness would lack a foundation. Just as, for example, [an action] being performed apart from the firmness of a stone floor...

A house consisting of pillars and walls does not stand firm; or just as medicine, even when consumed, does not produce health if it fails to expel the powerful humors (doṣas) by means of purgation, so it is in this case.
Response: It cannot be said so, for in that case, instability [would result].
The impressions of absolute knowledge will not arise, just as a house remains unstable even if constructed with pillars and walls, provided a firm foundation has not first been prepared; or,
Just as medicine taken without first expelling the stronger defects from the body through purgation— that is, without eliminating the morbid humors— does not cure the disease.

Now, one might object: "But from the statement, 'Then he should even abandon that' (Yogavāsiṣṭha, Sthiti 57.20), the abandonment of even the latent impression of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) is understood"; yet that too is incorrect, because there is nothing to be acquired within pure consciousness itself.
Having abandoned [desire for] another—
Objection: The abandonment of the desire for pure knowledge has also been enjoined, as is known from the following scriptural text:
"One should abandon even that" (Yogavāsiṣṭha,
Sthitiprakaraṇa 57.20). This cannot be justified, because once the desire for pure consciousness has ceased, there remains nothing else to grasp.

This is not a fault. The latent impression of pure consciousness (*cinmātra-vāsanā*) is of two kinds: that which is accompanied by the mind and intellect, and that which is devoid of them. The instrument is the mind (*manas*), while the intellect (*buddhi*) is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for agency. Thus, being vigilant, [one realizes] "I am pure consciousness with a one-pointed mind."

One should abandon that initial latent impression (*vāsanā*) of pure consciousness— which is designated by the term "meditation" (*dhyāna*)— that is accompanied by such coordination of agent and instrument as "I shall cultivate [this]"; however, one should adopt that which, through proficiency in practice, is devoid of the mediation of coordination such as agency and is designated by the term "absorption" (*samādhi*).
Reply: There is no harm; for the desire for pure knowledge is of two kinds: one is accompanied by the mind and intellect, and the other is devoid of them.

The mind is the instrument, and the intellect is that which is qualified by the notion "I am the doer. Therefore, one should form the desire: "I shall diligently practice the thought of pure knowledge."
"With a concentrated mind," which encompasses the notions of agent and instrument, constitutes the primary desire of pure knowledge,
as expressed by the term *dhyāna* (meditation).
That which is to be abandoned;
the other, which has become free from the interruption of the notions of agent and instrument through practice.
The capacity expressed by the term *samādhi*—
concentration— is to be maintained.
As for the definition of *dhyāna* and *samādhi*, Patañjali formulated them in his *sūtras*:
"In that state, meditation (*dhyāna*) is the one-pointed continuity of the cognition" (3.2);
"That same [meditation], when it appears as the object alone and is, as it were, devoid of its own form, is concentration (*samādhi*)" (3.3).
Thus have meditation and concentration been defined by Patañjali.
One should bow thus: "The uninterrupted flow of cognition toward that object is meditative absorption (dhyāna)" (Yoga Sūtra 3.2).
"When that [mind], having abandoned all forms, reflects only upon the meaning, it is concentration—*samādhi*" (ibid. 3.3).
Having attained stability in such a *samādhi* through practice characterized by long duration, uninterruptedness, and devotion, [one attains the goal].
He should also abandon that effort which is intended for the relinquishing of the subsequent pursuit of agent and instrument;
when he is firmly established in this concentration through long and constant efforts with great love, then he should give up even that.

That effort by which he abandoned the awareness of an agent and an instrument—[an objection is raised]: "If this is so, then even the effort to abandon that [awareness] must be abandoned; thus, there would be an infinite regress.
Objection: If it is so, then this very effort to abandon is also...

[If you argue] that it must be abandoned by a further effort and thus there would be no end to this process—it is not so; for, according to the analogy of the *kataka* powder, it brings about the cessation of both itself and others. Just as when *kataka* powder is thrown into turbid water, [it causes the impurities to settle and then itself dissolves].
Just as [a cloth] removes itself along with other dust particles, so too the effort for the sake of renunciation, while removing the coordination of agent and instrument,
will also remove itself; and when that [effort] has ceased, the impure latent impressions [also cease].
Because even the pure latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have been exhausted, the mind remains in a state free from impressions (*nirvāsana*). With this very point in mind, Vasiṣṭha said:
[Reply: It is not so. It will dissolve itself and others.
Just as the powder of the *kataka* (the clearing-nut tree,
*Strychnos potatorum*) acts: when the powder of the *kataka* is thrown into turbid water, it causes the impurities to settle, and along with...

It settles down of its own accord. In the same way, the effort to renounce, along with the dissolution of the notions of agent and instrument, will also dissolve by itself. And having dissolved, like impure desires, it [subsides].

Pure desires are also dissolved, and thus the mind remains free from desire. With this thought, Vasiṣṭha said: "Therefore, the mind bound by latent impressions (vāsanā) is fettered; the mind free from latent impressions is liberated."
O Rāma, quickly attain the state of extinction through discernment.
(Laghu-yogavāsiṣṭha 16.45)
"Therefore, bondage arises from desires, and the mind is liberated when it is free from desires. By means of discrimination, O Rāma, attain the state of desirelessness as soon as— "
"Through right observation of the truth, latent impressions (*vāsanā*) dissolve;
and with the dissolution of latent impressions, the mind becomes tranquil, like a lamp without oil. (LYV 16.45)
— (at that very place, 16.46)—
"Desires are dissolved by correctly discerning the truth. When desires are dissolved, the mind is extinguished."

"He who remains awake while established in deep sleep, for whom no waking state exists, whose consciousness is free from latent impressions—he is called liberated while living" (ibid. 16.45, 46). He is extinguished like a lamp without oil.
And thus it is said [in that same work, 5.92]:
"He who is awake while others sleep, who has no waking state, and whose intellect is free from desires, is called *jīvanmukta*."
(As stated in ibid. 5.92):
"He whose mind remains always awake with the fluctuations of its states pacified, as if in deep sleep..."
He who is always resorted to by the wise, like the moon endowed with its digits,
is remembered here as one who is liberated.
And likewise [it is said] in that very place (20.36):
"He whose mind, while waking, is always free from mental modifications, just as the mind is during sleep..."
The state is unaware of objects, and being a man of knowledge, he is like the full moon sought after by the wise; such a one is known as *jīvanmukta* (ibid. 20.36).
Having completely renounced everything from the heart, he who remains free from agitation is liberated; he is the Supreme Lord.
(In that very same place, 18.26) ||
"He who, possessed of vast intelligence, casts off all desires from the mind and remains free from agitation—
he is liberated, and he is the Supreme Lord" (ibid. 18.26).
Whether he practices meditative concentration or performs ritual actions— or whether he does neither—
one whose heart has cast away all desires and whose disposition is supreme is indeed liberated.
(In that very same place, 18.27) ||
"That great-souled one, whose heart is free from all expectations and who is noble-minded, is indeed liberated, whether he performs meditation and ritual acts or does not perform them" (ibid).
He for whom the mind is free from latent impressions has no need for inaction, nor does he have need for ritual acts;
he has no need for meditative concentration or the chanting of prayers.
(At that very place, 18.28) ||
‘He whose mind is free from desire has no concern with the performance or avoidance of actions, nor does he stand in need of meditation or the muttering of prayers’ (ibid. 18.28).
"The scriptures have been thoroughly investigated and long discussed among one another;
yet there is no state superior to the silence [of] one whose latent impressions have been completely abandoned" (ibid., 18.29). Thus it is said.
“The scriptures have been studied in detail, and for a long time our views and conclusions have been exchanged with one another;
the final determination is that there is no state superior to this state.”
"Of a sage brought about by the renunciation of desires" (ibid).
Furthermore, it should not be suspected that for one whose mind is free from latent impressions (*nirvāsana*), the worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) that is the cause of life would be lost.
Is this the loss of activities such as seeing with the eyes and so forth, or is it the loss of mental activity? Regarding this, Uddālaka [says]:
He refutes this: it cannot be apprehended that the life-sustaining activities would cease for a person whose mind is free from desire.
The cessation of activity must belong either to the eyes and other sense organs or to the mind. Regarding these, Uddālaka has refuted the former as follows:
"Even though this sense-faculty, such as the eye, is devoid of latent impressions (vāsanā), it functions by itself toward its own external object; latent impressions are not the cause here."
(Yogavāsiṣṭha 5.52.59; Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 24.70).
Thus: "Although free from desire, these senses, such as the eyes and so forth, function spontaneously toward external objects; therefore, desire..."
This is not the cause (YV 5.52.59; LYV 24.70). Vasiṣṭha refutes the second [position]:
"Just as the gaze falls without attachment upon objects in the sky that present themselves without effort, so too does the intellect of the wise man fall toward its objects."
(Yogavāsiṣṭha 4.23.44; Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 15.13).
Regarding this second [verse], Vasiṣṭha replies as follows:
"Just as the eye, free from attachment, falls upon objects in space..."
Or, like the horizon that is not brought near by any effort,
the mind of the wise man again conducts itself with the activities of ordinary life.
He himself explains the enjoyment of the *prārabdha* (commenced karma) by means of such an intellect:
"For when enjoyment is experienced after being fully understood, it leads to contentment;
a thief, once recognized and dealt with, becomes a friend and no longer acts as a thief."
"Just as a village procession encountered unexpectedly on a journey is watched by travelers,
even so is the splendor of enjoyment observed by the wise.
(Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 15.14, 15).
The justification for such a mind undergoing *prārabdha* is provided by Vasiṣṭha as follows:
"Just as when a thief is approached with the knowledge [of his identity]..."
Just as a thief, upon becoming friendly, does not steal,
so too when one enjoys objects of enjoyment with the knowledge that they are the cause of bondage, it brings satisfaction.
(LYV15:14). "Just as travelers on their way, unexpectedly encountering a festive procession in a village, gaze upon it, so too [do they behold] the beauty."
"the difference between those with latent impressions and those without is seen by the wise" (ibid.
15.15). He states the distinction even at the time of enjoyment: "Even at the time of enjoying... [there is a distinction between those with latent impressions and those without].
Regarding those with desire and those without it, as is described here in the *Jīvanmuktiviveka*:
"They do not succumb to exhaustion in times of adversity, just as a golden lotus does not fade at night."
They do not desire anything other than their natural state; they delight in the path of the learned.
—(In that very same place, 18.42) ||

— Just as the golden lotus does not close at the fall of night, so the wise, free from desire, do not become despondent in adversity; they do not long for anything other than what exists, and they follow [the truth].
In the footsteps of the wise (ibid. 18.42):
"They never abandon their state of eternal fullness, which is inwardly undisturbed and as beautiful as the moon, even in times of adversity—just as the moon does not lose its coolness."
— (In that very same place, 1.43) ||

"Even in adversity, the wise who are free from desire never abandon their perfection, tranquility, inner radiance, and coolness; just as the moon, even when eclipsed, does not relinquish its unperturbed nature."
[The qualities of a great being are] fullness, roundness of form, radiance, and coolness (ibid. 1.43).
"Those of vast intent maintain their boundaries like the ocean; like suns, the great do not transgress the law of nature."
(Tatraiva 1.45) Thus:
"The large-hearted— *vitatāśayāḥ*— the disinterested wise, hold fast to the limits of morality and propriety just as the oceans do."
"Do not transgress the bounds. Just as the sun does not abandon the fixed order of things [of rising and setting], so the great-souled ones undergo *prārabdha* without hesitation" (ibid. 1.45).
The same kind of conduct is also recorded for Janaka upon rising from his meditative absorption:
"Then, having remained silent for a long time, Janaka, having emerged from [samādhi], reflected with a mind characterized by tranquility upon the life of living beings. (60)
What is there to be accepted here that I should strive to accomplish?
What conceptualization can I have regarding the consciousness (citi) which is pure and established by its own nature? (61)
"I do not long for what has not been attained, nor do I abandon what has been attained;
I remain established in the self that is at ease—let whatever belongs to me remain mine.
Having reflected thus, Janaka performed his duties as they arose.
He rose up to act without attachment, just as the sun rises at the beginning of the day.
"He does not connect with the future, nor does he reflect upon the past;
he simply continues through the present moment while laughing" (ibid., 19.60–64).
Conduct of precisely this kind is recorded concerning Janaka after he had emerged from meditative absorption (*samādhi*):
"Janaka remained silent for a long time; then he awoke."
With a tranquil mind, he reflected upon the nature of the world:
"Is there anything here worth accepting? Is there anything to be accomplished through effort? What kind of conceptualization could there be?"
In me, who am self-existent, where is absolute knowledge? (Ibid.
"I do not desire what is not obtained, nor do I relinquish what is already obtained. Let that which is mine remain mine; being composed,"
"I abide in the Self" (ibid. 19.62).
Having resolved thus, Janaka arose to perform, without attachment, the work that presented itself.
Just as the sun rises to shine (ibid. 19.63):
"He neither speculates about the future nor dwells on the past; ever smiling, he acts within the living present."
Thus, it is well established that in this way, through the aforementioned destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*), the aforementioned liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) will come to be.
Therefore, it is thus concluded that *jīvanmukti*, as previously described, will follow from the aforementioned effacement of desires.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Dissolution of Latent Impressions," in the *Jīvanmuktiviveka* composed by the venerable Vidyāraṇya.
The end of the second chapter, concerning the effacement of desires. The third chapter:
On the Dissolution of the Mind.

Now we shall describe the dissolution of the mind (*manonāśa*), which is the means for liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). Although the mind necessarily dissolves when all latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are exhausted, nevertheless, if the dissolution of the mind is practiced independently and thoroughly, the destruction of the latent impressions is secured.
Now we shall describe the dissolution of the mind, which is the means to *jīvanmukti*.
Although the dissolution of the mind follows of its own accord—
All desires (latent impressions) stand effaced; nevertheless,
through the well-practiced dissolution of the mind, the effacement of desires is maintained individually.
Nor should it be said that the preservation of that [effacement] is accomplished solely through the practice of being tongueless, being a eunuch, and so forth.
Objection: The maintenance of the effacement of desires is achieved by the practice of tonguelessness and the like.
[Objection: For others, since the absence of the tongue and so forth is established by the fact that the mind has perished, there is no need for the exertion of practice.
[Reply: This cannot be said; for the mind [having been...]
Since the dissolution of the sense of being tongueless and so forth follows automatically,
no effort is required for their practice.
If it is argued that even there, the exertion of practicing the dissolution of the mind exists, [we reply:]...

Objection: Let it be granted that efforts toward the dissolution of the mind exist there through practices such as tonguelessness (*ajihvatva*) and so forth, since these are necessary; however, even when practiced, tonguelessness and the like do not become stable without the destruction of the mind. For this very reason, Janaka stated that the mind must be destroyed:
Reply: Let it be so, as it is required. For, in the absence of the dissolution of the mind, even well-practiced [virtues] such as silence and the like do not become stable. Therefore,

Janaka speaks of the necessity to dissolve the mind as follows: "It is established that for this tree of saṃsāra, which abounds in thousands of sprouts, branches, trunks, fruits, and shoots, the mind is the root."
(Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 19.53):
"The mind is accepted as the root of this tree of saṃsāra (transmigratory existence), which flourishes with thousands of [branches]."

“Sprouts, branches, leaves, and fruits— I consider that to be nothing but volition (*saṅkalpa*). Therefore, by the cessation of volition, I shall wither it away, so that the tree of saṃsāra reaches its withering.”
—(In that very place, 19.54) ||
"I understand that the mind is nothing other than desire;
by the cessation of desire, I shall destroy the mind so that the tree of saṃsāra is destroyed" (ibid. 54).
"I am awakened! I am awakened! I have seen the thief within myself;
here I shall slay this one named 'mind,' for I have long been slain by the mind."
—(at that very place, 19.55) thus:
"I am awakened, I am enlightened; I have discovered the thief named the mind, who stole my Self. I shall slay him."
"Now, for a long time, he has tormented me" (ibid., 55).
Vasiṣṭha also said:
"Of this tree of saṃsāra, which bestows every affliction..."
There is only one means: the restraint of one's own mind.
In that very place (17.1),
Vasiṣṭha also spoke thus:
"The tree of saṃsāra, which bestows all manner of afflictions..."
It has only one remedy: the control of one’s own mind.
"The rise of the mind is downfall; the destruction of the mind is great prosperity.
The mind of the wise man goes toward destruction, for the mind of the ignorant is indeed a shackle."
(In that very same place, 17.5) ||
"The ascent of the mind is its disappearance [from the Self], and great prosperity lies in the dissolution of the mind.
The mind of the knower dissolves; for the ignorant, however, it truly [persists]."
His fetters (ibid. 17.5):
"The latent impressions (vāsanās) leap about in the heart like midnight *vetālas* as long as the mind has not been conquered through firm practice on the single reality."
— (In that very same place, 15.23) ||
The tumult unleashed in the heart, as it were,
by the midnight demons of desire, shall persist until the mind is conquered through the concentration of attention.
The unity of reality (ibid. 15.23):
"For one whose pride of mind has perished and who has subdued the enemies that are the senses, the latent tendencies for enjoyment wither away like lotus ponds in winter."
(In that very same place, 15.22) ||
For one who has subdued the mind, cast off pride,
and conquered the enemies that are the senses, their cravings for enjoyment dissolve just like lotus plants in winter.
"Pressing hand against hand, grinding teeth against teeth,
and crushing limb against limb, one should first conquer one's own mind."
—(ibid. 15.18) || By pressing hand against hand, with the gnashing of teeth, and by striking limb with limb, one should conquer one’s own mind (ibid. 15.18).
"On this entire surface of the earth, those men are truly fortunate and possess virtuous minds who are not conquered by their own minds, even when they are counted among the subjects of men's talk."
— (In that very same place, 15.19) ||
‘In this vast world, those noble-minded ones are truly fortunate who have not been defeated by their own minds; they are worthy of being recorded in the chronicles of heroes’ (ibid. 15.19).

I bow to that imperishable one, like the risen moon, in whose heart-cavity the serpent of the mind— having fashioned its coils within and possessing the virulent poison of its flickering movements— has attained complete pacification.
—(In that very same place, 15.20) ||
"I praise that Imperishable One, who, having slain the serpent of the mind coiled within the hollow of his heart, has arisen like the full moon released from an eclipse."
"In the venom of desire" (ibid. 15.20):
"The mind is indeed the hub of this wheel of illusion on all sides;
if one stands having stepped upon it, then nothing can cause harm."
—(tatraiva 23.92) thus:
"The mind alone is truly the hub of the wheel of delusion revolving in all directions. If he remains [in that state], nothing can afflict him."
"With complete mastery over his own mind" (ibid. 23.92). Gauḍapādācārya has also said: "For all yogins, fearlessness depends upon the restraint of the mind."
