Vālmīki said this:
"Sitting down again and again with a one-pointed mind,
it is not possible to conquer the mind without an irreproachable method."
(Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 28.126)
“Even the practice of one-pointed attention through repeated sitting cannot conquer the mind without the aid of flawless reasoning. (LYV 28.126)
"Just as a wild, rogue elephant cannot be subdued without a goad,
so too the mind cannot be conquered without the application of skillful means.
“Just as a wild elephant in rut cannot be controlled without the use of a goad, so the mind cannot be brought under control without the employment of reasoning” (ibid. 28.127).
"Vasiṣṭha has correctly set forth the reasonings that cause the dissolution of the mind; for one who is established in those, the mind comes under control."—*Jīvanmuktiviveka*.
"Vasiṣṭha has properly described the reasonings (yogas)."
"Which lead to the dissolution of the mind; he who applies these controls the mind.
Restraint is considered to be twofold: both by force and by method."
The restraint of the intellect, the vital functions, and the senses is achieved through forceful control of the physical body.
Sometimes a certain [state] arises, and by that the mind is dissolved.
It is held that mastery over the mind is attained either through haṭhayoga or through reasoning. By exercising forceful control...
Over the seats of the organs of knowledge and action, certain kinds of attachments occasionally arise, which lead to the dissolution of the mind.
The acquisition of inner knowledge and association with the virtuous alone.
The complete relinquishing of latent impressions and the cessation of the movement of the vital breath.
Indeed, these arguments are well-established for the conquest of the mind.
(Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 28.128, 129)
‘The study of the knowledge of the Supreme Self, association with the virtuous, complete renunciation of desires, and control of the vital energy— these are well known as the perfect means.’
To conquer the mind (Laghu Yogavāsiṣṭha 28.128–129,
first line):
"Those who, despite these [proper] methods existing, attempt to restrain [the mind] by force..."
Having cast aside the lamp of consciousness, they seek to destroy darkness with collyrium.
—(In that very same place, 28.130) ||
"Those who apply haṭhayoga to control the mind when such effective means are available resemble those who, having abandoned a lamp, apply magical ointment to their eyes."
To dispel darkness (ibid. 28.130):
"Those who, being utterly deluded, strive to achieve mastery over the mind by force—they bind the intoxicated king of serpents with lotus fibers."
—(at that very place, 28.131)—thus [it is said]. *Jīvanmuktiviveka*:
Those deluded ones who attempt to control the mind by force, they are, as it were, binding a large, frantic elephant with a lotus-fiber.
"Breathing" (ibid. 28.131).

Restraining (*nigraha*) is of two kinds: forceful restraining (*haṭhanigraha*) and gradual restraining (*kramanigraha*). Among these, the organs of perception, such as the eyes and ears, and the organs of action, such as speech and hands, are restrained by force merely by obstructing their respective physical seats (*golaka*); by way of that illustration...
The fool thinks, "I shall likewise restrain the mind," yet it cannot be restrained, because its physical seat—the heart-lotus—cannot be blocked. Therefore, gradual restraint alone is appropriate.
And for gradual restraint, the means are precisely the attainment of spiritual knowledge (*adhyātmavidyā*) and so forth. That knowledge consists in [realizing] the falsity of the visible world.

It also makes known the self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) of the object of vision (*dṛgvastu*). Thus, when this [ignorance] perceives the absence of purpose in the visible objects within its own range and the lack of being an object for that which possesses purpose—the object of vision—it subsides by itself, like a fire without fuel. And so it is heard in scripture:

Control is of two kinds: violent control and gradual control. Of these, the former is performed by obstructing the organs of knowledge, such as the eyes, ears, and so forth, as well as the organs of action—

By force, one restrains the organs, such as the larynx, hands, and so forth, in their respective locations. A deluded person, through this example, falsely imagines that in this same manner he shall likewise control the mind. However, [the mind is not like that].
The mind cannot be controlled in that manner, because its center—
the lotus-like heart— is impossible to control. Therefore, gradual control is justified.
The means for gradual mastery are the study of the knowledge of the self and of others. This science of the self gives rise to the conviction that all objects of knowledge are unreal.
Having become convinced that objects and the knower are the self-evident reality, the mind finds that the objects of knowledge within its own range are useless, and realizes that—
O Knower, although the Reality is a beneficial thing, it is beyond the reach of the intellect and dissolves of its own accord, like a fire without fuel.
And the Śruti says thus:

"Just as a fire without fuel is extinguished in its own source, so too the mind, through the cessation of its fluctuations, is extinguished in its own source. (Maitrāyaṇī Upaniṣad 4.1; Pañcadaśī 19.111) — *Jīvan-mukti-viveka*
"Just as a fire without fuel goes out in its own place, even so the mind, through the cessation of activity, goes out in its own source. (Maitrāyaṇī Upaniṣad 4.4.1)

The *Pañcadaśī* (11.111) states: "The Self is the womb. For those two who do not correctly understand the reality even when it has been explained, and for him who forgets it, the only means is association with the virtuous (*sādhūnām saṅgama*). For the virtuous awaken one again and again, and cause one to remember. As for he who...

One who is afflicted by evil latent impressions such as the intoxication of learning is unable to follow the virtuous; for such a person, the means to abandon these impressions is the discernment previously described. However, if it is impossible to abandon them due to the intensity of those impressions—

The means is the cessation of the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Since both the vibration of the vital breath and latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are the motivators of the mind, when these two are restrained, the pacification of the mind is achieved. And regarding this motivating power, Vasiṣṭha says:
The word *yonih*— meaning "source"— signifies that the association with the virtuous is the means for both those who,
despite having received instruction, are unable to grasp the truth perfectly.

Those who forget even after having grasped [the teaching], because the virtuous remind and instruct them repeatedly in the truth. Those who are distressed by impure desires, such as the pride of learning...
and so forth, has no inclination to associate with the virtuous; for such a person, the only remedy is to abandon that desire through the aforementioned discernment.

If he is unable to remove those exceedingly strong desires, then the restraint of the vital energy (*prāṇa*) is the means for him. Since both desire and the vital energy agitate the mind, their control [is necessary].
will bring about tranquility.
Their stimulating nature is described by Vasiṣṭha as follows: "There are two seeds for the tree of the mind, which bears the creepers of its fluctuations."
The first is the vibration of the vital breath; the second is firm latent impression.
(Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 28.38)
"The mind, as it were, like a tree with climbing vines of transformation, has two seeds— one is the vital energy (*ojas*) and the second is strong desire" (*Laghu-Yogavāsiṣṭha*).
"The existent, all-pervading consciousness is awakened by the vibration of the vital breath;
from that [awakening] come endless perceptions, and from those, sufferings for the mind.
(Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 28.40–41)
“The omnipresent absolute intelligence, as it were, awakens through the vital energy, and this awakening brings in its wake endless miseries for the mind” (ibid).

Just as smiths blow upon a fire covered with ashes using two bellows, and that fire blazes up by means of the air produced from those bellows, so too consciousness— though veiled by ignorance, which stands in the place of wood— is [awakened] by the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) through the instrument of the mind (*citta*).

Being awakened, it blazes forth in the form of mental fluctuations (*cittavṛtti*). From that consciousness which takes the form of a blazing flame called mental fluctuation, sufferings arise. This very [consciousness] is impelled by the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇaspanda*).
The arising of the thought of enlightenment. And he himself said another [verse]:
"Just as a smith blows air into a fire covered with ash by means of a pair of bellows, and by that air blown by the bellows..."
Just as fire becomes kindled, so too the intellect,
though covered by ignorance, when awakened by the vital breath (*prāṇa*), blazes forth like fuel for a fire, using the mind as its material.
Mental transformation. Sufferings arise from that consciousness which exists in the form of radiant intelligences and is termed mental transformations. In this manner, the vital force bestows [them].
It arises in the mind. Regarding the other cause as well, he said:
"O Rāghava, that which is manifested by the consciousness of existence and that which has been experienced..."
Listen now to another arising of the mind, which is produced by latent impressions.
—(Yogavāsiṣṭha 5.91.28)
"Listen, O Rāghava, to another creation of the mind arising from desire, which is manifested by consciousness and likewise experienced" (YV 5.91.28).
"Due to the intense cultivation of the notion of a single object through firm habituation,
the extremely restless mind arises as the cause of birth, old age, and death. (Yogavāsiṣṭha 5.91.35)
"The steady repetition of thoughts regarding objects alone creates the restless mind, which is the cause of birth, old age, and death" (ibid).
Not only do the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and latent impressions (*vāsanā*) act as motivators of the mind, but they also act as mutual motivators. Thus it is said:
Vasiṣṭha says:
"The vibration of the vital breath arises from the power of latent impressions (vāsanā), and by that [vibration], latent impressions are produced;
thus occurs the sequence of seed and sprout for the tree of the mind."
—(Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 28.65)
For this very reason, he states that by the destruction of either one, both are destroyed:
"The life-force (*jīva*) and desire (*kāma*) are not only the causes of the mind, but they also arise from one another. Thus said Vasiṣṭha:
"Vitality and desire are mutually dependent— that is, they owe their existence to one another— and this introduces the law of the seed-and-sprout succession for the tree of the mind" (LYV 28.65).
Therefore, it is also described that the destruction of either one destroys both:
"There are two seeds for the tree of the mind: the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇaspandana) and latent impressions (vāsanā)."
"And when one of these two is exhausted, both quickly perish" (Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 28.64). Thus:
"Vital energy and desire are the two seeds for the tree of the mind."
"By the destruction of one, both are destroyed simultaneously" (ibid. 28.64).
He now states the means for their destruction and the fruit of that destruction:
"Through firm practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma), by means of the method imparted by the Guru,
and through the application of postures and diet, the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa) is restrained."
(Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 28.122) | The method for destroying these [impurities] and the result of that destruction are described as follows: Jīvanmuktiviveka.

By the steady practice of *prāṇāyāma* in the proper posture, together with the restraint of food and other means as instructed by the teacher, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is brought under control (An. Up. 4.87).
Because of acting without attachment, because of abandoning the cultivation of worldly existence,
and because of perceiving the destruction of the body, latent impressions do not arise.
(Annāpūrṇopaniṣad 4.88; Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 28.123)
‘By living the ordinary life without attachment,
abandoning worldly thoughts, and remaining mindful of the mortality of the body— desires do not arise. (Aṅguttara Nikāya)

"Through the complete abandonment of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the mind attains the state of non-mind (*acittatā*); and through the cessation of the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa-spanda*), do as you wish. (Up. 4.88; LYV 28.123)
—(Aṇṇapūrṇopaniṣad 4.86; Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 28.121) ||
“By completely abandoning desires, the mind becomes non-mind; this is also attained through the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa);
now do as you wish. (LYV 28.121)
"O Rāghava, I consider this alone to be the nature of the mind:
that which is the internal contemplation of an object as being a real entity and with a sense of relish."
(Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 28.57)
"In my opinion, the form of the mind is this: the thought of an internal object as real and with liking" (ibid. 28.57).
"When nothing whatsoever is cultivated that has the nature of being either to be abandoned or to be adopted..."
When one remains having abandoned everything, then the mind is not born.
— (In that very same place, 28.54) ||
"When one remains, having renounced everything, without any thought of what is acceptable or unacceptable, then the mind does not arise" (ibid. 28.54).
"When the mind, due to the constant absence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), no longer cognizes anything, then non-mindfulness (*amanastā*) arises,
which bestows supreme tranquility" (Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 28.55).
“When the mind, due to its desirelessness, does not function at all, then the state of mindlessness arises, which bestows supreme peace” (ibid. 28.55).
He states that in the absence of the non-arising of the state of mindlessness, there is a lack of peace:
"When one is firmly seized by the yakṣa of the mind, neither friends nor kinsmen,
nor teachers nor men, are able to protect [one]."
(Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 30.18).
Thus it is described that there can be no peace in the absence of mindlessness.
"He cannot be saved either by friends or relatives, or by teachers or others, he whose mind is, as it were, possessed by a ghost" (ibid. 30.18).

Regarding what was stated as "by means of the yoga of posture and diet," Patañjali set forth the definition, the method, and the result of posture (*āsana*) in three sūtras: "Posture is steady and comfortable" (*sthira-sukham āsanam*);
"By the relaxation of effort and [meditation on] the infinite... (*prayatna-śaithilyānanta-*).
"By means of the two attainments" (2.47); "thereafter, freedom from the affliction of dualities" (2.48).
The practice of *āsana*—posture—and of dieting has been mentioned previously; of these, the definition, the means, and...
The effects of *āsana* are described by Patañjali through three sūtras as follows:
"Posture is that which is firm and comfortable" (*Yogasūtra* 2.46).
‘By lessening the natural tendency [for restlessness] and meditating on the unlimited [posture becomes firm and pleasant]’ (ibid. 2.47).
"Once the seat is conquered, the dualities do not obstruct" (ibid). By whatever posture,

such as the lotus (*padmaka*) or the auspicious cross (*svastika*), a person’s placement of the body results in pleasure characterized by the absence of pain in the limbs and stability characterized by the lack of bodily movement— for that person, that very [posture] is [the conquered seat].
A comfortable seat is one where,
when the body is positioned in any posture such as the lotus (padmaka), the cross-legged (svastika), or others, no part of his body trembles.
Or if there is pain, then the posture (āsana) is firm and pleasant,
and that is what is most suitable for him. And the worldly means for this is the relaxation of effort, [as well as] walking, domestic duties, and pilgrimage.

One should diminish the mental exertion and enthusiasm directed toward activities such as ritual bathing and fire-offerings; otherwise, that enthusiasm will forcibly rouse the body and drive it toward whatever [object] it may be.
This is the common method for achieving [the goal].

This is the firmness of *āsana*. He should diminish his zeal for traveling, visiting places of pilgrimage or performing domestic chores, bathing [in sacred waters and the like], offering oblations, and so forth; otherwise, such...
Zeal would compel him to rise from his seat and send him wherever he might.
And the extraordinary means (alaukikopāya) is this Ananta, who remains steadfast, supporting the earth with his thousand hoods.
The meditation "I am that very one" is the infinite attainment of the mind (*cittānantasamāpatti*). Through this, the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) that accomplishes the aforementioned posture is produced.
The spiritual method for attaining it is to identify oneself [with that].
One meditates upon the serpent-god Ananta— who remains perfectly still while supporting the world with his thousand hoods— as "I am He.
This meditation is called *cittaikāgrya* (one-pointed concentration of the mind).
Ananta—the Infinite; and from this arises the "unseen" (merit), which in turn brings about the steadiness of the seat.
Once the seat is perfected, one is no longer struck by the pairs of opposites—such as cold and heat, pleasure and pain, honor and dishonor—as one was before. For such a person:
It is taught that a place suitable for the posture (āsana) is required—
once the posture has been mastered, [the yogi remains unaffected by] dualities such as heat and cold, pleasure and pain, and honor and...
Dishonor and the like cannot trouble him as they did before.
A suitable place for such a seat is prescribed by the Śrutis as follows: "Seated in a comfortable posture in a secluded place... (194).
Pure, with his neck and head held erect, his body upright.
(From the Kaivalyopaniṣad 4):
"In a secluded place, being pure (in body and mind), seated in a comfortable posture with the body, neck, and head held erect."
On a level, clean spot free from pebbles, fire,
and sand— this is the yoga of posture (*āsana-yoga*).
One should practice in a place free from sounds, water-bodies, and the like—
agreeable to the mind and not distressing to the eyes— taking refuge in a cave or a windless shelter.
And thus it is stated in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (2.10).
“Let yoga be practiced within a cave sheltered from strong winds, or in a place that is level, pure, free from pebbles, gravel, and fire, and undisturbed by the sound of water.”
"Or where there is no pool or river very near, yet which is pleasing to the mind and not offensive to the eye" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.10).
The practice regarding food is moderation in eating,
according to the scripture: "A yogin should always avoid both overeating and fasting" (Amṛtabindūpaniṣad 27).
This is the practice of *āsana* mentioned previously. The practice of diet consists in moderation in eating. Thus says the *Śruti*:
"A yogi should always avoid overeating and fasting."
The Blessed One has also said: "Yoga is not for him who eats too much, nor for him who does not eat at all. (Amṛtabindu Upaniṣad 27)
"Nor for one who is habitually over-sleeping, O Arjuna, nor for one who is never awake; yoga— which destroys suffering—
belongs to one who is moderate in food and recreation, moderate in exertion in actions,
and moderate in sleep and wakefulness."
—(Bhagavadgītā 6.16, 17). Thus the Blessed One also said:
"Indeed, yoga is not for one who eats too much, nor..."
For one who abstains excessively from food; it is not for him,
O Arjuna, who sleeps too much, nor for him who stays awake too much (BG 6.16).
"For one who is moderate in food and recreation,
moderate in exertion at work, and moderate in sleep and wakefulness, yoga brings an end to all sorrows" (ibid. 6.17).

The destruction of the mind through breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) by one who has mastered his posture is recorded in the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*: "Holding the body straight with its three parts even, having withdrawn the senses into the heart along with the mind..."
By means of the raft of Brahman, the wise man should cross over all the terrifying currents.
Having restrained his vital breaths here with disciplined effort,
he should breathe through the nostrils when the breath is exhausted;
for this body is like a carriage yoked to vicious horses.
"The wise man, being vigilant, should fix his mind [on the Self].
(Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.8, 9).
Thus it is stated in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad. By means of prāṇāyāma—
For one who has thus mastered *āsana*, the dissolution of the mind through the control of cosmic energy (*amā*) occurs:
"The wise man should hold his body steady."
With the three upper parts erect, he turns his senses, along with the mind, toward the heart; and by means of the boat of Brahman, he crosses over the fearsome torrents.
[The breath] through the nostrils. Then, he should restrain his mind without distraction, just as a charioteer restrains unruly horses (ibid).

There are two kinds of yogis: one who is free from the demonic endowments such as the intoxication of knowledge, and one who possesses them. Of these two, for the former, [the practice is] by means of meditation on Brahman.
When the mind has been restrained, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is restrained as its inseparable concomitant. With reference to that, the mantra "Raised three finger-breadths...
(*Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* 2.8) is recited.
There are two classes of yogis: the one who is free from...
There are demonic endowments, such as the pride of learning and so forth,
as well as those who possess them. Among these, for yogins of the first order, the *prāṇa* becomes naturally controlled.

They are controlled specifically by the restraint of the mind brought about through meditation on the Self, because they are concomitant with it. The scriptural passage, "Holding the three upper parts erect," and so forth (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.8), refers to this.
Class.

For the second [type of practitioner], when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is restrained through practice, the mind (*manas*) is restrained as a necessary consequence thereof. With reference to him, the mantra begins: "Having compressed the vital breaths... (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.9).
For the second class of yogis, when the *prāṇa* is controlled through practice, the mind— which is concomitant with it— becomes controlled; thus, the text says "controlling the mind."
and so forth (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.9).

The method of suppressing the vital breaths (prāṇa) will be explained. By that suppression, one's activity becomes disciplined; the activities of the mind, such as the intoxication of learning and so forth, are restrained. Regarding the restraint of the defects of the mind through the restraint of the vital breaths, another illustration is heard elsewhere:
The method for restraining the *prāṇa* will now be discussed.
Restraint of the *prāṇa* gives rise to a slackening of effort in worldly activities. Such mental behaviors as pride— [text continues]
Learning and the rest also become restrained. In another Śruti,
the control of the defects of the mind through the control of prāṇa has been explained as follows:
"Just as the impurities of mountain ores are burnt away by smelting,
so too are the defects produced by the senses burnt away through the restraint of the vital breath.
(Amṛtanādopaniṣad 7).
"Just as impurities are destroyed from mountain ore through smelting, even so, through the control of *prāṇa*, all evils pertaining to the senses are destroyed" (*Amṛtanāda Upaniṣad*).
Regarding this, the proof has been shown by Vasiṣṭha:
"That which is the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa-pavana) is indeed the very vibration of the mind (citta)."
"A wise person should exert great effort toward the cessation of the vibration of the vital breath" (Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 28.125).
The reason for this has been demonstrated by Vasiṣṭha as follows:

“The activities of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the functions of the mind are identical as one. Therefore, the wise person should strive with all effort to restrain the activities of the vital breath. (LYV)

The deities of the senses—mind, speech, sight, and the rest—having taken a vow, "We shall perform our respective functions without interruption," were seized by Death in the form of exhaustion. Yet that Death did not overcome the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Consequently, even while performing inhalation and exhalation incessantly, this *prāṇa* does not grow weary. Then, having reflected, the deities entered into the form of the *prāṇa*.
This very point is recorded by the Vājasaneyins:
"The deities of the mind, speech, sight, and the other organs,
having vowed to perform their respective functions without interruption..."
All actions were seized by Death in the form of exhaustion;
however, Death did not seize the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Therefore, although it is constantly exhaling and inhaling, the vital force—
It does not grow weary. Then all the gods, having reflected, assumed the form of the vital force (*prāṇa*). This matter is thus recorded by the Vājasaneyins: 198.

"This one is indeed the best among us, for whether moving or not moving, he neither suffers nor is harmed. Come, let us all assume his very form! They all assumed his form; therefore they are called by this name, "prāṇas" (vital breaths). (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.21)
"This indeed is the greatest among us; whether moving or unmoving, it neither feels pain nor is injured. Come, let us assume its form. They all assumed its form.
"Therefore, they are called *prāṇas* after it" (Br. Up. 1.5.21).

Thus, what is meant by the senses having the nature of *prāṇa* is that their activity is dependent upon *prāṇa*. And this is heard in the *Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa*, in the context of the discussion on the *sūtrātman*: [text follows].
Therefore, "the organs in the form of prāṇas" means all their functions depend upon the function of prāṇa. And this has been described in the Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa.
Regarding the "inner controller" (*antaryāmin*)—under the heading of the *sūtrātman*, the Self as the thread—in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*, it is stated:
"Vāyu indeed, O Gautama, is that thread; by Vāyu as the thread, O Gautama, this world and the other world, and all [beings]..."

"And the elements are held together by it. Therefore, O Gautama, they say of a dead man: 'His limbs have fallen apart,' for, O Gautama, they are held together by the thread of breath (vāyu). (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.2). Thus, because the movement of the vital breath (prāṇa) and the mind (manas) are co-existent, when the breath is restrained, the mind is restrained.
"Air, indeed, O Gautama, is that thread. By air, O Gautama, as by a thread, this world, the other world, and all beings are held together. Therefore, indeed, O..."
"O Gautama, they say of a person who dies that his limbs have become loosened; for they are held together, O Gautama, by air, as if by a thread" (Brhadaranyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.2).
Therefore, since the functioning of both the vital breath and the mind is mutually concomitant, by restraining the former, the latter is restrained.
Objection:
This "functioning together" is untenable,
because in deep sleep, although the vital breath (prāṇa) remains active, the mind (manas) does not so function.
The mind becomes non-functional. [Objection: No, because at that time the mind does not exist due to its having dissolved.
[Reply: It is not so, because the mind then remains.

It is resolved in its potential state and is, in a sense, non-existent. But is it not contradictory to say, "When the breath has ceased, one should breathe through the nose"? For we never see breathing in one whose breath has ceased—that is, in a dead person; nor is there a cessation of breath in one who is breathing and living.
Objection: The text, "When the vital force is destroyed,
one should breathe through the nostrils" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.9, quoted above), is self-contradictory, since nowhere do we find...
"A dead man, devoid of *prāṇas*, does not breathe, nor is the cessation of *prāṇa* observed in a breathing, living being.
Not so; for what is intended here is the exhaustion of the *prāṇas* due to their lack of intensity (*anulbaṇatva*), as in the cases of digging, cutting, and so forth.

Just as the force of the breath that occurs in one who is active, climbing a mountain, or running swiftly does not exist in one who is standing still, sitting, or sleeping; likewise, for one endowed with proficiency in *prāṇāyāma*, the breath becomes less than it was otherwise. It is with this very intention that it is heard in the scripture:

Reply: It is not so; by the word "destruction" (of *prāṇa*), diminished breathing is intended here—that is, neither too much nor excessive breathing. For the rate of breathing is faster in [that state].

Just as for one engaged in digging earth, felling a tree, climbing a hill, or running, the rate of respiration is much reduced compared to that of one who is standing, sitting, or sleeping; so too is it in this case.
He is more accomplished in *prāṇāyāma* than anyone else.
This very same idea is found in the following *śruti*: "Having become one whose breath is restrained therein, he should exhale very slowly."
(Kṣurikopaniṣad 5):
“Having restrained the prāṇa there (in the heart), one should exhale only slowly. (Kṣurikopaniṣad 5).

Just as a chariot drawn by vicious horses leaves the path and is led anywhere at all, yet is brought back onto the smooth road by a charioteer who firmly pulls the horses with the reins, so too the mind— which is being led hither and thither by the senses, latent impressions, and the like— is held steady when the rope of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is firmly grasped.
Regarding what was stated in the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* (2.9), "Having oppressed the vital breaths," the manner of that oppression of the vital breaths is heard elsewhere:
"Just as a chariot drawn by vicious horses is dragged away..."
Just as a horse that has strayed from its course is brought back to the right path by a charioteer who pulls it firmly with the reins, even so the mind remains under perfect control.
When [the mind] is dragged here and there by the senses, desire,
and so forth, if it is held firmly by the bridle of *prāṇa*. This refers to the method for controlling the mind mentioned previously in the text.
Regarding the passage "having restrained the prāṇa," etc. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.9, quoted above), it is described in another Śruti as follows:
"The Gāyatrī, together with the Vyāhṛtis, together with the Praṇava, and together with the Śiras..."
One should recite [the mantra] three times while restraining the breath; that is called prāṇāyāma.
(From the Amṛtanāda Upaniṣad, 11)
"He should mutter the formula known as Gāyatrī, together with the praṇava, the vyāhṛtis, and the śiras, three times while restraining the breath through pūraka, kumbhaka, and recaka."
This is called *prāṇāyāma* (*Amṛtanāda Upaniṣad*, 11):
"Three types of *prāṇāyāma* are taught: exhalation (*recaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*)" (10).
Having raised the wind into the sky and rendered it empty and selfless, one should apply it through the state of emptiness; such is the characteristic of exhalation (recaka).
(Amṛtanādopaniṣad 10, 12)
It is said that there are three types of *prāṇāyāma*— the regulation of the vital breath: exhalation (*recaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*),
and retention (*kumbhaka*) of the air (breath) (ibid.).
10). "One should practice by completely emptying the internal space through exhaling the air and retaining it—without allowing air to enter. This is the nature of *recaka*."
Prāṇāyāma (ibid. 12). *Jīvanmuktiviveka*: "Just as a man might draw up water through the stalk of a lotus with his mouth, so should the air be drawn in; this is the characteristic of *pūraka*. (13)
(Amṛtanādopaniṣad 13)
"Just as one draws up water through a lotus stalk, so too should one inhale air through the mouth; this is called *pūraka*. (Ibid., 13)
"One should neither inhale nor exhale, nor indeed move the limbs; in this manner one should practice for the duration of the *kumbhaka*— this is its definition" (Amṛtanādopaniṣad 14).
"Neither inhaling nor exhaling, one should practice holding the body perfectly motionless; this is the definition of kumbhaka" (ibid. 14).

In this context, having expelled the air within the body to the exterior and having made the bodily space empty, void, and devoid of self—that is, free of air—one should restrain it in the state of emptiness itself without allowing even the slightest air to enter. This is *recaka* (exhalation).
*Kumbhaka* (retention) is of two kinds: internal and external. Regarding both of these, Vasiṣṭha said:
In order to expel the air from within the body, one should force it upward and out through exhalation; in this manner,
making the internal space of the body void of air and empty.
Even if it enters in a minute quantity, one should maintain this state of emptiness; this is what is meant here by *recaka*. There are two kinds of *kumbhaka*: internal and external.
outward; and both are described by Vasiṣṭha as follows:
"When the apāna has subsided and the prāṇa has not yet arisen in the heart, that state which is experienced by yogins is the state of kumbhaka."
(Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 29.211)
When the apāna has subsided (or when the prāṇa has subsided into the apāna), until the prāṇa arises in the chest (the heart)—
this state for such a duration is experienced as kumbhaka.

"By the yogis" (LYV 29.211): "When the prāṇa has set outside, as long as the apāna has not yet risen— [during that interval] they know the external kumbhaka to be the state of full equilibrium" (tatraiva 29.216).
“When the *prāṇa* has gone outside and until the *apāna* has arisen, to that extent this state of complete equilibrium is known as external *kumbhaka*” (Ibid. 29.216).
In that context, inhalation (ucchvāsa) is opposed to internal retention (āntara-kumbhaka); exhalation (niḥśvāsa) is opposed to external retention (bāhya-kumbhaka);
and the movement of the limbs is opposed to both, as it interferes with either exhalation or inhalation.
Because [the practice] must necessarily occur; Patañjali also formulated the aphorism regarding breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) as occurring after the postures (*āsana*):
"When that [posture] is present...
Among these, inhalation (*pūraka*) is incompatible with internal [retention].
Retention (kumbhaka) is incompatible with exhalation, and exhalation is incompatible with external retention; moreover, physical movement is inconsistent with both,
because one of the two— either exhalation or inhalation— is certain to follow.
This occurs when the body is moved. Patañjali also described *prāṇāyāma* as the stage following *āsana* in his *Yoga Sūtras*, stating:
"When that [posture] is attained, the cessation of the movement of exhalation and inhalation is breath control" (Yogasūtra 2.49).
"The restraint of the flow of exhalation and inhalation follows upon this [attainment of posture]. (Yoga Sūtra)

[Objection: But surely, even though there is an absence of movement during *kumbhaka*, the movements of inhalation (*ucchvāsa*) and exhalation (*niḥśvāsa*) still exist during *recaka* and *pūraka*. If this is argued:
It exists in *kumbhaka*, as well as in *recaka* and *pūraka* in the form of exhalation and inhalation.
No, for by practicing excessive measures, the naturally established equilibrium of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is interrupted. That very practice—
The Sūtra replies: This is not so, because the natural even flow of the *prāṇa* is arrested by practicing [the breath-control] to a greater degree. The same...
Practice is set forth in the aphorism as follows:
"Its fluctuations are either external or internal or motionless; it is regulated by place, time, and number, and is long and subtle" (2.50).
"Its modifications are either external or internal, or motionless..."
"Otherwise, [the breath] is regulated by place, time, and number, being either long or short" (Ibid.
2.50). Recaka is the external movement; pūraka is the internal movement; kumbhaka is the arrested movement. Among these, each one—

It is to be examined by means of place (*deśa*) and other factors. For example: when exhalation (*recaka*) is established by its own nature, the breath, having issued from the heart, terminates at a distance of twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) directly in front of the tip of the nose; however, through practice, the air gradually issues forth from the navel or the foundation (*ādhāra*), reaching completion at a distance of twenty-four or thirty-six finger-breadths. In this regard:

When there is excessive effort in exhalation (*recaka*), it can be ascertained internally by the agitation of the regions starting from the navel; externally, it should be ascertained by holding a fine tuft of cotton and observing its movement. This is the examination of space (*deśa-parīkṣā*). The examination of time (*kāla-parīkṣā*) is performed by counting ten, twenty, thirty, or more repetitions of the *praṇava* during the period of exhalation. In this month, there are ten exhalations every day.
The examination of number is by means of such [counts] as twenty in the coming month, twenty in the next, thirty in the following month, and so forth; that is,
the breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) characterized by the aforementioned place and time, numbering ten, twenty, thirty, and so on, within a single day.

Examination of Number. This same principle should also be applied to inhalation (*pūraka*). Although no specific spatial pervasion is perceived during retention (*kumbhaka*), nevertheless, its pervasion by time and number is indeed perceived. Just as a mass of cotton, when condensed, becomes long, thin, and subtle when it is spread out, so too is the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
When practiced with an increase in place, time, and number, it becomes long and subtle due to its difficulty of being perceived.
He sets forth another method, distinct from the three beginning with exhalation (recaka), in the subsequent section.

Recaka is the outward flow, pūraka is the inward flow, and the cessation of movement is kumbhaka. Each of these is to be examined in terms of place, time, and number. For example, in its natural state—
The outward course of the breath, rising from the heart,
flows to a distance of approximately twelve finger-breadths from the tip of the nose and terminates there; however, through practice, the air gradually rises further.
From the navel (the solar plexus) or from the base (the mystical circle situated above the generative organ), it flows outward to the extent of twenty-four or thirty-six finger-breadths (inches).

roughly). In this *recaka*—where intense practice is being performed—the sensation of a stirring helps one discern the site, the navel or base, from which the breath rises. Externally, the range of the...
The breath can be ascertained by the movement of a thin piece of cotton held in front; thus, this is the test for the place. The test for the duration of the exhalation is made by repetition.
Of the *praṇava*— the syllable *Oṃ*— ten times, twenty times,
thirty times, and so forth. The number is tested by practicing ten *recakas* daily during this month, twenty during the next, and so on.
And thirty *recakas* in the month following that, and so forth.
The number of *prāṇāyāmas*— distinguished by the aforementioned time and place— performed in a single day, [may be] ten, twenty, or [more].
"Thirty," and so forth, is the test for the number. This same method of testing should also be adopted for *pūraka*.
Although the specific location or extent of the space cannot [be measured],...
In *kumbhaka*, both number and duration can certainly be known. Just as a piece of dense cotton becomes long when spread out and also subtle through rarification, so too—
Thus, the *prāṇa*, the vital breath, being practiced with increasing duration, location, and frequency, becomes long and also subtle due to its imperceptibility.
Patañjali describes another type of *prāṇāyāma*, distinct from the three beginning with *recaka*, in the following aphorism:
"The fourth [prāṇāyāma] is without regard for external or internal objects" (Yoga Sūtra 2.51).

The external *kumbhaka* is that performed immediately after exhaling all the air according to one's capacity; the internal *kumbhaka* is that performed immediately after filling the air according to one's capacity. Thus, when *kumbhaka* alone is practiced, disregarding exhalation (*recaka*) and inhalation (*pūraka*), it becomes the fourth in relation to the preceding three. [This is for those] afflicted by powerful defects such as sleep and lethargy.
The triad beginning with *recaka* [exhalation]; the fourth belongs to those free from defects—this is the distinction. He states the fruit of *prāṇāyāma* in a sutra:
"When all the air has been exhaled as much as possible, the retention performed thereafter is external *kumbhaka*."
Inhaling as much air as possible is internal *kumbhaka*; thus,
the practice of *kumbhaka* alone, regardless of *recaka* or *pūraka*, becomes the fourth when considered in relation to the preceding [stages].
Going three. The distinction is to be understood as follows:
the three *prāṇāyāmas*, such as *recaka* and so forth, are for those afflicted by powerful defects such as sleep, drowsiness, and the like.
The fourth [type of *prāṇāyāma*] is for those who are free from such defects.
The result of *prāṇāyāma* is described as follows:
"From that, the covering of light is destroyed" (YS 2.52).

"From that, the veil over the light of the *citta* becomes attenuated" (ibid. 2.52). The veil (*āvaraṇa*) of the luminous *sattva* is *tamas*, which is the cause of sleep, lethargy, and so forth; its destruction occurs. When it is destroyed—
He sets forth another result in the aphorism:
"The covering of light—that is, *sattva*—which is characterized by *tamas* and is the cause of sleep, lassitude, and so forth, is destroyed. This is the subsequent effect."
After the destruction of the veil, it is described as follows:
"And there is fitness of the mind for the *dhāraṇās*" (2.53), meaning, "The mind becomes fit for *dhāraṇā*. (Ibid., 2.53)
Dhāraṇā is the drawing and fixing of the mind upon a specific location, such as the base of the spine, the navel, the heart, the space between the eyebrows, or the aperture of Brahmā;
for it is stated in the Sūtra: "Dhāraṇā is the binding of the mind to a place" (3.1).
Dhāraṇā is the drawing and fixing of the mind on a particular [spot].
The sites (*pīṭha*), such as the base, the navel wheel, the heart,
the space between the eyebrows, the aperture at the crown of the head, and so forth, as described in the Sūtra: [text continues].
— "Dhāraṇā is the holding of the mind upon a particular object" (ibid. 3.1).
And the Śruti says:

"Having meditated upon the mind as the faculty of volition and having withdrawn it into the self, the wise man should likewise fix the self [therein]; this is proclaimed as *dhāraṇā* (concentration)."
Thus [it is said] in the *Amṛtanādopaniṣad* (16).
And the Śruti also says this: "The wise seeker, having thoroughly studied the mind— the instrument of thought— should concentrate it upon [the Self]."
"Holding onto such a state is described as *dhāraṇā*" (*Amṛtanāda Upaniṣad* 16).
By means of *prāṇāyāma*, one is restrained from the restlessness caused by the quality of *rajas* and from the lethargy and other traits caused by the quality of *tamas*.
The mind becomes fit for that concentration (dhāraṇā) when it is freed from fickleness— the effect of the quality of passion (rajas)— and from...
Laziness and other qualities born of the *tamas* attribute [are removed] through the practice of *prāṇāyāma*,
according to the passage from the *Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha* (28.122): "By the firm practice of *prāṇāyāma* and by the method imparted by the Guru..."

By the word "reasoning" (*yukti*), there is understood such things as the movement of the Meru in the form of the head as established among practitioners of yoga, the whirling of the uvula with the tip of the tongue, meditation on light at the navel-center and in the heart, and the use of drugs that induce forgetfulness, and so forth.
[This is] by means of the steady practice of *prāṇāyāma* together with its application...
"the application of the means prescribed by the teacher" (LYV 28.122).
The word *yukti*, "means," mentioned in the aforementioned verse, implies any one of the methods better known among [practitioners].

The yogis [practice] such things as moving the crown of the head, turning the uvula with the tip of the tongue, meditating on light at the navel-cakra and the heart, and the use of substances that induce heedlessness.

Thus, the means for the dissolution of the mind— namely, knowledge of the inner self, association with the virtuous, the exhaustion of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and the restraint of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*)— have been shown. Now, we shall describe *samādhi*, which is the means to that [dissolution].
Thus, the methods and means for the dissolution of the mind, such as the study of the science of the Self and so forth,
have been described. Now, another means for dissolving the mind is as follows:
Now, *samādhi* concentration will be explained. Regarding the mind endowed with five stages (*bhūmi*), *samādhi* consists of the two remaining stages after the abandonment of the first three stages.
And these stages have been shown by the author of the *Yogabhāṣya*: [text follows]
Excluding the first three, the final two states of the fivefold mental process are called *samādhi*— concentration. These states have been described by the commentator of the [Visuddhimagga].
The *Yogasūtra* states thus: "The states of the mind are the distracted, the deluded, the scattered, the one-pointed, and the restrained" (*Yogasūtrabhāṣya* 1.1).
"Scattered, clouded, gathered, one-pointed, and concentrated— these are the states of the mind" (Yogasūtrabhāṣya 1.1).

The mind existing amidst worldly scriptures and bodily impressions associated with the *āsura* (demonic) nature is *kṣipta* (distracted). That which is seized by sleep, lethargy, and so forth is *mūḍha* (deluded).

That which is occasionally joined with meditation, being superior to the distracted state, is *vikṣipta* (occasionally distracted). Among these, there is not even a suspicion of *samādhi* in the *kṣipta* and *mūḍha* states. However, in the *vikṣipta* mind, *samādhi* exists as a subordinate factor to distraction; it belongs to the category of yoga.
"It does not proceed" (in that very same work). Because it is included within distraction, it perishes immediately, like a seed placed within fire.

"But that which illuminates the object arisen in a one-pointed mind, attenuates the afflictions (*kleśa*), loosens the bonds of karma, and brings about cessation (*nirodha*)—that is designated as *saṃprajñāta-yoga*. (In that very same work).
"But when all modifications have ceased, there is asamprajñāta-samādhi" (in that same work). Therein, he formulates the aphorism regarding one-pointedness, which is the stage of samprajñāta-samādhi:
"The mind [is one-pointed] when it is absorbed in the divine attributes..."

The state of being distracted is known to occur when the mind is directed toward objects such as worldly affairs, learning, or the physical body. When the mind is overcome by sleep, lethargy, and so forth, it is known to be in a state of darkness. The...
The mind is said to be in a state of gathering when, at times,
it possesses contemplations, as this state is distinguishable from the state of scattering. [This applies to] the states of scattering and mental darkness.
The mind cannot possess concentration.
However, the occasional concentration occurring in the state of mental gathering cannot be counted as *yoga*, because it is subordinate.
"Having bowed to that state" (ibid. 1.1). *Jīvanmukti-viveka*:
Just as a seed is destroyed when placed in fire, so too is this concentration immediately destroyed because it exists within [the mind].
However, that concentration which,
in the one-pointed state of the mind, reveals the object in its true reality, removes the afflictions and loosens the bonds.
That which burns away karma and brings one closer to the state of concentration is called *samprajñāta* yoga. When all modifications of the mind have ceased, it is called *asamprajñāta*.
"Samādhi, or the state of concentration" (ibid. 1.1).
Among these, the one-pointed state in which *samprajñāta* samādhi occurs is described in the Sūtra as follows:
"The transformation of the mind's one-pointedness occurs when the past and present cognitions are identical" (3.12).
That is to say, the one-pointedness of the mind (*citta*) is when the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) that has subsided and the one that is currently arising are alike.

(Yoga Sūtra 3.12). "Quiescent" means past; "arisen" means present; "cognition" (*pratyaya*) refers to a mental modification (*cittavṛtti*). If the arisen cognition were to grasp the very same object that the past cognition grasped, then those two would be identical. Such [identity] belongs to the mind.
Transformation is called one-pointedness. He formulates the aphorism for *samādhi*, which is characterized by the intensification of one-pointedness:
"The subsided (*śāntaḥ*) means past; the arisen (*uditaḥ*) means present; ideation (*pratyaya*) means mental transformation."
When the object of a past transformation and the object of a present transformation are identical, then those transformations become similar. Such modification—
The stabilization of the mind is called one-pointedness. The nature of *samādhi* concentration is this increased one-pointedness,
which is described in the Sūtra as follows:
"The transformation of the mind into concentration consists in the destruction of its capacity to take in all objects and the manifestation of its capacity for one-pointedness" (3.11).
"The powers of apprehending all objects and concentrating on a single object— these two being respectively suppressed and brought forth..."
"respectively, the *citta* attains the modification called *samādhi*" (ibid.
The *citta*, being impelled by the quality of *rajas*, gradually grasps all objects. For the suppression of that quality of *rajas*:
Through the specific effort exerted by the yogin as he practices day after day, the tendency toward all objects (*sarvārthatā*) diminishes and one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*) arises;

such a transformation of the mind is called *samādhi*. Among the eight limbs of that *samādhi*, the five—restraints (*yama*), observances (*niyama*), postures (*āsana*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*)—are the external limbs. Regarding these, he formulates the sūtra on the restraints (*yama*):
The mind grasps all manner of objects, one by one, impelled by the quality of *rajas*. To restrain this, yogis apply special effort and cultivate the habit of contemplating all such objects.
By this means, distraction is diminished day by day and one-pointedness is increased; such a transformation of the mind is called concentration.
Of the eight constituents of *samādhi*-concentration, the first five— *yama*, *niyama*, *āsana*, *prāṇāyāma*, and *pratyāhāra*—
are preliminary. Among these, the *yamas* are the forbearances.
It is set forth in the Sūtra as follows: "Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness are the yamas" (2.30).
"Non-injury, truthfulness, non-theft, chastity, and..."

The abstentions from prohibited actions such as violence are called *yamas* (ibid.: "They are called *yamas* because they restrain the yogi from forbidden practices such as violence"). He formulates the *niyamas*:
"These are called *yamas* because they restrain the yogis."
From prohibited activities such as killing and the rest.
The *niyamas*, or religious observances, are described in the *sūtra* as follows:
"Purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord are the observances" (Yoga Sūtra 2.32).
"Internal and external purification, contentment, mortification, study, and worship of God are the *niyamas*" (ibid.).

The *niyamas* (observances) are so called because they restrain and direct [the practitioner] toward the dharma of desirelessness (*niṣkāmadharma*), which is the cause of liberation, after having turned them away from the dharma of desire (*kāmyadharma*), which is the cause of birth. The distinction between the practice of *yama* and *niyama* is recorded in the Smṛti:
"These restrain the yogis from motivated rituals..."

One should cause rebirth to arise and direct him toward performing desireless religious acts that lead to liberation; therefore, these are called observances (*niyama*). In the *Smṛtis*, a certain distinction regarding this is described.
Regarding the distinction between the *yamas* and *niyamas* and their practice, it is said: "A wise person should constantly perform the *yamas*, but should not [exclusively] perform the *niyamas*;
for one who fails to perform the *yamas* while devoting himself solely to the *niyamas* falls."
—(Manusmṛti 4.204)
“The observance of the *niyamas* is not mandatory, but one must always practice the *yamas*. He who practices only the *niyamas*, while avoiding the *yamas*, falls” (Manu Saṃhitā 4.204).
"One who possesses the observances (niyamas) but is not attached to the restraints (yamas) falls, whereas one who possesses the restraints but is indolent regarding the observances does not perish;
thus, having examined the restraints and the observances with the intellect,"
"He should direct his intellect toward those [practices] where *yamas* predominate. Thus it is said.
"He who does not attend to the *yamas*, but practices the *niyamas* well, falls; whereas he who practices the *yamas* well, even though..."
One who is lax regarding the *niyamas* does not become discouraged. Thus, having wisely determined the relative importance of *yama* and *niyama*,
one should direct the mind toward the practice of the greater number of *yamas*.
(Source untraced).
He sets forth the aphorisms on the fruits of *yama* and *niyama*:
the results of *yama* and *niyama* have been described.
Thus it is stated in the Sūtras:
"When non-violence is firmly established, hostility ceases in his presence" (Yoga Sūtras 2.35).
"When non-violence is established, all hostilities cease in his presence" (Yoga Sūtra 2.35).
"When truth is established, there arises the attainment of the fruits of actions" (Yoga Sūtra 2.36).
“(By the establishment of truthfulness) the yogi gains the power of attaining for himself and for others the fruits of action without performing the action” (ibid. 2.36). Jīvan-mukti Viveka.
"When non-stealing is firmly established,
all riches come to the yogi" (Yoga Sūtra 2.37).
Upon the firm foundation of celibacy, there is the attainment of vigor. (Yoga Sūtra 2.38)
"By the firm establishment of celibacy, vigor is attained" (Yoga Sūtra 2.38).
"By the firm establishment of non-possessiveness, there arises knowledge of how one came to be born" (Yoga Sūtra 2.39); that is, the absence of fear regarding birth and other such conditions.
"When he is established in non-appropriation, he attains the recollection of past lives" (ibid. 2.39). Thereafter, there is freedom from fear regarding rebirth.
"From purity comes disgust for one's own body and non-association with others. (Yoga Sūtra 2.40)
"When internal and external purity have been established, there arise disgust for one's own body and non-intercourse with others" (ibid. 2.40).
“Purification of the *sattva*, cheerfulness, one-pointedness, mastery over the senses, and fitness for the vision of the Self” (Yoga Sūtra 2.41) come into being.
“There also arise purification of the *sattva*, cheerfulness...”
"Of the mind, concentration, mastery over the senses, and fitness for the realization of the Self" (ibid. 2.41). These [qualities] come about when purity (*śauca*) is established.
"From contentment comes the attainment of unsurpassed happiness" (Yoga Sūtra 2.42).
‘From contentment comes supreme happiness’ (ibid);
‘The perfection of the sense organs results from the destruction of impurity through austerity’ (Yoga Sūtra 2.43).
“The result of mortification is the attainment of mastery over the sense organs and the body through the destruction of impurities” (ibid).
“From self-study comes communion with the chosen deity” (Yoga Sūtra 2.44).
"Through the repetition of the mantra, there is the realization of the intended deity" (ibid. 2.44);
"Success in samādhi comes from devotion to the Lord" (Yoga Sūtra 2.45).

‘By surrendering everything to Īśvara, samādhi arises’ (ibid. 2.45). Posture and breath-control have already been explained. He now formulates the aphorism for withdrawal of the senses: [The previous two] have been explained; he now provides the sūtra for pratyāhāra.
Posture and control of the vital breath have already been [explained].
Now, *pratyāhāra*— the withdrawal of the senses— is described in the *sūtra* as follows:
"The withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*) is when, in the absence of contact with their respective objects, the senses, as it were, conform to the nature of the mind" (Yoga Sūtra 2.54).
Thus: "The withdrawal of the senses consists in their relinquishing their own objects and assuming, as it were, the form of the mind-stuff."

Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are the objects; when the senses, such as hearing and the rest, are withdrawn from them, they remain as if imitating the very nature of the mind. And there is a scriptural passage to this effect:
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are the objects of the senses;
when the sense organs, such as hearing and the rest, are withdrawn from them, they remain as if assuming the form of the mind. The Śruti also [states this].
In this regard, it is said as follows:
"One should contemplate the five objects, beginning with sound, as well as the mind which is exceedingly fickle, as the rays of one's own self; that is called pratyāhāra (withdrawal)."
(From the Amṛtanāda Upaniṣad, section 5)

“The five senses, which have sound and the other [objects] as their domains, together with the mind whose nature is exceedingly fickle, are merely the rays (manifestations) of the Self, like the rays of the sun.”

Thinking in this manner is called ‘withdrawal’ (Amṛtanāda Upaniṣad 5). Those senses, such as hearing and the rest, for which sound and other objects are the domains are the five senses beginning with hearing; [and] the mind.
The withdrawal of these six [faculties] from sound and the other objects—which do not have the nature of the Self—and contemplating them as rays of the Self;
that is the meaning of *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal). He states the fruit of *pratyāhāra* in the aphorism:
"The five senses, hearing and so forth, having sound and so forth as their..."
The objects, the senses, and the mind— these six together— withdraw themselves from their respective objects, such as sound and the rest, which are non-self,
and regard them as the rays of the Self, which is Light; this...
This is *pratyāhāra*—such is the meaning of the sacred scripture (*śruti*). The result of withdrawal is described in the aphorism as follows:
"From that comes the supreme mastery over the senses" (Yoga Sūtra 2.55).

From that arises supreme mastery over the senses. (Now, by means of three sutras, he sets forth concentration—*dhāraṇā*, meditation—*dhyāna*, and absorption—*samādhi*. [The text continues: ...Now contemplation—*dhāraṇā*, meditation—*dhyāna*, and [absorption—*samādhi*]. (Yogasūtra 3.1–4)
Concentration (*samādhi*) is being presented by way of three sūtras as follows:
"Concentration is the binding of the mind to a single location" (*Yoga Sūtra* 3.1).
‘Dhāraṇā is the fixing of the mind upon a particular object’ (ibid. 3.1).
‘Dhyāna is the one-pointed continuity of cognition directed toward that [object]’ (Yoga Sūtra 3.2).
"An uninterrupted flow of knowledge regarding that object is meditative absorption— dhyāna" (ibid., 3.2).
"That same [state], when only the object appears and it is as if devoid of its own nature, is concentration— samādhi" (Yoga Sūtra 3.3).
"When that, having abandoned all forms, reflects only upon the meaning, it is concentration—*samādhi* (ibid. 3.3).
The locations such as the *ādhāra* and so forth have been described previously. Another location is now heard:"
Regions such as the mystic circle at the base (*mūlacakramaṇḍala*) and so forth have been described previously. Now, another location is defined in the *Śruti* as follows:

"Having meditated upon the mind as the faculty of volition and having withdrawn it into the self, the wise man should likewise fix the self [therein]; this is proclaimed as *dhāraṇā* (concentration). (Amṛtanādopaniṣad 16).
"Having studied the perceiving mind, the wise seeker concentrates it upon the Self and remains holding it fixed there;
this is called *dhāraṇā*, or contemplation. (Amṛtanāda Upaniṣad)
Upaniṣad 16):

"The effort consisting of the thought, 'Let the mind, which conceives all objects, conceive only the Self and nothing else'—this is concentration (*saṃkṣepa*) upon the Self. One-pointedness of cognition is a continuous flow whose sole object is reality. And that is of two kinds:"

Arising repeatedly after being severed, and [arising] continuously—these two, respectively, become *dhyāna* and *samādhi*. Both of these have been demonstrated by the practitioner who experiences all things:
"Let that mind which thinks of everything think of the [One]."
The self alone and nothing else— effort in this manner is concentration on the self.
The continuous flow of thought means a succession of transformations.
The modifications of the mind in the form of reality alone are of two kinds, occurring in a broken or an unbroken manner;
these are called meditation (dhyāna) and concentration (samādhi).
These two have both been demonstrated by Sarvānubhavayogin as follows:
"Since knowledge is said to arise from one-pointedness of mind (cittaikāgrya)..."
Therefore, meditation, which is the means for achieving that, is taught here according to the proper method.
(Muktikopaniṣad 2.49)
Just as the aforementioned knowledge arises correctly from the concentrated mind, so too is meditation— the means to that knowledge— now being duly described (Muktikopaniṣad 2.49).
"Having dissolved all modifications through the process of reversing their origination,
one should contemplate the remaining pure Being, which is consciousness and bliss.
(Muktikopaniṣad 2.50)

"Having dissolved all derivative entities back into their sources in the reverse order of their creation, contemplate that which remains— the ultimate source— which is pure existence and consciousness."
"And bliss [which is meditation]" (ibid. 2.50).
"The continuous flow of mental modifications in the form of Brahman, devoid of egoism, arising from the excellence of the practice of meditation, is samprajñāta-samādhi."
And as it is said in the *Muktikopaniṣad* (2.53):
"The continuous flow of the mental modifications in the form of the Self, which is Brahman, unmixed with the sense of ego, is [the state of liberation]."
"Samprajñāta-samādhi, which results from the superior practice of meditation" (ibid. 2.53).
And the venerable Bhagavatpāda cited this:
The supreme nature of consciousness is like the sky— once-shining, unborn, one, and imperishable;
it is untainted, all-pervading, and non-dual.
And that very [state] I am, eternally liberated—Om.
—(Upadeśasāhasrī 10.1)
His Holiness (Śaṅkarācārya) explained it as follows:
"I am the Supreme Brahman, which is pure consciousness, eternally manifest, unborn, one alone, and imperishable."
Unattached and all-pervasive like space, I am non-dual; therefore, I am eternally free. Om. (Upadeśasāhasrī 10.1) "But as for me, I am the pure Seer, whose nature is changeless."
By my very nature, I have no object whatsoever; being the unborn, infinite plenitude, I abide as the Self, complete everywhere— before, across, above, and below.
Thus [it is stated] in that very same place (10.2).
"I am pure and changeless consciousness, by nature devoid of objects to be illumined; unborn and established in the Self,
I am the all-pervading Brahman— before me, across, and everywhere."
Above, below, and in all other directions (ibid. 10.2):
"I am unborn, immortal, likewise undecaying, deathless, self-luminous, omnipresent, and non-dual. I am neither cause nor effect, exceedingly pure, eternally satisfied, and therefore liberated, Om."
— (at that very place, 10.3) thus.
“I am unborn, deathless, free from old age, immortal, self-luminous, all-pervading, and non-dual. Utterly pure, devoid of both cause and effect, and satisfied in the One.”
"Bliss! I am free! Yes! (ibid. 10.3).

Now, one might object: "Is not *samprajñāta-samādhi* [cognitive absorption] still a mental state? How then can it be cited as the locus for *samādhi*, the eighth limb that occurs immediately after *dhyāna*?"
Objection: How is *samprajñāta* samādhi, which is the primary [form of samādhi], mentioned in the place of the eighth ancillary (*aṅga*), namely samādhi, which follows meditation (*dhyāna*)?

This is not a fault, because there is no absolute difference [between the stages]. Just as a student reciting the Veda stumbles at every step and must repeatedly correct himself, whereas one who has mastered the Veda does not stumble when attentive, and even a teacher may stumble when inattentive or drowsy; so too, despite the identity of the object, [the results differ] according to the degree of ripeness.

The internal distinctions among the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), concentrations (*samādhi*), and discernments (*samprajñāta*) are to be understood. The triad beginning with *dhāraṇā* (retention) is the "internal limb" (*antaraṅga*) of discerning concentration (*samprajñāta-samādhi*) because it has the mind as its object. However, the five beginning with *yama* (restraint) are "external limbs" (*bahiraṅga*). This [distinction] he sets forth in the sūtra:

Reply: There is no harm, because they are not entirely different. Just as a boy, while studying the Vedas, stumbles at every step but corrects himself, so too does one who has completed [his studies].
Just as one who studies the Vedas with care commits no error, and even an unobservant or drowsy teacher does not stumble,
so too are the distinctions between *dhyāna* and *samādhi*.
And *samprajñāta* samādhi is to be understood as subdivisions of the same object according to the differences in its maturation. *Dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi* consist of the mind—
As their objects, these are essential means for *samprajñāta-samādhi*, whereas the five ancillaries— *yama* and so forth— are not of primary importance.
The same view has been expressed in the aphorism:
"These three are more internal than the preceding ones" (Yoga Sūtra 3.7).
"These three are more internal than those that precede."
(Yoga Sūtra 3.7).
Therefore, once the internal limb has first been attained through some merit, one need not exert excessive effort for the sake of attaining the external limbs.
Although Patañjali [mentions] the objects of *samprajñāta-samādhi*—namely, the gross elements, the subtle elements (*tanmātras*), the sense organs, the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and so forth—...

Various conceptual concentrations (*vikalpasamādhi*) have been elaborated in many ways; nevertheless, because they serve as causes for powers such as invisibility and are contrary to the concentration that is the cause of liberation, we do not pay them heed. And thus it has been aphorized:
"Therefore, if in the first instance these internal means..."

Since these are accomplished through certain religious merits, it is not necessary to exert great effort to attain the external ones. Although Patañjali has treated *samprajñāta* and *savikalpa* [samādhi] at length—
Although there are samādhis that have as their objects material objects,
the gross elements and subtle elements, the sense organs, and the ego-sense,
we do not wish to direct our attention toward them because—
Since these are the causes of occult powers such as invisibility and the like, they are contrary to *samādhi*, which leads to liberation.
This has been described in the Sūtra as follows:
"These are obstacles to samādhi, but they are powers in the worldly state" (Yogasūtra 3.38).

And as it is said: "Upon being invited by those in their respective stations, the yogi should neither feel attachment nor pride, for fear of the recurrence of undesirable consequences" (Yoga Sūtra 3.52).
Thus also:
"The yogi should not feel allured or flattered by..."

"Out of fear of evil once again, there were overtures from celestial beings" (ibid.). It is narrated that although Uddālaka was invited by the gods, he disregarded those gods and remained solely in non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*). This is understood in exactly the same way through both questions and answers.

"Occupying high positions"— *sthānins* refers to the gods (*indra* and so forth). The episode in the *Yogavāsiṣṭha Rāmāyaṇa*, *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* 54.64–66, relates that although Uddālaka was invited...
The gods, having attained the *nirvikalpa* samādhi, disregard even those [other] gods.
This same point is understood from the questions and [answers].
Śrī Rāma asked, and Vasiṣṭha replied as follows: Śrī Rāma— Vasiṣṭha—
Sri Sri Rama: "O best of the knowers of the Self, how is it that powers such as levitation and others [arise]?"

"O best among the knowers of the Self, how is it that [these signs] are not found here in the bodies of those liberated while living? (Laghu Yogavāsiṣṭha 28.1; YV 5.89.9). "jīvanmuktaśarīrāṇāṃ kathamātmavidāṃ vara..."
Powers such as traveling through the sky and so forth are not seen here.
—(Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 28.1)

"O Rāghava, even one who knows not the Self, though unliberated, certainly attains such powers as traveling through the sky by means of the power of substances, mantras, rituals, time, and personal capacity. (Tatraiva 28.2)
Vasiṣṭha: O Rāghava, through the power of certain substances, mantras, specific practices, time, and so forth, one may acquire such supernatural powers as levitation and the like.
This is not the domain of one who is still bound and ignorant of the Self; for the knower of the Self perceives only the Self.
Satisfied by the Self through the Self, he does not pursue ignorance.
—(At that very place, 28.3) ||
‘This object is not for one who knows the Self,
for that knower of the Self has regard only for the Self. He is satisfied in and by himself alone, and he does not go forth.’

"Whatever worldly phenomena there may be, those who know them to consist of ignorance—how indeed could one who knows the Self, having abandoned ignorance, immerse himself in them? (Jīvanmuktiviveka 28.3; Yogavāsiṣṭha 5.89.13)
(In that very same place, 28.5) ||
“How could he, who by knowing the Self has cast off ignorance and understands phenomenal existence to be a product of ignorance, immerse himself in those very things? (LYV 28.5; YV)
The powers of substances, mantras, rituals, time, and personal capacity effectively grant success;
however, none of them assist in the attainment of the state of the Supreme Self.
(In that very same place, 28.7) ||

"Some substance, mantra, practice, and time— all these have the power to bestow supernatural powers (*siddhi*) effectively, yet they do not assist in realizing the abode of the Supreme Self" (LYV 28.7; YV).
For that attainment of the Self which arises when the entire web of desires has been stilled— how can it be obtained by one whose mind is submerged in the longing for supernatural powers?
(In that very same place, 28.9) ||
“The realization of the Self occurs when desires have been entirely dissolved; how, then, can it be attained by one whose mind is immersed in the cravings for supernatural powers?”
"None of these worldly phenomena can please one who knows reality, just as the women of a wretched village cannot please a sophisticated city man who loves a refined courtesan. (LYV28.9; YV5.89.33)
—(Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra 18.34) —
"Nothing whatsoever in the world can attract the knower of Reality, just as a city-dweller, having a refined woman of the city as his wife, does not feel infatuated with others."

no curiosity arises in him regarding these webs of wonders."

"The self that is pure consciousness" (LYV 27.67; YV 5.77.30).

And it is said: "But he who, even though his self is cultivated, still desires the nets of supernatural powers, accomplishes those powers in due order by means of the substances used for attaining powers."
—(In that very place, 28.6; in the Yogavāsiṣṭha, 89.23) ||
"Whoever desires to gather supernatural powers (*siddhi*),
even while being ignorant of the Self, may achieve them one by one by means of those things that serve as instruments for supernatural powers. (LYV)

However, the *samprajñāta* samādhi, which has the Self as its object, is the cause for the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and for the *nirodha* samādhi; therefore, attention is paid to it here.
As the *samprajñāta* samādhi, concerned with the Self...
Because it leads to the destruction of desire and brings about the *nirodha-samādhi*, we have paid close attention to this.
Now, the *nirodha-samādhi* consisting of the fifth stage is examined. And he sets forth that cessation (*nirodha*) in a sūtra:
Now, the fifth state, *nirodha-samādhi*, is being defined. This *nirodha*—cessation—is described in the Sūtra as follows: [Jīvan-mukti-viveka]

"The transformation of cessation is the sequence of moments of the mind in cessation, characterized by the suppression of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of emergence and the manifestation of the latent impressions of cessation" (Yoga Sūtra 3.9). "By the suppression of the agitated impressions of the mind..."
"And by the arising of the saṃskāras of mastery, the mind, persisting in that moment of mastery, is said to attain the transformation of mastery" (Yoga-sūtra 3.9).
The impressions of emergence (*vyutthāna-saṃskāra*) are antagonistic to *samādhi*. These have been illustrated in the case of Uddālaka’s *samādhi*:
"The impressions of emergence (namely, those of *samprajñāta* *samādhi* or the first three stages) are opposed to *samādhi*..."
They have been explained in the episode of the *samādhi* of Uddālaka as follows: *tasmāt...* [text fragment].
"When shall I attain long-lasting rest in that supremely pure state free from mental constructs, like a cloud upon the peak of Mount Meru?"
Thus it is said in the *Laghu-yogavāsiṣṭha* (24.29).
"When shall I attain a state of tranquil abiding in that realm which is perfectly pure and devoid of mental construction, just as clouds rest upon the peak of Mount Meru? (LYV 24.29)
Thus, overcome by these reflections, the twice-born Uddālaka sat down again and again and diligently practiced meditation.
(In that very same work, 24.35) ||
The Brāhmaṇa Uddālaka, possessing this thought, while seated, practiced meditation with great vigor again and again. (LYV:
"But when the mind, as restless as a monkey, is led away by sense objects...")
He did not find a firm foundation for his composure that would grant him joy.

"Perhaps, immediately after abandoning external contact, he might secure the blissful state in *samādhi*, for his hand—fickle like a monkey—is being dragged away by the objects of the senses. (LYV 24.36; YV 5.51.39) "At one time, immediately after the abandonment of external contact..."
The monkey of his mind went toward the accumulations of internal tactile sensations.
(In that very same place, 24.37) ||
"But when external objects were abandoned,

"Sometimes, due to an internal touch, he grasps an external object;
