(In that very same place, 24.38) ||
"Sometimes withdrawing from internal things, he again perceives external objects; at other times, his mind flies away like a frightened bird. (LYV 24.38)
At times he perceives a pervasive radiance resembling the rising sun;
at times he sees only empty space; and at times he sees dense darkness.
(In that very same work, 24.39) ||
"Sometimes he sees a pervasive light like the risen sun, and yet again only emptiness, or sometimes utter darkness.
Again and again, as he comes according to his desire, these appearances manifest."
The hero cut them down with his mind, as if with a sword against enemies in battle.
—(In that very same place, 24.109) ||
Again and again, he severed with the sword of his mind the appearances of objects that arose of their own accord, just as a warrior cuts down his enemies in battle with a sword.
When the flood of conceptual constructions had been completely severed, he beheld within the sky of his heart that darkness which veils the sun of discernment, as black as flickering collyrium.
—(In that very same place, 24.110) ||
"The multitude of mental images having been severed, he saw the sun of discernment hidden by the quality of darkness (*tamas*), like a throbbing, dark-blue cloud. (LYV 24.110)
He also destroyed that [ignorance] with the sun of perfect knowledge;
when darkness had ceased within his mind, he beheld a mass of light.
He crushed it like a young elephant crushing a forest of land-lotuses.
(In that very same place, 24.111) ||
‘He dispelled even that darkness [of ignorance] with the sun of right knowledge; then, in his mind cleared of darkness, he beheld a mass of light. He destroyed even that mass.’

Just as a young elephant destroys a forest of hibiscus (*sthalapadma*), so too, when his splendor had subsided, the mind of that sage began to reel. (LYV 24.111) "When his radiance had ceased, the mind of the sage was reeling."
He fell asleep like a night-lotus, but he quickly shattered even that sleep.
(In that very same place, 24.112) ||
"When the light vanished, the sage’s mind reeled and fell asleep like a lotus closing at sunset; yet he immediately roused his mind from that slumber. (LYV 24.112)
When his sleep had passed away, the consciousness of space arose within him.
When that consciousness of space vanished, his mind became bewildered;
yet this noble-minded one wiped away even that delusion of the mind.
—(In that very place, 24.113) ||
"When he awoke, his mind perceived the form of space (*ākāśa*). When that awareness of space was destroyed, his mind became torpid. The magnanimous sage removed even that."
‘This lethargy [arose] from his mind’ (LYV 24.113). ‘Then, having reached an indescribable state free from radiance, darkness, sleep, delusion, and so forth, his mind rested for a moment’—
(in that same work, 24.114).
“Then the mind reached that ineffable state which is free from light, darkness, sleep, torpor, and so forth, and for a time experienced peace” (LYV 24.114; YV 5.54.53).

These latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of emergence are daily and moment by moment overcome by the yogi’s effort, which has cessation as its cause; and the latent impressions of cessation, being opposed to them, manifest. This being the case, cessation follows after the mind at every single moment. Such is this transformation of the mind toward cessation.

These mental transformations are overcome, day after day and moment after moment, by such efforts of the yogi as are the means for their control (cessation); and their opposites— namely, the factors of control— [are likewise cultivated].
Impressions are formed. When this is accomplished, the mind remains restrained from transformation in every single moment; and in this manner, the mind is transformed.
In the form of restraint— that is, the transformation of restraint.

Now, according to the principle that "all entities, except for the power of consciousness, undergo transformation at every moment," it must be asserted that there is a continuous flow of transformation in the mind at all times.

Objection: It must be admitted that the mind always undergoes modifications according to the rule that "everything, with the exception of pure consciousness (knowledge), is subject to transformation."
"Transformations at every moment" (*Tattvakaumudī* of Vācaspati Miśra on *Sāṃkhyakārikā* 5).
"Certainly. In that regard, for one whose mind is emergent, the flow of mental modifications (*vṛtti*) is manifest; but for one whose mind is restrained..."
Anticipating the question "How so?", he provides the answer in a sutra:
"Yes, it is indeed so. The flow of the transformations of the mind in its arisen state is evident. But how does this happen?"
The state of mental restraint is described in the aphorism as follows in the *Sāṅkhyakaumudī* (5):
"Then, from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*), there is a steady flow" (Yoga Sūtra 3.10). Its flow becomes steady through practice.
Just as when fuel, clarified butter, and oblations are poured into a fire, it blazes up with ever-increasing intensity, yet when the fuel and other materials are exhausted, at the very first moment—

Something subsides, and in each subsequent moment, tranquility increases. Thus, for one whose mind has been restrained, an ever-increasing calm flows forth. In this regard, the very latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by each preceding state of calm are the cause of each succeeding state of calm.
The Blessed One clearly described this "flowing of tranquility" (*praśāntavāhitā*):
Just as when one throws fuel and clarified butter into a fire,
its flames increase more and more, and then, as the fuel is gradually exhausted, the fire also becomes less and less;

In the same way, stability increases progressively within the restrained mind. Only those impressions (*saṃskāra*) that precede stability serve as the cause for the subsequent stability therein. This flow of...
Steadiness has been very clearly described by the Lord (Śrī Kṛṣṇa in the Bhagavadgītā) as follows:
"When the disciplined mind abides in the Self alone..."
When one is free from longing for all desires, then one is said to be disciplined (yukta).
(Bhagavadgītā 6.18)
“When the disciplined mind rests in the Self alone, free from longing for objects of enjoyment (whether seen or unseen),
then one is said to have attained yoga” (Bhagavad Gītā 6.18).
"Just as a lamp standing in a windless place does not flicker— this is the simile remembered for the yogin of restrained mind who practices yoga of the self."
—(In that very same place, 6.19) ||
‘Where the mind, restrained through the practice of yoga, comes to rest—that is the simile for the disciplined mind of a yogi practicing concentration on the Self’ (ibid.
6.19). ‘Where the mind, restrained through the practice of yoga, comes to rest...’
And wherein, beholding the Self by means of the self, one finds satisfaction within the self.
(In that very same work, 6.20)
“That in which the mind, restrained by the practice of concentration, comes to rest in tranquility; that in which, seeing the Self by means of the self, one rejoices in one’s own self” (ibid).
"That absolute bliss which is to be grasped by the intellect and is beyond the senses—
he who knows it, and being established therein, does not deviate from reality."
— (In that very same place, 6.21):
“That in which one knows the boundless bliss, beyond the reach of the senses and grasped only by the intellect;”
"Established in which, one never departs from reality" (ibid. 6.21):
"Having obtained which, one considers no other gain to be superior to it."
Established in which, one is not shaken even by heavy suffering.
(In that very same place, 6.22) ||
"That which, having attained, one thinks there is no greater attainment, and established in which one is not shaken even by the heaviest of sorrows" (ibid. 6.22).
One should know that disjunction from the union with suffering is designated as yoga.
‘That must certainly be practiced with a mind free from despondency.
(ibid., 6.23). ‘Let that be known as yoga which is the severance from...’
"the touch of pain. This is to be practiced with perseverance and with an undaunted mind" (ibid. 6.23).
He provides the aphorism for the means of achieving the concentration of cessation (*nirodhasamādhi*):
The means for *nirodha-samādhi*— the concentration of restraint—
is described in the aphorism as follows: “The other [samādhi] is preceded by the practice of the cognition of cessation and results in residual latent impressions” (*Yoga Sūtra* 1.18).
There is another samādhi, attained through the constant practice of the cessation of all mental activity,
in which the *citta* retains only the unmanifested impressions (*vāsanā*). (Pātañjala Yoga Sūtra)

*Virāma* is the cessation of mental activity; its *pratyaya* is the cause, namely the human effort for the sake of ceasing mental activity. Its *abhyāsa* is the repeated accomplishment thereof. That which is preceded by that [effort] and produced by it is [the *nirbīja-samādhi*], as stated in the immediately preceding sūtra.

Since *samprajñāta-samādhi* has already been described, the other, *asaṃprajñāta-samādhi*, is considered in relation to it. Because the true nature of the mind (*cittasvarūpa*), when devoid of mental fluctuations (*vṛtti*), is difficult to perceive, the mind remains in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). The Blessed One has clearly stated that this state is produced by the cognition of cessation (*virāma-pratyaya*).
Cessation (*virāmaḥ*) means the stopping of transformation. *Pratyayaḥ* means the cause of that, namely, the personal effort toward the cessation of transformation; it is practice.
The practice (*abhyāsa*) of that— meaning performing it again and again— is "preceded by that" (*tatpūrvakaḥ*), which means brought about by that.
As for *samprajñāta* samādhi, or conscious concentration...
By the word "other" (*anya*) in the immediately preceding aphorism, it is meant in relation to that *asamprajñāta* samādhi, namely, the superconscious concentration.
In that superconscious concentration (*asamprajñāta-samādhi*), the mind remains in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) alone, insofar as it is devoid of...
The nature of these transformations cannot be described. The Blessed One has clearly explained the practice of cessation as the progenitor [of that state] in this way:
Having abandoned all desires born of volition without exception,
and having restrained the entire collection of senses on all sides by the mind alone;
(Bhagavadgītā 6.24)
"Having completely renounced all desires born of the will, and having withdrawn the senses from all directions by the power of the mind; (Bhagavad Gītā 6.24)
“One should gradually come to rest by means of the intellect held with firmness;
having established the mind within the Self, one should not think of anything at all.”
(In that very same work, 6.25) ||
‘Let him gradually attain tranquility through a mind established in forbearance; having fixed his mind upon the Self, he should think of nothing else’ (ibid. 6.25).
"From whatever cause the restless and unsteady mind wanders away, from that very cause one should restrain it and bring it under the control of the Self alone.
"Let him withdraw the flickering and restless mind from whatever causes it to wander away, and bring it back under the control of the Self alone" (ibid. 6.26).

Desirable objects— such as garlands, sandalwood paste, women, sons, friends, houses, and fields— though possessed of many defects well-known to discerning people skilled in the scriptures on liberation, nevertheless conceal those defects through the power of beginningless ignorance and [cling] to them.
The mind conceives of correctness regarding sense objects; and from that conceptualization (*saṃkalpa*), desires arise in the form of "May this be mine. Thus it is recorded in the Smṛti:
"Though desired things such as flower garlands, sandalwood..."
Lodhra-paste, women, children, friends, houses, lands,
and the like are full of many evils, as is well known to discerning people who are well-versed in the discipline.

Although these are the causes of liberation, the mind— under the influence of beginningless ignorance— conceals all those evils and imagines them to be wholesome. From such imagination, desires arise.
It is born in the form of the thought, "Let this be mine. The Smṛti also states thus:
"Desire indeed has volition as its root; sacrifices are born from volition."
(Manusmṛti 2.3) ||
"I know your root, O Desire; you are indeed born from volition (saṃkalpa); even sacrifices are born from volition" (Manu Saṃhitā).
"I shall no longer form a mental resolve toward you; you shall perish, root and all.
(Mahābhārata, Śāntiparvan 171.25).
"O Desire! I know your origin; you are born from thought, without a doubt."
"Of imagination. No more shall I will you, and you shall be destroyed along with your very root" (Mahābhārata 12.171.25).
In that state, when the defects of sense-objects have been directly perceived through discernment (*viveka*), desires are abandoned like milk-rice vomited by a dog.

Intending to show that desires for the worlds of Brahmā and so forth, as well as for the eightfold powers such as *aṇimā*, must be abandoned just like those for sandalwood and other [objects], he said "all. He said "without remainder" so that desire might not arise again and again, as it does when one who observes the vow of fasting for a month abandons food during that month. Even when there is an absence of mental activity regarding the renunciation of desire, [desire may still arise] through the eyes and other [senses].
Even that activity directed toward form and so forth, which is established by its own nature, must be restrained by the mind alone when joined with effort.

It is said "on all sides" because one must not pursue even the vision of deities and the like. It is said "gradually" because cessation is intended to occur through the successive conquest of the stages (*bhūmikās*). And those four stages are heard of in the *Kaṭhavallīs*:
When, through discernment, the defects in the objects of enjoyment are realized, desires are abandoned, just as one avoids the gruel vomited by a dog. The word "entirely"—

The word *sarvān* (as quoted from BG 6.24 above) is used to imply the desires for the world of Brahmā and so forth, as well as for the eight occult powers (*aṣṭaiśvarya*), such as becoming minute (*aṇimā*) and the rest.
It should also be abandoned, just like the desire for garlands and such;
for example, when a man has taken a vow to fast during a particular month and, in observance of it, renounces eating.
Even in that month, the desire for food arises again and again;
to remedy such a situation, the word "entirely" (*aśeṣataḥ*)— meaning without reservation or exception— has been used.
used. Having abandoned desires, although there is no intentional activity of the sense-faculties, yet the ordinary...

The functioning of the eye and other faculties in perceiving forms and so forth is to be restrained by an active mind (the use of the term *manasā* indicates this). From every direction (*samantataḥ*).
This has been used to mean that no indulgence is to be granted even for the desire to behold the Divine, and so forth. Regarding the use of the term "gradually" (*śanaiḥ*):

The term *śanaiḥ* (gradually) is intended for attaining tranquility through successive stages. There are four such stages, as described in the *Kaṭhopaniṣad*: [1] *yato yato niścarati manaścañcalamasthiram*, [2] *tatas tato niyamyaitadātmanyeva vaśaṃ nayet*, [3] *praśāntamanasaṃ hyenaṃ yoginaṃ sukhamuttamam*, [4] *upaiti śāntarajasaṃ brahmabhūtamakalmaṣam*.
The wise man should restrain speech in the mind; he should restrain that mind in the self of knowledge;
he should restrain that knowledge in the Great Self; and he should restrain that in the Peaceful Self.
—(Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.13).
"The wise man should merge his speech into his mind, and his mind into his intellect. He should merge his intellect into..."
"The Cosmic Mind, and the Cosmic Mind in the Tranquil Self" (Kathopaniṣad 1.3.13).
Verbal activity is twofold: worldly and Vedic. That which takes the form of idle chatter and the like is worldly; that which takes the form of recitation (*japa*) and the like is [Vedic].
Vaidika: In that regard, because the worldly [speech] causes great distraction, the yogi should abandon it even at the time of emergence from meditation.
Therefore, it is stated in the Smṛti:
"The organ of speech has a twofold function: the worldly..."
Speech and Vedic speech. The ordinary is in the form of common conversation and so forth, while the Vedic is in the form of the recitation of passages and so forth from the scriptures. Of these two—
Ordinary speech causes distraction in various ways;
therefore, the yogi should avoid it even when he has arisen from meditative absorption. Thus, the Smṛti says:
"Silence, the yogic posture, yoga, endurance, the habit of solitude, freedom from desire, and equanimity— these seven belong to the Ekadaṇḍin. (Nārada Parivrajaka Upaniṣad 4.25).
"Silence, yogic posture, concentration, the practice of meditation, fortitude, dwelling in solitude, desirelessness, and equanimity— these seven are prescribed for [the practitioner]."
"the monk who carries a single staff" (Nārada Parivrājaka Upaniṣad 4.25). In the *Jīvan-mukti-viveka*:

"One should abandon recitation of prayers (*japa*) and other such practices during the samādhi of cessation. This is the first stage, the stage of speech. Having firmly mastered that stage through mere effort—whether in a few days, months, or years—one should thereafter strive for the second stage, the stage of the mind; otherwise,"

Like a multi-storied palace, all the higher stages of yoga would perish by the collapse of the first stage alone. Although the eyes and other senses are to be restrained, nevertheless their inclusion within the stage of speech or the stage of mind should be understood.
In the concentration of restraint, recitation and so forth should [be performed].
Having abandoned it, this is the first stage—the stage of speech.
This stage should first be brought under firm control through effort alone, within a matter of days, months, or years; thereafter—
One should attempt the second stage— the mental plane. Otherwise (if one attempts many stages simultaneously), the failure to conquer the first stage will lead to the collapse of all.
The stages of yoga collapse like a multi-storied building when its first floor falls; although the eyes and other senses must also be restrained, they should be understood [in this manner].
[This would mean] that [speech] is included within the stage of speech or the stage of mind.
But is it not the case that the instruction "one should restrain speech in the mind" is untenable? For there is no entering of one sense organ into another sense organ.
Objection: It was stated: "One should restrain speech..."
This is as stated in the *Kaṭha Upaniṣad* (1.3.13,
quoted above), and it cannot be justified because one sense-organ does not enter into another.

Not so; for the act of entry is not intended here. Between speech and mind, which both cause various distractions, what is intended here is the remaining of the mental activity alone by first restraining the operation of speech. When the restraint of speech has been naturally accomplished—just as it is with cows, buffaloes, horses, and the like—one should then restrain the mind within the self (*ātman*). The self is threefold.

[The Self is] the knower-self, the great-self, and the peaceful-self. Here, the term "knowledge" (jñāna) is intended to refer to the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), which has the nature of being a knower because it is situated here [in the heart]; for the mind, as an instrument, is that which is to be governed.
Because it is mentioned separately. Egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) is of two kinds: specific and general.

That which conceives itself specifically, as in "I am this person's son," is the specific form. That which conceives itself merely as "I am" is the general form, and that exists in all individual beings.
Because it is all-pervading, the Self is called "Great" (*mahān*). By means of these two forms of ego (*ahaṃkāra*), two Selves are conditioned.

There is also the unconditioned, peaceful Self (*śāntātmā*). All of this exists in the relationship of internal and external. The peaceful Self is within all, consisting of the single essence of consciousness (*cidekarasa*). Resting upon that is the unmanifest (*avyakta*), which is the root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) and consists of the power of inertia (*jaḍaśakti*). And that, first of all—

It manifests as the principle known as *mahat* (the Great One) in the form of the universal ego (*sāmānyāhaṃkāra*). From that, it manifests externally in the form of the specific ego (*viśeṣāhaṃkāra*), then externally in the form of the mind (*manas*), and then externally in the form of the organs of speech and so forth. With this in mind, the state of being progressively more internal is expressed as follows: [Sanskrit text omitted].
Reply: It is not so, because "entering" is not intended here.
What is intended here is that both this speech and mind are causes of various distractions; of these, by means of control—
Once the function of speech has been mastered, only the functions of the mind remain to be controlled.
When the control of speech becomes as natural as that [of the mind],...
Of cows, buffaloes, horses, and so forth, the mind should then be merged into the knowing-self (*vijñānātman*).
The self is of three kinds: the knowing-self, the great [self], and...
The Self and the Tranquil Self.
Here, the term "Self" refers to the egoism that is attributed as the knower— the Self appearing as the agent in the act of cognition.
It is the "knowing self"; since the mind, which is the instrument of knowledge, is to be controlled, it is therefore mentioned separately.
Egoism is of two kinds: individual and universal.
Thus, the manifest particular egoism expressed as "Here I am, the son of so-and-so" belongs to the individual form of egoism. And "I..."
"Am"—this much alone belongs to the universal form of egoism (*ahaṃkāra*). Since this universal variety exists in every individual, it is called "great" (*mahān*). Thus, there are two selves.
[These] are attributed respectively by the two forms of egoism (*ahaṃkāra*).
The tranquil self (*ātman*) is devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*). All of them stand in a relationship of internal and external [dependence]. That which is most internal is the tranquil one.
The Self, which is pure consciousness, in which exists as physical power the unmanifest (*avyakta*),
the primal nature (*mūla-prakṛti*), the cause; this [Self] manifests itself at—
First, it manifests in the form of universal egoism and is called the Great Principle (*mahat-tattva*, the intellectual principle). Beyond that, it manifests in the form of individual egoism;
and beyond that again, in the form of the mind (*manas*), and further still.
With reference to these, in the form of the organs such as speech and so forth,
the Śruti describes their progressive inwardness one by one as follows:
For the objects are higher than the senses, and the mind is higher than the objects;
the intellect is higher than the mind, and the Great Self is higher than the intellect.
"Beyond the Great is the Unmanifest; beyond the Unmanifest is the Puruṣa. There is nothing higher than the Puruṣa; that is the culmination, that is the supreme goal. (Katha Upaniṣad 1.3.10–11).
Beyond the senses are the objects; beyond the objects is the mind; beyond the mind, the intellect; beyond the intellect, the Great Self; beyond the Great Self, the...
‘Unmanifest; beyond the unmanifest is the Puruṣa. Beyond the Puruṣa there is nothing—this is the end, the supreme goal’ (Kaṭhopaniṣad 1.3.10–11).

This being so, one should restrain the mind—the instrument whose nature is that of a faculty and which serves as the means for various kinds of conceptual constructions and discursive thoughts—within the ego-maker (*ahaṃkartṛ*).
Having abandoned the activities of the mind, one should leave only the ego-maker remaining. Nor should it be said that this is impossible, for [the Lord] stated:
"I consider its restraint to be as difficult as that of the wind" (Bhagavad Gītā 6.34).
Since the Blessed One has thus provided an answer to Arjuna who spoke as above, [it follows that]:
"Therefore, the mind which produces a variety of thoughts, in the form of the instrument of deliberation..."
It should be merged into the egoity (*ahaṃkāra*). This means abandoning all mental activities and retaining only the egoity—the sense of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*).
It cannot be said that this is impossible, because in response to...
Regarding Arjuna’s statement, “To control it [the mind] seems to me as difficult as to control the wind” (BG 6.34), the Lord spoke as follows:

"Without doubt, O mighty-armed one, the mind is restless and difficult to restrain; yet, O son of Kuntī, it is brought under control through practice and dispassion. Yoga is unattainable by one whose self is unsubdued—this is my conviction;
but for one who has mastered the self and strives with the proper means, it can be achieved."
(Bhagavadgītā 6.35, 36) Thus it is said:
"Undoubtedly, O mighty Arjuna, the mind is restless and difficult to control; yet, through practice and dispassion, O son..."
The mind of Kuntī’s son can be restrained. I consider yoga difficult to attain for one who lacks self-control, but it is attainable by one who has self-control and strives through the proper means.

The "means" (ibid. 6:35, 36) will be explained by citing the sūtras of Patañjali regarding practice (*abhyāsa*) and dispassion (*vairāgya*). One who lacks firmness in the preceding stages is "one whose self is uncontrolled"; one endowed with that [firmness] is "one whose self is mastered. Gauḍapādācārya [describes] attainment through the means:
They state this with an illustration:
practice (*abhyāsa*) and detachment (*vairāgya*) will be explained later by citing the aphorisms of Patañjali. Who does not have mastery over [the mind]?
The preceding stages are intended by the term *asamyatātmā* (one whose self is not restrained), while one who possesses such restraint is called *vaśyātmā* (one whose self is mastered).
Ācārya Gauḍapāda has demonstrated through proper means how this is so.
Yoga is attained in this way:
"Just as the ocean might be emptied drop by drop with the tip of a blade of kusha grass, so too the restraint of the mind occurs through perseverance without weariness."
(Māṇḍūkya-kārikā 3.41):
"The mind is to be brought under control by undepressed effort; it is like emptying the ocean drop by drop."
"By the aid of a blade of *kuśa* grass" (*Māṇḍūkya-kārikā* 3.41).
"One should not contend with many, even if they are but one and powerful;
he meets with defeat, just as the ocean did from the *ṭiṭṭibha* bird."
"Though the mind is exceedingly powerful, it cannot withstand alone the manifold efforts of the yogi; it is defeated just as the ocean was defeated by the *tittibha* bird. (Source)

(untraced). Regarding this *Jīvanmuktiviveka*, those who know the tradition relate the following narrative: "It is said that the eggs of a certain bird, situated on the shore, were carried away by the surging tide of the ocean. That bird then set out, thinking, 'I shall dry up this ocean.'"

With the tip of his own beak, he cast out one drop of water at a time. Although he was being restrained by many birds and kinsmen, he did not desist; on the contrary, he even chose them as assistants. Seeing all of them suffering in various ways through the repeated acts of diving and rising, the compassionate Nārada sent Garuḍa to his side. Then—
"The ocean, drying up from the wind of Garuḍa’s wings, became terrified and brought those eggs back and gave them to the bird.
In this context, there is a story in the Vedāntic tradition as follows: The eggs of a certain bird that had been laid on the shore were carried away...

The ocean was carried away by the ebbing tide. Resolving to recover the eggs by drying up the sea, it began to discharge the water drop by drop with its beak. Although discouraged by its companions, [it persisted].

And toward many other birds as well, he did not desist, but rather requested their assistance. Seeing them suffering in various ways as they flew in and out of the ocean, the compassionate Nārada was moved.
And he dispatched Garuḍa to that place. Then the terrified ocean,
beginning to dry up due to the wind produced by the flapping of Garuḍa’s wings, returned those eggs.

Thus, when a yogin proceeds toward the supreme dharma through the cessation of the mind without weariness, Īśvara bestows his grace upon him. This lack of weariness is achieved by interspersing the practice with activities conducive to it from time to time, just as one eating rice occasionally tastes various other items such as sips and linctuses between mouthfuls. With this very intention in mind, Vasiṣṭha said:
Control of the mind is the highest religious act,
and the Lord aids the yogi in the same manner who is engaged in this with undaunted effort. Unwearied effort occurs.
By occasionally intermingling other favorable activities with it— just as one tastes other courses, such as soup or curd, between mouthfuls of rice. With this...
With this in view, Vasiṣṭha said as follows: "Of the mind's three portions, one should fill one with enjoyments, one with the scriptures,
and the remaining portion for the uninitiated with service to the guru in the noble lineage."
(Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 21.36)
“The beginner should follow the right path of yoga as follows: he should fill two parts of his mind with objects of enjoyment, one part with the study of the scriptures, and one [part] with...”

By attending upon his preceptor, one should fulfill one portion [of the day] with enjoyments, two portions with service to the guru, and one portion with reflection on the meaning of the scriptures. (LYV 21.36; YV)
(In that very same place, 21.37) ||

‘When he has made some progress, he should fill one part of his mind with objects of enjoyment, one part with reflection upon the scriptures, and the remaining two parts [with other meditative objects].’
One should fill the two parts of the mind daily by attending upon the preceptor—two parts with the scriptures and dispassion, and two parts with meditation and worship of the guru. (LYV 21.37; YV)
(tatraiva 21.38) Thus it is said: "When he has reached a very advanced stage, he should fill half of his mind with the study of scriptures and the practice of renunciation."
"The remaining half [is attained] through meditation and worship of the teacher" (LYV 21.38; YV 5.24.47).
Here, by the word *bhoga*, the activity of wandering for alms and so forth—which is the means of livelihood—and the activity appropriate to one's caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*) are expressed.

Having practiced yoga for a ghaṭikā or a muhūrta according to one's capacity, one should then attend upon the gurus for a muhūrta through listening to the scriptures or by service; then, for a muhūrta, one should attend to one’s own body, and for a muhūrta, reflect upon the yoga-śāstras; thereafter, one should practice yoga again for a muhūrta. Thus, making other activities subordinate to yoga, one should quickly master them.

At the time of sleep, one should calculate the *yoga-muhūrtas* occurring on that day. Thereafter, one should increase those *yoga-muhūrtas* on the following day, or in the next fortnight, or in the next month. In this way, even with the addition of just a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) to each *muhūrta*, the duration of the *yoga* becomes much greater within the span of a single year.
The term *bhoga*— objects of enjoyment— refers here to such acts as going out to beg for food for sustenance and other activities required according to one's social class (*varṇa*).
and stage of life. JĪVAN-MUKTI-VIVEKA:
He should practice yoga according to his capacity for one ghaṭikā or one muhūrta—that is, twenty-four minutes or forty-eight minutes.
Then, for one muhūrta, he should spend time with his teacher studying the scriptures and also serving him;
and the following muhūrta he should spend attending to his own needs.
Having attended to the body, he should then spend the next *muhūrta* studying the science of yoga, and thereafter practice yoga once more. Thus,
placing greater emphasis on yoga, he should integrate all other [activities] with it.
One should perform favorable activities with it and complete them quickly; then, retiring to bed, one should count the *muhūrtas* devoted to yoga, and thereafter increase those *muhūrtas*.

[The yoga] may occur on the following day, or in the following fortnight, or in the following month. In this manner, by adding even a single *muhūrta* to the *yoga-muhūrta*, the duration of the yoga will become greatly increased.
But this occurs in just one year. Nor should it be suspected that, if one relies solely on yoga, other activities would be neglected.
Because only one whose other activities have ceased has the qualification for yoga, for this very reason the renunciation of the knower (*vidvatsaṃnyāsa*) is required.
Therefore, a person devoted solely to that [yoga] becomes established in yoga through a gradual process, like a student, a merchant, or others.
One should not doubt that by applying oneself exclusively...
Otherwise, all other activities would be neglected,
for only he who has abandoned all other activities becomes fit for the practice of yoga; therefore, [the path of] *vidvatsaṃnyāsa*— the renunciation of the knower— is...
The renunciation of the knower is required; therefore, the person who devotes himself exclusively to practice attains yoga gradually,
just like a student or a merchant.
Just as a student, by reciting sequentially— quarter by quarter, half-verse by half-verse, verse by verse, pair of verses by pair of verses, and chapter by chapter—
becomes a teacher after ten or twelve years; and just as one engaged in trade...

Just as one who studies the Vedas gradually acquires a portion of them, so too, why should a practitioner— who begins together with those two, the merchant and the student, and exerts himself while being gripped by envy— fail to ascend to yoga within that same period of time, reaching the status of a lord of ten thousand, a lord of two hundred thousand, and so on, up to a lord of a hundred thousand or even a lord of ten million?
First a quarter of a ṛk, then a quarter, then a half, then a full ṛk, then two ṛks, and then a section; in this manner, after ten or twelve years, he becomes a teacher himself. *Jīvan-mukti-viveka*
Or, just as a merchant dealing in goods gains a profit of one rupee, then two rupees, and in this manner becomes a millionaire—
even so, starting from those [two], the student and the...
And for a trader practicing yoga with a competitive spirit,
why should he not attain yoga within that same amount of time? Therefore, by means of human effort, one should repeatedly suppress the arising of volitions and conceptualizations, as did Uddālaka.

Having abandoned [the mind] in the ego of "I-making" (*ahaṃkartṛ*), one should restrain the mind within the self of knowledge (*jñānātman*). Having conquered this second stage, when the natural state of "mindlessness" (*nirmanastva*)—like that of a child or a mute—has been attained, one should then restrain the clearly manifest self of knowledge, which is the form of the specific ego (*viśeṣāhaṃkāra*), into the unmanifest general ego (*sāmānyāhaṃkāra*), which is the principle of the Great (*mahattattva*). This is like one who has fallen into a slight drowsiness.
The specific ego-sense contracts by its own accord; likewise, for one who strives toward forgetfulness, the contraction of the ego-sense occurs even without drowsiness.

This third stage is identical to worldly lassitude (*tandrā*) and to the non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) postulated by the logicians; it is the state in which only the principle of the Great One (*mahat-tattva*) remains.
When this stage has been mastered through proficiency in practice, one [overcomes] this very [state] whose form is the universal ego (*sāmānyāhaṃkāra*).
One should establish the Great Self, free from all limiting adjuncts, within the tranquil state whose sole essence is consciousness.
"Having set aside the principle of Mahat, one should leave behind pure consciousness alone.
Therefore, having abandoned the functions of the deliberative mind, [one should abide in that state].
Those [states] that arise repeatedly through personal effort, such as that of Uddālaka,
one should dissolve the mind into the *ahaṃkāra* (ego-sense), which is the *jñānātmā* (the knowing self). When this second stage is overcome and...
When mindlessness has become as natural as that of a child or a mute, he should merge the distinct, individual ego— which is the clearly perceived knowing-self— into [the Supreme Self].
The indistinct universal ego, which is not clearly perceived— that is,
within the Great Principle (mahat-tattva)—
becomes naturally abbreviated for the individual egoity.
One who has become slightly languid; one who is striving to forget [it], whose individual egoity becomes contracted even without languor.

This is the third stage, which resembles the well-known *ālasya* (lassitude) and the undifferentiated knowledge (*aviśeṣa-jñāna*) according to the Tārkika school; and in this state, only the Great Principle (*mahat-tattva*) [remains].
The *mahat-tattva* remains.
When this stage is overcome through intense practice,
the Great Self (*mahān ātmā*) in the form of universal egoity (*sāmānya-ahaṃkāra*) should be merged [into the unmanifest].
In the Supreme Self, which is by nature pure consciousness and free from all attributes,
by removing the *mahat-tattva*, one...
"One should allow pure knowledge alone to remain" (source untraced).
Here too, the previously mentioned effort toward non-remembrance (*avismṛti*) becomes the means, even more so than that [mere presence]. As it is said:

Just as for one engaged in the study of a treatise, even though there is a dependence on the explanation of each preceding section before mastery is attained, once mastery is achieved, the meaning of the subsequent sections becomes manifest by itself; likewise, for a yogi who has properly mastered the preceding stages, the means to the subsequent stage becomes manifest by itself. Thus says the author of the *Yogabhāṣya*:
In this stage, the aforementioned effort toward forgetting alone becomes even more significant as a means.
Although he requires explanations for every single detail,
A person who has begun the study of the scriptures until he becomes well-versed in the subject, yet remains one who has not yet fully experienced the meaning of the remainder of the book.
It becomes clear of its own accord. Just as for the yogi who has perfectly mastered the preceding stage, the means for mastering the subsequent stage is revealed spontaneously.
This has been stated by the commentator on Yoga as follows: "Yoga is to be known through yoga; yoga proceeds from yoga.
That yogi who is vigilant through yoga rejoices for a long time."
(As stated in the *Yogasūtrabhāṣya* 3.6; *Saubhāgyalakṣmyupaniṣad* 2.7:
"By yoga, one should understand the subsequent stage of yoga; from the practice of yoga, yoga develops, and..."
Only the vigilant yogi attains that state of abiding bliss through yoga alone (*Yogasūtra-bhāṣya* 3.6; *Saubhāgyalakṣmī Upaniṣad* 2.7).

[Objection: But surely, between the principle of Mahat and the tranquil Self, a principle called the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), which is the material cause of Mahat, is cited in the Śruti. In that regard—
If it is asked, "Why is the restriction not stated?"—
the objection is: the principle which is the material cause of *mahat*, named the unmanifest (*avyakta*), has already been mentioned.
In the Śruti, [the term] *ned* is situated between the Great Self (*mahān ātmā*) and the Tranquil Self (*śānta ātmā*). Why should the Great Self not merge into that *avyakta*?

No; we say this because it would entail the consequence of dissolution (*laya*). Just as a jar, when ceasing in the absence of its material cause—water—does not dissolve, but rather dissolves into its material cause, namely clay; so too, the principle of Mahat does not dissolve into the Self (*ātman*), but dissolves into the Unmanifest (*avyakta*).

Furthermore, dissolution of one's own essential nature (*svarūpa-laya*) is not the goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*), because it is of no use for the realization of the Self. "But it is seen by a subtle intellect... (*Kaṭha Upaniṣad* 1.3.12).

This cannot be, we say; for in that case, since the vision of the Self was enjoined in the preceding verse— “by those who see the subtle with a subtle intellect”— and since the mention of *nirodha* (cessation) is intended to establish its subtlety, and because *laya* (dissolution) is already spontaneously established every day in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), making further effort redundant.
The question of the dissolution of the mahat-principle will arise.
Just as an earthen pot submerged in water— which is not its material cause— would not dissolve into it, that is, would...

Water does not become dissolved by losing its form into [mere] water; rather, within its own material cause, the clay, it is reduced to clay, losing its form. In the same way, the Great Principle (mahat-tattva) does not dissolve into the Self, but into...
The unmanifest, which is its material cause, dissolves.
The dissolution of its own form is not the goal of human life, because it does not subserve the vision of the Self. For it is...
Thus it was said: "But it can be seen by those subtle seers through their sharp and subtle intelligence" (Katha Śruti, Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.12).

In the preceding sentence, the propounding of the vision of the Self is intended to make the intellect sharp and subtle; furthermore, it serves to prevent the ordinary dissolution that normally occurs.
Every day during sleep, effort in this regard is futile. [From] *Jīvan-mukti-viveka*:
Now, even though it is a cause for perception...

If it is argued that the mind— having attained asamprajñāta-samādhi, which is established in the tranquil Self because it is accomplished through dhāraṇā, dhyāna, and samādhi, and because its state of one-pointedness has ceased— is devoid of fluctuations (vṛtti) like deep sleep, and therefore cannot be the cause of perception;

Objection: Since the means for seeing (realizing the Self) is conscious concentration— *samprajñāta-samādhi*— in the form of a one-pointed transformation brought about by [the practice of yoga], [how can the Self be perceived through the unconscious concentration, *asamprajñāta-samādhi*?]
Contemplation, meditation, and concentration—
the restrained mind that has attained superconscious concentration (*samādhi*) within the Tranquil Self— is devoid of transformation, like sleep.
[This] cannot be the means for seeing, because it is impossible to negate seeing that is established by itself (*svataḥ-siddha*). For this very reason...
Reply: This is not so, because the vision that is spontaneously accomplished cannot be prevented. Therefore, it has been said in the *Śreyomārga*:
The Path to the Higher Good (Sreyomārga) states:
"The mind, which by its very nature always exists in the form of both self and non-self,
should establish the view of non-self by means of the singular form of the self."

“The mental substance, by its own nature, always exists in the form of either the Self or the non-Self. By removing the perceptions of the non-Self, it should be maintained [in the state of the Self].”
"The form of the Self" (meaning that the mind necessarily assumes the form of the Self when the forms of the non-Self cease) (source untraced).

Just as a jar, while being produced, arises already filled with space by its very nature, whereas the filling with water, rice, and so forth occurs only later through human effort once the jar has been produced; and just as in that case, even when the water and other contents are removed, the space cannot be removed, and even when the mouth is covered, the space remains within; so too the mind, while being produced—

The mind arises already filled with the consciousness of the Self (*ātma-caitanya*). Once the mind has arisen, it subsequently assumes the form of mental modifications (*vṛtti*)—such as pots, cloths, forms, tastes, pleasure, and pain—under the influence of merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and other factors that cause experience, much like molten copper poured into a mold.
In this process, even though the non-self forms such as color and taste are excluded, the causeless aspect of consciousness (*cid-ākāra*) cannot be excluded. Therefore...
By means of the cessation-samadhi (*nirodha-samādhi*), which is characterized by the absence of mental activity and in which only the residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) remain—

subtle because it is directed solely toward the conscious self (*cidātman*) and one-pointed because of that focus— the Self is experienced without obstacle. It is with this very intention [that the following is said].
The Vārtikakāra and Sarvānubhava-yogin state:
"Just as a clay pot, while being fashioned, naturally becomes filled with space, so too [it is filled] by filling it with water, rice, and so forth."

This can occur only after [the self] has been produced and through personal effort. Just as a jar cannot be emptied of space even when it is emptied of water and other substances, for space certainly remains within it.
Even when the mouth is covered, likewise the mind is born, filled with the consciousness of the Self.
Once the mind has been born, under the influence of dharma...
Through merit and demerit— the causes of enjoyment and suffering—
transformations occur in the forms of jars, cloths, colors, tastes, pleasure, pain, and so forth, just as [changes occur] in molten [metal].
Copper takes the shape of the mold into which it is poured.
Even though the forms of non-self entities such as color, taste, and so forth are excluded from the mind, the form of that which is without cause—
Pure intelligence cannot be obstructed.
Therefore, the Self is experienced without impediment or hindrance by means of the mind that has become one-pointed.
It is intented, because it is directed toward pure consciousness alone; it is subtle, because all modifications have been restrained and it has been reduced to a mere latent impression.
Regarding the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samādhi),
both the Vārttikakāra and Sarvānubhavayogi have stated as follows:
The intellect’s assumption of forms such as pleasure and pain arises from causes such as merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*);
when its fluctuations are stilled, the mind becomes an illuminator of supreme bliss.
"This samādhi, named asaṃprajñāta, is dear to yogins" (Muktikopaniṣad 2.53–54).
"The mind assumes the forms of pleasure, pain, and so forth under the influence of merit and demerit; however, its assumption of the form of self-knowledge is not due to any external cause."
It is the very nature of the thing.
When the mind is free from all modifications, it reveals supreme bliss; this state is known as superconsciousness.
It is the concentration known as *asamprajñāta-samādhi*, which is favored by yogins (*Muktikopaniṣad* 2.53, 54).
Although the vision of the Self is established by its very nature, the practice of restraint (*nirodhābhyāsa*) is undertaken to ward off the perception of the non-Self (*anātman*).
Thus it has been said:
"Therefore, although self-realization is self-accomplished..."
To prevent the perception of a non-self, self-control is practiced.
Therefore, it has been said:
"Having fixed the mind upon the Self, one should not think of anything at all" (Bhagavad Gītā 6.25).
"Having established the mind in the Self, one should not think of anything else" (BG 6.25).
Since the Yoga-śāstra is concerned solely with the samādhi that treats the mind, the vision of the Self is not present therein during the samādhi of cessation (nirodha-samādhi).

This has been stated directly; however, it is also accepted by implication, since after formulating the aphorism, "Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind" (Yoga Sūtras 1.2), he subsequently formulated, "Then the seer abides in its own nature" (Yoga Sūtras 1.3).
The *Yogaśāstra* does not explicitly mention the realization of the self in the concentration brought about by restraint, insofar as it treats concentration solely as a means to liberation.
It is the treatment of the mind. However, this has been indirectly confirmed by formulating it thus:
"Yoga is the restraint of the mind from assuming various forms."
(Yogasūtra 1.2), and then formulating as follows:
“At that time (the time of concentration), the Seer (puruṣa)...”
"He rests in his own (unmodified) state" (ibid. 1.3).

Although the seer, being changeless, always abides in his own essential nature, nevertheless, when mental modifications arise and their reflection is cast upon him, the seer becomes as if unsteady due to non-discrimination from that reflection.
That too has been stated in the immediately following sūtra:
"Even though the Seer, being uniform, always abides in his own state, yet, by identifying with his own reflection..."
Reflected in the transformations arising therein within the mind, it is as if the Seer itself has undergone change.
This very point has also been mentioned in the immediately following [verse].
Thus the aphorism:
"In other cases, there is conformity with the modifications" (Yoga Sūtras 1.4).
"At other times [than that of concentration], the Seer..."
This is identified with the modifications [of the intellect] (ibid. 1.4).
It is also aphorized elsewhere:
"Experience is the non-distinction of the cognition of the sattva and the puruṣa, which are absolutely unmixed; [it is experience] because [the sattva] exists for the sake of another" (Yogasūtras).
Thus it is said [in Yogasūtra 4.22]: "The self-awareness of one's own intellect occurs when consciousness, which does not undergo transference, assumes the form of that [intellect].
It is also formulated elsewhere as follows:

"Enjoyment arises from the non-discrimination between the Puruṣa and the Sattva, though they are entirely distinct, because the functions of the latter are for the sake of another... (ibid. 3.36), and also as follows:
Since the essence of knowledge (the *puruṣa*) is immutable, when the mind assumes its form, it becomes conscious (ibid. 4.22).

Even when the referent of the term *tvam* (the "thou") has been purified by the samādhi of cessation (*nirodhasamādhi*) and directly realized, a further mental modification (*vṛtti*) called the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) arises through the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*) in order to make its identity with Brahman an object of cognition. Furthermore, the samādhi of cessation is not the sole means for the direct realization of the pure referent of the term *tvam*; rather, it may also be achieved by distinguishing it through the discrimination between consciousness (*cit*) and the insentient (*jaḍa*).
Because direct realization is possible. For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha said:
"Though purified and even realized through the concentration of restraint, the individual self (jīvātman)..."
In the Great Utterance "That Thou Art" (*tat-tvam-asi*), the word "Thou" (*tvam*)—
in order to establish its identity as Brahman, that is, its nature as the Universal Self—
is brought forth as another transformation in the form of Brahman.
That which is attained through the Great Utterance is called Brahmavidyā—
the self-knowledge, the knowledge of the one Self-existent Being.
Nirodha-samādhi is not the only means to realize it.
The pure, individual self denoted by "thou" is also realized by discriminating and separating the Spirit from matter; therefore, Vasiṣṭha spoke as follows:
"O Raghava, there are two methods for the destruction of the mind: yoga and knowledge.
Yoga is indeed the restraint of its fluctuations, while knowledge is correct discernment. — (Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 27.72).
"For some, yoga is unattainable; for others, the certainty of knowledge.
Therefore, the Lord, the Supreme God, declared these two methods" (ibid., 29.60). Thus it is said.
There are two ways to dissolve the mind, O Rāghava:
one is yoga and the other is knowledge. The restraint of the transformations of the mind is called yoga, and [the other is] right...
"Seeing is called knowledge" (LYV 27.72; YV 5.78.8).
And thus:
"Yoga is unattainable for some, while for others it is realization."
It is not possible [to achieve this] through right knowledge alone. Therefore, the Supreme Lord, God, spoke regarding the two varieties [of means]:
"But surely, even discrimination culminates in yoga, for at the time of vision there is a one-pointed mental state whose sole object is the Self."
Because its nature consists of momentary discernment.
Objection: The application of discernment becomes yoga itself, since at the time of realization—
The one-pointed transformation of the mind, perceiving the Self alone, momentarily assumes the form of conscious concentration (*samprajñāta-samādhi*). — *Jīvanmuktiviveka*

Certainly. Nevertheless, there is indeed a great distinction between the cognitive (*samprajñāta*) and the ultra-cognitive (*asamprajñāta*) [samādhis] in terms of their essential nature and their means of attainment.
The difference in their essential nature is evident from the presence or absence of mental modification (*vṛtti*).
As for the means of achievement (*sādhana*),
the triad beginning with concentration (*dhāraṇā*) is internal because it is of the same genus [as yoga],
whereas the others are external because they are of a different genus. And thus says the Sūtra:
Reply: Indeed it is so; yet there is a great difference between conscious and superconscious concentrations, both in terms of their essential nature and the means by which they are attained.
attain them. The difference in their nature is evident through the presence or absence of the transformation of the mind.
As for the means, [they consist of] reflection, meditation, and...

These three— concentration and so forth— being of a homogeneous nature with conscious concentration, fall within the internal category of means; however, being of a heterogeneous nature, they become external.
This refers to superconscious concentration (asaṃprajñāta-samādhi) which is devoid of mental transformation (vṛtti). In this regard, there is the following aphorism:
Of the non-discerning [samādhi],
and of the discerning [samādhi] which is without mental fluctuations.
"But even those are external to the seedless [samādhi]" (Yogasūtra 3.8).

Even though they are of a different class (*vijātīya*), it is not contradictory that they are "external" (*bahiraṅga*) because they are helpful by warding off many types of non-self-activity (*anātmavṛtti*).
To clarify that very helpfulness, he formulates the aphorism:
"Even though they are heterogeneous, by preventing many..."
Since these types of non-self transformations are beneficial,
their externality is not contradictory. Patañjali formulates this to make their benefit intelligible as follows:
‘For others, [this samādhi] is preceded by faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and discernment of reality’ (Yoga Sūtras 1.20).
‘To others, [this samādhi] comes through faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and discernment of the real.’

"knowledge filled with Truth)" (ibid. 1.20). In the *Jīvanmuktiviveka*, after having described samādhi by birth alone for certain gods and others in the preceding sūtra, this is now stated with regard to human beings. The conviction that "this very yoga of mine is the means for attaining the supreme goal of man" is faith (*śraddhā*). And that [faith] arises from hearing about its excellence.
And its excellence is recorded in tradition:
in the aphorism preceding this, the concentration of certain deities and others from their very birth has been described.
And this aphorism is intended for human beings.
The firm conviction that "this yoga alone is the means to attain the supreme goal of my life" is called *śraddhā* (faith). And having heard...
From the excellence of yoga arises such *śraddhā* (faith).
The *Smṛti* describes that excellence as follows: "The yogi is superior to the ascetics; he is considered superior even to the men of knowledge."
"And the yogi is superior to the performers of action; therefore, O Arjuna, become a yogi" (Bhagavad Gītā 6.46).
"The yogi is greater than the ascetics; he is so considered..."
He is superior even to those who possess knowledge, and he is also superior to those who perform ritual actions. Therefore, O Arjuna, be a yogi;
for [yoga] is the means to attain the highest world, being superior to austerities such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa*, as well as to rituals such as the *jyotiṣṭoma*.

Yoga is superior. Because it is an internal limb (*antaraṅga*) with respect to knowledge and because it is the cause of the mind’s repose, it is superior even to knowledge. For one who understands this, faith in yoga arises. When that faith has been cultivated, vigor—that is, enthusiasm—arises in the form:
"I shall accomplish yoga by all means. Through such enthusiasm, the limbs of yoga (*yogāṅga*) are to be practiced from time to time.

These are recorded in the Smṛtis. And when, through that Smṛti, the internal clarity (*adhyātmaprasāda*) arises from the correctly practiced concentration (*samādhi*), the wisdom that bears truth (*ṛtambharā prajñā*) emerges.
Since Yoga is the means for attaining the supreme world (the world of the Self), it is superior to austerities such as the *kṛcchra*.
Cāndrāyaṇa and the like, as well as rituals such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and others. Yoga is superior even to knowledge,
for as an internal means to knowledge, it renders the mind tranquil.
In one who possesses such understanding, faith in yoga arises.

"By all means. With such a resolve, the limbs of yoga are traditionally taught to be practiced according to their priority.

"Truth-bearing" (Yogasūtra 1.48).
In this context,

The meaning is: when there exists that internal clarity (*adhyātmaprasāda*) produced by the excellence of that samādhi. He provides the justification for its being "truth-bearing" (*ṛtaṃbhara*) in the sūtra:

*Ṛta* means truth, that is, the actual nature of things.
In itself; *bibharti*—here it means manifesting, that is, conveying or manifesting the Truth. *Tatra*—there, meaning after that clear intellect has been produced.
heightened concentration. The reason why it is called ‘truth-bearing’ (*ṛtambharā*) is described in the *sūtra* as follows: ‘The knowledge obtained from authoritative testimony and...’

The direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of those who have not attained yoga does not operate with respect to objects that are subtle, concealed, or distant. Those objects are known by non-yogis through scripture (*āgama*) and inference (*anumāna*). Furthermore, the wisdom (*prajñā*) born of scripture and inference has as its object only the general characteristics (*sāmānya*) of things.
Yogic direct perception, however, [perceives them directly].

Because it has a specific real object as its domain, it is called *ṛtambhara*. And he formulates a sūtra to establish that this yogic perception is an auxiliary factor for the attainment of *asaṃprajñāta-samādhi*:
"The latent impression (*saṃskāra*) born from that [perception] obstructs other latent impressions" (Yoga Sūtras 1.50).
However, non-yogis cannot perceive an object that is extremely subtle,
concealed behind something, or located at a great distance. These...
Objects come to the knowledge of non-yogins through inference and verbal testimony. Knowledge obtained through inference or testimony relates only to the universal (sāmānya).
of a thing. However, the scope of this yogic perception is the particularity (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a thing; therefore, it is called "truth-revealing" (*tattvābhāsaka*).
To establish the externality of this yogic perception...

Having described the external means for superconscious concentration (*samādhi*), Patañjali now describes the effort to restrain it as the internal means.
Thus it is stated in the aphorism: "Upon the cessation of that [vāsanā] as well, because of the cessation of everything, there is seedless samādhi" (Yoga Sūtras 1.51).
"By the restraint of even this [impression which obstructs...]"
"When all other mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) are restrained, there arises 'seedless' (*nirbīja*) *samādhi*" (ibid. 1.51).
This *samādhi* is similar to deep sleep and can be experienced by the witnessing consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*). And it is not...

It should not be suspected that this state is merely deep sleep (*suṣupti*) because of the absence of all mental modifications (*dhīvṛtti*), for there is a distinction based on the existence or non-existence of the very nature of the mind. As it was said by the teacher Gauḍapāda:
"The concentration just described resembles sleep..."

This is experienced by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣi-caitanya*). Due to the similarity [of this state] with the absence of all modifications of the mind, it must not be imagined as being anything other than *jīvan-mukti*.
They sleep alone, for they differ according to the presence or absence of the mind in its own form. This has been described by the teacher Gauḍapāda as follows:

The movement of the wise one whose mind has been restrained and is free from conceptual construction should be understood as being like that in deep sleep; it is not otherwise, nor is anything else equal to it.
"For that [mind] dissolves during deep sleep; when restrained, it does not dissolve.
That itself is the fearless Brahman, the light of knowledge extending everywhere" (Māṇḍūkya-kārikā 3.34–35).
The non-apprehension of duality is equal for both the Prājña and the Turya;
however, the Prājña is accompanied by seed-sleep (bīja-nidrā), whereas that [sleep] does not exist in the Turya.
The first two states are associated with dream and sleep; the wise one (prājña), however, is characterized by the absence of both dream and sleep.
Those who are certain do not perceive either sleep or dream in the fourth state (turya).
"Otherwise, for one who perceives [reality] incorrectly, there is dreaming; for one who does not know the truth, there is sleep.
When the error of these two has perished, one attains the fourth state (turiya).
(Māṇḍūkyakārikā 1.13–15). Thus it is said.
"One should know the state of the mind that,
being endowed with discernment and free from delusion, remains under control. This is the condition of the mind in deep sleep."

It is not like that, but is of a different kind: "In deep sleep the mind is withdrawn, but it is not so when the mind is restrained; for the restrained mind is indeed [the state of liberation]. (Māṇḍūkya-kārikā)
"The fearless Brahman, the light of whose omniscience is all-pervasive" (ibid. 3.35).
And thus:

The non-perception of duality is common to both the *prājña* and the *turīya*. However, the *prājña* is associated with sleep in the form of a cause (*kāraṇa-svapna*), whereas such sleep does not exist in the *turīya* (ibid. 1.13). *Jīvanmukti Viveka*

“The first two (viśva and taijasa) are associated with dreaming and sleep respectively; prājña is associated with sleep devoid of dreams. Those who know Brahman perceive neither sleep nor [dreaming].”
dreams in *turiya* (ibid. 1.14):
"Dreaming is the false cognition of reality, and sleep is the non-cognition of it. When this erroneous knowledge [in these states]..."

The first two are *viśva* and *taijasa*. The apprehension of the non-dual reality otherwise—namely, its manifestation in the form of duality—is what constitutes the dream state existing within *viśva* and *taijasa*. Ignorance of reality is sleep (*nidrā*), and that...
It exists within Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña. The "reversal" (viparyāsa) of those two—dream and sleep—which constitute their essential nature, is false knowledge (mithyājñāna).
When that [false knowledge] is exhausted through wisdom (vidyā), one attains—that is, experiences—the fourth state (turīya), the non-dual reality.
"The first two" (ādyau) refers to Viśva and Taijasa. "Wrong..."
Apprehension (*anyathā-grahaṇam*) means the appearance of non-dual reality in the form of duality; this is present in both *viśva* and *taijasa*, and is called "dream. Non-apprehension—
The non-manifestation of reality is called ‘sleep’ (*nidrā*), which is present in *viśva*, *taijasa*, and *prājña*.
The essence of dreaming and sleep is inversion (*viparyaya*).
When false knowledge is destroyed by the knowledge of reality, the fourth state— that is, the non-dual entity—
is attained, which means it is experienced; this is the meaning.

Granted, there may indeed be a great difference between asamprajñāta-samādhi and deep sleep; however, for one who desires to see reality, there is no need for that [samādhi] as a means to vision for the sake of liberation while living (jīvanmukti),
even when there is a requirement for samādhi.
For one who has seen reality, the bondage of afflictions such as passion and hatred ceases even in deep sleep.
[Objection: Let there be such a great difference [between the two states].
sleep and superconscious concentration. Although *samādhi* is required as a means to realization for one who wishes to realize the Truth, it is not necessary to attain [the goal].

"Jīvanmukti belongs to one who has already realized the Truth, because even the bondage of afflictions in the form of love, hatred, and so forth, is removed by sleep. This is not so. Is it that occasional sleep, which occurs naturally every day, removes the bondage? Or...?

Is it through practice that [the afflictions] cease to exist continuously? Even regarding the first case, does this refer to the cessation of the bondage of afflictions existing at the time of deep sleep, or to those existing at other times?
Reply: It is not so. It is the sleep which will remove the bondage...
It must be either that which occurs spontaneously every day at certain times, or the other, which has been produced through practice and continues at all times. If...
If the first type of sleep is intended, then the question will arise whether it removes bondage at the time of sleep or at some other time.
Not the first, because it is not applicable; for even in the deep sleep (*suṣupti*) of the ignorant, there is no bondage of afflictions (*kleśa*), otherwise [excessive] exhaustion would result.

Not the second, because it is impossible; for the destruction of an affliction existing at one time by means of a deep sleep occurring at another time is not possible; otherwise, the destruction of afflictions during the waking and dreaming states of the ignorant would also result.
Nor can uninterrupted practice be performed during deep sleep, because that state is caused by the exhaustion of karma.
Therefore, even for one who knows reality, there is indeed a need for asamprajñāta-samādhi for the destruction of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The first [alternative] is not possible, since it does not apply [to a realized person].

Furthermore, even for an ignorant person, there is no bondage of afflictions during sleep; otherwise, exhaustion would ensue there. Nor is the second [alternative] possible, because it is logically untenable.

The afflictions of one period of time cannot be destroyed by the sleep of another period of time; otherwise, even the ignorant would experience the destruction of the afflictions of both the waking and dreaming states.
As for the result: even the continuity of sleep cannot be practiced during sleep, since sleep is induced by the cessation of activities.
Therefore, even one who knows reality requires a superior...

[One practices] conscious concentration (*samprajñāta-samādhi*) in order to destroy the afflictions (*kleśas*). Of that concentration, the first stage (*bhūmi*) is the cessation of speech, as in the case of cows, horses, and the like; the second is the absence of mind (*amanastva*), as in the case of infants, the dull-witted, and so forth; the third is the absence of ego (*ahaṃkāra*), as in the state of drowsiness; [and the fourth is] the absence of the principle of cosmic intellect (*mahattattva*), as in deep sleep.

The fourth [quarter]: with reference to these four stages, it has been said, "One should gradually come to rest. And in this process of coming to rest, the intellect sustained by fortitude (*dhṛti*) is the means. For the restraint of the Great Principle (*mahat*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), mind (*manas*), speech (*vāk*), and so forth—which naturally flow outward with intense velocity like a river eroding its banks—requires great steadfastness.

*Viveka* is discernment. Having examined whether the preceding stage has been mastered or not, one should commence the next stage if it has been mastered; however, if it has not been mastered, that very same stage must be practiced again. One should thus discern this from time to time, as stated in the half-verse beginning with "ātmasaṃstham" (Bhagavad Gītā 6.25).
The practice of the fourth stage is also recorded. The teacher Gauḍapāda says:
"Control of speech—that is, silence—such as is found in cows, horses, and so forth, is the first stage of that superconscious concentration (*asaṃprajñāta-samādhi*)."

The second stage is mindlessness, such as is found in children, idiots, and the like; the third state is the absence of egoity, as experienced in lassitude; and the absence of the Great [Principle]...
The principle of *mahat-tattva*, as in the state of deep sleep, is the fourth stage.
With this tetrad of stages in view, it has been said:
"One should attain tranquility gradually (i.e., by stages)" (*Bhagavad Gītā* 6.25).

6.25). In this attainment of tranquility, the intellect established in patience is the means. Infinite patience is required for the control of the great principle (*mahat*), egoity (*ahaṃkāra*), the mind (*manas*), and the senses, such as speech.
and so forth, which are flowing outward with tremendous speed, just like a torrent tearing away its banks.
*Buddhiḥ*—here it means discrimination. After...

One examines whether mastery over the preceding stage has been attained or not; if it is found to have been attained, an attempt is made toward the next stage. If it has not been attained, then that [same stage] should be practiced.
One should attempt it again; thus, one should very carefully observe the progress in the course. "Well-established in the Self" (ātmasaṃstha)—thus [it is said] by the latter.
The control of the fourth stage has also been described through the latter half of this verse (BG 6.25) and the following verse.
Ācārya Gauḍapāda says as follows:

One should restrain the mind when it is distracted by sensual enjoyments through skillful means; likewise, one should restrain it when it is overly tranquil or in a state of lethargy, for desire and lethargy are of the same nature. 42.
Recalling that all is suffering, one should turn away from the enjoyment of sensual pleasures;
by recollecting that all is unborn, one no longer perceives anything as born. (43)
One should collect the mind for the sake of awakening, and again pacify it when it is distracted;
one should recognize it when it is accompanied by passion, and once it has attained equanimity, one should not move it.
— (Māṇḍūkya-kārikā 3.42–44) | “The mind, distracted by desires and enjoyments,
should be brought under control by proper means; likewise [the mind of] one liberated while living (jīvan-mukta).”
The mind that delights in the pleasure of inactivity (*laya*)—
for the state of inactivity is as harmful as the state of desires (*Māṇḍūkya-kārikā* 3.42).
Turn the mind away from the enjoyment of desires,
remembering that they produce only suffering. Do not perceive created objects, remembering that all this is the unborn.
The Self (ibid.
3.43): "If the mind becomes inactive, rouse it [from *laya*]; if distracted, make it tranquil. Understand its true nature."

When the mind contains the seed of attachment. Once the mind has attained equanimity, do not disturb it again: "One should not savor the bliss therein; being free from attachment, one should abide in wisdom" (ibid.).
One should diligently unify the mind that is emerging with that which is motionless. ||45||
When the mind neither dissolves nor is distracted again, being unshakeable and free from appearances, then Brahman is realized. 46.
—(Māṇḍūkya-kārikā 3.45–46).
★ The yogi must not taste the bliss [arising from samādhi]; he should become detached from it through practice.
If, after attaining steadiness, his mind again seeks external objects, he should, with great effort, make it one with the Self (ibid. 3.45).
‘When the mind does not lapse into inactivity and is not distracted by desires— that is to say, when it remains unshakable and does not give rise to appearances— it indeed...’
"becomes Brahman" (ibid. 3.46);
[it] should lead to dissolution.

There are four states of the mind: those characterized by lethargy, distraction, impurity, and equanimity. Among these, when the mind is being restrained and has turned away from sense objects, if, by the force of previous habituation, it is inclined toward deep sleep;
At that time, one should properly awaken that mind either by the effort of uplifting it or by removing the causes of dissolution.
The causes of dissolution are the remnants of sleep, indigestion, overeating, and fatigue. Therefore they say:
"There are four states of the mind: dissolution (*laya*),..."
It is a trance-like state (a form of hypnosis), distraction, deep attachment, and the attainment of equanimity. While the mind is being restrained and turned away from sense objects,
Sometimes, if due to prior habit it turns toward sleep in order to enter a state of inactivity, it should then be aroused by timely efforts or by eliminating such causes.
Those factors which give rise to that state should be properly understood.
These include insufficient sleep, indigestion, overeating, and physical [exertion].
Exertion is the cause of lethargy (*laya*). Therefore, it is said:
"Having completed one's sleep, eating little and well-digested..."
"In a secluded place, free from fatigue, abandonment, and obstacles, one should always sit without thirst and without effort;
or else, one should restrain the vital breaths according to the path of one's own practice."
(Saubhāgyalakṣmyupaniṣad 2.2) Thus:
"He should eat light, easily digestible food in moderation, complete his sleep, avoid physical exertion, and remain free from desire."
The practitioner should always sit in a place that is solitary and free from disturbances; or he should restrain the vital breath in the manner to which he is accustomed (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.2).
If the mind, having been raised from its latent state, should become distracted by the enjoyment of desires due to the force of daily waking habits,

then one should repeatedly withdraw the mind from that distraction by means of reflecting upon all the sufferings inherent in objects of enjoyment as well-known to those who possess discernment, and by contemplating the reality of the non-dual Brahman— which is free from birth and other such conditions— as established in the scriptures, preceded by the vision of the objects of enjoyment [as they truly are].
One should pacify it.
If the mind, having arisen from a state of inactivity, becomes distracted under the influence of the habitual tendencies of daily life, [one should pacify it].
Then, by recollecting all the vices well-known among the wise regarding objects of enjoyment, and also by recollecting [the consequences of] desires and pleasures—

Bring the mind repeatedly to the perception of the objects of enjoyment— the Brahman, the absolute Reality, devoid of birth and other attributes, as it has been well described in the scriptures— through the *Jīvanmuktiviveka*.
[The mind] is under control [of itself] rather than by distractions.

*Kaṣāya* is a sharp defect of the mind. A mind seized by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of intense passion, hatred, and so forth, sometimes remains as if concentrated, free from lethargy and distraction, yet one-pointed in suffering; one should recognize the mind to be of such a nature.

One should understand [the state] through the discernment of the concentrated mind. Having realized, "This is unconcentrated," one should apply a remedy for the impurity characterized by lethargy and distraction. By the word *sama*, Brahman is denoted, according to the traditional teaching: "The Supreme Lord abiding equally in all beings" (*Bhagavad Gītā* 13.28).

Deep attachment is a very powerful vice of the mind. It is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of extremely intense love and hatred; and when the mind is seized by it, it sometimes remains, as it were, [in a state of suspension].
In samādhi, free from lethargy and distraction and one-pointed amidst suffering, one should understand the mind in such a state; that is,
one should know it by distinguishing it from the [ordinary] mind.
In concentration. Having recognized it as being unconcentrated, one should counteract that attachment just as one would counteract lethargy and agitation. The word *sama* expresses "evenness."
Brahman—the Supreme Self. As the Smṛti says:
"The Supreme Lord, pervading all beings, is 'Equanimity' (samatva).
When the impurities of attachment and distraction have been removed, Brahman is attained as equal by the mind through the process of elimination. And that [Brahman], once attained as equanimity..."

One should not cause the mind to waver through the delusion of depression (*laya*) or agitation (*kaṣāya*). Having discerned the onset of depression and agitation with subtle intelligence, one should, with great effort, establish the mind for a long time in that state of equilibrium (*samaprāpti*). When it is thus established, supreme bliss, which is the very nature of Brahman, perfectly manifests. As it has been said:
When the mind is freed from inactivity, distraction, and deep attachment, it attains the state of remaining equanimity,
which is Brahman. Mistaking that state for inactivity or deep attachment—
Once this has been realized, one must not disturb the mind that has attained equanimity. With a sharp and subtle intellect,
one should distinguish between the states of non-activity and deep attachment, and thereby settle [the mind].
The mind, through immense effort, remains for a long time in a state of equanimity. When the mind is thus established, the supreme bliss— *Jīvanmukti-viveka*— [arises].
It is the essence of Brahman; thus it arises in its full splendor. Accordingly, there is a scriptural passage: śrutiśca bhavati—
"That infinite bliss which is perceived by the intellect and is beyond the senses"
— (Bhagavad Gītā 6.21). "When he feels that infinite bliss which is perceived by..."
"which is beyond the senses" (BG 6.21).
"The bliss that arises when the mind, its impurities shaken off by *samādhi*, is established in the Self..."
"It cannot then be described by speech; it is grasped by one's own inner organ itself" (Maitrāyaṇī Upaniṣad 4.9).
There is also a Śruti on this point as follows:
"The bliss of a mind whose impurities have been washed away by concentration and which has entered the Self— [that cannot...]"
It cannot, therefore, be described by words. It is grasped by the internal organ itself (*Maitrāyaṇī Upaniṣad* 4.9).
