For one who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta), there is no occasion for the application of *smṛti*, yet it serves to bring benefit to the world; therefore, the Lord says:
"Even considering the welfare of the world, you ought to act."
(Bhagavadgītā 3.20):
"Furthermore, you should perform action for the purpose of setting people on the right path" (BG 3.20).

And the world to be gathered is threefold: the disciple, the devotee, and the indifferent. Among these, when the teacher is a yogin whose face is turned inward, the disciple’s mind suddenly finds rest after attaining supreme confidence in the reality taught by him, due to an extraordinary degree of conviction in his authority. Therefore, it is heard in scripture:

Those to be guided fall into three categories: the disciple, the devotee, and the neutral. Among them, the disciple’s firm conviction in the authority of his inward-turned yogic teacher leads to implicit faith.
Faith in the principle taught by Him; and the mind of such a disciple soon becomes tranquil.
Therefore, the Śruti says this:
"For that high-souled one who has supreme devotion for the Divine, and for the teacher as for the Divine, these truths thus declared indeed shine forth" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.23).

‘If these truths are told to a noble-minded person who feels the highest devotion toward God and toward his spiritual teacher (*jīvan-mukti-viveka*) as toward God himself, then they will surely shine forth.’
"It is an inner experience" (Śvet. Up. 6.23).
And it is also recorded in the Smṛti:
"The man of faith, who is intent upon that and has his senses restrained, attains knowledge."
"Having attained knowledge, one reaches supreme peace before long" (Bhagavadgītā 4.39).
The Smṛti also says this:
"He who is full of faith and zeal and has subdued his senses obtains knowledge; having obtained knowledge, he quickly attains supreme peace" (Bhagavad Gītā 4.39).
A devotee who serves a yogin by providing food, shelter, clothing, and so forth, takes upon himself that yogin’s austerity.
Thus it is heard in scripture: "His sons inherit his property; his friends his good deeds, and his enemies his evil deeds."

The indifferent person (*taṭastha*) is also of two kinds: the believer (*āstika*) and the non-believer (*nāstika*). Among these, the believer, having observed the practice of the right path by the yogi, himself proceeds upon the right path. And so says the *Smṛti*:
"The devotee serves the yogi by providing food, shelter..."
and so forth, partakes himself of the austerity of the yogi. The Śruti says the same:
"His sons inherit his property; friends obtain his virtues."
and his enemies take upon themselves his sins’ (source untraced; quoted by Ācārya Śaṅkara in his commentary on Brahmasūtra 3.3.26).
Furthermore, those who are indifferent are also of two kinds: those who believe...

the existence of God, another world, and so forth, as well as the lack of belief in such things. Among these, the former, having observed the righteous conduct of a yogi, follows the right path of life himself. The Smṛti...
It is likewise stated [in the Bhagavad Gītā]:
"Whatever a great man practices, that very thing other people do;
whatever standard he sets, the world follows it."
(Bhagavadgītā 3.21):
"Whatever a great man does, that others follow; whatever standard he establishes, that the world follows. (BG 3.21)
Even an atheist, when beheld by a yogi, is liberated from sin. As it has been said:
"For one whose intellect proceeds toward reality until it reaches direct experience, all those who come within the range of his vision are liberated from all sins."
(Sūta-saṃhitā 2.20.44).
Thus it is said: even an atheist is liberated from sins merely by the sight of a yogi.
"Whose intellect, having ascertained reality, has reached the state of realization— everyone who comes within his sight is liberated from all sins" (Sūta-saṃhitā 2.20.44).

Having intended to express that the yogin is thus beneficial to all living beings, it is recited: "He has bathed in the waters of all sacred fords; he has given away the entire earth; he has performed a thousand sacrifices; and he has fully worshipped all the gods."
"Even though he is worthy of worship by the three worlds, his own fathers were rescued from saṃsāra by him alone whose mind attained stability for even a moment in the contemplation of Brahman.
(Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 6.16.34).
The yogi benefits all living beings in the manner indicated by this verse: "He has bathed in all the sacred fords; he has bestowed [all gifts]..."
He who has conquered the entire world, performed thousands of sacrifices,
and worshipped all the gods— his ancestors are liberated from saṃsāra, and he himself is honored.

"Even in the three worlds, whose mind, while contemplating Brahman, attained tranquility for a moment" (LYV 6.16.34). From the *Jīvanmuktiviveka*: "By him, his lineage is purified, his mother has fulfilled her purpose, and the earth itself becomes meritorious."
‘Whose mind is merged in that Supreme Brahman, this ocean of boundless consciousness and bliss’ (Sūta-saṃhitā 2.20.45).
"By him who is an infinite ocean of consciousness and bliss,
his lineage is sanctified; through him the purpose of his mother’s life is attained, and the world is rendered holy" (Sūta Saṃhitā).

Not only is austerity (*tapas*) the nature of the yogi’s scriptural practice alone, but it is also the nature of every worldly activity. Thus, the Taittirīyas, in the final section (*anuvāka*) of their own branch concerning Nārāyaṇa, record the greatness of even the knower (*vidvan*). And in the first part of that section, the limbs of the yogi [are described].
They are mentioned as the constituent materials of the sacrifice:

"Of that sacrifice of one who knows thus, the self is the sacrificer, faith is the wife, the body is the fuel, the chest is the altar, the hair is the sacrificial grass (barhis), the head is the ladle (veda), the heart is the sacrificial post, desire is the clarified butter, anger is the animal victim, austerity is the fire, self-restraint is the immolator, and liberality is the sacrificial fee."
"Speech is the Hotṛ, breath is the Udgātṛ, the eye is the Adhvaryu, the mind is the Brahman, and the ear is the Agnīdh. (Nārāyaṇopaniṣad 80).
Thus, not only are the prescribed activities [of a yogi], but...
Not only are [these] established by the scriptures, but all worldly activities are also of the nature of religious austerity (*tapas*). For example,
the followers of the Kṛṣṇa-Yajurveda’s Taittirīya school...
In the final chapter (the eightieth) of their *Nārāyaṇopaniṣad*, they even chant the glory of a yogi. In the first portion of that chapter,
the limbs of a yogi are chanted as being the constituent elements [of the body].
The limbs of the sacrifice are as follows: "The self of him who knows thus is the sacrificer of that sacrifice; faith is the wife; the body is the sacrificial fuel; his..."
The chest is the sacrificial altar; his body hairs are the sacrificial grass (*barhis*);
the tuft of hair on the crown of his head is the tuft of sacrificial grass (*darbha*); his heart is the sacrificial fire.
His stake is [the body], his desire is the clarified butter, his anger (or mental resolve) is the victim, his austerity is the sacrificial fire,
his self-restraint is the slayer, and his renunciation is the sacrifice.
His speech is the Ṛgvedic priest, his vital breath is the Sāmavedic udgātṛ, his eye is the Yajurvedic adhvaryu,
his mind is the Atharvavedic priest, and his ear is the...

"The priest who kindles the sacrificial fire" (referring to all Vedic priests). And here, the word "gift" (*dāna*) must be supplied [to complete the sense of] "dakṣiṇā," as in: "Now, as for austerity, charity, uprightness, non-violence, and truthfulness—these are his sacrificial fees" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.17.4).

Because it is so recorded by the Chandogas. In the middle portion of the aforementioned section, the activities of the yogi and the periods of his life are recorded as being of the nature of the constituent rites of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice; and in the latter portion, they are recorded as being of the nature of the constituent rites of all sacrifices: "Insofar as he restrains himself, that is the initiation (*dīkṣā*); what he eats, that is the sacrificial offering (*havis*); what he drinks, that is his drinking of Soma."

What he enjoys is the *upasads*; what he moves about, sits down, and rises up is the *pravargya*; his mouth is the *āhavanīya* fire; whatever *vyāhṛti* there is is the oblation (*āhuti*); whatever discernment (*vijñāna*) he has, that he offers as a libation; what he eats in the evening and in the morning is the fuel-sticks (*samidh*);
the morning, midday, and evening are the *savana*s; day and night are the *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa* sacrifices; and the half-months...

"The months are the Cāturmāsya sacrifices; the seasons are the Paśubandhas; the years and the Parivatsaras are the Ahargaṇas; this entire sacrifice is indeed the renunciation of all possessions (sarvavedasa), and death is its final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha)" (Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 80).
In the preceding text, the word *dāna*—meaning "giving up"—[is used].
The term ‘dakṣiṇā’ (sacrificial fee) is to be understood here. For the Chandogas chant thus:
“Austerity, charity, uprightness, non-violence, and...”
"Truthfulness— these are the gifts for the priest" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad).
In the middle portion of the aforementioned chapter, the activities and the lifespan of a yogi are described as follows:
The form of the acts pertaining to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice has been described by the final portion in the same manner as the form of the acts of all sacrifices.
"As long as [the life] is maintained—that is the consecration; what he eats is the oblation; what he drinks is his drinking of *soma*; and whatever he rejoices in is the *upasad*-observance."
His moving about, sitting, and rising— all these three are the Pravargya ceremony; his mouth is the consecrated fire for receiving oblations,
and his utterance is the offering.
His fire-offering is his knowledge; whatever he eats in the evening and in the morning is the sacrificial fuel;
his morning, midday, and evening meals are the three [oblations].
The libations of Soma-juice are his days and nights; the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices are his fortnights and months; and the Cāturmāsya observances are his seasons.
The animal sacrifices are his days; the full sacrificial years known as *saṃvatsara* and *parivatsara* are his. Indeed, it is that very sacrifice in which one bestows all of one's possessions.
"The priest is at the end, and his death is the final bath after the sacrifice" (Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 80).

"Sarvavedasaṃ" means that which has the giving away of all one's possessions as its sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Here, by the word "this" (*etad*), the period beginning with the day and night and ending with the full year under discussion is referred to.

The lifespan of the yogin, characterized by the totality of all time, is what is intended here; the meaning is that such a lifespan constitutes a sacrificial session (*sattra*) accompanied by the gift of one's entire being (*sarvasva*). In the final portion of the aforementioned section, there is recorded for one who meditates upon the yogin—who is the essence of all sacrifices—the fruit consisting of gradual liberation (*kramamukti*), characterized by identity with the sun and the moon, which are the causal and effected Brahman respectively.

"This Agnihotra-sacrifice indeed lasts until old age and death. He who, knowing this, dies during the northern course of the sun, having attained the greatness of the gods, goes to union with the sun. But he who dies during the southern course, having attained the greatness of the ancestors, reaches union with and the same world as the moon. These two are the greatnesses of the sun and the moon; [it is] for these that the Brāhmaṇa..."
"The wise man conquers; therefore he attains the greatness of Brahman, and from that, the greatness of non-Brahman"—this is the Upaniṣad (Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 80).
"Possessing all wealth" (*sarvavedasa*) means:

Accompanied by a gift of all one's possessions. The word "this" (*etad*) in the phrase "in this sacrifice" (*etasmin yajñe*) indicates the entire aggregate of time, ranging from day and night up to a year.
This refers to the lifetime of the yogi; that is, the entire life of the yogi is a sacrifice in which he gives away whatever he possesses as a gift.
In the final portion of the aforementioned Upaniṣad, it is chanted:
"He who worships the yogi as the embodiment of all sacrifices attains the fruit consisting of identity."
With the sun and moon—Brahman as both effect and cause—and which consists of gradual liberation. *Jīvan-mukti-viveka*:
"This life of the yogi until old age and death (due to old..."
Aging indeed is the *agnihotra* sacrifice; he who, knowing this,
dies during the period when the sun moves northward [the summer solstice], attains that glory.
of the gods alone and then becomes identified with the sun;
and he who, knowing this, dies during the winter solstice,
attains the glory that belongs to the ancestors alone and becomes [identified with them].
Absorbed in the moon, or abiding in the world of the moon—
the brāhmaṇa who knows thus attains the splendor of the sun and the moon, and thereafter gains the splendor of...
"Brahman, and thereafter he attains the glory of Brahman"—

this is the Upaniṣad (Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 80). Whatever conduct of a yogin exists, bounded by old age and death, that [conduct] begins with the Agnihotra prescribed in the Vedas and ends with the year-long sacrificial sessions (saṃvatsara-sattra).

One who meditates on the nature of karma in this way attains *sāyujya*— identity— with the sun and the moon through the intensity of their contemplation. Through the mildness of their contemplation, having attained the same world as them and experienced the glory of the sun and the moon in that world, one thereafter ascends further.

Thereafter, in Satyaloka, one attains the majesty of the four-faced Brahmā. Having produced the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) there, one thereafter attains Kaivalya—the majesty of the Supreme Brahman, whose nature is truth, knowledge, and bliss. Thus [ends] the Upanishad; by this, [the fruit] of the aforementioned knowledge—
And the conclusion of the treatise expounding this [topic] is now being made:
all the activities of a yogi until his old age and death are in the form of sacrifices as described in the Vedas.
Beginning with the *agnihotra* up to the *saṃvatsara* sacrifice,
he who worships a yogi with this thought attains union with the sun and moon through intense meditation; in the event that...
If his meditation is not intense, he attains the worlds of the sun and moon and there experiences their splendor; thereafter,
he attains the splendor of the four-faced Brahmā in the world of truth.
In Satyaloka; there, in the world of truth, he realizes the truth and then attains the glory of the Supreme Brahman,
whose nature is Truth, Knowledge, and Bliss.
Unity. By these two words, "This is the Upaniṣad," both the knowledge and the books that expound it as described are indicated.

Conclusion. Thus, in this manner, the second purpose of *jīvanmukti*, which consists of the nature of austerity (*tapas*), is established. The third purpose is the absence of contradiction. Indeed, neither a worldly person nor a follower of a particular sect perceives external activity in a Lord of Yogis who is inward-turned.
Someone contradicts [this]. Worldly contradiction is of two kinds: in the form of quarrel and in the form of censure.
In that regard, how indeed could a worldly person quarrel with a yogi who is free from anger and the like? And that freedom from such states is recorded in the Smṛti:
Therefore, the second purpose of the practice of religious austerity (*jīvanmukti*) is thus established.
Absence of disagreement is the third purpose of *jīvanmukti*.
No one, whether a householder or a follower of another creed,
can oppose a master yogi who is inwardly withdrawn and does not look outward.
Outward activities. Customary disagreement is of two kinds, in the form of quarreling and censuring. How could a worldly person engage in a quarrel with a yogi who is devoid [of such attachments]?
Regarding anger and so forth? Non-anger and the like are described in the *Smṛti* as follows:
"One should not return anger to one who is angry; when reviled, one should speak kindly" (*Manusmṛti* 6.48).
"One should endure harsh words and should not despise anyone" (ibid., 6.47).
"One should not respond to anger with anger, and when reviled should wish one well; when insulted, one should endure it."

"One should be patient and should not insult anyone" (Manusmṛti 6.48). If it is argued that these qualities, such as the absence of anger and so forth, are traditionally prescribed for the renunciation of those seeking knowledge (*vividiṣā-saṃnyāsa*), which is prior to the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), which in turn is prior to the renunciation of the knower (*vidvat-saṃnyāsa*), and that this latter is prior to liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*):
Objection: But jīvanmukti is preceded by vidvatsaṃnyāsa, which is itself preceded by the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), and that in turn is preceded by the desire to know (vividiṣā).
How is it that these virtues— such as freedom from anger and so forth— are prescribed for practice in the *smṛtis* regarding *saṃnyāsa*,
yet are mentioned here [in this context] once again? *Jīvanmuktiviveka*.

Certainly! For this very reason, anger and the like are impossible even to suspect in one who is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). If anger and the like do not exist even in the most recent stage—the renunciation of the seeker (*vividiṣā-saṃnyāsa*)—then how could they exist in the superior stage of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), how much less in the renunciation of the knower (*vidvat-saṃnyāsa*), and how much less in liberation while living? Therefore, [anger] does not coexist with the yogi.
A worldly quarrel may occur; nor should a disagreement in the form of censure be suspected, because the state of being censurable is not certain. And thus it is recorded in the Smṛti:
[Reply: Indeed, it is so. Therefore, anger and the like cannot even...

This should not be doubted regarding one who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta). If even in the lowest stage of renunciation for the sake of seeking knowledge (vividisā-saṃnyāsa) qualities such as anger are absent, then how could they possibly exist in the superior stage of realized knowledge? And...
In the even higher state of *vidvatsaṃnyāsa*,
where [even this] is not possible, what need is there to mention the supreme state of *jīvanmukti*? Therefore, a worldly person can never grasp it.
One should not suspect a quarrel with a yogin, nor even a disagreement in the form of censure, because the blameworthiness of the yogin is unascertained. This is described as follows:
Thus says the Smṛti:
"He whom no one knows as existent or non-existent, as unlearned or deeply learned, as well-behaved or ill-behaved— he indeed is a true ascetic (yati)."
— (Vasiṣṭha-smṛti 6.40)— thus it is said:
"A true ascetic is indeed he whom no one knows to be of noble birth or of low birth, ignorant or learned, a rogue or..."
"virtuous" (Vasiṣṭha Smṛti 6.40; Nārada Parivrājaka Upaniṣad 4.34).

"Existent and non-existent" refers to high and low castes. Does even a follower of another school contradict [the truth] regarding the objects of knowledge established by the scriptures, or regarding the conduct of yogis? Regarding the first point, the yogi does not refute the objects of knowledge established by other scriptures, [saying]: "Know Him alone as the one Self, and nothing else..."

This is in accordance with such scriptural passages as, "Release your speech" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.5), and "One should not meditate on many words, for that is a weariness of speech" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.21). Nor does he establish the subject matter of his own treatise before an opponent.

"One seeking grain should discard the straw entirely; having realized the Supreme Brahman, one should cast off all else like a firebrand," and so forth—because [this work] is devoted to the meaning of such scriptural passages. (From the *Amṛtabindūpaniṣad* 18 and *Amṛtanādopaniṣad* 1). *Jīvanmuktiviveka*.
By "goodness and badness" (*sadasattva*) and "high and low birth," what is meant here is [the status of] caste.
A follower of another creed might disagree with this.
the tenet or the conduct of a yogi. Regarding the first alternative,
there is no possibility, because the yogi does not dispute other doctrines in accordance with the injunctions of the Vedas.
It is as follows: “Know that non-dual Self alone and abandon all other talk” (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.5).
"Let him not think of too many words, for that is exhausting to the organ of speech" (Brhadaranyaka Upanishad 4.4.21).
Nor does the yogi defend his own tenet against [others].
The disputant should proceed in accordance with the following instructions,
which are consistent with the meaning of the Śruti: "The yogi should abandon all books, just as one who needs water abandons the vessel."
"Grain casts aside the chaff" (Amṛtabindu Upaniṣad 18).
"The yogi, having realized the supreme Brahman, should cast them (the books) aside like a torch" (Amṛtanāda Upaniṣad).
Upadeśa 1):
When a yogin perceives even his opponent as his own self, what need is there to mention the desire for victory?
Furthermore, every non-materialist (laukāyatika) non-Buddhist (tairthika) who accepts liberation likewise [engages] in the conduct of a yogin.

It ought not to be contradictory; for although the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) propounded in the various systems of liberation—such as those of the Ārhatas, Buddhists, Vaiśeṣikas, Naiyāyikas, Śaivas, Vaiṣṇavas, Śāktas, Sāṃkhyas, Yogins, and others—are manifold, the eightfold yoga consisting of *yama*, *niyama*, and so forth, which is the means to liberation, is of a single form.
Therefore, by virtue of this non-contradiction, the Lord of Yoga is universally accepted. Having this very point in mind:
Vasiṣṭha said:
When the yogi perceives even the adversary as his own self,
how then could the desire for victory arise?
Except for the materialists, followers of all creeds who believe in liberation cannot disagree with the activities of a yogi; for such is the teaching of the Jaina scriptures.

The Buddhist, Vaiśeṣika, Naiyāyika, Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Śākta, Sāṅkhya, Yoga, and other systems dealing with final liberation, despite their differences regarding the nature of that liberation, [all agree on its essential character].
The agreement regarding the very same means for that [attainment],
namely the eight-limbed yoga consisting of *yama*, *niyama*, and so forth; therefore,
the master yogi is indisputably honored by all.
Vasiṣṭha speaks with this very intent: "O high-minded one, pure knowledge enters him whose birth is his last, just as pearls enter an excellent bamboo flute."
(Yogavāsiṣṭha, Upaśamaprakaraṇa, 6.8)
"O great-minded one, just as fine pearls enter into the finest bamboo, so does the totality of radiant knowledge quickly enter him whose present birth is his last. (YV 5.6.8)
Nobility, amiability, friendliness, gentleness, liberation, and wisdom always attend upon him, just as women dwell within the inner apartments.
—(In that very same place, 6.9) ||
"Just as noblewomen always resort to the inner apartments,
so too do magnanimity, cordiality, friendship, benevolence,
liberation, and wisdom always resort to such [a person]."
"A yogi (ibid. 9):
All people desire him who is sweet in his gentle conduct, just as forest deer in the woods long for the flute with its sweet sound."
—(In that very same place, 6.12) ||
"Just as in the forest wild deer pursue the sweet sound of the flute, so do all people pursue him (the yogi) who is sweet and of charming conduct" (ibid., 12). Jīvan-mukti-viveka.
He who always remains awake with a mind whose mental fluctuations are stilled as if in deep sleep,
like the moon endowed with its digits, is [truly] wise.
"He who is ever wide awake in mind, yet remains without [mental activity], is remembered here as one who is liberated.
(Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 16.22).
"He who remains mentally ever wide awake..."
One who possesses no objective mental transformations such as those occurring in sleep,
and whose company— like the full moon— is ever sought after by the learned for their erudition, is known to be liberated.
In this world (LYV 16.22):
"Just as toward a mother, both the harsh and the gentle attain tranquility;
so do all beings here place their trust in one who possesses tranquility."
(Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 4.62).
"All beings— whether harsh or gentle— place their trust and find peace in him (the yogi) who is perfectly tranquil, even as..."
All creatures find peace and rest by placing their trust in their own mother:
"Among ascetics, the learned, sacrificial priests, and kings;
among the powerful and the virtuous—it is only the man of tranquility who truly shines."
(tatraiva 4.66) Thus it is said:
"Among ascetics, scholars, officiating priests, kings, powerful men, and those rich in excellent qualities..."
"the tranquil [yogi] alone shines" (ibid. 4.66).

Thus, the third purpose of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), which consists in the absence of contradiction and is uncontradicted, is established. As for the fourth and fifth purposes, which consist in the destruction of suffering and the manifestation of bliss, they are contained within the bliss of Brahman, which is of the nature of knowledge and bliss.
Both of these have been established in the fourth chapter; they are here stated in brief:
thus is the third purpose of *jīvanmukti*, namely the absence of contradiction, proven beyond doubt.
The fourth and fifth purposes— namely, the disappearance of sorrow and the appearance of happiness— have been treated in the *vidyānanda*, the fourth chapter of the *Brahmāṇa*.
(Pañcadaśī, Chapter 14). Both of these are now being described here in brief:
"If a person should know the Self, realizing 'I am this,'..."
"Desiring what, or for the sake of what, should one suffer for the body?
(Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.12)
‘If a man knows the Self as “I am this,” then desiring what, and for whose sake, would he suffer on account of the body? (Brhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.12; Pañcadaśī 14.5).

By such scriptural passages as these, the destruction of worldly suffering is declared. Furthermore, scriptural texts such as, "Indeed, at that time he does not grieve, thinking: 'Why did I not do good? Why did I do evil? (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.9), speak of the destruction of suffering consisting of anxiety regarding merit and demerit—the causes of future existence. The manifestation of bliss is threefold: [all...]
The attainment of desires, the state of having accomplished all that was to be done, and the state of having attained all that was to be attained. The attainment of all desires is threefold:

being the witness of all, being untouched by desire in all circumstances, and being the nature of the enjoyer of all. For one who knows, "I am indeed that Brahman which is the pervasive consciousness as witness within all bodies from Hiraṇyagarbha down to the level of stationary objects," it is as if in his own body.

Even in other bodies, there exists the state of being a witness to all desires. With this in mind, it is heard in scripture: "He enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahman" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1).
In the world, that which consists in being unassailed by desire regarding enjoyments already experienced is called the attainment of desires. And thus, [there is] the enjoyment of all—

For one who perceives defects in [worldly] objects and knows reality, there is the attainment of all desires because of being unassailed by desire in every respect. For this very reason, it is stated in the scripture (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.8.1): "And of the learned Śrotriya who is unassailed by desire," regarding the joys that begin with the sovereign of the earth and extend up to Hiraṇyagarbha, each increasing a hundredfold over the preceding. [This occurs] by way of its nature as Being (*sat*), its nature as Consciousness (*cit*), and its nature as Bliss (*ānanda*).
Intending that one who contemplates their own self as abiding everywhere possesses the state of being the enjoyer of all, it is heard in scripture thus:
[By this Śruti and others, the cessation of this worldly sorrow is described].
"Indeed, such a person is not tormented by the thought: 'Why did I not do what is good? Why did I do what is evil?
(Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.9). Jīvan-mukti-viveka.
Thus, this Śruti and other texts describe the cessation of sorrow in the form of anxiety regarding merit and demerit, which give rise to future births.
Happiness appears in three ways: through the fulfillment of all desires, through the performance of duties, and through the attainment of what is attainable.
The attainment of all desires occurs again in three ways: through the state of witnessing all, through complete desirelessness, and through the state of experiencing all things.

He who has realized his own identity as Brahman in the form of witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) residing within all bodies, from Hiraṇyagarbha down to the immobile beings, possesses the state of being a witness.
He enjoys all desires in all bodies as if in his own. With this very intent, the Śruti says: "Being one with the omniscient Brahman, he enjoys..."
"simultaneously all desires" (ibid. 2.1).
In this world, the absence of desire for objects of enjoyment after they have already been enjoyed is called attainment (*prāpti*).
of desires. And thus, the desirelessness of the enlightened one, due to his perception of the defects in all forms of enjoyment, is equivalent to the attainment of all desires.
Therefore, the Śruti (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.8.1) mentions: "Of the one learned in the Vedas and untouched by desire," while describing the degrees of happiness increasing hundredfold.
Beginning from the sovereign monarch of the world up to Hiraṇyagarbha—
He who is conscious of His own Self as pervading everywhere.

In the form of reality, consciousness, and bliss, [the Self] exists in the state of enjoying all objects of enjoyment. With this in view, the Śruti says: "I am food, I am food, I am food; I am the eater of food, I am the eater of food, I am the eater of food."
—(Taittirīyopaniṣad 3.10)— "I am food, I am food, I am food;
I am the eater of food, I am the eater of food, I am the eater of food. (Although...)
"I am the non-dual Self, yet I am the enjoyer and the object of enjoyment" (ibid. 3.10.6).
Furthermore, the state of having accomplished all that was to be done is recorded in the Smṛti:

"For the yogi who is satisfied by the nectar of knowledge and has accomplished his purpose, there is nothing whatsoever left to be done; if there were anything to be done, he would not be a knower of reality. (Jābāladarśanopaniṣad 1.23 and Uttaragītā 1.13)
And the state of one who has fulfilled his duties is described in the Smṛti as follows:
"The yogi who has drunk the nectar of knowledge to his fill..."
"One who, having attained contentment, has thus fulfilled his obligations, has nothing further to do; and if there remains something for him to do,
he is not yet enlightened" (Śrī-Jābāladarśana-Upaniṣad).

"However, that person who delights only in the Self, who is satisfied with the Self, and who finds contentment in the Self alone—for him there is no duty to be performed. (Bhagavad Gītā 3.17; Pañcadaśī 1.23; Uttaragītā 1.13)
(Bhagavadgītā 3.17):
"But the man who is devoted to the Self, who is satisfied with the Self, and who finds contentment in the Self alone— he has no [duty]."
"the obligatory duty" (BG 3.17).

Furthermore, the state of having attained what was to be attained is heard in scripture: "O Janaka, you have indeed attained fearlessness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.2.2), "therefore it became all that" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10), and "he who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself."

And so it is stated in the *Muṇḍakopaniṣad* (3.2.9). Now, one might object: "Since these two—the destruction of suffering and the manifestation of bliss—are accomplished by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) alone, they do not constitute the specific purpose of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). This is not so; for what is intended here in the *Jīvanmuktiviveka* is the preservation of those two once they have been attained. Just as the knowledge of reality, though already arisen previously, becomes firmly secured through *jīvanmukti*.

In this way, these two also become well-guarded. Now, if it is the case that there are five purposes for liberation while living (jīvanmukti), one must say that the master yogi who remains composed is superior even to the knower of reality (tattvavid) who engages in worldly affairs; yet that [superiority] has been refuted by the questions and answers between Rāma and Vasiṣṭha:
The state of attaining that which ought to be attained is described in the Śruti as follows:
"O Janaka, you have attained That which is free from..."
"From fear of it, the wind blows" (Bṛ.
Up. 4.2.2). "Therefore, it became all" (ibid. 1.4.10). And likewise: "He who knows Brahman indeed becomes Brahman" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad).
Objection: Since these two—the disappearance of sorrow and the appearance of happiness—are accomplished by [the means], [what is the need for knowledge?]
Since they consist of the knowledge of reality alone, they cannot constitute the purpose of *jīvanmukti*.
Reply: This is not so, for their protection is implied here.
Just as the knowledge of reality, though it arose previously, is preserved by *jīvanmukti*, so too these two remain well-protected.
Objection: When the five purposes of *jīvanmukti* have been established in this manner, it must be admitted that the master yogi absorbed in samādhi is superior to [the one liberated while living].
An enlightened one who remains engaged in worldly activities;
however, this position has been refuted through the dialogue between Rāma and Vasiṣṭha as follows:
Śrī Rāma said:

"O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, is there anyone who, though engaged in worldly affairs, remains ever composed and rests as if awakened? Is there anyone who, having resorted to solitude, abides in the discipline of meditative absorption?"
But of these two, which is the superior? Tell me this, O Blessed One.
(Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 25.5–6)
Sri Rama: "O holy sage, Lord of the welfare of all beings, please tell me which of these two is superior: he who has awakened from his meditative absorption, or [he who remains absorbed]?"
"Though performing ordinary acts, he is tranquil as if in *samādhi*, like one who always remains in meditative concentration in a secluded place"? (LYV 25.5, 6)
Vasiṣṭha:
For one who perceives this collection of qualities as not being the self, that inner coolness which arises is called "samādhi. (7)
Having ascertained that "I have no connection with visible objects," one becomes cool;
whether engaged in worldly affairs or devoted to meditation, one remains so. (8)
O Rāma, if these two are perfectly equal and thoroughly cooled, that which constitutes internal coolness is the fruit of infinite austerity. (9)
(Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 25.7–9).
Vasiṣṭha said: “The inner coolness—the tranquility of one who perceives this world as merely a combination [of elements]...”
That which consists of the three modes and is non-self is called concentration (ibid., 7).
Someone might remain active in the worldly way and...
Someone may be absorbed in meditation, being cool and tranquil among them due to the conviction: "I am unconnected with this phenomenal world" (ibid., 8).
"O Rāma, both of these are perfectly equal, provided they are absolutely cool within. Such inner coolness is the result of infinite religious austerity" (ibid. 9).

This is not a fault. Here, it is merely established that the state of inner coolness, which consists in the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*), must necessarily be accomplished; however, the superiority of the dissolution of the mind (*manonāśa*) occurring immediately thereafter is not being denied. He himself clarified this intended meaning—that "coolness" refers to the pacification of craving—as follows:

Reply: There is no harm in this; for it is precisely this much that is being established—that the inner coolness consisting of the effacement of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*) in the form of *jīvanmukti-viveka* must be accomplished.
And it is not the superiority of the subsequent dissolution of the mind that is being refuted. Vasiṣṭha himself clarifies the implied meaning of "coolness" as the quenching of thirst.
[This refers to] enjoyment).
"But when inner coolness has been attained, the world is cool;
for those tormented by inner thirst, the world consists of the burning of a forest fire. (24)
(In that very same place, 25.24) ||
“When inner coolness is attained, the entire world becomes cool; but for those who burn within from desire, the world is a forest conflagration” (ibid. 25.24).
But is it not the case that here we find both a censure of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and a praise of worldly activity?
"If the mind of one established in the state of meditative absorption is restless with its fluctuations, then his concentration is equal to the frantic dancing of a madman. (10)
"If the mind of one who is engaged in the dance of madness has its latent impressions (*vāsanā*) exhausted,
then his mad dancing is equal to absorption in Brahman (*brahmasamādhi*). — (Ibid., 25.10–11).
Objection: But here— in the following verses— it is observed that *samādhi* is disparaged and engagement in worldly activities is praised as follows:
‘If the mind of one in the state of concentration is restless due to transformation, that concentration of his is tantamount to a mad dance’ (ibid. 25.10).
"But if the mind is free from desire even in the state of frantic dance, then this frantic dance of his is equivalent to *brahma-samādhi*— the superconscious concentration" (ibid).

Not so; for here, while accepting the excellence of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) itself, it is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) that is censured. This is the intended meaning of the statement: although meditative absorption is superior to ordinary worldly activity (*vyavahāra*), if it is accompanied by latent impressions, then it is indeed inferior to activity free from such impressions; thus, it is not true *samādhi*. When both the one in *samādhi* and the worldly agent are equally ignorant of reality (*atattvajña*) and possessed of latent impressions, then, because meditative absorption is a merit (*puṇya*) that leads to rebirth in higher worlds, [it is inferior].

Praise: When both [the seeker and the master] are established in knowledge and free from latent impressions (*vāsana*), even then this samādhi in the form of the dissolution of the mind (*manonāśa*)—which preserves liberation-in-life (*jīvanmukti*) consisting of the exhaustion of latent impressions—is indeed highly commendable. Therefore, since the Lord of Yogis is preeminent, it is established that there is no obstacle whatsoever to *jīvanmukti*, which possesses five purposes.
Reply: It is not so. For here, while acknowledging the excellence of samādhi alone, desire is disparaged.
The simple meaning of the aforementioned verses is as follows:
Although *samādhi* is superior to worldly activities, if it is fraught with desire, then it is truly inferior to desireless worldly activities; thus, it is not *samādhi* at all. When a person...
When one in a state of meditative concentration and a person engaged in worldly activities are both unenlightened and possessed of desire,
the state of concentration is superior because it possesses such a quality.
That leads to the attainment of higher worlds. And when both are enlightened and free from desire, then also this concentration in the form of the dissolution of the mind [occurs].
That which protects *jīvanmukti* in the form of the cessation of desire is, of course, superior.
Therefore, because the master yogi is superior, it is established—
He declares that there is no obstacle whatsoever to his attainment of *jīvanmukti* along with its fivefold objects.
Thus ends the section on the nature of *jīvanmukti* in the *Jīvanmuktiviveka* composed by the venerable Vidyāraṇya.
The fourth chapter, titled "The Investigation of the Two Purposes."

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Purpose Served by the Attainment of Jīvanmukti," in the *Jīvanmuktiviveka* composed by Śrīmad Vidyāraṇya. Fifth Chapter: The Section on the Renunciation of the Knower (*Vidvatsaṃnyāsa*)
An Inquiry into the Renunciation of the Knower.
Thus, liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) has been described by way of its essential nature, its means of proof, its instruments, and its purpose. Now, that which is conducive to it—
We shall now describe the renunciation of the knower (*vidvatsaṃnyāsa*). This renunciation of the knower is set forth in the *Paramahaṃsopaniṣad*;
having quoted that Upaniṣad, we shall explain it.
Therein, first, the text introduces a question concerning the one qualified for the renunciation of the knower:
Thus, *jīvanmukti*, together with its nature, proof, means, and purpose, has been defined. Now, *vidvatsaṃnyāsa*, which is subordinate to *jīvanmukti*, is being defined. And...
The renunciation of the wise (*vidvat-sannyāsa*) has been set forth in the *Paramahaṃsa Upaniṣad*; quoting from that very Upaniṣad, we shall explain it.
At the beginning of that Upaniṣad, there is a question concerning...
The renunciation of the wise (vidvat-saṃnyāsa) is introduced as follows:
"Then Nārada, having approached the Blessed One, said: 'What is this path of the Paramahaṃsa yogins, and what is their state?'"
Then Nārada, approaching the Lord, asked him thus: “What is the path and what is the state of the yogis who are *paramahaṃsas*?”

Although no counter-correlative for the immediate succession required by the word *atha* appears here, nevertheless, the subject to be inquired into is the renunciation of the knower (*vidvat-saṃnyāsa*). And in that regard, the qualified seeker is one who has realized the truth, who, being distracted by worldly activities, desires the repose of the mind as described in the *Jīvanmukti-viveka*. Therefore, the meaning of the word *atha* is the immediate succession following the attainment of such a qualification.

The two terms were stated in order to exclude the *kevalayogin* and the *kevalaparamahaṃsa*. A *kevalayogin*, due to the absence of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), becomes attached to the wondrous displays of yogic sovereignty—such as knowledge of the three periods of time and the power of moving through space—and exerts himself in various specific forms of self-restraint (*saṃyama*) for those ends. Consequently, he falls away from the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*). On this point, the aphorism has already been cited previously: [Yoga Sūtra 3.51].
"Those are obstacles to concentration, but they are accomplishments upon emergence" (Yoga Sūtras 3.38).
Although nothing whatsoever appears to precede this that would be implied by the word *atha* ("then"), nevertheless, the subject of [the discourse]...

The question here concerns *vidvatsaṃnyāsa* (the renunciation of the knower). One who is enlightened, yet distracted by worldly activities and desiring tranquility of mind, is fit for this; therefore, having attained such [a state]—
The word "then" (tadā) means "possessing [the aforementioned] qualifications.
Both words are used to exclude the "yogi alone" (*kevala-yogin*) or the "paramahaṃsa alone" (*kevala-paramahaṃsa*).
Used together.
Only the yogi— that is, one who is unenlightened and practices yoga solely due to a lack of enlightenment— becomes...
Attached to the miraculous feats of occult powers such as omniscience, levitation, and so forth, one endeavors to acquire them through the application of their respective methods.
Samyama consists of contemplation (dharana), meditation (dhyana), and concentration (samadhi).
In this manner, one falls away from the attainment of the goal of life. The aphorism that describes this meaning is as follows: [Yoga Sutra 3.51].
It has already been quoted as follows:
“These are obstacles to samādhi; yet they are powers in the worldly state” (Yogasūtra 3.38).

But the *kevalaparamahaṃsa*, having understood through the discrimination of reality (*tattvaviveka*) the worthlessness of supernatural powers (*aiśvarya*), becomes dispassionate. This too has been illustrated: "But the *kevalaparamahaṃsa*... [and so forth].

The realization of reality becomes unattached. This has also been quoted previously as follows: "These powers of the conscious self manifest here in this manner; thus, curiosity does not arise regarding its wondrous webs. (67)
—(Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha 27.67).
“All these manifestations in this manner are but the essence of the Self, which is pure consciousness”; understanding this,

The phrase "text and covering" (*acchādanam ca*) refers to a pair of sandals and the like. Regarding this, there is the following *smṛti*: "A pair of loincloths, a garment, and a patched cloak to ward off the cold."
"One should also take up the two sandals and should not keep anything else" (Hārītasaṃhitā 6.728; Laghuviṣṇusmṛti 4.7).
"Utilization for one's own body" means the warding off of shame by means of the loincloth, and the avoidance of disturbances from cattle, snakes, and so forth by means of the staff.

By means of clothing, there is the warding off of cold and other such things. By the word "and" (ca), he includes the warding off of touching impure places by means of sandals. What is called "benefiting the world" is the accomplishment of merit for others through their engagement in appropriate salutations and the giving of alms, once they have recognized his highest stage of life (*uttamāśrama*) by signs such as the staff. By the word "and," [he implies] the maintenance of the boundaries of the stage of life (*āśramamaryādā*).
This implies the maintenance of what is obtained through the conduct of the learned.
With the intention that the acceptance of a loincloth and so forth is merely permissive, he prohibits its being primary:
"He may accept a pair of loincloths and an upper garment."
"A patched garment for protection against the cold, and even a pair of sandals; but nothing else should he take" (Hārīta Saṃhitā 6.728; Laghu-Viṣṇu-Smṛti 4.7).
"For one's own bodily use" (*svaśarīropabhoga*) means that one should be modest with the pair of loincloths. The staff is intended for protection against cattle, snakes, and the like.
Covering is intended for protection against the cold. By the word "and" (*ca*), the avoidance of contact with impure places by means of a pair of sandals is intended for the sake of one's welfare.
"Benefit for the people"— meaning *lokasyopakāraḥ*— refers to the fact that people,
recognizing him by the signs such as the staff and so forth that he belongs to the highest stage of life (*parama-āśrama*), will honor him.

One should acquire religious merit by performing appropriate acts such as salutation, giving alms, and so forth; furthermore, the word "and" (*ca*) also implies the observance of proper conduct (*vṛtta*).
One should maintain one's conduct according to the propriety of the stage of life as transmitted by the wise elders;
the acceptance of the loincloth and other requisites is conducive solely to this end.
This being the case, its lack of ultimate reality is prohibited as follows:
"And that does not exist in a primary sense" (Paramārthasāra Upaniṣad 1).
"And that is not essential" (Paramahaṃsa Upaniṣad 1).
Even the possession of a loincloth and other such items is not the primary rule for this Paramahaṃsa yogin;
rather, it is merely a secondary alternative (anukalpa). This is because, for the seeker-renunciant (vividiṣā-saṃnyāsin), the taking up of the staff is considered the primary rule.
The prohibition of being separated from the staff is recorded in the Smṛti:
"The acceptance of the loincloth and so forth, which has been prescribed, is not the essential rule for a yogin-paramahaṃsa."
Although the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra* permits [the use of a staff] only as a substitute, the acceptance of the staff has been made mandatory for a *vaidika-saṃnyāsin*,
and the *smṛti* prohibits its separation, stating:
"The union of the staff and the self is ordained for all times;
a wise man should not go even three throws of an arrow's distance without his staff" (Sannyāsopaniṣad 2.11).

Even regarding the expiation for the loss of the staff, a hundred *prāṇāyāmas* are prescribed in the traditional texts: "Upon abandoning the staff, one should perform a hundred [repetitions]. "The contact of the staff with the body should always be maintained;
the wise should not go beyond its length by more than three [times]."
"the range of the arrow, without the staff" (Sannyāsopaniṣad 2.11).

He shows the primary rule for the *yogin*-paramahaṃsa by means of a question and answer.

It is described through the following dialogue:

“What, then, is the essence? The essence is this: without a staff, without a topknot, without a sacred thread, without a covering, the Paramahaṃsa wanders about” (Paramahaṃsa Upaniṣad 1.2).

The phrase "not the tuft" (*na śikham*) should be understood as a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*) involving a change in gender. Just as the seeker who desires knowledge (*vividiṣu*) is primary when devoid of both the tuft and the sacred thread, so too the yogi becomes primary when devoid of both the staff and the covering;

this is for the purpose of examining whether the staff possesses the characteristics of being made of bamboo and the like, and whether the covering possesses the characteristics of being a patched garment and the like.

If the mind is occupied with procuring and protecting such things as staffs and the like, yoga—characterized by the cessation of mental fluctuations—will not be accomplished. That, however, is not tenable, according to the maxim: "One does not marry off a maiden for the sake of obstructing her excellence.

The use of the neuter gender in the phrase "na śikhām" ("no tuft") is archaic. Regarding the seeker-paramahaṃsa,
there is the absence of the tuft on the head as well as the sacred thread.

And this is improper, according to the maxim: "no one gives his daughter in marriage to a groom in order to kill him."
Anticipating the question, "In the absence of a blanket and so forth, what will be the protection against the discomfort of cold and the like? the Śruti says this: 332.
"Neither cold nor hot, neither pleasure nor pain, and free from honor and dishonor, as well as the six waves" (Paramahaṃsa Upaniṣad 2).
"The paramahaṃsa-yogin is neither cold nor hot..."
Neither happy nor unhappy, neither honored nor dishonored, and free from the six waves (Paramahamsa Upaniṣad 2).

For the yogin whose mental fluctuations have been entirely ceased, there is no cold, because its cause is absent. Just as for a child absorbed in play—who, even though lacking clothing and other protections, feels no cold even during the early morning of the winter and late winter seasons—so too, for the yogin absorbed in the Supreme Self, there is an absence of cold. Furthermore, during the summer season, there is an absence of heat.

It should be understood in exactly the same way. The word "ca" (and) serves to include the absence [of cold] during the rainy season. When cold and heat are not perceived, the absence of the pleasure and pain produced by them is logically established. During the summer, cold is pleasant; during the winter, it is cold.
That which produces suffering is the opposite of what has been stated; this should be understood as applying to heat. *Māna* is honor bestowed by another person;

*avamāna* is contempt. When the yogi does not perceive any other person distinct from his own self, then honor and contempt are removed far away. The word "and" (*ca*) includes the absence of dualities such as enemy and friend, attachment and aversion, and so forth.

The six waves are hunger, thirst, grief, delusion, old age, and death. Since these three pairs of opposites pertain respectively to the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the mind (*manas*), and the body (*deha*), it is appropriate for the yogi who is oriented toward the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) to abandon them.
For a yogi whose all mental transformations—
The functions [of the senses] are restrained due to the absence of awareness of them. Just as a child absorbed in play feels no cold on a winter morning even though naked, so too the yogi.

One who is absorbed in the supreme Self does not feel cold. In the same way, it should be understood that there is no sensation of heat during the summer. The word "and" (*ca*) in the text "nor hot" [indicates this].
"Na cosnam" implies the absence of rain during the rainy season. When there is no sensation of heat and cold,
there is an absence of the pleasure and pain caused by them.
Established.
Cold is pleasant during the summer and unpleasant during the winter; in the case of heat, the opposite of the above.
This is to be understood. In the *Jīvan-mukti-viveka*,
"honored" (*manah*) means being treated with reverence by other people, and "dishonored" (*avamānaḥ*) means being censured.
Red. When the yogi has no perception of anyone other than his own self, honor and dishonor are far removed from him. The final word "and" implies their opposites.
Such as friend and foe, love and hatred, and so forth. The six waves are hunger and thirst, sorrow and delusion, and old age and death.
The abandonment of these three pairs, which are the attributes of the vital breath, the mind, and the body respectively,
is appropriate for the yogi who is oriented toward the true nature.

Regarding the soul—that is, one intent on realizing the Self—one might object: "Granted that there is an absence of cold and other such sensations during the state of meditative absorption (samādhi), yet in the state of emergence (vyutthāna), afflictions such as censure would surely trouble this person just as they do a worldly being. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Having abandoned censure, pride, envy, deceit, arrogance, desire, hatred, pleasure, pain, lust, anger, greed, delusion, joy, malice, egoism, and so forth" (Parama Upaniṣad 2).
"Let there be an absence of cold and the like during concentration..."
Anticipating the doubt that "even though he is free from tradition, when outside of it, censure and the like must torment him just as they do an ordinary worldly person," the Śruti says this:
"Having abandoned censure, pride, selfishness, hypocrisy, insolence,
wish, hatred, pleasure, pain, desire, anger, avarice, delusion, joy, envy, egoism, and so forth" (Paramahaṃsa-).
2) Panisad:

Censure (*nindā*) is the attribution of faults to oneself by various persons. Pride (*garva*) is the mental state of thinking, "I am superior to others. Envy (*matsara*) is the cognition that one is equal to others in terms of knowledge, wealth, and so forth. [In the presence] of others...

Hypocrisy (*dambha*) is the ostentatious display of practices such as recitation (*japa*) and meditation (*dhyāna*). Arrogance (*darpa*) is a firm conviction in [one's own] power to revile others and the like. Desire (*icchā*) is the longing for wealth and other such things. Hatred (*dveṣa*) is the inclination toward the killing of enemies and similar acts. Happiness (*sukha*) is the composure of the intellect resulting from the acquisition of favorable objects and the like; its opposite is suffering (*duḥkha*). Lust (*kāma*) is the longing for women and other such objects. Anger (*krodha*) is the agitation of the intellect produced by the frustration of one’s desired ends.
Greed (*lobha*) is the inability to relinquish wealth that has been acquired. Delusion (*moha*) is the perception of benefit in what is harmful and the perception of harm in what is beneficial.
Joy (*harṣa*) is a modification of the intellect (*dhīvṛtti*) that manifests the pleasure residing in the mind and serves as the cause for the expansion of the face and other such signs.
Envy (*asūyā*) is the attribution of faults [to others]. Egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) is the delusion of selfhood regarding the aggregate of the body, senses, and so forth.

The notions of "mine-ness," "propriety," and so forth, regarding objects of enjoyment are what are meant here. The word "and" (ca) includes the opposites of the aforementioned censure and so on, such as praise and the like. Having abandoned all these—censure and the rest—one should remain, having relinquished them through the practice of the dissolution of the previously mentioned latent impressions (vāsanā); this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Regarding the phrase "in the virtues of others," by the word "etcetera" (ādi),
when various individuals find fault with me, that is called [the third type of patience].
Censure; the notion, "In wealth and learning I must excel others," is selfishness; the notion, "I am greater than others," is pride; hypocrisy consists in the display of outward piety.
Praying, meditating, and so forth in the presence of others is hypocrisy; a strong will to deride is insolence; longing for wealth and the like is desire;
hatred consists in the will to kill enemies; and pleasure consists in—

The pleasant state of the mind upon the acquisition of favorable objects is happiness; its direct opposite is suffering. Longing for women and so forth is desire; anger consists in the agitation of the mind.

Born from the frustration of not obtaining desired objects; avarice consists in the inability to endure parting with one's gains; delusion consists in perceiving the good as evil and the evil as good; joy is...
That transformation of the mind which gives rise to a beaming face indicating a pleasant state of mind; envy consists in finding fault with the good qualities of others; egoity consists in—
This refers to conceiving the combination of the body, the senses,
and so forth as the self. In the text, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) implies the sense of "belonging to me" (*mama*) and propriety (*yuktatva*).
objects of enjoyment. The use of the word ‘and’ (ca) in the text refers to the opposites of censure and so forth, such as praise and the like.
Abandoning all such censures and the like— meaning, through the practice of the eradication of latent impressions— the yogi should remain indifferent toward them; this is the conclusion.

Anticipating the doubt that "abandonment of one's own body is not possible while it still exists," the Śruti says: "Since one's own body is seen like a corpse, that body is cast off" (Parama Upaniṣad 2).
"It is not possible to give them up"— thus he further says:
For the yogi-paramahaṃsa, his own body appears like a corpse, because it has been abandoned— that is, separated from [the self].
From the Self (*Paramahaṃsopaniṣad* 3):

That which was formerly one's own body is now perceived by the yogi as something separate from the consciousness of his own self, like a corpse. Just as a person of faith, out of fear of touching it, observes a dead body while standing at a distance, so does this [yogi].

Fearing the arising of the delusion of identity, the yogi remains vigilant and continuously discriminates the body from the conscious self (*cidātman*). For that reason, the body has been discarded from the conscious self, being destroyed by the teachings of the teacher, the scriptures, and personal experience. Consequently, because the body, when separated from consciousness, is seen to be like a corpse, even though it exists—
The intention is that the abandonment of censure regarding the body is possible.

Now, one might object: just as a delusion concerning direction, even after it has arisen and been destroyed by the sight of the sun rising, may sometimes persist, so too, if doubt regarding the self and the body were to occasionally persist within the self, the affliction of censure and the like would recur again and again.
Anticipating this objection, he says: "He is eternally free from that which is the cause of doubt, misconception, and false knowledge" (Pañcadaśī Upaniṣad 2).
The body which was his own previously is now regarded [as distinct].

The yogi regards it as a dead body because it is distinct from his own self, which is pure consciousness. Just as a person of faith, fearing contact, gazes upon a corpse from a distance, so too does the yogi view it.
Therefore, the yogi always carefully discriminates the body from the Self, which is pure consciousness, fearing that a false identification of the two might arise. For this very body—
It has been degraded by the precepts of the teacher,
the teachings of the scriptures, and one's own experience— that is,
it has been discriminated from pure consciousness. Therefore—
The point is this: it is possible to relinquish censure and the like even while the body still exists, because that body, being dissociated from consciousness, appears just like a corpse.

Just as the confusion that arose regarding the cardinal directions, though dispelled by seeing the rising sun, may sometimes reappear, even so [is it with] the doubt and other [defilements] concerning...
At times, the identification of the body with the self may occur, which would again cause pain to the self through censure and the like;
anticipating such a doubt, the Śruti says this: "The paramahaṃsa-yogī is forever free from the cause."
Regarding doubt, misconception, and erroneous knowledge (*viparyaya-jñāna*) (*Paramahaṃsa Upaniṣad* 2):

"Is the self endowed with attributes such as agency, or is it devoid of them?"—this and the like constitute doubtful cognition (*saṃśaya-jñāna*). [And] "The self is of the very nature of the body and so forth" [is misconception].

Perverted knowledge (*viparīta-jñāna*). Both of these relate to the subject who experiences (*bhoktṛ-viṣaya*). However, what is intended here as false knowledge (*mithyā-jñāna*) relates to the object of experience (*bhogya-viṣaya*).

That [false knowledge] is of many kinds, as clarified in the *Bhagavadgītā* (6.24): "Desires arising from mental constructs. Its cause is fourfold: [the perception of] the permanent, the pure, the pleasant, and the self in that which is impermanent, impure, painful, and non-self.

This is because of the aphorism in the *Yoga Sūtras* (2.5): "Nescience (*avidyā*) is the cognition [of the permanent, the pure, the pleasant, and the self] in that which is impermanent, impure, painful, and non-self. The first is the delusion of permanence regarding impermanent things such as mountains, rivers, and oceans. The second is the delusion of purity regarding the impure bodies of one's sons, wife, and so forth. The third is the delusion of pleasure regarding pain, such as agriculture, trade, and the like. [The fourth is the delusion of self regarding what is not the self, such as the "self consisting of food" (*annamaya*) and others, or secondary selves such as sons and wives.]

And the fourth is the delusion that the non-Self is the primary Self. The cause of these—doubt and the rest—is ignorance (*ajñāna*), which veils the reality of the non-dual Brahman-Self, along with its latent impressions (*vāsanā*). That ignorance has been removed for the *paramahaṃsa* yogin through the awakening to the meaning of the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*); however, the latent impressions have been removed through the practice of yoga. As was illustrated in the [previous] example...

Even when the ignorance that causes confusion regarding the directions has ceased, the conventional behavior of delusion continues as before due to the persistence of its latent impressions (*vāsanā*). However, for the yogi, since he is devoid of the two causes of delusion, how could doubt and the like continue? It is with reference to this absence of continuation that it is said the yogi is eternally free from those two causes. Even though there is the cessation of ignorance and its latent impressions, [the question remains] of that...
Because there is no destruction of cessation (*nivṛtti*), its eternality is to be understood. He states the reason for that eternality: "Its consciousness is eternal" (*Parama-upaniṣad* 2).
Doubt consists in such uncertainty as: "Is the Self..."

*Jīvan-mukti-viveka* (The Discrimination of Liberation while Living)
Ignorance is the apprehension of the impermanent, the impure, the painful, and that which is not the self as being permanent, pure, pleasant, and the self (ātman), respectively (Yoga Sūtra 2.5).
The first is the erroneous conception of permanence regarding impermanent things such as mountains, rivers, and oceans;

The second is [the misconception] regarding sons, wife, and so forth; the third is the false notion of happiness in painful occupations such as agriculture and commerce; and [the fourth is] falsely taking...

The cause of these— doubt and the rest— is ignorance along with its latent impressions, which conceal the true nature of the non-dual Brahman, the Supreme Self.
The ignorance of the yogī-paramahaṃsa has been destroyed by understanding the meaning of the great Vedic scriptures,

The Śruti declares the cause of this eternal cessation as follows:

"The yogi-paramahaṃsa is forever conscious of That" (Paramahaṃsa Upaniṣad 2). Because it is a pronoun, the word *tat* here denotes a well-known object; it refers to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) as established in all the Vedāntas.
That yogi who possesses constant consciousness of that Supreme Self is "one whose consciousness is eternally fixed on That. For the yogi [meditates] on Him alone...

Following the scriptural injunction, "The wise Brāhmaṇa, having understood, should practice wisdom" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.21), one eliminates mental distractions through yoga and continuously cultivates wisdom directed solely toward the Supreme Self.
Therefore, because awakening is eternal, the cessation of ignorance and its latent impressions—which are to be destroyed by that awakening—is also eternal; this is the meaning.
The word "it" (*tad*), being a pronoun, refers to something that is very well known; here, it denotes the "Supreme Self" (*paramātman*) celebrated in all the Upaniṣads.
The yogi whose awareness of That, the Supreme Self,
is constant— he is "ever-aware of That" as referred to by the Śruti. For, in accordance with the instructions of...
Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (4.4.21): The wise seeker of Brahman, having learned the Self alone, should practice wisdom (*prajñā*); thus the yogi, having attained it...
Having removed the distractions of the mind through the practice of yoga, one should constantly exercise in the wisdom concerning the Supreme Self. Therefore, insofar as this knowledge...
The cessation of ignorance and its latent impressions— which can be destroyed by knowledge alone— is likewise permanent.
To ward off the suspicion that the Supreme Self, who is being realized in this way, might be aloof like the Lord of the logicians, [the text] states:
"That very [Self] is its own abiding" (Parama-upaniṣad 2).
The Supreme Self—thus being experienced—
The Self does not stand apart from the individual soul like the omnipotent God of the Nyāya school. To exclude such a separation, the Śruti declares as follows:

“The yogi abides in that which is his very self alone” (Paramahaṃsa Upaniṣad 2). Having thus ascertained that the Supreme Brahman, which is to be known through the Vedānta, exists as his very self and is not other than himself— this is the *Jīvanmuktiviveka*.
The state of the yogi comes about.
He shows the manner in which that yogi experiences Brahman: [the yogi] being firmly convinced that he himself is identical...
One who is united with the Supreme Self— that which is known from the Upaniṣads and nothing else— abides in That. The Śruti describes the manner in which the yogi attains this state.
The knowledge of Brahman is as follows:
"I am indeed that which is peaceful, immovable, the mass of non-dual bliss and consciousness; that alone is my supreme abode" (Paramahamsa Upanishad 2).
"I am indeed He alone, who is tranquil, motionless, and nothing but non-dual bliss and consciousness; and that alone is my supreme state" (Paramahaṃsa Upaniṣad 2).
In the three words beginning with "tam," the accusative case is to be understood in the sense of the nominative. That Supreme Self—who is peaceful, free from distractions such as anger;

who is immovable, devoid of actions such as going; who is free from internal differences of the same or different classes, and whose sole essence is Being-Consciousness-Bliss—that alone am I. That very reality of Brahman is my supreme abode, O yogi.
