Furthermore,
The nominative case endings in the first three words of the text are to be understood as nominatives. The Supreme Self is "tranquil," meaning free from such distractions as anger.
and so forth; motionless—free from such activities as going and the like;
free from duality—that is, devoid of the three kinds of difference: essential, specific, or external. [A tree...]

A stone is different (extrinsically) from [a rock]; an oak is different (specifically) from a poplar; in the same tree, the blossom is different (intrinsically) from the leaf. All these differences...
[who are absent] in Brahman— He who is of uniform existence,
consciousness, and uninterrupted bliss— I am none other than He alone.
The same— that is, the true knowledge of Brahman— is my highest state, namely the yogi’s real form, his essential nature,
and not this form conditioned by the state of being.

The agent and the enjoyer are such only insofar as they are imagined through ignorance. The learned have described by way of illustration how bliss is realized and why bliss is not realized at present.
Although the Self is none other than the Supreme Brahman, as it is said:
"The clarified butter residing within the bodies of cows does not nourish their limbs."
That very same thing fashioned by karma is, moreover, its own medicine.
"Thus the Supreme Lord resides within the body of all like clarified butter;
yet, without worship, the God does not bestow benefit upon men.
(Bṛhadyogiyājñavalkyasmṛti 9.30–31).
"Just as clarified butter, though present within the body of a cow, does not nourish her body, yet acts as a medicine for her if extracted by the proper means; even so..."
Thus, the Supreme Lord pervades everyone like clarified butter, yet He does not bestow well-being— bliss— upon men unless that Divine Lord is approached with devotion. (BY)

If practitioners of ritual action (karmiṇaḥ)—such as teachers, fathers, or brothers—who were well-known in the yogin’s former stage of life, being dull-witted due to their faith, should seek to delude him by imputing the status of a heretic (pāṣaṇḍitva) based on his lack of the topknot, sacred thread, twilight prayers, and so forth, then...
To prevent the arising of delusion, he shows the yogin’s present certainty:
"Should those blind followers of ritualistic observances, who were known in the previous stage of the yogin's life..."
His teacher, father, brother, and others confound him by accusing him of heresy, [citing] the absence of the principle that "just as ghee residing within the body does not produce strength in cows."
Having emerged, joined with their karma, that great power was bestowed upon them.
Likewise, Viṣṇu, though residing within the body, does not bring about the welfare of men without being propitiated;
for he is the omnipresent Supreme Lord.

— (Garuḍa Purāṇa 227.2, 3) || Regarding the *Jīvanmukti-viveka*: [the renunciation of] the topknot, the sacred thread, the morning and evening prayers (*saṃdhyā*), ritual worship (*upāsana*), and so forth, in order to restrain such [practices].
To clarify the firm conviction of the yogi, the Śruti describes it as follows:
"That alone is the tuft, and that alone is the sacred thread; for by the knowledge of the oneness of the Supreme Self and the individual self, their very distinction is shattered."
"That [knowledge of Brahman] alone is the tuft of hair, and that alone is the sacred thread; by means of it— " (Parama-upaniṣad 2).
The knowledge of the unity of the individual self and the Supreme Self, wherein their distinction is destroyed— that alone is *saṃdhyā* (Paramahaṃsa Upaniṣad 2).

The knowledge of the Supreme Brahman, which is to be known through the Vedāntas, is itself the substitute for the external topknot (*śikhā*) and sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) that constitute parts of ritual action (*karman*). Furthermore, by means of the two *ca*s, other components of ritual—namely the mantras and the sacrificial materials—are also included. Whatever happiness, such as that of heaven, is produced by rituals accomplished through the topknot and other such limbs, all of that is obtained solely through the knowledge of Brahman; this applies to every form of worldly pleasure.

Because it is but a fraction of the bliss of Brahman; for the Śruti says: "Other beings subsist on a mere measure of this very bliss" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.32). With this very intent, the followers of the Atharva Veda declare in the Brahmopaniṣad:
[the knowledge of the Supreme Brahman... which is realized—

The realization of the Upaniṣads— which is the knowledge of Brahman— substitutes for the external tuft of hair (*śikhā*) and the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), which are constituent parts of ritual acts; the double use of the word "and" (*ca*) in the text implies this.
The formulas and other requisite materials, which also constitute the components of the rituals;
and the bliss of heaven and so forth, which are born of sacrifice.
All rites, of which the topknot and so forth constitute the constituent parts,
are attained solely through the knowledge of Brahman, because all objective bliss is but a mere fraction of [the bliss of] Brahman.
of Brahman. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Śruti states thus:
"On a mere fraction of this very bliss, other beings subsist" (Bṛ.

With this in view, it is chanted in the *Brahmopaniṣad* of the Atharvaveda as follows: "Having performed the tonsure along with the top-knot, the ignorant man should discard the external thread; he should instead maintain that which is the imperishable Supreme Brahman as his thread. (*Brahmopaniṣad*, 6)
“The wise man (vipra), having shaved his head together with the topknot, should discard the external sacred thread and wear that which is the imperishable Supreme Brahman.”
The sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) (Brahmopaniṣad 6):
"They say it is called *sūtra* because of its indication; the supreme state is indeed named *sūtra*.
He by whom that *sūtra* is known is a true Brahmin who has reached the further shore of the Vedas" (ibid., 7).
“That which manifests is called the thread; this thread is the supreme state, namely the Supreme Brahman. The *vipra*—the one learned in the Vedas—who has known this thread...”
"He has transcended the Vedas" (meaning he has become fully conversant with them) (ibid. 7).
"By whom all this is strung together like clusters of gems on a thread..."
The yogi who perceives the reality of the knowledge of yoga should uphold that sūtra. (In that same work, verse 8)
“The yogi who is fully skilled in yoga and has realized reality should wear that thread upon which all this [phenomenal world] is strung, just as rows of jewels are strung upon a cord.”
(As cited in ibid., 8):
"The wise man, established in the supreme yoga, should abandon the external thread;
he who possesses true consciousness should wear this thread which is the state of Brahman."
By upholding that Sūtra, one shall become neither impure from remnants of food nor ritually unclean. (In that same work, verse 9)
"The enlightened one, firmly established in the supreme form of yoga, should abandon the external sacred thread—
he who perceives Brahman in the form of this thread."

One should invest oneself with it. By wearing this thread, one becomes neither impure nor defiled (ibid. 9). "Those for whom the thread has entered within, who wear the sacrificial knowledge as their sacred thread—they alone in this world are knowers of the thread, and they are truly those who wear the sacrificial thread" (ibid. 10).
“Those who wear within the knowledge in the form of the sacred thread are truly the knowers of the thread in this world; they alone are indeed invested with the sacred thread. (Ibid.)

"Those whose crest is knowledge, who are established in knowledge, and who wear the sacred thread of knowledge—for them, knowledge alone is the supreme purifier; knowledge is said to be their [purifier]. (In that same work, 11)
"For those who are firmly established in knowledge, knowledge is their topknot, and knowledge is the sacred thread they wear; for them, knowledge is the ultimate."
"Knowledge, it is said, is purity itself" (ibid.
11). "He whose crest consists of knowledge, like the flame of a fire, is called a man of the crest—a wise man—and not others who merely wear hair" (ibid. 12).
"He who has no crest other than the crest of knowledge, like the flame of fire— he is called the enlightened wearer of the crest; others are merely wearers of hair" (ibid.).
"But those Brāhmaṇas and others who are entitled to perform Vedic rites— by them this Sūtra is to be maintained, for it is indeed remembered as an auxiliary to those rites. (Ibid., 13)
Those performing rituals should wear this external sacred thread, for according to the Smṛtis, it indeed constitutes a constituent part of the sacrificial rite (ibid. 13).

"Those who know Brahman understand that he whose topknot consists of knowledge and whose sacred thread also consists of that [knowledge] possesses the entirety of the status of a Brāhmaṇa. (In that same work, verse 14).
"In whom the topknot is made of knowledge and the sacred thread is also made of knowledge— know that in him, who is fully skilled in the Vedic lore, resides the state of being a *brāhmaṇa*."
"Complete" (ibid., 14). 344.
"This is the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), which is the supreme goal;
one who knows this should be considered a wearer of the sacred thread. Those who know that regard him as a true sacrificer" (ibid., 15).

"This is the supreme sacred thread (yajñopavīta) and this is the final refuge; knowing this, one becomes truly invested with the sacred thread, and those who know the sacrificial rites regard him as such."
"to be the [true] sacrificer" (ibid. 15).

Therefore, just as the tuft of hair (*śikhā*) and the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) exist for the yogi, so too does the twilight devotion (*saṃdhyā*) exist. Through the knowledge of the unity of those two—the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), which is accessible through the scriptures, and the individual self (*jīvātman*), which is accessible through the notion of "I"—arising from the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*).

The distinction perceived through delusion is indeed utterly shattered; moreover, the non-recurrence of delusion is the specific characteristic of that shattering. This cognition of unity is called "saṃdhyā" (the junction) because it arises at the junction (*saṃdhi*) between the two selves, just as the ritual to be performed at the junction of day and night is called *saṃdhyā*. This being so, the yogi cannot be deluded by those who are dull-witted due to their faith.
It is possible.
Therefore, just as the yogi possesses the topknot (*śikhā*) and the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), so too does he possess the *saṃdhyā* (the religious rites performed at the junctions of time).
[The worship of] *hṛdaya* and so forth during the three divisions of the day. [This concerns] the erroneously conceived difference between the Supreme Self,
known from the scriptures, and the individual self (*jīva*).
That which is known through the sense of "I" is indeed utterly destroyed by the knowledge of their non-duality arising from the Great Upaniṣadic texts.
The specialty of this destruction is that the error never returns again. This is because of the realization of the oneness of the two selves.
That which arises at the point of union of the two selves is called *sandhyā* (the juncture), just as the religious rite to be performed at the juncture of day and night is so named.
The night is called *sandhyā*. This being the case, the yogi cannot be confounded by those who stubbornly adhere to ritualistic observances (*karmakāṇḍa*).
To the question, "What is this path? the answer has been stated in such passages as, "This is his own son" (*Parama Upaniṣad* 1).

Having given a concise answer to the question "What is its state? with the words beginning "The Great Person," he now elaborates upon it with the words beginning "Doubt, misconception... and so forth.
He concludes that very point with: "Having renounced all desires, there is the supreme abiding in non-duality" (Parama-upaniṣad 3).

The answer to the question "What is the way? has been given by the words "He renounces his son," and so forth; and the answer to the question "What is the state? has been given by the Great Soul, first in brief and then...
This has been explained in detail [in the passage beginning] with "Doubt, misapprehensions... and so forth;
and now the Śruti concludes by saying:
"The ultimate abiding is in non-duality, after having discarded..."
"Free from all desires" (Paramahaṃsa Upaniṣad 3).
Since anger, greed, and the like are preceded by desire, by the abandonment of desire, all defects of the mind are likewise abandoned.
With this very intention, the Vājasaneyins have recorded: "Now, indeed, they say that this person consists entirely of desire."
(Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad 4.4.5). Therefore, for one whose mind is free from desire, an unimpeded state in non-duality is established.
Through the abandonment of desire, all evils of the mind—such as...
Anger, avarice, and the like are abandoned because they arise from desire. With this very intention, the Vājasaneyins of the Veda have chanted as follows:
"However, others say that the self is identified with desire alone" (Br. Up. 4.4.5).
Therefore, the uninterrupted abiding of one who is free from desire—

The non-dual state of mind of a yogi is possible. Now, raising the objection that those who have renounced with the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā-saṃnyāsins*), being possessed of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the rule regarding the taking up of the staff, do not accept a *paramahaṃsa* yogi who is without a staff, he says:
"He by whom the staff of knowledge is held is called a *ekadaṇḍin*.
He by whom a wooden staff is held, who eats all things and is devoid of knowledge,
goes to the terrible hells known as Mahāraurava— [he] who is destitute of the qualities of forbearance, knowledge, dispassion, tranquility, and so forth."
He who lives by mere alms is a sinner and a destroyer of the ascetic’s way of life.
"Having understood this distinction, he is a Paramahaṃsa" (Parama-upaniṣad 3.3).
This anticipates the concern that a yogi without the staff might not be recognized as a Paramahaṃsa by those seeking renunciation (*vividiṣā-saṃnyāsins*).
If one still has the impression that the staff should be accepted in accordance with the scriptural injunction, the Śruti further says this:
"He who has taken up knowledge as his staff is called a bearer of the single staff; but he who carries a wooden staff while devoid of knowledge eats all kinds of food and goes to [hell]."

The terrible hell called Mahāraurava. He who is devoid of such virtues as forbearance, understanding, non-attachment, and tranquility, and who subsists solely on alms, is [the one destined for that place].
He is a sinner who violates the moral conduct of the ascetics. Having realized this distinction between the staff of knowledge and the wooden staff, he becomes a *paramahaṃsa*. *Parama*...

(Haṃsopaniṣad 3.3) This single staff of the Paramahaṃsa is of two kinds: the staff of knowledge (jñānadaṇḍa) and the wooden staff (kāṣṭhadaṇḍa). Just as for the Tridaṇḍins there are the staff of speech (vāgdaṇḍa), the staff of mind (manodaṇḍa), and the staff of action (karmadaṇḍa)—or, according to another reading, the staff of body (kāyadaṇḍa).
Its threefold nature is likewise. The three types of staffs, such as the staff of speech and so forth, are recorded by Manu;
the single staff of the Paramahaṃsa is of two kinds:
the staff of knowledge and the wooden staff, just like the three types.
A *tridaṇḍin* ascetic possesses three staffs, such as the staff of speech, the staff of mind, and the staff of action. Manu has described the staff of speech and the others as follows:
"The staff of speech, the staff of mind, and likewise the staff of action—
he by whom these are restrained within his intellect is called a *tridaṇḍin* (one who possesses the triple staff)."
"Having cast aside this triple staff among all beings, and having restrained desire and anger, a person then attains perfection. (Manu Smṛti 12.10, 11).
"He who is ever vigilant regarding these three 'staves'— namely,
those of speech, mind, and action— is called a *tridaṇḍin*, a yogi who bears the triple-staff (*daṇḍa* signifying self-restraint)."
"Control" (*gupti*) refers to complete mastery over speech, mind, and body (Manusmṛti 12.10). "A man becomes liberated by directing these three forms of control."
"towards all beings, having completely subdued desire and anger" (ibid. 12.11).
Dakṣa recalls their true nature:
"The staff of speech, the staff of mind, and likewise the staff of action—
he whose these staffs are restrained is called a *tridaṇḍin*.
One should practice silence regarding the staff of speech, and non-exertion regarding the staff of action."
"But for the mental staff, breath-control (prāṇāyāma) is prescribed. Thus it is said.
Dakṣa describes their nature as follows:
"He is called a *tridaṇḍin*—one possessing triple restraint—who..."
He maintains constant control over his speech, mind, and actions (Vāyupurāṇa 17.6).
"To control his speech, he should observe silence; to..."

To control his actions, he should practice equanimity and *prāṇāyāma*; the restraint of the vital breath is prescribed for the purpose of controlling his mind (quoted in Viśveśvara’s *Yatidharmasaṃgraha*).
(Śivasarasvatī, p. 122; Sannyāsopaniṣad 2.97).
There is a reading in another Smṛti: "The staff of action is eating little. Such possession of the triple-staff (tridaṇḍitva) exists even for the Paramahaṃsa.
With this in mind, the Grandfather (Brahmā) records in the Smṛti:
"The ascetic who is a paramahaṃsa is designated as the fourth state (turya) as enjoined by the Vedas;
endowed with restraints (yama) and observances (niyama), he bears the triple staff (tridaṇḍa) and is the very form of Viṣṇu. Thus says another Smṛti.

"One should practice frugality in order to control one's actions" (source untraced). This threefold restraint must also be observed by a *paramahaṃsa*; with this in mind, the Grandfather (*Pitāmaha*) says:
Thus: "The stage of the yogi-paramahaṃsa is the fourth as enjoined by the Śruti; he is endowed with self-restraint (yama) and religious observances (niyama), and carries the triple staff (tridaṇḍa)."
"Control is Viṣṇu incarnate" (source untraced).

This being so, just as silence and other such practices possess the nature of a staff (*daṇḍa*) because they are the means for subduing speech and the other senses, likewise knowledge possesses the nature of a staff because it is the means for subduing ignorance and its effects. That Paramahaṃsa alone by whom this staff of knowledge is held [is truly such].

The primary one is called the *ekadaṇḍī* (the single-staffed). Since there is the possibility that the mental staff of knowledge (*jñānadaṇḍa*) might be forgotten due to occasional distractions of the mind, a wooden staff is carried as a reminder to prevent that. A Paramahaṃsa who carries a wooden staff without understanding this secret essence of the meaning of the scriptures, merely intending to achieve the goals of human life through outward appearance alone—[he is not a true ascetic].

A person, due to being subject to various kinds of torment, falls into the terrible hell known as Mahāraurava. The reason for this is stated: seeing him in the guise of a Paramahaṃsa, all people, under the delusion that he is a man of knowledge, feed him in their respective homes.
And this man, greedy of the tongue, eats all food without making a distinction between what is forbidden and what is permitted. By that, he incurs sin (*pratyavāya*).

[He] attains [it]. As for those Smṛti statements such as "The mendicant is not defiled by the fault of food" (Saṃnyāsopaniṣad 72) and "He may wander among the four castes," these refer to those possessed of knowledge. And since this [person] is devoid of knowledge, his descent into hell is justified. For this very reason, Manu states the rules for alms-seeking for an ascetic who lacks knowledge:

Therefore, just as the observance of silence and so forth are called "staff" (danda)— that is, restraint— because they are the causes of restraint over speech and the other faculties, so too is knowledge, which is the cause...
The control of ignorance and its effects is considered a staff. That paramahaṃsa who carries this staff of knowledge is alone called a true ekadaṇḍin, a bearer of the single staff.
At times, due to some distraction of the mind, there may occur forgetfulness of this mental staff of knowledge; in order to restrain such an occurrence, the wooden staff is carried.

A reminder: the *paramahaṃsa* who, ignorant of the esoteric meaning of the scriptures, carries the wooden staff (*khāṇḍika*) thinking that he can attain the ultimate goal through the mere change of dress.
The object of life leads to the dreadful hell known as Mahāraurava, for it is filled with afflictions and fraught with manifold miseries.
The reason for this is as follows: seeing him in the guise of a *paramahaṃsa* and mistaking him for an enlightened one (*jīvanmukta*), everyone feeds him in their own homes. And...
This ignorant and greedy person, without discriminating between what should and should not be consumed, eats all kinds of food indiscriminately and thereby commits a transgression.

Those *smṛti* texts, such as "The fault incurred by eating forbidden food does not affect renunciants" (*Sannyāsopaniṣad* 72), and "One should beg from members of all four castes," and so forth, refer to...
[This practice] is intended only for enlightened *sannyāsins*. However, since this *paramahaṃsa* is devoid of knowledge, hell is appropriate for him;
for it is precisely for this reason that Manu prescribes restrictive rules regarding his begging.
For the unenlightened sannyāsin, [it is said]:
"He should never seek alms by means of portents or omens, nor by the science of astrology and bodily marks, nor by instructions or discourses. (50)
"He who eats [only] what is left over from the food of others and wanders about is truly a mendicant; for an ascetic who is addicted to begging becomes attached even to sense-objects.
(Manu Smṛti 6.50, 55)
"The ascetic must never desire to secure alms by predicting portents or interpreting omens, nor by prophesying according to astrology, palmistry, or medicine, nor even..."
According to the exposition of the moral code and the scriptures (*Manusmṛti* 6.50):
"He should go for alms once a day and never indulge in [other activities]."
"obtaining more. For, whoever is attached to abundant alms would likewise become attached to the objects of enjoyment (ibid).
However, regarding one who practices for the sake of knowledge, it is thus recorded in the Smṛti:
"A Parahaṃsaka may eat once or twice; by whatever means possible, he should always remain devoted to the practice of knowledge. Thus it is said.
"A Paramahaṃsa may eat once or twice a day,

and by whatever means possible, he should always practice knowledge" (source untraced). This being so, having understood the difference between the staff of knowledge (*jñānadaṇḍa*) and the wooden staff (*kāṣṭhadaṇḍa*)— namely, their respective natures as superior and inferior— one should [choose] the superior.
It must be acknowledged that he alone who wields the staff of knowledge is the primary Paramahaṃsa.
This being the case,
after realizing the distinction between the [ordinary] staff and the staff of knowledge...
And the wooden staff, representing respectively the superior and the inferior— he who carries the staff of knowledge is the true Paramahaṃsa.

Granted that for the Paramahaṃsa who possesses direct realization (abhijña), there may be the staff of knowledge (jñānadaṇḍa) and no insistence on a wooden staff; yet, one might ask, what is his entire other mode of conduct like? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says:
"Clad in the sky (space), he offers neither salutation nor the utterance of *svadhā*; he is subject neither to blame nor praise, and he should be guided by chance."

"A monk neither brings forth nor dismisses; there is no mantra for him, no meditation, no service, no object of focus, and no non-object; he is neither separate nor not separate, neither "I" nor "you," neither "all" nor even one who abides in a state of homelessness.
Such a monk does not take possession of gold or other such things, nor does he look toward the world or its opposite" (Parama Upaniṣad 4).
For the knowing *paramahaṃsa*, let there be only the staff of knowledge and no insistence on carrying a wooden staff; but of what nature are all his other possessions?
Anticipating such a question, the Śruti further says:
"The mendicant has the quarters of the sky as his garment."
(Naked), without salutation, neither offering oblations or libations to the gods or the departed ancestors, nor pronouncing blessings, without censure, and without praise, one should...
remain contented with whatever comes by chance; neither summoning nor dismissing, without a sacred formula,
without meditation, without worship, without conceptualization, and without [expectation].
Neither different nor identical to its denotation, neither "I" nor "you," nor "all"— the mendicant remains even without an abode.
He should not accept a vessel made of gold or similar materials.
"Nor should he accept people, nor even look at them" (Paramahaṃsa Upaniṣad 4).
*Āśāmbara* means one whose garment or covering is the quarters of the sky (*āśā*) themselves, which constitute the directions (*diśaḥ*). As for that which...
The statement of the Smṛti:
"The regions of the sky—that is, the cardinal directions—are his garment, his covering. Regarding the Smṛti text which speaks thus:
"Having put on one garment from above the knees to below the navel,

and having put on a second as an upper garment, he may wander among the houses"— this refers to one who is not a yogi. For this very reason, it was stated previously that "and that is not the primary [practice]."
‘He should clothe himself with a piece of cloth covering the region between the navel and the knees, and wearing a second piece as an upper garment, he should go for alms.’
The phrase "from house to house" (source untraced) refers to one who is not a yogi; therefore, it was stated previously that "this is not essential" (Paramahaṃsa Upaniṣad 1).
Although another Smṛti states: "If there should be one who was previously a renunciant and is indeed equal in terms of dharma,
salutation must be offered to him, but never to anyone else."

Thus, even so, because that [state] is the domain of those who have not yet attained yoga (*ayogin*), no salutation should be performed toward this [text]. For this very reason, it is cited in the definition of a Brāhmaṇa in the *Mahābhārata* (Śāntiparvan, Mokṣadharma 237.24): "free from salutation and free from praise."
Although another *smṛti* states:
"He should salute a senior monk of his own order, but never others" (*Mahābhārata* 13, App. 10.181), nevertheless—

It also refers to one who is not a yogi; therefore, prostration is not mandatory toward a *paramahaṃsa*. It is for this very reason that, in defining a *brāhmaṇa*, it has been said: "He neither bows nor praises."
(Mahābhārata 12.237.24).

The desire for *svadhā* (ancestral offerings) obtained at sacred sites such as Gayā and Prayāga due to the dullness of faith is prohibited. In the preceding section, by the statement beginning with “censure and pride” (Parama-upaniṣad), suffering [arises] from self-reproach caused by others.

In this context, however, praise and censure directed toward others by oneself are prohibited. "Spontaneity" means the absence of insistence; one should not exercise compulsion in any worldly activity. As for the insistence on the worship of the gods that is prescribed in the Smṛtis—such as "begging for alms, recitation, purification, bathing, meditation, and the worship of the gods"—[it refers to a different matter].
"these six must be performed in every way, like the punishment of a king"—
with this in mind, it was taught that there is no invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth, intending that this also applies to those who are not yet liberated (*ayogin*).
Regarding the offering of oblations and libations to the deceased:
For such a person, the performance of ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) at sacred sites such as Gayā and Prayāga—which arises from blind adherence to faith—is forbidden.
This is indicated by the scriptural passage beginning with "Censure, pride... (*Paramahaṃsa Upaniṣad* 2).
As previously cited, the infliction of pain upon the yogi by others through censuring him has been prevented; however,
in the present text, the yogi is forbidden from slandering or praising.
Others. The state of being content with whatever comes by chance means the absence of insistence. The yogi-paramaha-
One must not obstinately insist upon anything whatsoever in ordinary life. Regarding the obligatory nature of the worship of the deities as prescribed by the Smṛti:
"Begging for alms, the recitation of sacred formulas, purity, bathing,
meditation, and the worship of the gods— these six must always be performed like the command of a king" (quoted in *Yatidharma*).

The *Pramāṇasaṃgraha* of Viśveśvara Sarasvatī (p. 62), among other sources, also refers to one who is not a yogi; with this in mind, [the text] has chanted, “without summoning” (*Paramahaṃsopaniṣad* 4), and so forth.

The distinction between these two is that *dhyāna* (meditation) is single-minded recollection, whereas *upāsana* (devotional worship) is continuous recollection. Just as for the yogi there is an absence of worldly activities such as praise or censure, and just as there is an absence of religious-legal (*dharmaśāstra*) activities such as the worship of deities, so too there is no engagement with the science of knowledge (*jñānaśāstra*) regarding such matters as the "object of perception" (*lakṣya*) or the "non-object of perception" (*alakṣya*). That which exists is the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*).

This [Self] is that which is indicated by the term *tvaṃ* (thou) in the sentence *tat tvam asi* (That thou art). Consciousness qualified by the body and so forth is not the indicated meaning (*lakṣya*), but rather the literal meaning (*vācya*). And that literal meaning is distinct from the referent of the term *tat* (That), whereas the indicated meaning is non-distinct. The literal meaning residing in one's own body is fit for the conventional usage "I," while that residing in another's body is fit for the conventional usage "thou. The indicated meaning, however, is...

"Both that which is expressible— consisting of the two types [subject and object] endowed with consciousness— and all other insentient things in the world are fit for worldly transaction"— no such conceptual construction exists for the yogin, because his mind has come to rest in Brahman.

For this very reason, that monk must remain without a fixed abode. If he were to establish a monastery for the sake of a permanent residence, then, through the sense of "mine" regarding it, his mind would become distracted by its loss or gain. With all this in mind, the teacher Gauḍapāda said:
"Free from praise, free from salutation, and likewise free from the utterance of *svadhā*;
with a dwelling that is both moving and unmoving, the ascetic should live according to chance.
— (Māṇḍūkyakārikā 2.37).
The distinction between meditation and worship lies respectively in remembering [the object] once and remembering it constantly.
As the yogi is not concerned with worldly activities, [he remains absorbed].

Whether it be worldly affairs such as praise, slander, and the like, or whether he is free from the obligatory duties such as the worship of deities prescribed by the scriptures— even so, he has none.
One should not concern oneself at all with metaphysical discussions regarding the implicit and explicit meanings of a text and so forth.
For example, none of such thoughts [deliberative...]
Regarding the functions of the mind: "The consciousness in the form of a witness, which is implied by the word 'thou' in the text 'That thou art,' is the consciousness disguised [as the ego]."
The body and so forth are not merely implied, but are directly denoted; they are distinct from the consciousness signified by the word "That" in the text,
yet identical with the implied witness-consciousness (sākṣin).

The consciousness that constitutes one's own body is denoted by the term "I," while that which constitutes another's body is denoted by the term "thou. Both the connotation and the denotation of "thou" [are likewise consciousness].
"Everything consists of consciousness; the other, namely the unconscious world, is referred to as 'all'"— such a thought indeed occurs to a yogi,
for his mind has attained tranquility in Brahman.
Therefore, the mendicant (yogi-paramahaṃsa) indeed remains without a fixed abode. However, if he makes a monastery his permanent residence, a sense of ownership toward it will arise.

Furthermore, mental distractions will naturally arise due to the loss or gain pertaining to the monastery. Having considered all this, Ācārya Gauḍapāda says: “The enlightened saṃnyāsī does not praise [any deity]...”
He does not salute [any superior] and does not perform rites for the propitiation of the ancestors. Regarding both the body and the self as his abode, he remains content with whatever [he receives].
"comes by chance" (Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad Kārikā 2.37).
Just as a monastery is not to be accepted, so too he should not take even a single vessel for alms or for rinsing the mouth made of gold, silver, or other such materials. Regarding this, Yama says:
Just as a yogi should not accept a monastery as his residence,
so too he should not accept, not even a single vessel made of gold, silver, or similar materials, as an alms-bowl.
A cup for sipping water. Yama says the same thing: "Golden vessels and those made of black iron—these are unfit vessels for ascetics; a mendicant should avoid them. Thus it is said.
“Vessels made of gold or iron are not vessels for yogins; the mendicant should avoid them. (Source unidentified)
Manu also says:
"His vessels should be non-metallic and free from blemishes;
their purification with water is prescribed, just as that of the *camasa* cups at a sacrifice."
"An alābu gourd, a wooden bowl, one made of clay, or likewise one of bamboo— these, Svāyambhuva Manu declared, are the vessels for ascetics. (Manu 6.53, 54).
Manu also says this:
"His vessels should be without leaks and not made of metal; their purification is prescribed by means of water, just as..."
In the sacrifice, the vessels for drinking *soma* are cleansed with water alone. Those made of gourd, wood, or earthenware, as well as those made of bamboo— these are the vessels of the ascetic.
As has been prescribed by Manu, the son of Svayambhū (Manu-smṛti 6.53–54), Baudhāyana also states:
"Either upon leaves gathered by oneself, or again, upon those that have fallen off naturally..."
One should not eat from the leaves of the vaṭa, aśvattha, or karañja trees.
"Even in times of distress, one who eats from bronze vessels does not consume impurity;
nor [should one eat] from vessels of gold, silver, copper, earthenware, tin, or lead.
Thus also says Baudhāyana.
‘He should eat from leaves that have been plucked by himself or have fallen of their own accord, but not from the leaves of the banyan, the holy fig, or the karañja.’
*Glabra*). "He should never eat, even in times of distress, from a vessel made of bell-metal, or of gold, silver, or copper."
"Nor from earthenware, nor from vessels of tin or lead; for he who eats from such vessels eats impurity" (source untraced).
Likewise, one should not accept the world, that is, people or a circle of disciples. Regarding this, Manu says:
‘One should always wander alone for the sake of perfection, without a companion;
for seeing the perfection of solitude, one abandons [the world] and is not lost.
(Manu 6.42) Thus it is said.
Medhātithi also states:
"In the same manner, he should not accept a 'world,' meaning people—that is, disciples. Manu says the same thing as follows:
"He should wander alone without assistance to attain the goal of human existence, seeing that the goal is achieved by one who is alone;
for he who is alone neither gives nor receives."
"Seating, the loss of the alms-bowl, accumulation, gathering of disciples, sleeping during the day, and idle talk—these six are the bonds for an ascetic. (Manusmṛti 6.42).
"Seating, the loss of the bowl, accumulation, the gathering of disciples, sleeping by day, and idle chatter—these six are the causes of bondage for an ascetic."
Medhātithi also says: (as found in the *Sannyāsa Upaniṣad*):
"Dwelling, longing for vessels, saving for future use, accepting disciples, sleeping during the day, and idle talk—"
"These six are the causes of bondage for an ascetic" (Sannyāsa-upaniṣad 79).
"Beyond one day in a village, beyond five days in a city..."
Any place other than during the rainy season is designated as a seat (āsana).
"At any time other than the rainy season, staying in a village for more than one day and in a town for more than five days is described as dwelling" (ibid. 80).
"Even if not a single one of the aforementioned vessels, such as the alābu and others,
is possessed by a mendicant who subsists on alms, that is called the 'loss of the bowl'."
‘A mendicant and others who subsist on alms, such as a brahmacārin and so forth, should not collect even one additional vessel made of gourd beyond what has been prescribed.’
And the rest as previously described, which is called the longing for vessels (ibid. 81):
"But the grasping of a second [object], such as a staff, once one has already been taken up..."
Accumulation is proclaimed to be for the purpose of enjoyment at a later time.
The acceptance of a second staff or similar items, other than those already in one's possession, for the purpose of using them in the future, is described as "saving for future use" (ibid. 82).
"The acceptance of disciples for the sake of service, gain, honor, or fame,
and not out of compassion— that should be known as the gathering of disciples [for selfish ends]."
The selfish motive of acquiring personal services, adoration,
and fame is to be known as "acceptance of disciples" (ibid., 83). *Jīvan-mukti-viveka*.
Knowledge is called day because of its luminosity, and ignorance is called night;
negligence in the practice of knowledge is said to be sleeping during the day.
“Knowledge is called day because it illumines, and ignorance is night. Negligence in the practice of knowledge is called sleeping during the day” (ibid., 84).
"Except for discourse concerning the inner self, talk regarding the life of mendicancy, praise of the gods,
inquiries about the way, or seeking favor— all other conversation is called idle chatter.
"All conversations, with the exception of those concerning the Self..."
Regarding mendicancy, the praise of deities, blessings, and inquiries made along the way and so forth are called "idle talk" (*saṅkathā*).
As stated in the same source: "It is not merely that one should not accept the world consisting of disciples; rather, for him..."

He should not even look at or observe the world, because that serves as a cause for bondage. By the word "na ca" (and not), it is intended that he should not perform anything else that is prohibited by the Smṛti. Medhātithi points out that which is so prohibited:
"Not only should he not take people with him as..."
O disciples, he should not even look at them, for that leads to bondage. The word "not" in the text implies that the ascetic should not even perform such actions as are prohibited.
In the *smṛtis*, prohibited acts are described by Medhātithi as follows:
"Immovable things, moving beings, seeds, metallic objects, poison, and weapons..."
An ascetic should not accept these six things, just as he would avoid urine or excrement.
"Alchemy, the doctrine of action, astrology, buying and selling, and various crafts—one should avoid these as one would another's wife. Thus it is said.
"The ascetic should not take these six: [the aforementioned five] and immovable property..."
Movable property, seed, metal, poison, and weapons—one should regard these as being like excrement (as quoted in YDS p.
107; Sannyāsa Up. 2.91).
"He should avoid alchemy, litigation, astrology, commerce, and various arts and crafts, just as he would the wife of another" (quoted in YDS p. 107).
The avoidance of those obstacles that pertain to the worldly and Vedic activities of the yogin has been stated.
Now, having demonstrated the ultimate obstacle through a question and answer, he describes its avoidance: [the avoidance of those obstacles which are connected...]

The activities of the yogi—both those pertaining to common practice and those based on scripture—have been described. Now, the Śruti, describing the greatest obstacle by means of a dialogue of questions and answers, says: "Abandon..."
It is as follows:
"If it is asked, 'What is the obstacle? there is indeed an obstacle. Because if a monk should look upon gold with a sense of attachment (*rasena*), he becomes a slayer of a Brahmin (*brahmahā*).
Because if a monk should touch gold with a sense of attachment, he becomes a *paulkasa*. Because if a monk [should take gold]..."
"If it were to be accepted with relish, he would be a destroyer of his own self. Therefore, a mendicant must neither look upon gold, nor touch it, nor accept it with relish" (Parama Upaniṣad 4).
"If there is any great obstacle, what is it?"
"Of course there is a great obstacle. For if the mendicant should look upon gold with longing, he becomes a slayer of a Brahmin; for if the mendicant should touch gold..."
Through longing he becomes a paulkasa; for if the mendicant should take gold with longing, he becomes a slayer of the self.
"Therefore, the mendicant should not look at, touch, or take gold with longing" (Paramahaṃsa Upaniṣad 4).
The prefix *ā-* has the sense of pervasion (*abhivyāpti*), because it is stated that "the prefix *ā-* [is used] in the sense of slightness and pervasion. Regarding pervasion:

An "obstructor" (*bādhaka*) is one who causes absolute obstruction; having asserted its existence, such obstructiveness regarding gold is now described. If gold should be seen with passion—that is, with longing—and with earnestness, then that observer, even if he be a mendicant, would become a slayer of a Brahmin (*brahmahā*). This is because, through attachment to gold, he would always be striving for its acquisition and preservation, and thus, in order to avoid its loss, [he becomes bound].

Having refuted the Vedānta texts that establish the falsity of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*), he instead relies upon its reality. Consequently, the non-dual Brahman established by the scriptures is effectively destroyed by that mendicant; therefore, he would be a slayer of Brahman (*brahmahā*).
And so it is recorded in the Smṛti:
The prefix ‘a’ in the Sanskrit word *abādhaka* (non-obstructive) signifies completeness, for it has been stated: “‘A’ denotes the slight and the comprehensive. (From *Jīvan-mukti-viveka*)
[This refers to] lexicographers. A comprehensive obstacle is a great obstacle;
and the Śruti, having declared its existence, states that gold is that obstacle.
If gold is gazed upon with longing— that is, with great yearning—
then the gazing mendicant becomes a slayer of a Brahmin. Due to his attachment to gold, he constantly exerts himself [for its acquisition].
It establishes the attainment and preservation of that [knowledge], and in order to prevent its uselessness, it refutes the Vedānta doctrines which explain the unreality of the phenomenal world.
its reality. Thus, the unique Brahman—which has been well established by the scriptures—is, as it were, slain by this mendicant. Therefore, he becomes a slayer of Brahman.
Regarding the Brahmin: the Smṛti also says the same thing as follows:
"He who says 'Brahman does not exist,' he who hates the knower of Brahman, and he who speaks of a non-existent Brahman—these three are slayers of Brahman."

"He is to be known as a slayer of a Brahmin, excluded from all dharmas. And: "If gold is touched intentionally, then that monk who touches it becomes a *paulkasa*—like a barbarian (*mleccha*)—due to his fallen state. And this state of being fallen is recorded in the Smṛti:
"He who says that Brahman does not exist, he who hates a knower of Brahman, and he who teaches the difference between the individual self and the universal self— these..."
"Three are the slayers of a Brāhmaṇa" (source untraced).
And likewise: "Know him to be an outcaste who is the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa" (source untraced).
If gold is touched with longing, then the mendicant who touches it falls to the state of a paulkasa— that is, he becomes like a mleccha (barbarian). The Smṛti describes this downfall as follows:
Falling prey to temptation in this way: "That monk certainly falls [from his state] in whom two things exist:
the intentional emission of semen and the accumulation of material goods. Thus it is said.
‘The downfall of the mendicant is certain who has committed these two: the intentional emission of semen and the hoarding of wealth’—as quoted in the *Yogadrstisamuccaya* (p. 110).

Gold must not be accepted even with a prior desire for it. If it is accepted, then that monk would have killed the unattached conscious self (cidātman), which is the witness of the body, senses, and so forth; for, having set aside its state of non-attachment, he has identified his own self as an enjoyer in relation to objects such as gold. Gold must not be taken with longing; if it is taken, the mendicant becomes, as it were, the slayer of the pure intellect, which is the unattached witness of the body.
the senses and so forth. For, by denying the state of non-attachment of his own self, he is convinced that it is the enjoyer of gold and other such riches. Such is the contradiction.
Perception is equivalent to all sins, as the Smṛti describes:
"He who represents himself as something other than what he truly is..."
"What sin has not been committed by that thief who steals his own self?
— (Mahābhārata 1.68.26).
What sin remains to be committed by the thief?
"What a self-deceiving fellow, who understands the self contrary to its true nature! (Mahābhārata 1.68.26).
Furthermore, it is heard that the worlds of those who destroy themselves are devoid of even a trace of happiness and are enveloped in manifold suffering.
"Sunless indeed are those worlds, shrouded in blind darkness;
to them go after death those people who are slayers of the Self.
(Īśopaniṣad 3)

Moreover, the Śruti declares that the slayer of the self goes to such worlds as are devoid of even a trace of happiness and abound in manifold forms of suffering, as follows: [from the *Jīvan-mukti-viveka*]
"Verily, those worlds are shrouded in blinding darkness; to them go all after death who are slayers of the Self" (Īśā Upaniṣad 3).

By the word "ca" (and) in the phrase "dṛṣṭaṃ ca" (and seen), "śrutaṃ ca" (and heard) is conjoined. By the word "ca" in "spṛṣṭaṃ ca" (and touched), "kathitaṃ" (spoken of) is conjoined. By the word "ca" in "grāhyaṃ ca" (and to be grasped), "vyavahṛtaṃ" (transacted) is conjoined. Just as seeing, touching, and grasping, so too listening to accounts of gold preceded by desire, speaking of its qualities, and transacting such things as its purchase are causes of demerit.
Therefore, the meaning is that [this applies] to a monk who causes fault;
for [faults such as] looking at gold with desire and so forth—
The meaning is that looking at gold and other such acts are to be avoided. The text states the result of avoiding gold:
the word "and" in the phrase "and should not look" implies that one should also not hear of gold; the phrase "and should not touch" implies...
"One should not speak of gold" and "one should not take gold" imply that one should not trade in gold.
This is the essential meaning of the scriptural injunction regarding gold.
Whatever concerns gold— whether hearing of it,
speaking of its merits, or dealing with it— with longing leads likewise to downfall, just like seeing, touching, or taking it.
Gold with longing. Since the seeing, touching, taking, and so forth of gold with longing are harmful, therefore the seeing and other acts regarding gold should be avoided by the mendicant.
The Śruti describes the result of renouncing gold as follows:
"All desires residing in the mind turn away; one is not agitated by suffering and is free from longing for pleasure; there is renunciation of attachment everywhere;
one has no affection for the auspicious or the inauspicious; one neither hates nor rejoices; and the movement of all the senses comes to rest."
"He abides in the Self alone" (Parama Upaniṣad 4).
"All desires dwelling in his mind vanish; he is not afflicted by suffering, and he is free from longing."
Possessing the joy of renunciation toward all attachments—
